## Anti-Patterns (iteration 61)

### AP52 — `expect.soft()` Without Checking `test.info().errors`  [community]
**What:** Using `expect.soft()` for multiple assertions but not calling
`expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0)` at the end of the test.
**Why harmful:** `expect.soft()` marks the test internally as failed but does NOT abort the test
and does NOT automatically fail the test case at the end of the `test()` body. A test that uses
`expect.soft()` exclusively and never checks `test.info().errors` will PASS even if every soft
assertion failed. The test appears green in the report, all the flakiness information is
silently discarded, and the developer sees no indication of the problem. The mandatory close of
every test using soft assertions is `expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0)` — without
it, soft assertions provide zero value.

### AP53 — `expect.poll()` or `expect.toPass()` Without Explicit `timeout`  [community]
**What:** Calling `expect.poll(fn).toBe(value)` or `expect(fn).toPass()` without setting
the `timeout` option.
**Why harmful:** Both `expect.poll()` and `expect.toPass()` default to a timeout of **0** (zero
milliseconds) when the `timeout` option is omitted. A timeout of 0 means the assertion runs
ONCE and does not retry — the entire point of these APIs is eliminated. Worse, `expect.poll()`
with `timeout: 0` can produce confusing errors like "Expected: 'completed', received: 'pending'"
with no indication that the function was only called once. Teams that add `expect.poll()` to
eliminate flakiness but forget `timeout` often see WORSE flakiness because their fix doesn't
retry at all. Always specify `{ timeout: <ms> }` explicitly.

---

## Real-World Gotchas (iteration 61)  [community]

**Gotcha 52 — `expect.toPass()` Default Timeout Is 0 — Tests "Pass" Without Retrying**  [community]
A team migrating from `page.waitForTimeout(3000)` to `expect.toPass()` found that their E2E
flakiness rate *increased* after the migration. Root cause: every `expect.toPass()` call was
missing the `{ timeout: 10_000 }` option. With `timeout: 0`, the block executed once, the
assertion failed, and the test reported a hard failure — not a retry. The waitForTimeout had
at least delayed the single assertion attempt by 3 seconds (masking the timing issue), while
the `toPass()` with no timeout failed immediately. Fix: always pass `{ timeout: N }` — Playwright
documentation does not prominently display the 0-default in the main API reference. The
Playwright team notes this is a known footgun: the next major version may change the default
to the global timeout, but as of v1.52, you must specify it explicitly.

**Gotcha 53 — MTBF Scoring Resets Silently After Test Case Rename**  [community]
Teams that track per-test MTBF (Pattern 107) using the test name as the identity key discover
that renaming a test case during refactoring (e.g., "should create user" → "creates user correctly")
silently resets that test's failure history to zero. The renamed test appears as a brand-new test
case with no failure record — its accumulated MTBF data is orphaned under the old name. Teams at
scale (Spotify, Canva) solve this by assigning a stable test ID via custom metadata (`test.info().annotations`
in Playwright, `test.meta` in Vitest) and tracking MTBF by that ID rather than the display name.
The ID is a short hash of the original test path + name, set at authoring time and preserved across
renames. This is particularly important for regression detection: a test with a history of 30%
flakiness that gets renamed looks "clean" to the scoring system, hiding that the root cause was
never fixed.

### Pattern 109 — Vitest `--retry.condition` for Error-Pattern-Specific Retry  [community]

The `--retry.condition` CLI option (Vitest 4.1) accepts a **regex pattern** matched against the
error message of a failing test case. Only failures whose error message matches the pattern trigger
a retry — all other failures fail immediately. This is the most precise retry mechanism available:
instead of retrying every failure (which hides real regressions), you enumerate the known-transient
error signatures and retry only those.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — retry only known-transient failures
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Retry up to 2 times, but ONLY for these transient error classes:
    retry: {
      count: 2,
      delay: 500,
      // Only retry network timeouts, ECONNRESET, and DB pool exhaustion.
      // Real assertion failures ("Expected: X, received: Y") will NOT retry.
      condition: /ETIMEDOUT|ECONNRESET|ECONNREFUSED|pool.*exhausted|socket hang up/i,
    },
  },
});
```

```typescript
// Alternative: CLI usage for CI environments
// npx vitest --retry.count=2 --retry.delay=500 \
//   --retry.condition="ETIMEDOUT|ECONNRESET|pool.*exhausted"

// Example: separate retry budgets per test project
// vitest.config.ts with multiple projects
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      {
        // Unit tests: no retry — deterministic
        test: { name: 'unit', include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'], retry: 0 },
      },
      {
        // Integration tests: retry transient infra errors only
        test: {
          name: 'integration',
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
          retry: {
            count: 2,
            delay: 1_000,
            condition: /ETIMEDOUT|ECONNRESET|ECONNREFUSED/i,
          },
        },
      },
      {
        // E2E tests: retry browser launch and network errors only
        test: {
          name: 'e2e',
          include: ['e2e/**/*.test.ts'],
          retry: {
            count: 3,
            delay: 2_000,
            condition: /browser.*closed|Target.*closed|net::ERR_/i,
          },
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});
```

**Why this eliminates over-retry:** A generic `retry: 3` on all tests means a test case with a
real assertion defect (`Expected: 200, received: 500`) wastes 3 retry cycles before failing. With
`condition`, the real regression fails on attempt 1, saves CI time, and the transient infra error
retries cleanly. Track which condition patterns fire in your reporter — if a pattern fires >10%
of runs, the underlying infra issue warrants a dedicated fix, not more retries.

### Pattern 110 — Vitest `--sequence.shuffle.tests` + `--sequence.seed` for Reproducible Order-Dependency Debugging  [community]

Order-dependent flakiness — where test case B passes only if test case A ran first — is the
hardest class to reproduce because it is invisible in a fixed-order run. Vitest's `--sequence.shuffle`
flags combined with `--sequence.seed` provide a two-phase workflow: (1) expose the dependency by
randomizing order, (2) reproduce the exact failing order by replaying the seed.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — always shuffle in CI to continuously expose order-dependency
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    sequence: {
      shuffle: {
        files: true,   // randomize which file runs first
        tests: true,   // randomize test case order within each file
      },
      // seed is set via CLI or env var — omit here to generate fresh seed each run
    },
  },
});
```

```bash
# CI workflow: capture seed, run tests, log seed on failure
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# generate a seed for this CI run
SEED=$RANDOM

echo "Running tests with seed: $SEED"
npx vitest run --sequence.seed="$SEED" --sequence.shuffle.files --sequence.shuffle.tests

EXIT_CODE=$?
if [ $EXIT_CODE -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "::error title=Order-Dependency Detected::Failing seed: $SEED"
  echo "Reproduce locally: npx vitest run --sequence.seed=$SEED --sequence.shuffle.files --sequence.shuffle.tests"
fi
exit $EXIT_CODE
```

```typescript
// Verifying a suspected order-dependent test case in isolation:
// Step 1: identify the failing pair (test A then test B fails; test B alone passes)
// Step 2: use test.describe.serial to run them in that exact order
import { describe, test, expect, beforeEach } from 'vitest';

// antipattern: shared mutable state leaking between test cases
let sharedCounter = 0;

describe.serial('order-dependency demo (broken)', () => {
  test('test A: increments counter', () => {
    sharedCounter += 1; // leaks state — next test sees counter = 1
    expect(sharedCounter).toBe(1);
  });

  test('test B: FAILS if test A ran first', () => {
    // expects fresh counter, but gets counter = 1 from test A
    expect(sharedCounter).toBe(0); // fails when test A ran first
  });
});

// fix: reset shared state in beforeEach
describe('order-dependency fixed', () => {
  beforeEach(() => { sharedCounter = 0; }); // reset per test case
  test('test A', () => { sharedCounter += 1; expect(sharedCounter).toBe(1); });
  test('test B', () => { expect(sharedCounter).toBe(0); }); // always 0 now
});
```

**Workflow for teams:** Add `--sequence.shuffle.files --sequence.shuffle.tests` to the nightly
CI run but NOT to the developer PR run (to keep PR runs stable). When a nightly run fails, the
logged seed lets any engineer reproduce the exact failure locally in under a minute. Pair with
`--reporter=json` to capture test execution order in the artifact.

### Pattern 111 — Playwright `page.consoleMessages()` and `page.pageErrors()` for Flakiness Diagnosis  [community]

Added in Playwright v1.56, `page.consoleMessages()` and `page.pageErrors()` return the **accumulated
log of browser console output and uncaught page errors** respectively. This is the cleanest way to
detect client-side JavaScript errors that cause intermittent test failures without adding custom
`page.on('pageerror')` listeners to every test case.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// afterEach hook — fail any test case that had uncaught page errors
// (common cause of flakiness: a JS error fires, React error boundary catches it,
// the UI looks correct visually, but the next assertion fails on degraded state)
test.afterEach(async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  const pageErrors = page.pageErrors();

  if (pageErrors.length > 0) {
    // Attach errors as test annotation for the Playwright report
    for (const err of pageErrors) {
      testInfo.annotations.push({
        type: 'page-error',
        description: err.message,
      });
    }

    // Fail the test case if there were uncaught page errors
    // (use expect.soft if you want to continue despite errors)
    expect(pageErrors, 'Unexpected page errors detected during test').toHaveLength(0);
  }
});

// diagnose console warnings as flakiness signal
test('checkout flow completes without console errors', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Order confirmed')).toBeVisible();

  // Retrieve accumulated console messages — filter to errors/warnings
  const consoleMessages = page.consoleMessages();
  const errorMessages = consoleMessages.filter(
    m => m.type() === 'error' || m.type() === 'warning'
  );

  // Attach for debugging — do not fail on warnings (too noisy), fail on errors
  if (errorMessages.length > 0) {
    testInfo.annotations.push({
      type: 'console-errors',
      description: errorMessages.map(m => `[${m.type()}] ${m.text()}`).join('\n'),
    });
  }

  const consoleErrors = consoleMessages.filter(m => m.type() === 'error');
  expect(consoleErrors, 'Unexpected console errors during checkout').toHaveLength(0);
});

// clear between navigation steps when testing multi-page flows
test('multi-step wizard with per-step error tracking', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/wizard/step-1');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next' }).click();

  // Clear accumulated messages after step 1 before proceeding to step 2
  page.clearConsoleMessages();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next' }).click();

  // Now only step-2 console messages are captured
  const step2Errors = page.consoleMessages().filter(m => m.type() === 'error');
  expect(step2Errors).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Why this reduces flakiness:** Many E2E test cases fail because a React/Vue component throws an
uncaught error that the framework catches silently (error boundary) but the resulting degraded
state causes an assertion to fail several steps later. Without `page.pageErrors()`, the error trace
points to the assertion — not to the original JavaScript error three steps earlier. With this
pattern, the uncaught error is surfaced immediately, reducing diagnosis time from 30+ minutes
(re-running with extra logging) to zero (the error is in the report).

---

### Pattern 112 — Playwright `await using` Async Disposables for Automatic Test Context Teardown  [community]

Playwright v1.59 introduced `async disposable` support on several APIs. Objects returned from
methods like `page.addInitScript()` and `page.exposeBinding()` implement `[Symbol.asyncDispose]`,
enabling the TypeScript 5.2+ `await using` syntax for deterministic, automatic cleanup. This
eliminates the most common source of test isolation defects: forgetting to call cleanup methods
in `afterEach`.

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.2+ required — tsconfig.json: { "target": "ES2022", "lib": ["ES2022", "esnext.disposable"] }
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('init script auto-cleaned up via await using', async ({ page }) => {
  // await using — cleanup is automatic when the block exits (pass OR fail)
  // Without this, forgetting "await initScript.dispose()" leaks the script
  // across tests and causes shared-state flakiness
  await using initScript = await page.addInitScript(() => {
    // Inject a test flag before any page scripts run
    window.__TEST_ENVIRONMENT__ = true;
  });

  await page.goto('/');
  // initScript.dispose() is called automatically at end of test
  // even if the expect below throws — no manual cleanup needed
  await expect(page.getByTestId('env-banner')).toHaveText('Test environment');
});

// Pattern: multiple disposables in a single test case — all cleaned up in LIFO order
test('multiple disposables with LIFO teardown', async ({ page }) => {
  await using binding = await page.exposeBinding('trackEvent', (_source, event: string) => {
    console.log(`[TEST] Event tracked: ${event}`);
  });

  await using script = await page.addInitScript(() => {
    // Override analytics to use the exposed binding
    window.analytics = { track: (e: string) => (window as any).trackEvent(e) };
  });

  await page.goto('/onboarding');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Get Started' }).click();

  // Both `script` and `binding` disposed automatically in reverse order
  // (script first, then binding — LIFO)
  await expect(page.getByText('Welcome')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Why this eliminates a class of flakiness:** The most common async teardown defect is:
test A calls `page.exposeBinding('helper', fn)` and does not dispose it; test B navigates to
the same page and the stale binding from test A fires unexpectedly, causing assertion failures
in test B. With `await using`, even if the test case throws, TypeScript guarantees the dispose
call runs — it is not possible to forget cleanup. Teams adopting this pattern report eliminating
a class of shared-binding flakiness entirely (similar elimination to using `using` for file handles).

**Migration checklist:**
- `tsconfig.json`: `"target": "ES2022"` and `"lib": ["ES2022", "esnext.disposable"]`
- Replace `const x = await page.addInitScript(...)` + `afterEach(() => x.dispose())` with `await using x = await page.addInitScript(...)`
- Verify `strictNullChecks: true` — TypeScript emits better disposal error messages with strict mode

### Pattern 113 — pytest `--randomly-seed=last` for Reproducing Randomized Failures in Python  [community]

The `pytest-randomly` plugin randomizes test case execution order in Python suites using
`pytest-random-order` or `pytest-randomly`. Both plugins support `--randomly-seed=last`, which
reruns the test suite with the exact seed from the previous run — enabling engineers to reproduce
an order-dependent failure in one command after seeing it in CI.

```python
# conftest.py — capture and log the random seed used each run
import pytest

def pytest_configure(config):
    """Log the random seed to the terminal and to a CI artifact."""
    seed = getattr(config, '_randomly_seed', None)
    if seed is not None:
        print(f"\n[pytest-randomly] Seed: {seed}")
        # Write to a file so CI can upload as artifact and engineers can reproduce
        with open("test-random-seed.txt", "w") as f:
            f.write(str(seed))

# Usage in CI:
#   pytest --randomly-seed=random          # generate fresh seed each run
#   cat test-random-seed.txt               # inspect used seed after failure
#   pytest --randomly-seed=last            # reproduce using last run's seed
#   pytest --randomly-seed=42              # reproduce a specific known seed


# Example: order-dependent test cases exposed by shuffling
import pytest

# This test suite has a hidden order-dependency:
_shared_registry: dict = {}  # module-level shared state — FLAKINESS SOURCE

class TestRegistryOperations:
    def test_register_item(self):
        # Leaks state: adds 'item1' to shared registry
        _shared_registry['item1'] = 'value1'
        assert 'item1' in _shared_registry

    def test_list_is_empty_at_start(self):
        # Only passes if test_register_item DID NOT run first
        assert _shared_registry == {}  # fails when test_register_item ran before

    # Fix: use a fixture that provides an isolated registry per test case
    @pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
    def isolated_registry(self, monkeypatch):
        """Replace module-level registry with a fresh dict for each test case."""
        fresh_registry: dict = {}
        monkeypatch.setattr('tests.test_registry._shared_registry', fresh_registry)
        yield fresh_registry
        # monkeypatch auto-restores the original after the test case completes
```

```python
# pyproject.toml — enable randomization by default in all runs
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = "--randomly-seed=random"
# To disable randomization for a specific run:
# pytest --randomly-dont-shuffle-module
```

**Why this is critical for Python teams:** Python's module-level state (class attributes,
module globals, `@lru_cache` cached values) is the most common source of order-dependent flakiness
in Python test suites. The `monkeypatch` fixture (built-in to pytest) is the canonical fix — it
replaces module attributes and restores them automatically. `pytest-randomly` with `--randomly-seed=last`
makes the reproduction loop from "CI failed" to "I can reproduce locally" under 30 seconds.

### Anti-Patterns (Cycle 19)

#### AP54 — Using `--retry.count` Without `--retry.condition` in Vitest  [community]
**What:** Setting `retry: { count: 3 }` globally in Vitest config without a `condition` regex.
**Why harmful:** Every failing test case — including those with deterministic assertion failures
(`Expected: 200, received: 404`) — retries 3 times before reporting. A 1,000 test suite with
10 failing tests wastes 30 extra test executions per CI run, adding minutes to wall-clock time.
Worse, it erodes the signal: if a real regression retries 3 times before failing, engineers
assume the failure might be transient and re-run rather than investigating immediately. Always
pair `retry.count` with a `condition` regex that matches only known-transient error signatures.

#### AP55 — Ignoring `page.pageErrors()` Accumulation Between Navigation Steps  [community]
**What:** Calling `page.pageErrors()` only at the end of a multi-step test case, without clearing
between steps using `page.clearPageErrors()`.
**Why harmful:** A JavaScript error thrown during step 1 accumulates in `pageErrors()`. When the
test case inspects `pageErrors()` after step 5, all errors from all steps are mixed together.
The assertion `expect(pageErrors).toHaveLength(0)` fails with step-1 errors even when steps 2–5
were clean. The error report becomes unactionable — engineers cannot tell which step introduced
the error. Fix: call `page.clearPageErrors()` and `page.clearConsoleMessages()` at the start of
each logical step when testing multi-page or multi-navigation flows.

#### AP56 — Forgetting `esnext.disposable` in `tsconfig.json` for `await using`  [community]
**What:** Using the `await using` syntax with Playwright async disposables without configuring
`"lib": ["ES2022", "esnext.disposable"]` in `tsconfig.json`.
**Why harmful:** TypeScript silently falls back to compiling `await using` as a regular `const`
assignment, emitting no `[Symbol.asyncDispose]()` call. The object is not disposed — cleanup
code does not run — and the developer sees no error or warning. The test case appears to work,
but the binding/initScript leaks across tests exactly as if `await using` had not been used at
all. The resulting shared-state flakiness is particularly hard to diagnose because the code *looks*
correct. Always verify disposal by checking that `tsconfig.json` targets ES2022 and the
`esnext.disposable` lib entry is present.

### Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 19)  [community]

**Gotcha 54 — Trunk Auto-Quarantine Unblocks CI but Creates Invisible Coverage Holes**  [community]
Teams using Trunk's auto-quarantine feature (which quarantines flaky tests without code changes
and excludes them from blocking the pipeline) report a secondary problem: after 6 months, 8–15%
of their test suite is quarantined but still listed as passing in the "main suite" coverage report.
Coverage tools count quarantined test cases as covering code, but they never run in CI. Root cause:
the quarantine system operates at the CI result layer, not the coverage layer. Fix: maintain a
separate coverage baseline run that excludes quarantined test cases, and set a numeric quarantine
limit (Pattern 53's infection model). When quarantine count exceeds the limit, block new PRs until
the backlog is reduced. Trunk's own documentation recommends weekly quarantine review with owner
assignment via integrated ticketing.

**Gotcha 55 — `--sequence.shuffle` Exposes Order-Dependencies That `--runInBand` Masks**  [community]
Teams migrating from Jest to Vitest who set `--runInBand` (single-threaded execution) to "fix"
order-dependent flakiness discover that the fix disappears when they enable `--sequence.shuffle`.
The reason: `--runInBand` runs test files in the same deterministic alphabetical order every time,
so order-dependent test cases that depend on specific file ordering always get the state they
expect. Shuffling breaks this assumption. The correct fix is never `--runInBand` alone — it is
resetting shared state in `beforeEach` / `afterEach`. Use `--runInBand` only for initial diagnosis
(to confirm the issue is parallelism-related), then fix the underlying shared state.

**Gotcha 56 — `page.requests()` Retains Only the Last ~100 Requests**  [community]
Teams using `page.requests()` (Playwright v1.56+) to diagnose network-related flakiness in long
E2E test cases discover that requests early in the test are evicted from the buffer. The retention
limit is approximately 100 requests — in a checkout flow that makes 150 API calls across 8 steps,
the first 50 calls are gone by the time the test ends. Teams that need full network capture for
flakiness diagnosis should use HAR recording (`page.routeFromHAR()` or tracing with network events
enabled) rather than `page.requests()` for test cases with high request volume.

|---------|-------------------|-------------|----------------------|
| Every failing test retries 3× — CI run inflated | `retry.count` without `retry.condition` | Pattern 109 (condition regex for transient errors only) | AP54 (global retry without condition) |
| Order-dependent failure reproduced in CI but not locally | Fixed execution order locally | Pattern 110 (`--sequence.shuffle` + seed capture) | Running without shuffle in CI |
| E2E test fails on assertion 5 steps after the real error | No page error monitoring | Pattern 111 (`page.pageErrors()` in afterEach) | Checking only the final assertion |
| `await using` does not clean up — binding leaks | Missing `esnext.disposable` in tsconfig | Pattern 112 (tsconfig lib + TS 5.2+ target) | AP56 (missing tsconfig lib entry) |
| Python order-dependent failure not reproducible locally | Random seed not captured | Pattern 113 (`--randomly-seed=last` + seed artifact) | Running without seed capture |
| Quarantined tests counted in coverage — false confidence | Auto-quarantine at CI layer, not coverage layer | Maintain separate coverage run excluding quarantined tests | Gotcha 54 (Trunk auto-quarantine coverage hole) |
| `page.requests()` missing early network calls in long test | 100-request retention limit | Use HAR recording for high-volume tests | Gotcha 56 (requests() retention limit) |

### Pattern 114 — Vitest `vi.setTimerTickMode()` for Async-Safe Timer Flakiness Elimination  [community]

Vitest 4.1.0 introduces `vi.setTimerTickMode()`, which controls **when** fake timers advance
after `vi.useFakeTimers()` is called. Three modes are available:

- **`'manual'`** (default): Timers only advance when you explicitly call `vi.advanceTimersByTime()`,
  `vi.runAllTimers()`, etc. Use this for full deterministic control.
- **`'nextTimerAsync'`**: Automatically advances to the next scheduled timer after each macrotask.
  Use this when your production code awaits timers internally and you cannot easily control when
  timers fire from the test body — prevents the "test hangs forever" class of async flakiness.
- **`'interval'`**: Advances timers automatically at a real-time interval (milliseconds). Use this
  for animation or polling loops where you want the test to exercise real scheduling cadence.

**Why this matters:** Before 4.1, async code that depended on timers firing between `await` points
required manual interleaving of `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync()` calls inside the test body — easy
to get wrong, and the source of "hangs only in CI" when async scheduling differs between environments.
`'nextTimerAsync'` eliminates this by making the timer advancement automatic after each microtask flush.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — project-level timer mode for integration tests
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    fakeTimers: {
      // toFake restricts WHICH timer APIs are faked — prevents over-mocking
      toFake: ['setTimeout', 'clearTimeout', 'setInterval', 'clearInterval', 'Date'],
    },
  },
});
```

```typescript
// In an individual test: per-test timer tick mode override
import { vi, test, expect } from 'vitest';

// MANUAL mode — full explicit control (default)
test('manual timer control — polling loop fires exactly N times', async () => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  vi.setTimerTickMode('manual');

  let pollCount = 0;
  const polling = setInterval(() => { pollCount++; }, 1_000);

  vi.advanceTimersByTime(3_500); // fires at 1000ms, 2000ms, 3000ms
  expect(pollCount).toBe(3);

  clearInterval(polling);
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

// nextTimerAsync mode — prevents "hangs waiting for timer" in async code
test('nextTimerAsync mode — async code awaits timer internally', async () => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  vi.setTimerTickMode('nextTimerAsync');

  async function fetchWithRetry(attempt = 0): Promise<string> {
    if (attempt < 2) {
      await new Promise<void>(res => setTimeout(res, 500));
      return fetchWithRetry(attempt + 1);
    }
    return 'success';
  }

  // Under nextTimerAsync, each awaited setTimeout fires automatically —
  // no manual vi.advanceTimersByTime calls needed
  const value = await fetchWithRetry();
  expect(value).toBe('success');

  vi.useRealTimers();
});

// interval mode — animation frame / polling cadence testing
test('interval mode — 60fps animation loop processes all frames', async () => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  vi.setTimerTickMode('interval', 16); // 16ms ≈ 60fps

  let frames = 0;
  const rafHandle = setInterval(() => { frames++; }, 16);

  // Real 100ms passes, auto-advancing by 16ms each tick
  await new Promise<void>(res => setTimeout(res, 100));
  clearInterval(rafHandle);

  expect(frames).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(6);
  vi.useRealTimers();
});
```

**Why `'nextTimerAsync'` eliminates a whole class of CI flakiness:** In CI, the Node.js event
loop scheduler may flush microtasks at different points than local development. Code that does
`await delay(500)` internally can stall the test runner if the fake timer never advances because
the test body never calls `vi.advanceTimersByTime()`. `'nextTimerAsync'` makes the advancement
automatic — the timer fires after every `await` point, matching the production scheduling
behaviour regardless of CI scheduler variance.

### Pattern 115 — Vitest `vi.mockObject()` for Partial-Mock Shared State Prevention  [community]

`vi.mockObject()` (Vitest 3.2.0+) deeply mocks all method properties of a given object while
preserving non-function property values. This prevents the "partial mock leaks real implementation"
class of flakiness — where one test case mocks `service.fetchUser` but leaves `service.cacheResult`
real, and a subsequent test case unexpectedly writes to a shared cache.

The `{ spy: true }` mode wraps all methods with spies that preserve their original implementation
while tracking calls — the correct choice for most flakiness-prevention use cases, because it
avoids accidentally silencing side-effects that should fail loudly.

```typescript
// service.ts
export const userService = {
  fetchUser: async (id: string) => { /* real network call */ },
  cacheResult: (key: string, value: unknown) => { /* writes to module-level cache */ },
  _cache: new Map<string, unknown>(),
  maxRetries: 3,   // non-function: preserved as-is by vi.mockObject()
};
```

```typescript
// user-service.test.ts
import { vi, test, expect, beforeEach, afterEach, describe } from 'vitest';
import { userService } from './service';

describe('UserService — mockObject isolation', () => {
  let mockedService: ReturnType<typeof vi.mockObject<typeof userService>>;

  beforeEach(() => {
    // Deep-mock ALL methods — no accidental real-implementation leaks
    mockedService = vi.mockObject(userService);
    // maxRetries (number) is preserved: mockedService.maxRetries === 3
    // fetchUser and cacheResult are now vi.fn() — return undefined by default
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    vi.clearAllMocks();
  });

  test('fetchUser returns mocked value without hitting network', async () => {
    mockedService.fetchUser.mockResolvedValue({ id: '1', name: 'Alice' });
    const user = await mockedService.fetchUser('1');
    expect(user).toEqual({ id: '1', name: 'Alice' });
    // cacheResult is also mocked — does NOT write to shared _cache
    expect(mockedService.cacheResult).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });

  test('spy mode — tracks calls while preserving implementation', () => {
    // Use spy: true when you need the REAL implementation but also call tracking
    const spiedService = vi.mockObject(userService, { spy: true });
    // fetchUser still calls real implementation — useful for integration tests
    expect(spiedService.fetchUser).toBeTypeOf('function');
    expect(spiedService.cacheResult).toBeTypeOf('function');
  });
});
```

**Anti-pattern this prevents:** Using `vi.spyOn(service, 'fetchUser').mockResolvedValue(...)` on
individual methods while leaving other methods real. If `cacheResult` writes to a module-level
`Map`, that mutation persists across test cases — classic shared state flakiness. `vi.mockObject()`
mocks the whole object atomically.

### Pattern 116 — Vitest `vi.defineHelper()` for Actionable Stack Traces in Custom Assertions  [community]

When custom assertion helpers fail, Vitest stack traces by default point *inside* the helper
function rather than to the test line that invoked it. `vi.defineHelper()` (Vitest 4.1.0+)
wraps the helper so errors point to the **call site** — the exact test line that triggered the
failure. This eliminates the "why does the error say line 42 inside assertUserShape.ts?" class
of diagnosis time waste, which manifests as "I can't tell which test case is failing" in test
suites with many shared assertion helpers.

```typescript
// test-helpers/assertions.ts
import { expect, vi } from 'vitest';

// Without vi.defineHelper: stack traces point inside this file (confusing)
// With vi.defineHelper: stack traces point to the test line that called it (actionable)

export const assertUserShape = vi.defineHelper((user: unknown) => {
  expect(user).toMatchObject({
    id: expect.any(String),
    name: expect.any(String),
    createdAt: expect.any(Date),
  });
});

export const assertPaginatedResponse = vi.defineHelper(
  (response: unknown, expectedCount: number) => {
    expect(response).toMatchObject({
      items: expect.any(Array),
      total: expect.any(Number),
      page: expect.any(Number),
    });
    expect((response as { items: unknown[] }).items).toHaveLength(expectedCount);
  }
);

export const assertNoFlakySideEffects = vi.defineHelper(
  async (fn: () => Promise<void>, globalsBefore: Record<string, unknown>) => {
    await fn();
    for (const [key, before] of Object.entries(globalsBefore)) {
      expect((globalThis as Record<string, unknown>)[key]).toEqual(before);
    }
  }
);
```

```typescript
// user-api.test.ts
import { test } from 'vitest';
import { assertUserShape, assertPaginatedResponse } from '../test-helpers/assertions';
import { fetchUsers } from '../api/users';

test('GET /users returns valid user shapes', async () => {
  const response = await fetchUsers({ page: 1, limit: 10 });
  assertPaginatedResponse(response, 10);         // error points HERE, not inside helper
  response.items.forEach(user => assertUserShape(user)); // same
});
```

**Why this reduces flakiness diagnosis time:** In CI logs where flaky test cases fail
intermittently, the first question is "which line in which test triggered the failure?" Without
`defineHelper`, the stack shows an internal line of the assertion helper — developers waste time
cross-referencing. With `defineHelper`, the stack points directly to the test line, cutting
mean-time-to-diagnose for intermittent assertion failures by ~60% in test suites with deep
assertion helper hierarchies.

### Pattern 117 — Playwright `tracing.group()` for Flakiness-Scoped Trace Navigation  [community]

Playwright v1.49 introduced `tracing.group()` (and `tracing.groupEnd()`) to organize trace
actions into **named visual groups** in the Playwright Trace Viewer. For flakiness diagnosis,
this transforms a flat list of 200+ actions (clicks, navigations, network requests) into a
folded hierarchy where each group corresponds to a logical test phase. When a test case is
flaky, you open the trace and immediately see *which group* contains the anomaly — instead of
scrolling through 200 individual actions.

**Note:** The Playwright team recommends `test.step()` over direct `tracing.group()` in test
bodies, as `test.step()` integrates with the full test reporter infrastructure. Use
`tracing.group()` in fixtures, page objects, and helper utilities where `test.step()` is not
accessible.

```typescript
// page-objects/checkout-page.ts
import { Page } from '@playwright/test';

interface CardDetails { number: string; expiry: string; cvc: string; }

export class CheckoutPage {
  constructor(private readonly page: Page) {}

  async completeCheckout(cardDetails: CardDetails): Promise<string> {
    // Groups all card-fill actions in the trace under a named fold
    await this.page.context().tracing.group('checkout: fill card details');
    await this.page.locator('[data-testid="card-number"]').fill(cardDetails.number);
    await this.page.locator('[data-testid="card-expiry"]').fill(cardDetails.expiry);
    await this.page.locator('[data-testid="card-cvc"]').fill(cardDetails.cvc);
    await this.page.context().tracing.groupEnd();

    await this.page.context().tracing.group('checkout: submit and await confirmation');
    await this.page.locator('[data-testid="submit-order"]').click();
    await this.page.waitForURL('**/order-confirmation/**');
    const orderId = await this.page.locator('[data-testid="order-id"]').textContent();
    await this.page.context().tracing.groupEnd();

    return orderId ?? '';
  }
}
```

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — enable traces on all retries for comparison
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    trace: 'retain-on-failure-and-retries', // captures all retries for side-by-side diff
  },
});
```

```typescript
// tests/checkout.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { CheckoutPage } from '../page-objects/checkout-page';

test('checkout flow completes with valid card', async ({ page }) => {
  const checkout = new CheckoutPage(page);

  // test.step() preferred in test bodies — appears in all reporters
  await test.step('navigate to checkout', async () => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
  });

  await test.step('complete checkout', async () => {
    const orderId = await checkout.completeCheckout({
      number: '4111111111111111',
      expiry: '12/28',
      cvc: '123',
    });
    expect(orderId).toMatch(/^ORD-\d{8}$/);
  });
});
```

**Key insight for flakiness diagnosis:** When `retain-on-failure-and-retries` is enabled, you
get one trace per retry attempt. Groups make it possible to compare *which group* differed
between the passing and failing attempt — network requests inside
"checkout: submit and await confirmation" on attempt 1 vs attempt 2 reveal whether the
flakiness is a timing issue during form submission or a race condition during order
confirmation redirect.

### Pattern 118 — Playwright `tracing.startHar()/stopHar()` for Network Flakiness Root Cause Analysis  [community]

Playwright v1.60 promotes HAR recording from a routing feature to a **first-class tracing API**
via `tracing.startHar()` / `tracing.stopHar()`. Unlike `page.requests()` (which retains only
the last ~100 requests per Gotcha 56), HAR recording captures the *complete* network history
for the entire test case with full request/response bodies, timing data, and headers.

For flakiness diagnosis, HAR recording enables:
1. **Cross-retry comparison**: Save `attempt-0.har` and `attempt-1.har`, compare with any HAR
   diff tool to identify the exact request that differed between a passing and failing run.
2. **URL filtering**: Use `urlFilter` to capture only the API calls you care about, keeping HAR
   files small enough for automated diffing.
3. **mode: 'full'** vs `'minimal'`: Use `'full'` for diagnosis (includes timing and security
   data); `'minimal'` only for replay scenarios.

```typescript
// fixtures/har-capture.fixture.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

// Fixture that saves a HAR file per retry attempt for network flakiness diagnosis
export const test = base.extend<{ harCapture: void }>({
  harCapture: [async ({ context, testInfo }, use) => {
    const harPath = testInfo.outputPath(`network-attempt-${testInfo.retry}.har`);

    await context.tracing.startHar(harPath, {
      content: 'embed',
      mode: 'full',         // REQUIRED for flakiness diagnosis — includes timing data
      urlFilter: /\/api\//, // Only capture API calls — skip static assets
    });

    await use();

    await context.tracing.stopHar();

    // Attach HAR to the test report so it appears in CI artifacts
    if (testInfo.status !== 'passed') {
      await testInfo.attach(`network-attempt-${testInfo.retry}`, {
        path: harPath,
        contentType: 'application/json',
      });
    }
  }, { auto: true }],
});
```

```typescript
// tests/payment-api.integration.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '../fixtures/har-capture.fixture';

test('payment API responds within 200ms on all retries', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.locator('[data-testid="pay-now"]').click();

  // If this test case is flaky, compare attempt-0.har vs attempt-1.har:
  // different timing on the /api/payment endpoint reveals the root cause
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="confirmation"]')).toBeVisible({
    timeout: 5_000,
  });
});
```

**Critical distinction from `mode: 'minimal'`:** Anti-pattern AP57 below covers this — using
`mode: 'minimal'` for flakiness diagnosis loses request timing and security metadata. Timing
data is the most diagnostic field for "why did this request take 4 seconds on retry 2 but 80ms
on retry 1" — always use `mode: 'full'` when diagnosing flakiness.

### Pattern 119 — FlakyDoctor Neuro-Symbolic Classification for ID/OD Flakiness  [community]

FlakyDoctor (ISSTA 2024, Intelligent-CAT-Lab) implements a **neuro-symbolic repair** loop for
flaky Java test cases: static analysis classifies the test case as Implementation-Dependent (ID)
or Order-Dependent (OD), then an LLM (GPT-4 or Magicoder-S-DS-6.7B) generates patch candidates
that a symbolic layer validates against compilation and execution.

**ID vs OD taxonomy** (the root cause patterns apply across all languages):
- **Implementation-Dependent (ID):** The test case itself contains a time-dependent assertion,
  floating-point comparison, or non-deterministic ordering assumption. The fix lives inside the
  test case.
- **Order-Dependent (OD):** The test case relies on state left by a previously executed test
  case. The fix adds setup/teardown to the polluter or victim test case.

**Practical ID/OD classifier for TypeScript teams** (FlakyDoctor itself targets Java; this
TypeScript adaptation implements the same classification heuristics):

```typescript
// scripts/flaky-classifier.ts
import * as fs from 'fs';

interface FlakyCaseReport {
  file: string;
  testName: string;
  category: 'ID' | 'OD' | 'UNKNOWN';
  evidence: string;
}

function classifyFlakiness(testFile: string): FlakyCaseReport[] {
  const content = fs.readFileSync(testFile, 'utf-8');
  const reports: FlakyCaseReport[] = [];

  // ID signals: timing, floating-point, non-injected randomness
  const idSignals: Array<{ re: RegExp; evidence: string }> = [
    { re: /\bnew Date\(\)/g,         evidence: 'Date() construction without fake timer injection' },
    { re: /Date\.now\(\)/g,          evidence: 'Date.now() without vi.useFakeTimers()' },
    { re: /Math\.random\(\)/g,       evidence: 'Math.random() — seed this or inject via parameter' },
    { re: /toBe\(\d+\.\d{4,}\)/g,   evidence: 'Deep float equality — use toBeCloseTo(value, digits)' },
    { re: /await\s+new Promise[^)]+setTimeout[^)]+0\)/g,
                                     evidence: 'setTimeout(0) sleep — replace with vi.waitFor()' },
  ];

  // OD signals: module-level mutable state that persists between test cases
  const odSignals: Array<{ re: RegExp; evidence: string }> = [
    { re: /^(?:let|var)\s+\w+\s*=/m, evidence: 'Module-level mutable variable (OD risk in parallel runs)' },
    { re: /\.mockImplementation/g,   evidence: 'mockImplementation not reset — confirm afterEach clearAllMocks' },
    { re: /globalThis\.\w+\s*=/g,   evidence: 'globalThis mutation without afterEach restore' },
  ];

  const testNames = content.match(/(?:test|it)\(\s*['"`](.+?)['"`]/g) ?? ['unknown test'];
  const firstName = testNames[0] ?? 'unknown';

  for (const { re, evidence } of idSignals) {
    if (re.test(content)) {
      reports.push({ file: testFile, testName: firstName, category: 'ID', evidence });
    }
  }
  for (const { re, evidence } of odSignals) {
    if (re.test(content)) {
      reports.push({ file: testFile, testName: firstName, category: 'OD', evidence });
    }
  }

  return reports;
}

// Usage: npx ts-node scripts/flaky-classifier.ts src/**/*.test.ts
const [, , ...files] = process.argv;
files.forEach(f => {
  const reports = classifyFlakiness(f);
  if (reports.length > 0) {
    process.stdout.write(JSON.stringify(reports, null, 2) + '\n');
  }
});
```

**Key finding from FlakyDoctor's ISSTA 2024 study:** 19 patches accepted in PRs to Apache Pinot,
Dropwizard, Moquette, and Jackson — all addressing test cases that static analysis alone could not
fix because the fix required understanding the test's *intent*. LLM-generated patches succeeded
where rule-based fixers failed because the model could infer whether the intent was "assert
ordering" (OD) or "assert a specific value" (ID) and generate the appropriate teardown or mock
injection.

**Adoption note for TypeScript projects:** FlakyDoctor requires Python 3.10.12, Java 8/11, Maven
3.6.3, and Linux. The classification script above provides the ID/OD heuristic without the Java
runtime. Pair it with an LLM API call (Claude with prompt caching for cost efficiency) to generate
patch suggestions — the same neuro-symbolic loop applies.

### Anti-Patterns (Cycle 20)

#### AP57 — Using `tracing.startHar()` with `mode: 'minimal'` for Flakiness Diagnosis  [community]
**What:** Calling `context.tracing.startHar('trace.har', { mode: 'minimal' })` to capture
network activity for flaky test case investigation.
**Why harmful:** `mode: 'minimal'` records only the information needed for HAR *replay*
(URL, method, response body). It omits request and response timing, security information,
cookies, and headers — precisely the fields that reveal why a request took 4 seconds on retry
2 versus 80ms on retry 1. When engineers open the HAR to diagnose flakiness and find no timing
data, they conclude "the network is fine" when the actual root cause is a slow database query
on the first call that warms a cache. Always use `mode: 'full'` for any HAR file whose purpose
is flakiness diagnosis. Only use `mode: 'minimal'` when the HAR is used exclusively for route
replay via `page.routeFromHAR()`.

#### AP58 — Mixing `vi.runAllTimers()` with `vi.setTimerTickMode('nextTimerAsync')`  [community]
**What:** Calling `vi.runAllTimers()` (or `vi.advanceTimersByTime()`) inside a test case after
setting `vi.setTimerTickMode('nextTimerAsync')`.
**Why harmful:** In `nextTimerAsync` mode, timers advance automatically after each macrotask.
If you also call `vi.runAllTimers()` in the test body, you double-fire timers: the automatic
advancement fires one set of timers, then `runAllTimers()` fires all remaining timers (and any
that were re-queued by the first fire). This can cause timers to fire 2–5× more than production
code expects, generating duplicate event emissions, double fetches, and assertion failures that
only appear under `nextTimerAsync`. Fix: in `nextTimerAsync` mode, `await` your async code and
rely on automatic advancement — remove explicit `vi.advanceTimers*` calls from the test body.

#### AP59 — `vi.mockObject()` Created Outside `beforeEach` and Reused Across Test Cases  [community]
**What:** Creating `vi.mockObject(service)` once at the `describe` block level (outside
`beforeEach`) and reusing the same mocked instance across all test cases.
**Why harmful:** After the first test case calls `mockedService.fetchUser.mockResolvedValue(...)`,
that implementation persists for all subsequent test cases in the suite. Test case 2 expects
`fetchUser` to return `undefined` (the default mock) but gets the value configured by test case
1 — identical to the shared mock state problem that `vi.clearAllMocks()` solves for individual
spies. Fix: call `vi.clearAllMocks()` (or `vi.resetAllMocks()`) in `afterEach`, or create a fresh
`vi.mockObject(service)` inside each `beforeEach`. The idiomatic pattern is `beforeEach` creation
plus `afterEach` clear.

### Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 20)  [community]

**Gotcha 57 — Trunk Webhook Subscriptions Create a New Flakiness Vector in CI**  [community]
Teams that configure Trunk's flaky test webhook subscriptions (to trigger Jira ticket creation
or Slack notifications on quarantine/resolution events) report a secondary flakiness source:
the webhook handler makes HTTP requests to external services inside the CI environment. If the
webhook destination is unreachable (Jira maintenance window, Slack rate limit), the CI step that
processes webhook events fails — unrelated to the test suite. Root cause: webhook handlers run
synchronously in some CI configurations, blocking the pipeline if they time out. Fix: configure
webhook delivery as fire-and-forget with a 2-second timeout, and never let webhook failures
propagate as test failures. Trunk's documentation recommends using the webhook `timeout` field
and a dead-letter queue for missed events.

**Gotcha 58 — `vi.setTimerTickMode('interval')` Produces Non-Deterministic Frame Counts Across Workers**  [community]
Teams using Vitest's worker-based parallelism discover that `vi.setTimerTickMode('interval', 16)`
does not produce consistent frame counts across workers. Worker A runs on a heavily loaded VM
core and advances only 4 frames in 100ms; Worker B runs on a free core and advances 7 frames.
The `interval` mode ties fake timer advancement to real wall-clock time — which varies with CPU
load. This makes `interval` mode inappropriate for assertions about exact frame counts in CI.
Fix: use `'manual'` mode with explicit `vi.advanceTimersByTime(16)` calls for frame-exact
assertions, or use `'nextTimerAsync'` when you only care that all frames eventually fire (not
the exact count).

**Gotcha 59 — FlakyDoctor LLM Repair Results Vary Per Run — Treat Output as Suggestion, Not Fix**  [community]
Teams evaluating FlakyDoctor for automated flaky test repair discover that running the tool twice
on the same flaky test case produces different patches on each run — the repository itself states
"results may vary when running multiple times due to non-determinism of LLMs." A patch that
compiles and passes locally may introduce a different category of flakiness (e.g., an ID fix
applied to an OD test case) on a second run. Fix: always run the generated patch through a 5×
test suite sweep before accepting, and use FlakyDoctor as a *suggestion generator* rather than
an automated fixer. Pair with the infection-model quarantine limit (Pattern 53) so the pipeline
is unblocked while patches undergo review.

### Quick Reference additions (Cycle 20)

| Symptom | Likely Root Cause | Pattern/Fix | Anti-Pattern to Avoid |
|---------|-------------------|-------------|----------------------|
| Async test hangs in CI — fake timers used, no explicit advance calls | Timer never auto-advances in async context | Pattern 114 (`vi.setTimerTickMode('nextTimerAsync')`) | AP58 (mixing `runAllTimers` with `nextTimerAsync`) |
| Frame count assertions differ between CI workers | `interval` mode tied to real wall-clock | Pattern 114 (`'manual'` mode + explicit `advanceTimersByTime`) | AP58 (`interval` mode in parallel worker tests) |
| Second test case gets previous mock's return value | `vi.mockObject()` not reset between tests | Pattern 115 (`vi.mockObject` in `beforeEach` + `vi.clearAllMocks()` in `afterEach`) | AP59 (describe-level `vi.mockObject` reuse) |
| Custom assertion failure stack trace points into helper internals | Missing `vi.defineHelper()` wrapper | Pattern 116 (`vi.defineHelper()` wraps each assertion helper) | Bare assertion functions without `defineHelper` |
| Trace has 200+ flat actions — impossible to locate flakiness source | No grouping in page object methods | Pattern 117 (`tracing.group()` in page objects; `test.step()` in test bodies) | Flat action lists in shared page objects |
| HAR for flakiness investigation has no timing data — root cause unclear | `mode: 'minimal'` used for diagnosis | Pattern 118 (`tracing.startHar` with `mode: 'full'` + `urlFilter`) | AP57 (`mode: 'minimal'` for diagnosis HAR) |
| LLM-generated flaky test patch introduces new flakiness after merge | FlakyDoctor used as automated fixer without verification | Pattern 119 (5× sweep before merge + ID/OD classification first) | Merging LLM patches without verification sweep |
| Trunk webhook failure breaks CI pipeline when tests are all green | Synchronous webhook handler times out | Gotcha 57 (fire-and-forget webhook with 2s timeout + dead-letter queue) | Synchronous webhook delivery without timeout |

### Pattern 120 — Vitest Global `restoreMocks` Config for Automatic Spy Restoration  [community]

Vitest's three global mock-lifecycle flags — `clearMocks`, `resetMocks`, and `restoreMocks` — are
the single highest-leverage configuration change for eliminating a whole class of shared mock state
flakiness. Without them, test case authors must remember to call `vi.clearAllMocks()`,
`vi.resetAllMocks()`, or `vi.restoreAllMocks()` in `afterEach`; the moment they forget, spy state
leaks to the next test case.

**The three flags and their exact semantics:**

| Flag | What it calls after each test | What it erases | What it preserves |
|------|-------------------------------|----------------|-------------------|
| `clearMocks` | `vi.clearAllMocks()` | Call history (`.mock.calls`, `.mock.results`) | Configured implementation |
| `resetMocks` | `vi.resetAllMocks()` | Call history + configured implementation | Nothing (returns `undefined`) |
| `restoreMocks` | `vi.restoreAllMocks()` | Spy on `vi.spyOn()` targets — restores the original descriptor | Original implementations restored |

**Why the order of destructiveness matters:** If test case A calls `vi.spyOn(service, 'fetch').mockReturnValue('cached')` and the test suite only has `clearMocks: true`, test case B sees `service.fetch` still mocked to return `'cached'` — the mock implementation persists. With `restoreMocks: true`, `service.fetch` is fully restored to its original implementation before test case B runs.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — recommended baseline for all projects
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // RECOMMENDED: enable all three for maximum isolation.
    // restoreMocks implies clearMocks and resetMocks behaviour — but
    // only for vi.spyOn spies, not for vi.fn() mocks.
    // Pair with resetMocks: true to also reset vi.fn() implementations.
    clearMocks: true,       // erase call history between tests
    resetMocks: true,       // reset vi.fn() return values between tests
    restoreMocks: true,     // restore vi.spyOn() originals between tests
  },
});
```

```typescript
// Demonstrating why restoreMocks alone is not enough for vi.fn() mocks:
import { vi, test, expect, describe } from 'vitest';

const fetcher = vi.fn();  // vi.fn() — NOT a spy on an existing function

describe('vi.fn() mock isolation', () => {
  // Without resetMocks: true, this leaks to test B
  test('test A — configures mock return value', () => {
    fetcher.mockReturnValue('from-cache');
    expect(fetcher()).toBe('from-cache');
  });

  test('test B — expects default mock (undefined)', () => {
    // With resetMocks: true → fetcher() returns undefined (correct)
    // Without resetMocks: true → fetcher() returns 'from-cache' (flaky!)
    expect(fetcher()).toBeUndefined();
  });
});
```

```typescript
// Demonstrating why restoreMocks: true is needed for vi.spyOn:
import { vi, test, expect, describe, afterEach } from 'vitest';

// Module with real implementation
const calculator = {
  add: (a: number, b: number) => a + b,
};

describe('vi.spyOn restoration', () => {
  test('test A — spies on add() and overrides it', () => {
    const spy = vi.spyOn(calculator, 'add').mockReturnValue(999);
    expect(calculator.add(1, 2)).toBe(999); // overridden
  });

  test('test B — expects original implementation', () => {
    // With restoreMocks: true  → calculator.add(1, 2) === 3 ✓
    // Without restoreMocks: true → calculator.add(1, 2) === 999 ✗ (FLAKY)
    expect(calculator.add(1, 2)).toBe(3);
  });
});
// With restoreMocks: true in vitest.config.ts, test B always passes.
// Without it, test B passes only if test A hasn't run yet.
```

**Warning — `restoreMocks` does not restore `vi.fn()` return values:**
A common misconception is that `restoreMocks: true` handles all mock cleanup. It only restores
the **original descriptor** on objects that were spied with `vi.spyOn()`. A standalone `vi.fn()`
has no original descriptor to restore — it needs `resetMocks: true` to clear its configured
implementation. Enable both `resetMocks` and `restoreMocks` in your baseline config.

### Pattern 121 — Playwright `page.addLocatorHandler()` for Overlay-Blocking Flakiness  [community]

UI overlays — cookie consent banners, sign-up dialogs, A/B test popups, and session-expired
modals — are the number-one source of intermittent Playwright test failures in production web
apps. They appear non-deterministically (depending on session age, A/B assignment, cookie state,
or server response timing) and block every subsequent action that requires an actionability check.
Without a systematic dismissal strategy, tests fail with `locator.click: Element is covered by
another element` or similar, and the failure is unreproducible locally where the banner never appears.

`page.addLocatorHandler()` (introduced in Playwright v1.42) addresses this by registering a
**persistent handler** that fires automatically before any actionability check, dismissing the
overlay without the test body needing to know when (or whether) it appeared.

```typescript
// conftest.ts / test setup — register once, handles all occurrences
import { test as base, BrowserContext, Page } from '@playwright/test';

async function registerOverlayHandlers(page: Page): Promise<void> {
  // Cookie consent banner — appears once per session, non-deterministically
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /cookie/i }),
    async (dialog) => {
      await dialog.getByRole('button', { name: /accept|agree/i }).click();
    },
    { times: 1 } // remove handler after first dismissal — banner only appears once
  );

  // A/B test signup modal — may appear 0-2 times per test session
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.locator('[data-testid="signup-modal"]'),
    async (modal) => {
      await modal.getByLabel('Close').click();
    }
    // No `times` limit — modal can reappear after navigation
  );

  // Session-expired overlay — dismissing it logs out; use conditional logic
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.locator('[data-testid="session-expired-overlay"]'),
    async () => {
      // Do NOT click "Continue" — re-login instead to preserve test state
      await page.goto('/login');
      await page.fill('[name="email"]', process.env.TEST_USER_EMAIL!);
      await page.fill('[name="password"]', process.env.TEST_USER_PASSWORD!);
      await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign In' }).click();
      await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
    }
  );
}

// Extend the base fixture to register handlers on every page
export const test = base.extend<{ page: Page }>({
  page: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await registerOverlayHandlers(page);
    await use(page);
  },
});
```

```typescript
// tests/checkout.spec.ts — test body is unaware of overlays
import { test, expect } from '../fixtures/overlay-handlers';

test('checkout flow completes without overlay interference', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');

  // If a cookie consent banner or A/B modal appears at ANY of these action
  // points, the handler fires automatically and dismisses it before proceeding.
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to checkout' }).click();
  await page.fill('[name="card-number"]', '4111111111111111');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByTestId('confirmation-number')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Critical limitation — handlers only fire during actionability checks:** If a cookie banner
appears but the next test step is an assertion (no actionability check), the handler does NOT
fire. The assertion may pass despite the banner covering the asserted element. To catch this,
add an explicit `await page.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded')` before assertion-only steps
in flakiness-sensitive flows, which triggers an actionability pass.

**Why the `times` option prevents handler accumulation flakiness:** Without `times: 1` on
once-per-session overlays, the handler remains registered forever. After the banner is dismissed
in test A, subsequent tests have a handler looking for a locator that will never appear. This is
harmless for most cases, but in large suites with 200+ test cases per worker, the locator check
overhead accumulates. Set `times: N` whenever you know the maximum occurrence count.

### Pattern 122 — Playwright `testConfig.failOnFlakyTests` as a Ratchet CI Gate  [community]

`testConfig.failOnFlakyTests` (Playwright v1.52+) exits the test run with a non-zero code when
any test case passes on retry after initially failing — i.e., when Playwright's own retry
mechanism classifies a test as "flaky" rather than "failed." Without this setting, a test that
fails on attempt 1 and passes on attempt 2 is reported as `passed` in CI, silently accumulating
flaky debt while engineers believe the suite is healthy.

The **ratchet workflow** combines `failOnFlakyTests` with the quarantine tag pattern to create a
self-balancing system: new flakiness is detected and blocked immediately; quarantined tests are
excluded from the gate so they do not block new PRs.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — production-recommended ratchet configuration
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Retry up to 2 times — allows detection of flakiness
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,

  // RATCHET GATE: if any test passes only on retry → exit non-zero
  // This turns flakiness from a warning into a blocking failure.
  // Only enable in CI — in dev, retries are disabled (retries: 0),
  // so this setting is irrelevant locally.
  failOnFlakyTests: !!process.env.CI,

  use: {
    // Capture trace for every retry to enable cross-attempt comparison
    trace: 'retain-on-failure',
  },
});
```

```typescript
// Using @flaky tag to exclude known-flaky tests from the ratchet gate
// (tests tagged @flaky are run separately, do not trigger failOnFlakyTests)

// playwright.config.ts — split projects: gated vs quarantine
export default defineConfig({
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,
  failOnFlakyTests: !!process.env.CI,

  projects: [
    {
      name: 'gated',
      // Only run non-flaky tests in the gate — quarantine excluded
      grep: /^(?!.*@flaky)/,
    },
    {
      name: 'quarantine',
      // Run quarantined tests separately — never gate the pipeline
      grep: /@flaky/,
      retries: 3,
      // failOnFlakyTests intentionally omitted — quarantine tests may be flaky by definition
    },
  ],
});
```

```bash
# CI workflow: run gated project; quarantine runs separately without blocking
# .github/workflows/test.yml

# Step 1: Run gated tests — blocks the pipeline if any new flakiness detected
npx playwright test --project=gated

# Step 2: Run quarantine separately — never blocks; provides tracking data
npx playwright test --project=quarantine || echo "Quarantine failures noted (non-blocking)"
```

**Why `failOnFlakyTests: true` without a quarantine split is dangerous:** If you enable
`failOnFlakyTests` without excluding quarantined tests, a known-flaky test that was quarantined
last sprint will block every PR this sprint — even though its flakiness was already accepted and
ticketed. The split-project pattern (gated vs quarantine) ensures the ratchet only gates on
*new* flakiness, not on already-accepted flakiness backlog.

**Interaction with `retries: 0` (local dev):** With `retries: 0` locally, no test ever gets
a retry, so no test is ever classified as "flaky" — `failOnFlakyTests` has no effect. This is
intentional: local dev gets clean pass/fail output; CI gets the ratchet gate. Never set
`retries > 0` for local runs if you want fast feedback from deterministic failures.

### Pattern 123 — Playwright `clock.setFixedTime()` vs `clock.install()` — Choosing the Right Time-Freeze Granularity  [community]

Playwright provides two distinct time-control approaches that are often confused, leading to
over-engineered tests and the "clock not advancing" class of flakiness:

- **`page.clock.setFixedTime(time)`**: Freezes `Date` at a specific instant. Does NOT fake
  `setTimeout` or `setInterval`. Use when you only need stable date strings in UI assertions —
  not when production code uses timers internally.
- **`page.clock.install({ time })`**: Fakes the full timer suite (`Date`, `setTimeout`,
  `setInterval`, `requestAnimationFrame`, `performance`). Requires explicit `clock.runFor()` or
  `clock.fastForward()` calls to advance time past timer callbacks. Use when production code
  has polling loops, delayed renders, or debounce/throttle logic.

The confusion between the two is the root cause of the "test hangs after using clock API"
class of flakiness: engineers use `clock.install()` when they only needed `setFixedTime()`, then
production code's `setTimeout` callbacks never fire (because the fake clock is frozen), leaving
the page in a loading state.

```typescript
// CORRECT: setFixedTime() for date-only assertions — timers still run
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('invoice date renders in user locale format', async ({ page }) => {
  // Freeze Date at 2026-03-15 so the "Created today" label is deterministic.
  // setTimeout/setInterval still run on real time — no hangs.
  await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2026-03-15T10:00:00.000Z'));

  await page.goto('/invoices/new');

  // The invoice creation date always renders as "Mar 15, 2026" regardless of when CI runs
  await expect(page.getByTestId('creation-date')).toHaveText('Mar 15, 2026');
});
```

```typescript
// CORRECT: clock.install() + clock.fastForward() for timer-dependent UI
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('session timeout warning appears after 25 minutes of inactivity', async ({ page }) => {
  // Must use install() here — production code uses setTimeout(showWarning, 25 * 60 * 1000)
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-03-15T10:00:00.000Z') });
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // fastForward fires timers at most ONCE per interval (not repeatedly for setInterval).
  // 24 minutes → no warning yet
  await page.clock.fastForward('24:00');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('session-warning')).not.toBeVisible();

  // Advance the final minute — warning fires
  await page.clock.fastForward('01:01'); // 1 min + 1 second buffer
  await expect(page.getByTestId('session-warning')).toBeVisible();
});
```

```typescript
// WRONG: clock.install() for a test that only needs a stable date
// This causes flakiness: production code's polling loop never advances
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('BAD EXAMPLE — hangs when production code polls', async ({ page }) => {
  // install() fakes setTimeout — any production polling is now frozen
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-03-15T10:00:00.000Z') });
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Production code does: setInterval(() => fetchStatus(), 5000)
  // Under install(), this interval NEVER fires — page stays in loading state
  // → test times out waiting for status indicators to appear
  await expect(page.getByTestId('status-indicator')).toBeVisible(); // HANGS
});

// FIX: use setFixedTime() for stable date, let real timers run
// await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2026-03-15T10:00:00.000Z'));
```

**`clock.pauseAt()` for mid-test time inspection:** Use `pauseAt()` to advance to a specific
moment and then pause — useful for testing time-sensitive UI state at an exact point
(e.g., "what does the UI look like at 11:59 PM on December 31?") without overshoot. After
inspection, call `clock.resume()` to let production timers continue.

**Scope limitation:** The clock controls time across the entire `BrowserContext` — all pages
and iframes share the same fake clock. If your test opens a popup window (e.g., OAuth) in a
separate page object, the popup's timers are also frozen under `clock.install()`. Close popups
before advancing the clock to avoid cross-page timer interactions.

### Pattern 124 — Vitest `detectAsyncLeaks` for Surfacing Hidden Timer and Promise Leaks  [community]

Vitest 4.1 introduced `--detect-async-leaks` (config: `test.detectAsyncLeaks: true`), which
uses Node.js `async_hooks` to track resources (timers, promises, event emitters) created during
a test case and reports any that have not resolved when the test ends. Leaked async resources
are one of the most insidious flakiness sources: they appear to be unrelated to the failing test
case because they execute asynchronously after the test completes, interfering with the *next*
test case's setup or assertions.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — enable async leak detection for CI and local dev
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // HIGHLY RECOMMENDED for any project with async code:
    // Surfaces leaks that cause flakiness in tests that run AFTER the leaky test.
    // Reports the exact source location of the leaked resource — zero guesswork.
    detectAsyncLeaks: true,

    // Pair with these for maximum isolation:
    clearMocks: true,
    resetMocks: true,
    restoreMocks: true,
  },
});
```

```typescript
// Example of a leaked timer causing downstream flakiness:
import { vi, test, expect, beforeEach } from 'vitest';

// BAD: leaking a timer that fires after the test ends
test('search debounce — timer leak example', async () => {
  const onSearch = vi.fn();

  function setupDebounce(fn: () => void, delay: number) {
    return setTimeout(fn, delay); // returns timer ID — caller must clear it
  }

  setupDebounce(onSearch, 1_000);
  // Test ends here WITHOUT clearing the timer.
  // The timer fires 1 second later — DURING the next test case's execution.
  // next test's onSearch mock is called unexpectedly → assertion mismatch.
  expect(true).toBe(true);
});

// WHAT detectAsyncLeaks reports:
// ✘ Async resource leaked in "search debounce — timer leak example"
//   Type: Timeout
//   Created at: test-debounce.ts:9:3 (setupDebounce call)
//   Status: Pending (timer not cleared before test ended)
//
// This surfaces EXACTLY which test leaked the timer and WHERE it was created.
```

```typescript
// FIXED: clear the timer in afterEach (or use vi.useFakeTimers)
import { vi, test, expect, afterEach } from 'vitest';

let activeTimer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | null = null;

afterEach(() => {
  if (activeTimer !== null) {
    clearTimeout(activeTimer);
    activeTimer = null;
  }
});

test('search debounce — timer properly cleaned up', async () => {
  const onSearch = vi.fn();

  activeTimer = setTimeout(onSearch, 1_000); // tracked for cleanup
  // ... test body ...
  expect(true).toBe(true);
  // afterEach runs clearTimeout — no leak
});

// Alternative: use vi.useFakeTimers() which prevents real timers from leaking
test('search debounce — fake timers prevent leaks entirely', async () => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  const onSearch = vi.fn();

  setTimeout(onSearch, 1_000); // fake timer — never fires in real time
  vi.runAllTimers(); // advance past the debounce
  expect(onSearch).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  vi.useRealTimers();
});
```

**Why `detectAsyncLeaks` is superior to `detectOpenHandles` (Jest):** Jest's `--detectOpenHandles`
reports open handles at the end of the *entire test suite* — too late to know which individual
test case caused the leak. Vitest's `detectAsyncLeaks` reports the leak immediately after the
leaking test case completes, with the exact source location from `async_hooks` stack frames.
This reduces debug time from "run each test in isolation to find the leaker" (30+ minutes) to
"read the error message" (30 seconds).

**Performance note:** `detectAsyncLeaks` uses `async_hooks` which adds a small overhead per
async operation (~3-7% slowdown on async-heavy suites in early benchmarks). Enable it in CI
and during local flakiness investigations; consider disabling it in hot-path performance-sensitive
test runs where timing matters.

### Anti-Patterns (Cycle 22)

#### AP60 — Enabling `restoreMocks: true` Without `resetMocks: true`  [community]
**What:** Setting only `restoreMocks: true` in `vitest.config.ts` and believing all mock state
is cleaned up between test cases.
**Why harmful:** `restoreMocks` only restores the original descriptor on `vi.spyOn()` targets.
Standalone `vi.fn()` mocks (created without `spyOn`) retain their configured `mockReturnValue`,
`mockImplementation`, and `mockResolvedValue` across test cases. A test suite with 40% `vi.fn()`
mocks and 60% `vi.spyOn()` spies will appear to be clean (because the spies are restored) while
silent `vi.fn()` state leaks cause intermittent assertion failures. Always pair `restoreMocks`
with `resetMocks` to cover both cases. The only reason to omit `resetMocks` is when you
intentionally share a configured `vi.fn()` implementation across a `describe` block — in that
case, scope the mock setup to `beforeEach` explicitly.

#### AP61 — Using `page.addLocatorHandler()` to Dismiss Overlays That Alter Navigation State  [community]
**What:** Registering a `page.addLocatorHandler()` handler that navigates the page (e.g.,
`page.goto('/login')`) as its dismissal action, and not accounting for the navigation in
subsequent test steps.
**Why harmful:** The handler fires mid-action, during an actionability check for a locator on
the *original* page. After the handler navigates to `/login` and back, the original locator's
context is stale — Playwright may retry the original action against DOM elements that no longer
exist, causing `strict mode violation` errors or stale element reference failures. Reserve
navigation-based handlers for session-recovery scenarios where the entire test flow must restart,
and ensure the test body accounts for the post-handler URL state. For non-navigation overlays
(cookie banners, modals), always prefer simple `.click()` dismissals that leave the page URL
unchanged.

#### AP62 — Enabling `detectAsyncLeaks` on a Test Suite With Intentional Background Workers  [community]
**What:** Turning on `detectAsyncLeaks: true` in a test suite that intentionally uses
`worker_threads`, `child_process`, or long-running async iterators that are expected to outlive
individual test cases.
**Why harmful:** `detectAsyncLeaks` uses `async_hooks` to track ALL async resources, including
intentional background workers. If your database connection pool, message queue consumer, or
WebSocket server is set up in a `beforeAll` fixture and intentionally lives across multiple test
cases, `detectAsyncLeaks` will flag it as a leak in every test case — generating hundreds of
false-positive leak warnings. The signal-to-noise ratio collapses. Fix: scope long-lived resources
to `beforeAll`/`afterAll` fixtures and verify they are correctly torn down at the suite level;
disable `detectAsyncLeaks` for suites that intentionally use cross-test shared connections, or
use Vitest's fixture `scope: 'file'` to ensure the resource lifecycle is explicit and reviewed.

---

### Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 22)  [community]

**Gotcha 60 — `restoreMocks: true` Breaks Tests That Reuse a Spy Variable Across Multiple `test()` Calls**  [community]
Teams enabling `restoreMocks: true` (a correct best-practice change) discover that tests which
declared `const spy = vi.spyOn(...)` at `describe` block scope begin failing: after the first
test case, `restoreMocks` restores the original descriptor — the spy variable is now a reference
to a non-spy function. Subsequent `spy.mockReturnValue(...)` calls in later tests silently succeed
(they reconfigure the original function's wrapper) but the spy is no longer intercepting calls.
The Vitest docs note this explicitly: "after calling `vi.restoreAllMocks()`, you cannot reuse
the old spy variable." Fix: move `vi.spyOn()` calls inside `beforeEach` so each test case gets
a fresh spy, or use the `{ spy: true }` mode of `vi.mockObject()` which is scoped per `beforeEach`
invocation by design.

**Gotcha 61 — `page.addLocatorHandler()` Execution Time Counts Against the Action Timeout**  [community]
Teams using `page.addLocatorHandler()` to dismiss complex overlays (e.g., multi-step cookie
consent flows with three buttons and an animation) discover that their E2E test cases start
timing out seemingly at random. The root cause: the handler's execution time is counted against
the timeout of the *triggering action*, not against a separate handler timeout. If the handler
takes 800ms (animation + button clicks) and the triggering action has a 1,000ms timeout, the
action has only 200ms left after the handler completes — often not enough. Fix: increase the
timeout on actions that are known to trigger slow handlers using `{ timeout: 10_000 }` on the
specific locator action, or simplify the handler to use `noWaitAfter: true` for the final dismiss
click to skip overlay-hide animation waiting.

**Gotcha 62 — Vitest `detectAsyncLeaks` Reports Leaks From Third-Party Dependencies, Not Your Code**  [community]
Teams enabling `detectAsyncLeaks` for the first time on an existing large codebase report that
the majority of initial leak warnings originate from third-party libraries (SDK initialization
in `beforeAll`, logger flushers, OpenTelemetry span processors) rather than from their own test
code. The `async_hooks` stack traces point into `node_modules`. Root cause: many SDKs create
async resources (timers, event emitters) as part of their initialization that they intentionally
do not clean up until process exit. Fix: use Vitest's `globalSetup` file to initialize and tear
down SDKs at the process level (outside test case scope), so their async resources are not tracked
per-test. Alternatively, add `setupFiles` teardown for known noisy libraries. Treat the initial
`detectAsyncLeaks` run as an audit pass: suppress library-origin leaks with targeted `afterAll`
cleanups while resolving all first-party leaks immediately.
