## Cycle 32 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 236 — Playwright `page.clock.install()` for Deterministic Date/Time in Browser Tests  [official]

Playwright v1.45+ ships `page.clock`, a full browser-level clock API that replaces brittle workarounds that inject a fake `Date` via `page.addInitScript()`. `page.clock.install()` intercepts `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `requestAnimationFrame`, and `performance.now()` in the page context. Unlike `page.addInitScript()` patches, the clock API survives page reloads and integrates with Playwright's auto-wait so that `page.clock.runUntil()` cooperates with pending network requests.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('subscription renewal banner shows 7 days before expiry', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install the clock BEFORE navigation so the fake Date is in place
  // from the first JavaScript evaluation on the page.
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-06-01T00:00:00Z') });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Advance time to 7 days before the hard-coded subscription expiry (2026-06-25).
  // The banner component uses Date.now() internally — no app code change needed.
  await page.clock.fastForward('18d'); // now 2026-06-19

  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /subscription renew/i })).not.toBeVisible();

  await page.clock.fastForward('5d'); // now 2026-06-24 — within 7-day window
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /subscription renew/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('1 day');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `page.clock.install()` must be called before `page.goto()` to intercept the initial page load's timer code. Calling it after navigation is undefined behaviour — timers already registered before clock installation are unaffected. See AP48 (previous cycle) for the specific failure mode.

**When NOT to use:** Integration tests that intentionally need real wall-clock time to validate TTL-based caches or JWT expiry in a live API. For those cases, inject a time parameter into your API call rather than manipulating the browser clock.

**Named alternative:** `vi.setSystemTime()` for Vitest unit tests that control `Date.now()` without a browser; `jest.useFakeTimers({ now: new Date(...) })` for equivalent Jest control in non-browser environments.

[official]

---

### Pattern 237 — Vitest `test.concurrent` With `expect.soft()` Batch Assertions for Parallel Stability  [official]

When a suite has many independent assertions about the same API response, running them in `test.concurrent` eliminates cumulative async setup overhead. Combining concurrent execution with `expect.soft()` (which accumulates failures instead of aborting on first mismatch) means one assertion failure reports ALL failing assertions in a single run — avoiding the serial "fix one, discover the next" debugging cycle that extends flakiness investigation.

```typescript
import { describe, test, expect, vi, beforeAll } from 'vitest';
import { fetchUserProfile } from '../src/api/user';

vi.mock('../src/api/user');

const mockProfile = {
  id: 'u-001',
  name: 'Ada Lovelace',
  role: 'admin',
  email: 'ada@example.com',
  createdAt: '2024-01-15T00:00:00Z',
};

describe.concurrent('UserProfile shape assertions', () => {
  beforeAll(() => {
    vi.mocked(fetchUserProfile).mockResolvedValue(mockProfile);
  });

  test('has correct id', async () => {
    const profile = await fetchUserProfile('u-001');
    expect.soft(profile.id).toBe('u-001');
    expect.soft(profile.id).toMatch(/^u-/);
  });

  test('has correct role and name', async () => {
    const profile = await fetchUserProfile('u-001');
    expect.soft(profile.role).toBe('admin');
    expect.soft(profile.name).toBeTruthy();
    expect.soft(profile.name.length).toBeGreaterThan(2);
  });

  test('has valid ISO timestamp', async () => {
    const profile = await fetchUserProfile('u-001');
    expect.soft(profile.createdAt).toMatch(/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T/);
    expect.soft(new Date(profile.createdAt).getTime()).not.toBeNaN();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `describe.concurrent` shares the same worker unless `pool: 'vmThreads'` is configured. If individual tests within the `concurrent` block mutate module-level state (e.g., re-assigning a `let` variable), race conditions between the concurrently-executing tests can produce non-deterministic assertion failures. Reserve `concurrent` for purely read-only or fully isolated tests.

**When NOT to use:** Tests that perform write operations on a shared database, shared in-memory store, or shared mock return value — concurrent access will produce interleaved mutations. Use `describe` (serial) or explicit per-test fixtures instead.

**Named alternative:** `describe` (default serial) for any state-mutating test group; Playwright's `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' })` for parallel E2E at the browser context level.

[official]

---

### Pattern 238 — MSW v2 `http.passthrough()` for Selective Real-Network Requests in Tests  [community]

In large Next.js or Remix test suites, MSW intercepts all HTTP by default. When a test legitimately needs a real request (e.g., a Next.js font preload or a CDN health-check that is not part of the feature under test), adding a `http.passthrough()` handler explicitly whitelists that URL pattern rather than disabling MSW entirely. This avoids the common flaky-test pattern of toggling MSW on and off between tests, which leaves a race window where the service worker is partially deregistered.

```typescript
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { http, HttpResponse, passthrough } from 'msw';

const server = setupServer(
  // Allow real requests to the Next.js font CDN — not under test.
  http.get('https://fonts.googleapis.com/*', () => passthrough()),

  // Allow real requests to the internal health endpoint.
  http.get('/api/health', () => passthrough()),

  // Mock the feature endpoint deterministically.
  http.post('/api/checkout', async ({ request }) => {
    const body = await request.json() as { items: string[] };
    if (body.items.length === 0) {
      return HttpResponse.json({ error: 'Cart is empty' }, { status: 400 });
    }
    return HttpResponse.json({ orderId: 'ord-test-001' }, { status: 201 });
  }),
);

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());
```

**Tradeoff:** Combining `passthrough()` for certain URLs with `onUnhandledRequest: 'error'` provides a tight net — any unhandled URL that is neither mocked nor explicitly passed through causes a test failure, making accidental real network calls visible immediately. However, if a new real dependency is added to the production code but not whitelisted in the test setup, all tests using that code path fail with "Unhandled request" — a signal, not noise.

**When NOT to use:** When running tests in a fully sandboxed CI environment with no external network access. In that scenario, `passthrough()` for external URLs will cause network errors. Use `HttpResponse.json(...)` mocks for every external call instead.

**Named alternative:** MSW `server.use(http.get(pattern, () => passthrough()))` per-test override for one-off passthrough needs; `nock.enableNetConnect(pattern)` for projects using nock.

[community]

---

### Pattern 239 — `AbortSignal.timeout()` for Deterministic Fetch Timeouts Without `setTimeout` Races  [official]

Tests that call `fetch()` inside a timeout wrapper using `Promise.race([fetch(url), new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(...), 5000))])` are fragile: the `setTimeout` fires on the fake timer clock if `vi.useFakeTimers()` is active, causing the timeout to trigger in 0 real milliseconds. `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` is handled by the native fetch implementation independently of the JavaScript timer queue, so fake timers do not interfere with it. This makes timeout tests deterministic whether or not fake timers are installed.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';

// Production code under test — uses AbortSignal.timeout instead of a manual
// setTimeout race to avoid fake-timer interference.
async function fetchWithTimeout(url: string, ms: number): Promise<Response> {
  return fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms) });
}

describe('fetchWithTimeout', () => {
  it('resolves when fetch completes within timeout', async () => {
    const mockFetch = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(
      new Response(JSON.stringify({ ok: true }), { status: 200 }),
    );
    vi.stubGlobal('fetch', mockFetch);

    const response = await fetchWithTimeout('https://api.example.com/data', 3000);
    expect(response.status).toBe(200);
    vi.unstubAllGlobals();
  });

  it('rejects with AbortError when signal fires', async () => {
    // Use an immediately-aborting signal to simulate a timeout without
    // relying on real time passage or fake timer advancement.
    const abortedSignal = AbortSignal.abort(new DOMException('Timeout', 'TimeoutError'));
    const mockFetch = vi.fn().mockRejectedValue(
      new DOMException('The operation was aborted', 'AbortError'),
    );
    vi.stubGlobal('fetch', mockFetch);

    await expect(
      fetch('https://api.example.com/data', { signal: abortedSignal }),
    ).rejects.toThrow('The operation was aborted');
    vi.unstubAllGlobals();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `AbortSignal.timeout()` is a browser/Node 18+ API. In Node 16 environments (some older CI images), the static method does not exist — tests will throw `TypeError: AbortSignal.timeout is not a function`. Always guard with a Node version check in CI pipelines or pin the test container to Node 18+.

**When NOT to use:** When the timeout logic itself is the unit under test — e.g., verifying that your wrapper correctly interprets the `AbortError` into a user-facing error message. In those cases, passing an explicitly pre-aborted `AbortSignal.abort()` signal gives more explicit control than `AbortSignal.timeout()`.

**Named alternative:** `AbortController` + `setTimeout` with `controller.abort()` for full manual control; `Promise.race` with a helper `sleep` function for environments that lack `AbortSignal.timeout`.

[official]

---

### Pattern 240 — Playwright `page.waitForResponse()` Predicate Before Click to Prevent Response-Race Assertions  [official]

A common flakiness root cause: a test clicks a button, then immediately asserts on the result that only appears after the network response completes. `page.waitForResponse()` started BEFORE the click creates a `Promise` that resolves only when the matching response is received. Awaiting both the click and the response-promise together via `Promise.all()` guarantees the assertion only runs after the UI has processed the response.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('submitting the create-user form shows the new user in the table', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/admin/users');

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add user' }).click();
  await page.getByLabel('Name').fill('Ravi Shankar');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('ravi@example.com');

  // Start waiting for the POST /api/users response BEFORE clicking Submit.
  // If we awaited the click first, the response might arrive before
  // waitForResponse() starts listening — a race that passes locally
  // (fast machine) but fails on slow CI runners.
  const [response] = await Promise.all([
    page.waitForResponse(
      (resp) => resp.url().includes('/api/users') && resp.status() === 201,
    ),
    page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click(),
  ]);

  const body = await response.json() as { id: string; name: string };
  expect(body.name).toBe('Ravi Shankar');

  // UI assertion: the new row is visible in the table.
  await expect(page.getByRole('row', { name: 'Ravi Shankar' })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `waitForResponse()` matches the FIRST response that satisfies the predicate during the Promise race. In tests that trigger multiple sequential API calls (e.g., create → fetch list), the predicate must be specific enough to avoid matching an earlier unrelated response. Use both URL pattern and status code in the predicate.

**When NOT to use:** When the action does not trigger a network request (pure client-side state transitions) — `waitForResponse()` will timeout. For client-side-only actions, use web-first assertions (`toBeVisible`, `toHaveText`) directly.

**Named alternative:** `page.waitForURL()` when the response causes a navigation; `page.waitForRequest()` when you need to assert on the outgoing request payload rather than the response.

[official]

---

### Pattern 241 — Vitest `vi.useFakeTimers()` With `shouldAdvanceTime: true` for Real-Time-Aware Code  [official]

Some production code under test reads `Date.now()` on every tick to compute elapsed time (e.g., a debounce, a polling loop, or an animation frame scheduler). If `vi.useFakeTimers()` is installed without `shouldAdvanceTime: true`, `Date.now()` is frozen at install time. The code sees zero elapsed time on every tick, producing incorrect output and flaky assertions. Setting `shouldAdvanceTime: true` causes the fake clock to advance with real wall-clock time while still being manually advanceable.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { createPollingWatcher } from '../src/polling/PollingWatcher';

describe('PollingWatcher — elapsed-time based back-off', () => {
  afterEach(() => {
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });

  it('doubles poll interval after first failure', async () => {
    // shouldAdvanceTime: true lets Date.now() return increasing values
    // so the watcher's elapsed-time calculation works correctly.
    vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true });

    const fetchFn = vi.fn()
      .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('network error'))
      .mockResolvedValue({ status: 'ok' });

    const watcher = createPollingWatcher(fetchFn, { intervalMs: 100 });
    watcher.start();

    // Advance past the first poll interval (triggers the failure).
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(150);
    expect(fetchFn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);

    // The watcher should have doubled the interval to 200 ms.
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(250);
    expect(fetchFn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);

    watcher.stop();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `shouldAdvanceTime: true` makes the clock tick with wall time, which introduces a small real-time dependency. On an extremely slow CI runner, the wall-clock advance may outpace `advanceTimersByTimeAsync()`, causing assertions to see more ticks than expected. For pure unit tests, prefer `shouldAdvanceTime: false` (default) and advance time manually to maintain full determinism.

**When NOT to use:** Tests that need the clock completely frozen to test a specific snapshot of time (e.g., verifying that a timestamp field is set to exactly the installed time). Use `vi.setSystemTime(new Date(...))` for pinning the clock to a fixed value.

**Named alternative:** `vi.setSystemTime()` for point-in-time Date mocking; `sinon.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ['Date', 'setTimeout'] })` for projects using sinon.

[official]

---

### Pattern 242 — Jest `--shard` With Consistent Hash Seed for Reproducible Shard Assignment  [official]

Jest's `--shard=N/M` splits test files across M parallel CI runners. Without a consistent seed, the hash function used to assign files to shards can vary between Jest versions or across environments with different file system ordering. A flaky test that only appears in certain shard combinations (due to a specific concurrency pattern or shared resource) disappears when the sharding assignment changes. Locking the shard seed via `--testSequencer` with a custom deterministic sequencer makes shard assignments reproducible and debuggable.

```typescript
// jest-sequencer.ts — custom TestSequencer that uses a deterministic hash
// to assign tests to shards consistently across environments.
import { Sequencer as DefaultSequencer, Test } from '@jest/test-sequencer';
import crypto from 'crypto';

export default class DeterministicSequencer extends DefaultSequencer {
  sort(tests: Test[]): Test[] {
    // Stable sort: SHA-256 of the relative test path, truncated to 8 hex chars.
    return [...tests].sort((a, b) => {
      const hashA = crypto
        .createHash('sha256')
        .update(a.path)
        .digest('hex')
        .slice(0, 8);
      const hashB = crypto
        .createHash('sha256')
        .update(b.path)
        .digest('hex')
        .slice(0, 8);
      return hashA.localeCompare(hashB);
    });
  }
}
// jest.config.ts: testSequencer: './jest-sequencer.ts'
// CI: jest --shard=1/4 --testSequencer=./jest-sequencer.ts
```

**Tradeoff:** A custom sequencer bypasses Jest's built-in "run slowest tests first" optimization that improves overall CI wall-clock time. Benchmark total run time before and after adopting a deterministic sequencer — if the slowest shard becomes significantly slower, add duration-based tie-breaking to the hash sort.

**When NOT to use:** Projects with fewer than ~20 test files where sharding overhead exceeds parallelism gains. Also avoid if tests genuinely have inter-shard dependencies (a design smell that should be fixed first).

**Named alternative:** Playwright's built-in `--shard` (already deterministic by file path hash); Vitest's `--shard` with `sequence.sequencer` config.

[official]

---

### Pattern 243 — Playwright `expect(page).toHaveURL()` With Regex for Navigation Race Prevention  [official]

After clicking a link or submitting a form that causes navigation, asserting on the resulting page content immediately can race with the navigation. `expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/expected-path/)` uses Playwright's web-first auto-wait — it retries until the URL matches the pattern, providing a navigation gate before further assertions without any `waitForNavigation()` or `waitForURL()` imperative call.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('login redirects to dashboard with welcome banner', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('user@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('correct-password');

  // Click submit — navigation to /dashboard will follow.
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();

  // Web-first assertion: retries until URL matches /dashboard.
  // This gates all subsequent assertions on navigation completion.
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/dashboard/);

  // Only runs after URL confirms navigation — no race condition.
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toHaveText('Welcome back');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('user-menu')).toBeVisible();

  // Verify no error banner appears (important negative assertion).
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).not.toBeAttached();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `toHaveURL()` with a regex matches partial URLs — `/dashboard` matches `/dashboard`, `/dashboard/profile`, and `/my-dashboard`. Use a more anchored regex like `/^.*\/dashboard$` or `expect(page).toHaveURL('https://app.example.com/dashboard')` (exact string) if path specificity matters.

**When NOT to use:** SPAs that manage route changes via `history.pushState()` without a real browser navigation — `toHaveURL()` still works (Playwright listens to the History API), but if the URL update is async and not coupled to the render, the URL may update before the component tree is ready. Add a subsequent `toBeVisible()` assertion on a key element.

**Named alternative:** `page.waitForURL(pattern)` for the imperative equivalent; `page.waitForNavigation()` (deprecated in favour of `waitForURL`) for older codebases.

[official]

---

### Pattern 244 — Vitest `globalSetup` Lifecycle for One-Per-Run Container Spin-Up  [official]

Integration tests that start a real database, Redis, or other container inside `beforeAll()` hooks incur container startup cost in every test file that uses the hook. With Vitest's `globalSetup`, the container starts once for the entire test run and teardown is guaranteed even on test failure. This eliminates the race condition where parallel test files fight over the same container port during simultaneous `beforeAll()` execution.

```typescript
// vitest.global-setup.ts
import { GenericContainer, StartedTestContainer } from 'testcontainers';

let pgContainer: StartedTestContainer;

export async function setup() {
  pgContainer = await new GenericContainer('postgres:16-alpine')
    .withExposedPorts(5432)
    .withEnvironment({
      POSTGRES_USER: 'test',
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: 'test',
      POSTGRES_DB: 'testdb',
    })
    .start();

  const host = pgContainer.getHost();
  const port = pgContainer.getMappedPort(5432);

  // Expose the dynamic port to all test files via process.env.
  process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL =
    `postgresql://test:test@${host}:${port}/testdb`;
}

export async function teardown() {
  await pgContainer?.stop({ timeout: 10_000 });
}

// vitest.config.ts: globalSetup: ['./vitest.global-setup.ts']
```

**Tradeoff:** `globalSetup` runs in the main Vitest process, not in worker threads. Code in `globalSetup` cannot import Vitest globals (`describe`, `expect`, etc.) and cannot use `vi` mock utilities. It is purely for infrastructure setup. For per-test database state isolation, combine `globalSetup` (container lifecycle) with `beforeEach` transaction rollback.

**When NOT to use:** Unit tests that should not have external infrastructure dependencies. Reserve `globalSetup` for integration/E2E test configurations. Having `globalSetup` in a shared `vitest.config.ts` used by unit tests will slow down unit test runs with unnecessary container startup.

**Named alternative:** `@testcontainers/ryuk` resource reaper for automatic container cleanup without explicit teardown; Docker Compose with a fixed port for simpler (non-dynamic) local setups.

[official]

---

### Pattern 245 — React Testing Library `waitFor()` With Single Assertion for Reliable Async UI Updates  [community]

Placing multiple assertions inside a single `waitFor()` callback causes subtle flakiness: if the first assertion passes but the second does not yet, `waitFor()` retries the ENTIRE callback. The first assertion re-runs (passing again), but the second still fails. On the next retry, if an intermediate render causes the first assertion to momentarily fail, `waitFor()` resets its internal state and restarts the timeout window — leading to an asymptotic retry loop that eventually times out rather than surfacing the real failing assertion. Use one assertion per `waitFor()`.

```typescript
import { render, screen, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { NotificationCenter } from '../src/components/NotificationCenter';
import { server } from '../src/mocks/server';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';

test('unread count badge decrements after marking notification as read', async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();

  server.use(
    http.get('/api/notifications', () =>
      HttpResponse.json([
        { id: 'n-1', message: 'PR approved', read: false },
        { id: 'n-2', message: 'CI passed', read: false },
      ]),
    ),
    http.patch('/api/notifications/:id', () =>
      HttpResponse.json({ success: true }),
    ),
  );

  render(<NotificationCenter />);

  // Wait for data load — single assertion per waitFor.
  await waitFor(() =>
    expect(screen.getByTestId('unread-badge')).toHaveTextContent('2'),
  );

  await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /mark PR approved as read/i }));

  // Separate waitFor for the decrement — avoids the combined-callback retry trap.
  await waitFor(() =>
    expect(screen.getByTestId('unread-badge')).toHaveTextContent('1'),
  );

  expect(screen.queryByRole('button', { name: /mark PR approved as read/i }))
    .not.toBeInTheDocument();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Using multiple `waitFor()` calls increases total assertion wait time in the worst case (each `waitFor` has its own timeout clock). If the assertion sequence must complete within a hard deadline, wrap each call in `waitFor(..., { timeout: 3000 })` to set per-assertion ceilings rather than relying on the global `asyncUtilTimeout`.

**When NOT to use:** When asserting that multiple values update simultaneously as part of a single atomic state transition (e.g., both a loading spinner disappearing AND the result appearing). In that case, a single `waitFor()` with both assertions is fine because they should all become true at the same render cycle.

**Named alternative:** `findByRole()` / `findByText()` as syntactic sugar for `waitFor(() => getBy...())` — equivalent semantics, more readable for single-element queries.

[community]

---

### Pattern 246 — Playwright `test.step()` With `box: true` for Flakiness-Isolated Step Reporting  [official]

Playwright v1.51+ supports `{ box: true }` on `test.step()`. A boxed step collapses all its children in the trace viewer into a single entry — only the step boundary is visible, not the individual sub-actions. This prevents "trace noise" where dozens of sub-actions obscure the root step that failed, speeding up flakiness diagnosis. Boxed steps also appear in HTML reporter output as a single collapsible unit rather than a flat list of actions.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

async function loginAsAdmin(page: Parameters<typeof test>[1]['page']): Promise<void> {
  await test.step('Login as admin', async () => {
    await page.goto('/login');
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('admin@example.com');
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('admin-secret');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/admin\/dashboard/);
  }, { box: true }); // Collapse all sub-actions in trace viewer.
}

test('admin can delete a user account', async ({ page }) => {
  await loginAsAdmin(page);

  await test.step('Navigate to user management', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Users' }).click();
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/admin\/users/);
  }, { box: true });

  await test.step('Delete target user', async () => {
    const targetRow = page.getByRole('row', { name: 'test-user@example.com' });
    await targetRow.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' }).click();
    await page.getByRole('dialog').getByRole('button', { name: 'Confirm' }).click();
    await expect(targetRow).not.toBeAttached();
  }, { box: true });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `box: true` option is only available in Playwright ≥ v1.51. If your team runs multiple Playwright versions across projects, guard this option with a version check or extract it into a shared helper that conditionally passes the option. Older Playwright versions silently ignore unknown `test.step()` options — no error is thrown, but the boxing is not applied.

**When NOT to use:** During active debugging of a flaky step where you need to see every sub-action. In that case, remove `box: true` temporarily to expose the full trace. `box: true` is a production CI optimisation, not a debugging tool.

**Named alternative:** `test.step()` without `{ box: true }` for standard step nesting; Playwright fixture composition for reusable multi-step login flows that do not need custom step naming.

[official]

---

### Pattern 247 — Vitest `vi.waitFor()` for Polling-Based Async Condition Assertions  [official]

For tests that check conditions that are not driven by an explicit Promise or event (e.g., a background process that writes to an in-memory store, a server-sent event handler that updates a class variable), `vi.waitFor()` polls the assertion callback with configurable interval and timeout. Unlike React Testing Library's `waitFor()`, Vitest's `vi.waitFor()` is runtime-agnostic and works in Node.js integration tests without a DOM renderer.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { EventDrivenCounter } from '../src/counters/EventDrivenCounter';
import { EventEmitter } from 'node:events';

describe('EventDrivenCounter — asynchronous increment', () => {
  let emitter: EventEmitter;
  let counter: EventDrivenCounter;

  beforeEach(() => {
    emitter = new EventEmitter();
    counter = new EventDrivenCounter(emitter);
    counter.start();
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    counter.stop();
  });

  it('increments count when 5 "tick" events are emitted', async () => {
    for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
      // Emit asynchronously — the counter processes events in microtask queue.
      setImmediate(() => emitter.emit('tick'));
    }

    // Poll until count reaches 5 — no explicit Promise to await.
    await vi.waitFor(
      () => expect(counter.count).toBe(5),
      { timeout: 2000, interval: 50 },
    );

    expect(counter.isRunning).toBe(true);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vi.waitFor()` uses real timers by default. If `vi.useFakeTimers()` is active in the test, `vi.waitFor()`'s internal polling interval is also fake — the condition will never be re-checked unless fake time is manually advanced inside the `waitFor` callback, resulting in a timeout. Either use `vi.waitFor()` with real timers or advance the clock inside the polling loop.

**When NOT to use:** When the condition update is driven by a Promise that can be directly awaited — `vi.waitFor()` adds unnecessary polling overhead. Use direct `await` on the Promise instead.

**Named alternative:** RTL `waitFor()` for DOM-bound async assertions; `page.waitForFunction()` in Playwright for browser-side condition polling.

[official]

---

### Pattern 248 — Playwright `page.addLocatorHandler()` for Automatic Interstitial Dismissal  [official]

Interstitial dialogs (cookie banners, session-expiry warnings, newsletter pop-ups) appear asynchronously and block interactions on the underlying page. Tests that hard-code a dismissal click before each action are fragile — if the interstitial does not appear (e.g., a feature flag is off in one environment), the dismissal click fails the test. `page.addLocatorHandler()` registers a handler that Playwright triggers automatically whenever the locator becomes visible, before retrying the blocked action — eliminating the need to predict when the interstitial appears.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  // Auto-dismiss cookie consent banner if it appears during any action.
  // Playwright retries the blocked action after the handler completes.
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /cookie consent/i }),
    async (dialog) => {
      await dialog.getByRole('button', { name: 'Accept all' }).click();
      // Wait for the dialog to detach before Playwright continues the blocked action.
      await expect(dialog).not.toBeAttached();
    },
  );

  // Auto-dismiss session-expiry modal if it appears.
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /session expired/i }),
    async (dialog) => {
      await dialog.getByRole('button', { name: 'Refresh session' }).click();
      await expect(dialog).not.toBeAttached();
    },
  );
});

test('user can complete checkout despite cookie banner', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/shop');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
  // Cookie banner may or may not appear here — handler dismisses it automatically.
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/checkout/);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `addLocatorHandler()` handlers run asynchronously between action retries. If the interstitial appears DURING an action (e.g., mid-type in a text field), Playwright may abort and retry the action — this can cause double-typing. Guard interactive handlers with `not.toBeAttached()` after the dismissal to ensure the overlay is fully gone before Playwright re-attempts the original action.

**When NOT to use:** When the interstitial contains important user-facing content that should be tested (e.g., a consent form). In that case, test the interstitial explicitly in a dedicated test rather than auto-dismissing it. Auto-dismissal masks untested UI paths.

**Named alternative:** `page.route()` to block the request that loads the interstitial; `test.beforeEach()` with an explicit navigation to a pre-consented URL via `storageState`.

[official]

---

### Pattern 249 — Vitest `pool: 'vmThreads'` for Full ES Module Isolation Between Test Files  [official]

The default `pool: 'threads'` shares the same V8 heap context between test files in a worker thread, relying on module cache clearing between files. Edge cases (native Node addons, global prototype mutations, `Symbol` identity checks) can leak between files even with module cache clearing. `pool: 'vmThreads'` runs each test file in a separate V8 `vm.Context`, providing the same isolation as separate processes but with lower startup cost than `pool: 'forks'`.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Full V8 context isolation — each test file gets its own vm.Context.
    // Use when: native addons, Symbol identity checks, prototype mutations.
    pool: 'vmThreads',

    poolOptions: {
      vmThreads: {
        // Increase heap per context for memory-intensive integration tests.
        memoryLimit: '512mb',
        // Reuse contexts for test files in the same module graph for performance.
        useAtomics: true,
      },
    },

    // Combine with --isolate for maximum per-test isolation (slower but safe).
    isolate: true,

    // Example: integration test files that use native SQLite bindings.
    include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
    exclude: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vmThreads` has a known incompatibility with some CommonJS modules that use `require.main === module` checks — the `vm.Context` changes the module identity, causing these checks to always return `false`. Audit native or legacy CJS dependencies before migrating from `threads` to `vmThreads`.

**When NOT to use:** Simple unit tests with no native addons and no global state mutations. The added startup cost per `vm.Context` (~20–50 ms) is wasteful for small isolated functions. Use the default `pool: 'threads'` for unit tests and reserve `vmThreads` for integration test suites.

**Named alternative:** `pool: 'forks'` for maximum compatibility (separate OS processes) at the cost of higher memory usage; `--isolate=false` for raw performance in zero-state-leak projects.

[official]

---

### Pattern 250 — Playwright Soft Assertions for Non-Blocking Multi-Field Form Validation Checks  [official]

When verifying a form's error state after invalid submission, asserting each error message with `expect()` stops the test at the first failing assertion — hiding the true scope of what broke. `expect.soft()` accumulates ALL failures and reports them together after the test body completes, giving a full picture of which validation messages are missing or incorrect without multiple re-runs.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('form shows all required-field errors on empty submit', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/register');

  // Submit without filling any fields.
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create account' }).click();

  // Soft assertions — all run regardless of individual failures.
  // A single re-run surfaces ALL missing/incorrect validation messages.
  await expect.soft(page.getByText('Name is required')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByText('Email is required')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByText('Password must be at least 8 characters')).toBeVisible();
  await expect.soft(page.getByText('You must accept the terms')).toBeVisible();

  // Hard assertion: the form must NOT have navigated away.
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/register/);

  // This line checks ALL accumulated soft failures — if any soft assertion
  // failed, the test fails HERE with a consolidated report.
  expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `expect.soft()` failures are accumulated in `test.info().errors` but do NOT stop test execution. If a later action depends on a soft-asserted element being present (e.g., clicking the error message to see a tooltip), the action will throw a hard error rather than a soft failure. Place any dependent actions after checking `test.info().errors.length`.

**When NOT to use:** Critical path assertions where a failure should halt the test immediately (e.g., confirming that the user is authenticated before testing features that require auth). Use hard `expect()` for gatekeeping assertions.

**Named alternative:** Vitest `expect.soft()` for equivalent batch-assertion semantics in unit tests; custom error accumulator pattern with `try/catch` for assertion libraries that lack soft-assertion support.

[official]

---

### Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 32)  [community]

**Gotcha 97 — Playwright `page.addLocatorHandler()` Fires on Hidden Matches, Blocking Unrelated Tests**  [community]
`page.addLocatorHandler()` uses the locator's default visibility matching — it fires whenever the locator BECOMES ACTIONABLE, not merely visible. If you add a handler for a `getByRole('dialog')` that matches a dialog present on the page in a non-visible state (e.g., `display: none` in an open shadow root), Playwright may still trigger the handler on pages where the dialog is conceptually absent. WHY this surprises teams: they assume "triggers when visible" means "only triggers when the user can see it," but Playwright's actionability includes elements in shadow DOM that are not rendered to screen. Always add a `page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Exact Name' })` name-anchor to the locator, or use `locator.filter({ hasNotText: '' })` to constrain the match.

**Gotcha 98 — Vitest `vi.mock()` With Factory Returning `undefined` Silently Passes — Real Module Used**  [community]
If a `vi.mock('../services/analytics', () => undefined)` factory returns `undefined` instead of an object, Vitest 3.x silently falls back to the real module rather than throwing. Tests that should be isolated from the analytics service call the real implementation, causing network errors in CI when the analytics endpoint is unreachable. WHY this is hard to detect: test assertions may still pass (if the analytics call is fire-and-forget), and the test only flakes when the network is slow enough to delay cleanup, leaving an unhandled Promise rejection in the next test's microtask queue. Always return an object from `vi.mock()` factories, even `{}` for fully silent mocks.

**Gotcha 99 — MSW `server.resetHandlers()` in `afterEach` Does Not Reset the Baseline Server Configuration**  [community]
`server.resetHandlers()` removes handlers added via `server.use()` during the test but PRESERVES the baseline handlers passed to `setupServer()`. If a baseline handler is accidentally stateful (e.g., a handler that uses a captured `let requestCount = 0` in the outer scope), the state persists across all tests even after `resetHandlers()`. WHY teams are confused: they assume `resetHandlers()` is a full server reset to the initial state. It is not — it only undoes `server.use()` overrides. To reset stateful baseline handlers, define them as factory functions called fresh in each test, or use `server.close()` / `server.listen()` in `beforeEach`/`afterEach` (expensive but fully clean).

**Gotcha 100 — Jest `fakeTimers` Clears `setImmediate` Callbacks, Breaking Node.js Streams in Tests**  [community]
`jest.useFakeTimers()` replaces `setImmediate` with a fake equivalent by default. Node.js readable streams rely on `setImmediate` to flush data asynchronously — when faked, stream data callbacks are never invoked unless fake timers are advanced. Tests that read a stream and assert on its output hang indefinitely under fake timers without `jest.runAllImmediates()`. WHY this is non-obvious: the stream appears to emit no data, leading teams to suspect a mock or encoding issue rather than a timer interaction. Fix: either call `jest.runAllImmediates()` after the stream write, or configure `jest.useFakeTimers({ doNotFake: ['setImmediate'] })` to preserve real `setImmediate` behaviour.

**Gotcha 101 — Playwright `storageState` Saved While Auth Cookies Are Still Being Written Captures Incomplete State**  [community]
`await page.context().storageState({ path: 'auth.json' })` captures cookies and localStorage at the moment of the call. If the application sets an auth cookie asynchronously (e.g., a `Set-Cookie` response from a background API call that the login page fires after the redirect), the cookie may not yet be in the context when `storageState()` runs. Tests that load `auth.json` in CI then start without the auth cookie and fail with a 401. WHY this races: the login page redirect resolves before all background requests complete. Fix: await `page.waitForResponse(resp => resp.url().includes('/api/session'))` (or the relevant background auth request) before calling `storageState()` to guarantee all cookies are written.

**Gotcha 102 — Vitest Snapshot Tests Flake When `toMatchSnapshot()` Receives OS-Dependent Formatting**  [community]
`expect(output).toMatchSnapshot()` captures the exact string. If the string contains file paths (e.g., error stack traces, source maps), the path separator differs between macOS/Linux (`/`) and Windows (`\`). Snapshots committed on macOS fail on Windows CI runners and vice versa. WHY this is intermittent: teams run tests locally on a consistent OS and never notice — the flakiness only appears when a new OS is added to the CI matrix or a Windows developer joins the team. Fix: normalise path separators before snapshotting (`output.replace(/\\/g, '/')`), or use `toMatchInlineSnapshot()` with a regex matcher for the path portion: `expect(error.stack).toMatch(expect.stringContaining('at fetchUser'))`.

### Quick Reference additions (Cycle 32)

| Symptom | Likely Root Cause | Pattern/Fix | Anti-Pattern to Avoid |
|---------|-------------------|-------------|----------------------|
| Date/time assertions flake between time zones in CI | `Date.now()` not controlled; CI runner uses UTC while dev uses local time | Pattern 236 (`page.clock.install()` before navigation, pinned to UTC) | Asserting on `toLocaleDateString()` output without pinned locale/timezone |
| Concurrent test assertions race on shared mock return value | `vi.mocked(fn).mockReturnValue()` mutated by concurrently-executing test | Pattern 237 (`describe.concurrent` only for read-only tests; isolate mutable mocks) | Using `mockReturnValue` in `beforeAll` for a concurrently-executed describe block |
| MSW handler "Unhandled request" error breaks tests after new API call added | Missing handler for new endpoint; `onUnhandledRequest: 'error'` catches it | Pattern 238 (`http.passthrough()` for non-test URLs; explicit mock for feature URLs) | Setting `onUnhandledRequest: 'warn'` — silently swallows missing handlers |
| `fetch()` inside test times out inconsistently with fake timers active | `setTimeout`-based timeout wrapper intercepted by fake timer clock | Pattern 239 (`AbortSignal.timeout()` — unaffected by fake timer queue) | `Promise.race([fetch(), new Promise(t => setTimeout(reject, 5000))])` with fake timers |
| Response assertion runs before API returns; passes on fast CI, fails on slow | Network request not awaited before DOM assertion | Pattern 240 (`Promise.all([page.waitForResponse(), click()])`) | `click()` then immediately `expect(result).toBeVisible()` |
| Polling-loop tests fail because `Date.now()` returns same value every call | Fake timers freeze `Date.now()` at install time | Pattern 241 (`vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true })`) | `vi.useFakeTimers()` default with elapsed-time-dependent production code |
| Flaky test only appears in specific CI shard combination | Non-deterministic shard assignment; file order varies by runner | Pattern 242 (custom `DeterministicSequencer` with SHA-256 hash sort) | Default Jest sequencer with `--shard` — assignment varies across environments |
| Assertions after form submit race navigation — pass locally, fail on slow CI | Navigation not awaited before content assertions | Pattern 243 (`expect(page).toHaveURL(/path/)` web-first navigation gate) | `click()` then immediately `getByRole('heading')` without URL assertion |
| Container startup in `beforeAll` causes port collision across parallel test files | Multiple files start container simultaneously; port 5432 already bound | Pattern 244 (`globalSetup` for single-run container lifecycle) | `beforeAll(() => startContainer())` in every integration test file |
| `waitFor()` with multiple assertions times out instead of failing cleanly | Second assertion in combined `waitFor()` callback fails; first re-runs on retry | Pattern 245 (one assertion per `waitFor()` call) | `waitFor(() => { expect(a); expect(b); })` — combined callback retry trap |

### Pattern 251 — Playwright `page.screencast` Streaming for Real-Time Flakiness Video Evidence  [official]

Playwright v1.59 introduced `page.screencast`, a real-time video streaming API that writes frames to a buffer as the test runs rather than archiving a video only on completion. Unlike `video: 'on'` in `playwright.config.ts` (which buffers and archives on test end), `screencast` makes frames accessible during execution. For flaky tests that hang and time out, the archived video is often incomplete or absent; the screencast API captures all frames up to the hang point.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { createWriteStream } from 'fs';
import path from 'path';

test('checkout flow — screencast for flakiness investigation', async ({ page }) => {
  // Start screencast before navigation so the full page load is captured.
  // Frames are written immediately to disk — no data loss on timeout or OOM kill.
  const screencastPath = path.join(
    test.info().outputDir,
    `screencast-retry${test.info().retry}.webm`,
  );
  const writeStream = createWriteStream(screencastPath);
  const screencast = await page.screencast();

  // Pipe each incoming frame chunk to disk immediately.
  screencast.on('data', (chunk: Buffer) => writeStream.write(chunk));

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByLabel('Card Number').fill('4111111111111111');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay Now' }).click();

  // This assertion is the flaky point — screencast captures all frames before the hang.
  await expect(page.getByTestId('order-confirmed')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 20_000 });

  // Stop the screencast and close the write stream.
  await screencast.close();
  await new Promise<void>((resolve) => writeStream.end(resolve));

  // Attach path to test result so Playwright HTML reporter links it.
  test.info().attachments.push({
    name: 'screencast',
    path: screencastPath,
    contentType: 'video/webm',
  });
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**

- **Use when:** A flaky test hangs mid-execution and the archived video (`video: 'on'`) is consistently empty or truncated. Screencast writes frames in real time, so partial runs are still useful.
- **Do NOT use when:** Running all tests in the full CI suite — the continuous frame write has higher disk I/O than archived video, and the webm files accumulate quickly. Scope it to a dedicated `flaky-investigation` Playwright project.
- **Alternative:** `trace: 'on'` with `live: true` (Pattern 83) captures DOM + network without video; use screencast when visual layout (CSS transitions, animations) is the suspected root cause.

[official]

### Pattern 252 — Vitest `test.extend` Lifecycle Hooks With Type-Aware Fixtures for Leak-Free DB Isolation  [official]

Vitest 4.0 added lifecycle hook support (`beforeEach`, `afterEach`) directly inside `test.extend` fixture definitions, with full type inference from the extended context. This eliminates the pattern of shipping raw database handles through fixtures and separately managing teardown in test bodies — the fixture now owns both setup and teardown with type-safe context access.

```typescript
// test-utils/db-fixture.ts
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres';
import { Pool } from 'pg';

interface DbFixture {
  db: ReturnType<typeof drizzle>;
  cleanup: () => Promise<void>;
}

// test.extend with lifecycle hooks: teardown is guaranteed even when test body throws.
export const test = baseTest.extend<DbFixture>({
  // db fixture: each test gets a fresh connection in a rolled-back transaction.
  db: async ({}, use) => {
    const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL! });
    const client = await pool.connect();
    await client.query('BEGIN');

    const db = drizzle(client as never);

    // yield to the test body — all writes run inside this transaction
    await use(db);

    // guaranteed teardown: always rolls back, even on test failure
    await client.query('ROLLBACK');
    client.release();
    await pool.end();
  },

  // cleanup helper: exposes a manual mid-test reset
  cleanup: async ({ db }, use) => {
    const cleanupFn = async () => {
      await db.execute('TRUNCATE TABLE test_events RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE');
    };
    await use(cleanupFn);
    // afterEach equivalent: runs after every test that uses this fixture
    await cleanupFn();
  },
});
```

```typescript
// checkout.test.ts — using the extended test fixture
import { test } from '../test-utils/db-fixture';
import { expect } from 'vitest';
import { OrderService } from '../src/services/OrderService';

test('creates order and writes event log entry', async ({ db, cleanup }) => {
  // db is a fresh in-transaction Drizzle instance — no rows from previous tests
  const svc = new OrderService(db);
  const order = await svc.create({ userId: 'user-1', amount: 4900 });

  expect(order.id).toMatch(/^order-/);
  // cleanup is available mid-test for specific isolation scenarios
  await cleanup();
  const events = await db.execute('SELECT * FROM test_events');
  expect(events.rows).toHaveLength(0);
  // After the test, the fixture's ROLLBACK runs automatically — zero DB state leakage.
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**

- **Use when:** Integration test suites that share a real PostgreSQL test instance and need per-test isolation without spinning up containers per test.
- **Do NOT use when:** Pure unit tests that mock all DB calls — the fixture overhead is wasted. Use `vi.mock()` instead.
- **Alternative:** `aroundEach` pattern (Pattern 67) for a more functional wrapping style without the `extend` boilerplate.

[official]

### Pattern 253 — Jest 30 `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` for Async ESM Singleton Reset  [official]

Jest 30 adds `jest.isolateModulesAsync()`, the async counterpart to `jest.isolateModules()`. It creates a sandboxed module registry for the duration of the callback, then restores the original registry. This is the correct fix for singletons that use async module-level initialization (e.g., a DB connection pool created via top-level `await`), which `jest.resetModules()` cannot safely reset without risking partially-initialized module state.

```typescript
// src/DatabasePool.ts — singleton with top-level await (common in ESM)
const pool = await createPool({ max: 10, idleTimeoutMs: 30_000 });

export async function query(sql: string, params: unknown[]): Promise<unknown[]> {
  return pool.query(sql, params);
}

export async function closePool(): Promise<void> {
  return pool.end();
}
```

```typescript
// DatabasePool.test.ts — per-test module isolation via isolateModulesAsync
import { describe, it, expect } from '@jest/globals';

describe('DatabasePool — ESM singleton isolation', () => {
  it('creates a fresh pool per isolated scope', async () => {
    await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
      // Inside this callback: fresh module registry — top-level await re-runs,
      // a NEW pool is created. Previous test pool connections cannot interfere.
      const { query } = await import('../src/DatabasePool');
      const result = await query('SELECT 1 AS n', []);
      expect(result).toEqual([{ n: 1 }]);
    });
    // Outside callback: original module registry is restored.
  });

  it('does NOT share pool state with previous test', async () => {
    await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
      // Brand-new module instance — pool starts fresh, no connection state from test 1.
      const { query, closePool } = await import('../src/DatabasePool');
      const result = await query('SELECT 2 AS n', []);
      expect(result).toEqual([{ n: 2 }]);
      await closePool();
    });
  });
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**

- **Use when:** ESM modules with top-level `await` initialization that produce singleton state (connection pools, config objects loaded from env, feature flag clients).
- **Do NOT use when:** Modules without async initialization — use `jest.isolateModules()` (synchronous variant) which is cheaper.
- **Alternative:** Vitest `vi.resetModules()` + dynamic `import()` inside test body for Vitest projects; dependency injection to avoid module-level singletons entirely.

[official]

### Pattern 254 — Playwright `locator.filter({ hasNot })` to Eliminate False-Positive Interstitial Matches  [official]

Playwright locators that match a broad role (e.g., `getByRole('alert')`) can hit hidden or detached DOM nodes from a previous navigation or animation frame, producing intermittent assertion failures because the locator matched the wrong element. The `filter({ hasNot })` option narrows the match by excluding elements that contain a specified sub-locator, making the assertion target unambiguous even when remnant nodes are present in the DOM.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('success banner appears after form submit — no stale error match', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/contact');
  await page.getByLabel('Name').fill('Alice');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('alice@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Message').fill('Hello from the contact form.');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send' }).click();

  // BAD (intermittent): getByRole('alert') may match a hidden server-error alert
  // left in the DOM from a previous test navigation or from a loading state.
  // await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Message sent!');

  // GOOD: filter out any alert that contains error language — the success alert
  // does not contain 'error' or 'failed', so only the success banner matches.
  const successAlert = page
    .getByRole('alert')
    .filter({ hasNot: page.getByText(/error|failed|invalid/i) });

  await expect(successAlert).toContainText('Message sent!');
  await expect(successAlert).toBeVisible();
});

// Advanced: combining filter() with and() for unambiguous multi-criteria locator
test('payment status badge is "Completed" not "Processing"', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/orders/ORD-001');

  // Narrow to status badges that: (a) are inside the order details section,
  // (b) do NOT contain "Processing" (which can linger during animation).
  const completedBadge = page
    .getByTestId('order-status-section')
    .getByRole('status')
    .filter({ hasNot: page.getByText('Processing') })
    .and(page.getByText('Completed'));

  await expect(completedBadge).toBeVisible({ timeout: 10_000 });
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**

- **Use when:** A broad locator intermittently matches the wrong element due to stale DOM nodes from navigation transitions, skeleton loaders, or CSS animation states.
- **Do NOT use when:** The element you want to exclude is visually the same role — use `getByTestId` or `aria-label` to directly target the correct element instead of filtering out the wrong one.
- **Alternative:** `locator.nth(0)` can work but is fragile to DOM order changes; `locator.last()` is equally fragile. Prefer semantic filters over positional ones.

[official]

### Pattern 255 — Vitest `--detect-async-leaks` Flag for Surfacing Orphaned Timers and Handles  [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduced the `--detect-async-leaks` CLI flag, which uses Node.js `async_hooks` to track all pending async resources at test boundaries. Any resource (timer, file handle, network socket, database connection) that is still open when a test ends is reported with a source location. This converts "test suite hangs and CI times out" into a deterministic failure with a stack trace pointing to the exact leak origin.

```typescript
// polling-service.test.ts — demonstrates leak detection in action
import { describe, test, expect, afterEach, vi } from 'vitest';
import { PollingService } from '../src/PollingService';

describe('PollingService — async leak detection', () => {
  let service: PollingService;

  afterEach(async () => {
    // Without this stop() call, the setInterval inside PollingService
    // remains active after the test ends.
    // --detect-async-leaks reports: "Leaked resource: Timeout (setInterval)
    //   created at PollingService.ts:14"
    await service?.stop();
  });

  test('polls every 500ms and accumulates results', async () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    const mockFetch = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ status: 'ok' });
    service = new PollingService(mockFetch, { intervalMs: 500 });
    service.start();

    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1_500);

    expect(mockFetch).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
    vi.useRealTimers();
    // If stop() is omitted in afterEach, --detect-async-leaks reports the setInterval.
  });

  test('reports correct poll count after explicit stop', async () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    const mockFetch = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ status: 'ok' });
    service = new PollingService(mockFetch, { intervalMs: 500 });
    service.start();
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(2_000);
    await service.stop(); // also called in afterEach — idempotent stop is safe

    expect(mockFetch).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(4);
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });
});
```

```bash
# CI: run with leak detection on integration tests only (overhead: ~15-30% slower)
npx vitest run --detect-async-leaks src/**/*.integration.test.ts

# Output when a leak is detected:
# FAIL src/services/polling-service.test.ts > PollingService > polls every 500ms
# AsyncLeakError: 1 async resource(s) leaked after test:
#   Timeout (setInterval) created at:
#     PollingService.ts:14:5  new PollingService()
#     polling-service.test.ts:22:14  test body
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**

- **Use when:** A CI suite intermittently hangs at the end (all tests green, worker never exits) — the classic symptom of a leaked timer or handle.
- **Do NOT use when:** Running in all-tests mode on every PR — `async_hooks` adds runtime overhead. Run nightly or on-demand for specific integration suites.
- **Alternative:** Jest `--detectOpenHandles` for the equivalent in Jest projects; `why-is-node-running` npm package for manual investigation without test-runner integration.

[official]

### Pattern 256 — Playwright `expect.poll()` for Eventually-Consistent External API State  [official]

`expect.poll()` wraps a custom async callback in Playwright's retry engine — it calls the callback repeatedly on an interval until the assertion passes or the timeout expires. This is the correct tool for asserting on state that Playwright cannot observe directly (background jobs, queue consumers, database writes triggered by a UI action) without resorting to `page.waitForTimeout()` or manual `while` loops.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('order placed via UI is visible in admin API within 8 seconds', async ({ page, request }) => {
  // Place the order through the UI.
  await page.goto('/shop');
  await page.getByTestId('product-buy-btn').first().click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Confirm Order' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Order placed!')).toBeVisible();

  // The admin API is updated by a background queue worker — it is NOT instant.
  // expect.poll() retries the API call every 500ms until the assertion passes.
  await expect.poll(
    async () => {
      const response = await request.get('/api/admin/orders?status=placed&limit=1');
      const body = await response.json();
      return body.total;
    },
    {
      intervals: [500, 1_000, 2_000], // backoff: 500ms → 1s → 2s → 2s remaining
      timeout: 8_000,                 // matches background worker SLA (8 seconds)
      message: 'Admin API did not reflect the placed order within 8 seconds',
    },
  ).toBeGreaterThan(0);
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**

- **Use when:** Asserting on state driven by background jobs, queue consumers, webhooks, or eventual-consistency propagation delays where direct locator assertions are not possible.
- **Do NOT use when:** State that IS directly observable via a Playwright locator — use `expect(locator).toBeVisible()` which has built-in auto-wait. `expect.poll()` skips Playwright's locator retry optimization.
- **Alternative:** `expect(locator).toBeVisible({ timeout })` for DOM state; `vi.waitFor()` (Vitest) for equivalent polling in unit/integration tests; `page.waitForFunction()` for custom JS-evaluated conditions.

[official]

### Pattern 257 — Jest 30 `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()` for `requestAnimationFrame`-Driven Flakiness  [official]

Jest 30 introduces `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()`, which advances fake timers exactly one frame boundary — resolving all pending `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks without requiring knowledge of the exact millisecond duration. Before this, tests had to call `jest.advanceTimersByTime(16)` — a magic number that breaks when the code uses `rAF` with a non-standard frame rate or when the frame duration constant is changed in production code.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';
import { AnimatedCounter } from '../src/AnimatedCounter';

describe('AnimatedCounter — rAF-driven animation', () => {
  beforeEach(() => { jest.useFakeTimers(); });
  afterEach(() => { jest.useRealTimers(); });

  it('increments display value on each animation frame', () => {
    const container = document.createElement('div');
    const counter = new AnimatedCounter(container, { from: 0, to: 100, durationMs: 1_000 });
    counter.start();

    // Before any frame: display shows starting value.
    expect(container.textContent).toBe('0');

    // Advance one frame boundary — ONE rAF callback fires.
    jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame();
    const valueAfterFrame1 = parseInt(container.textContent ?? '0', 10);
    expect(valueAfterFrame1).toBeGreaterThan(0);

    // Advance to mid-animation.
    for (let i = 0; i < 30; i++) jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame();
    const midValue = parseInt(container.textContent ?? '0', 10);
    expect(midValue).toBeGreaterThan(valueAfterFrame1);
    expect(midValue).toBeLessThan(100);

    // Advance past animation end — counter shows final value.
    for (let i = 0; i < 30; i++) jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame();
    expect(container.textContent).toBe('100');
  });

  it('calls onComplete callback after final frame', () => {
    const onComplete = jest.fn();
    const container = document.createElement('div');
    const counter = new AnimatedCounter(container, { from: 0, to: 10, durationMs: 100, onComplete });
    counter.start();

    // Fast-forward all frames.
    jest.runAllTimers();
    expect(onComplete).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  });
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**

- **Use when:** Testing any UI component that uses `requestAnimationFrame` for animation, scroll virtualization, or canvas rendering — the frame-boundary semantic is self-documenting and resilient to frame rate changes.
- **Do NOT use when:** Code that uses `setTimeout` exclusively and has no `rAF` dependency. Use `jest.advanceTimersByTime()` for that case to keep timing semantics explicit.
- **Alternative:** Vitest `vi.advanceTimersToNextFrame()` (Vitest 4.0+) for equivalent behavior; `sinon.clock.tick(16)` for projects using sinon fake timers.

[official]

### Pattern 258 — Playwright `page.pickLocator()` Interactive Mode for Selector Audit of Flaky Tests  [official]

Playwright v1.59 added `page.pickLocator()`, which enters an interactive element-picking mode where hovering highlights elements and prints the recommended locator. While primarily a developer tool, it has a direct QA application: auditing existing tests whose locator strings are suspected root causes of intermittent failures. Running `pickLocator()` in a headed test confirms whether the current locator is unique and whether a more resilient alternative exists.

```typescript
// locator-audit.spec.ts — run with --headed to use interactively
// npx playwright test locator-audit.spec.ts --headed --debug
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('interactive locator audit — identify fragile selectors causing flakiness', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Enter pick mode: hover over the element the flaky test targets.
  // Playwright prints the recommended locator to the terminal.
  // Exit pick mode: press Escape or click the element.
  // This is a developer diagnostic step, NOT an assertion.
  await page.pickLocator();
});
```

```typescript
// Production replacement: use the result of a pickLocator audit
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('downloads report PDF via accessible button', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/reports');

  // Before audit: page.locator('.reports-grid .col:nth-child(3) .download-btn')
  // After pickLocator audit: unambiguous role locator survives DOM restructuring.
  const downloadBtn = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Download Q1 Report' });

  await expect(downloadBtn).toBeEnabled();

  // Start waiting for download BEFORE click — never miss fast downloads.
  const [download] = await Promise.all([
    page.waitForEvent('download'),
    downloadBtn.click(),
  ]);
  expect(download.suggestedFilename()).toMatch(/Q1.*\.pdf$/i);
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**

- **Use when:** A test flakes with "strict mode violation" or "element not found" and you suspect the locator is matching multiple or zero elements after a DOM change.
- **Do NOT use when:** Automated CI runs — `pickLocator()` requires a headed browser and user interaction. It is a developer diagnostic tool only.
- **Alternative:** Playwright Trace Viewer's "Explore" panel for reviewing locators in a recorded trace; `locator.count()` assertion in a debug test to verify uniqueness before the main assertion.

[official]

### Pattern 259 — Vitest `expect.schemaMatching()` for Structural API Response Validation  [official]

Vitest 4.0 introduces `expect.schemaMatching()`, which validates a value against a Standard Schema v1 compatible schema (Zod, Valibot, ArkType). This replaces brittle `toEqual({ id: expect.any(String), ... })` object matchers that silently pass when the API returns unexpected extra fields or drops required fields. Schema-validated assertions catch structural drift — a common source of false-green tests where a field rename is not caught by loose matchers.

```typescript
// api-response.test.ts — schema-validated response assertions
import { test, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { z } from 'zod';
import { fetchUserProfile } from '../src/api/userProfile';

// Define the schema once — reuse across unit, integration, and contract tests.
const UserProfileSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().uuid(),
  email: z.string().email(),
  displayName: z.string().min(1),
  createdAt: z.string().datetime(),
});

describe('fetchUserProfile', () => {
  it('returns a structurally valid user profile', async () => {
    vi.stubGlobal('fetch', vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({
      ok: true,
      json: async () => ({
        id: 'a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890',
        email: 'alice@example.com',
        displayName: 'Alice',
        createdAt: '2026-01-15T09:30:00.000Z',
      }),
    }));

    const profile = await fetchUserProfile('a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890');

    // schemaMatching() validates the ENTIRE structure — not just sampled fields.
    // If the API renames 'displayName' to 'name', this fails immediately (not silently).
    expect(profile).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(UserProfileSchema));
  });

  it('fails fast when API response drops a required field', async () => {
    vi.stubGlobal('fetch', vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({
      ok: true,
      json: async () => ({
        id: 'a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890',
        email: 'alice@example.com',
        // displayName intentionally missing — schema violation
        createdAt: '2026-01-15T09:30:00.000Z',
      }),
    }));

    const profile = await fetchUserProfile('a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890');

    // Fails with a precise schema error, not a cryptic deep-diff message.
    await expect(
      () => expect(profile).toEqual(expect.schemaMatching(UserProfileSchema))
    ).toThrow(/displayName/);
  });
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**

- **Use when:** Testing API clients or contract boundaries where structural drift is a known flakiness risk (backend renamed a field, new required field added without coordinating with frontend tests).
- **Do NOT use when:** Asserting on internal implementation details where the structure is controlled entirely by the same codebase — simpler `toEqual({ ... })` matchers are sufficient.
- **Alternative:** Manual Zod `.parse()` call inside the test body; `expect.objectContaining()` for partial structural checks; MSW handler type safety for response shape enforcement at the network layer.

[official]

### Pattern 260 — Playwright `browser.bind()` + External CDP Client for Agentic Flakiness Observation  [official]

Playwright v1.59 added `browser.bind()`, which makes a launched browser available to external clients over a CDP connection. In a flakiness context, this enables an "observer" process — a separate script, LLM agent, or monitoring daemon — to attach to a running test's browser and inspect DOM state, network logs, or JavaScript errors without modifying the test code itself. This is particularly useful for low-frequency flaky tests (< 5% failure rate) that cannot be reliably instrumented via direct test changes.

```typescript
// observer-sidecar.ts — attaches to a bound browser and records diagnostic info
import { chromium } from '@playwright/test';

async function observeAndRecord(cdpEndpoint: string): Promise<void> {
  // Connect to the test's bound browser as an external observer.
  const browser = await chromium.connectOverCDP(cdpEndpoint);
  const [context] = browser.contexts();
  const [page] = context.pages();

  // Listen for console errors and page crashes in real time.
  page.on('console', msg => {
    if (msg.type() === 'error') {
      process.stderr.write(`[observer] console.error: ${msg.text()}\n`);
    }
  });
  page.on('pageerror', err => {
    process.stderr.write(`[observer] pageerror: ${err.message}\n${err.stack}\n`);
  });
  page.on('requestfailed', req => {
    process.stderr.write(
      `[observer] requestfailed: ${req.method()} ${req.url()} — ${req.failure()?.errorText}\n`
    );
  });

  process.stderr.write('[observer] Attached — monitoring for errors...\n');
  await browser.waitForClose();
}

// In a Playwright globalSetup or fixture:
// const cdpEndpoint = await browser.bind();
// observeAndRecord(cdpEndpoint); // fire-and-forget; output captured as CI artifact
```

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — configure the flaky investigation project for external observation
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [{
    name: 'flaky-observation',
    testMatch: '**/*.flaky.spec.ts',
    use: {
      // slowMo gives the observer process time to capture state between actions.
      slowMo: 100,
    },
  }],
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**

- **Use when:** A flaky test has a very low reproduction rate and you cannot modify the test code (vendored test, separate repo). The observer attaches externally with zero test code changes.
- **Do NOT use when:** Flaky tests with high reproduction rates — just add `page.on('pageerror')` directly to the test's `afterEach` (Pattern 111) for simpler instrumentation.
- **Alternative:** Playwright Trace Viewer with `live: true` tracing (Pattern 83) for full DOM+network capture without a separate process; `playwright-cli show` dashboard for real-time monitoring.

[official]

### Pattern 261 — Jest 30 `expect.arrayOf()` for Stable All-Elements API Array Assertions  [official]

Jest 30 adds `expect.arrayOf(value)` — a matcher that asserts every element of an array matches the given condition. The predecessor `expect.arrayContaining([expect.any(String)])` only verifies that AT LEAST ONE element of that type exists — it passes for empty arrays and for arrays with mixed types. `arrayOf` enforces that EVERY element matches, preventing false-green tests on responses that return fewer items than expected or return items of the wrong type.

```typescript
// api-list.test.ts — stable list-shape assertions with arrayOf
import { describe, it, expect, jest } from '@jest/globals';
import { listProducts } from '../src/api/products';

describe('listProducts', () => {
  it('returns an array where every element has a numeric price', async () => {
    jest.spyOn(global, 'fetch').mockResolvedValue({
      ok: true,
      json: async () => ([
        { id: 'p1', name: 'Widget', price: 9.99 },
        { id: 'p2', name: 'Gadget', price: 24.99 },
      ]),
    } as Response);

    const products = await listProducts();

    // arrayOf: EVERY element must satisfy the condition — catches partial responses.
    expect(products).toEqual(expect.arrayOf(
      expect.objectContaining({
        id: expect.any(String),
        name: expect.any(String),
        price: expect.any(Number),
      })
    ));
    // Also assert non-empty: arrayOf does NOT catch empty arrays.
    expect(products.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  });

  it('illustrates why arrayContaining is insufficient for all-elements checks', () => {
    // arrayContaining: passes for both — both have at least one string
    expect(['a', 'b', 'c']).toEqual(expect.arrayContaining([expect.any(String)]));
    expect(['a', 2, null]).toEqual(expect.arrayContaining([expect.any(String)])); // PASSES (bug!)

    // arrayOf: only the all-strings array passes — mixed-type array fails correctly
    expect(['a', 'b', 'c']).toEqual(expect.arrayOf(expect.any(String)));
    // expect(['a', 2, null]).toEqual(expect.arrayOf(expect.any(String))); // FAILS — correct!
  });
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**

- **Use when:** Asserting on list API responses where every element must conform to a schema — catches both structural drift and empty-response false-greens in a single assertion.
- **Do NOT use when:** Asserting on just a specific SUBSET of an array's items — use `expect.arrayContaining()` for "contains at least these" semantics.
- **Alternative:** Vitest `expect.arrayOf()` (equivalent API available via Vitest matchers); Zod `z.array(schema).parse()` for full schema enforcement.

[official]

### Pattern 262 — Vitest `vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true })` for Elapsed-Time-Dependent Code  [official]

The default `vi.useFakeTimers()` freezes `Date.now()` at the installation timestamp. Code that measures elapsed time by computing `Date.now() - startTime` gets `0` on every call, breaking polling loops, rate limiters, and debounce guards that rely on elapsed time to decide whether to fire. The `shouldAdvanceTime: true` option makes `Date.now()` advance with real wall-clock time while all scheduled callbacks (setTimeout, setInterval) still require explicit advancement.

```typescript
// src/RateLimiter.ts — uses elapsed time to enforce minimum call interval
export class RateLimiter {
  private lastCallTime = 0;

  isAllowed(minIntervalMs: number): boolean {
    const now = Date.now();
    const elapsed = now - this.lastCallTime;
    if (elapsed >= minIntervalMs) {
      this.lastCallTime = now;
      return true;
    }
    return false;
  }
}
```

```typescript
// rate-limiter.test.ts — shouldAdvanceTime: true makes Date.now() reflect elapsed time
import { vi, describe, test, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { RateLimiter } from '../src/RateLimiter';

describe('RateLimiter', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    // shouldAdvanceTime: true — Date.now() advances with real time.
    // Callbacks (setTimeout) still require explicit vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync() calls.
    vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true });
  });

  afterEach(() => { vi.useRealTimers(); });

  test('allows first call immediately', () => {
    const limiter = new RateLimiter();
    expect(limiter.isAllowed(1_000)).toBe(true);
  });

  test('blocks second call before minimum interval elapses', async () => {
    const limiter = new RateLimiter();
    limiter.isAllowed(1_000); // establishes lastCallTime

    // Advance clock by 500ms — Date.now() reflects this via shouldAdvanceTime.
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(500);

    // Only 500ms elapsed: below the 1000ms minimum — should be blocked.
    expect(limiter.isAllowed(1_000)).toBe(false);
  });

  test('allows call after minimum interval elapses', async () => {
    const limiter = new RateLimiter();
    limiter.isAllowed(1_000);

    // Advance past the minimum interval.
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1_100);
    expect(limiter.isAllowed(1_000)).toBe(true);
  });
});
```

**Use when / Do NOT use when / Alternative:**

- **Use when:** Code measures elapsed time via `Date.now()` subtraction (rate limiters, debounce, throttle, cache TTL) and you need fake timer control for callbacks while still having `Date.now()` advance naturally.
- **Do NOT use when:** Code does NOT depend on elapsed `Date.now()` — the default frozen `Date.now()` is simpler and eliminates all wall-clock race conditions.
- **Alternative:** `vi.setSystemTime(Date.now() + 1100)` for point-in-time Date advancement without continuous advancement; Playwright `page.clock.fastForward()` for browser-side equivalent.

[official]
