## Cycle 36 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns 281–295

---

#### Pattern 281 — `failOnFlakyTests` CI Gate: Promote Flakiness From Warning to Hard Failure

Playwright 1.52 introduced the `failOnFlakyTests` configuration option (and its `--fail-on-flaky-tests` CLI counterpart) that causes the entire test run to exit with a non-zero code whenever any test is classified as "flaky" — that is, it failed on the first attempt but passed on a subsequent retry. Without this option enabled, Playwright silently reports flaky tests in the summary but exits 0 if no tests ultimately failed all retries; this lets flaky tests slip through unnoticed on merge trains. Enabling `failOnFlakyTests` on CI makes flakiness a blocking signal just like a real failure, forcing engineers to address instability before merging. The gate is most powerful when combined with `retries: 2` in CI config — a passing-after-retry pattern is the exact definition of a flaky test that the gate catches. Locally, leave `failOnFlakyTests: false` to avoid blocking development iterations.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Only enable the hard-failure gate on CI
  failOnFlakyTests: !!process.env.CI,

  // CI needs retries to give tests a chance to demonstrate flakiness
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,

  use: {
    // Capture trace on all retries so you can compare passing vs failing run
    trace: 'on-all-retries',
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff note:** A strict gate accelerates flakiness remediation but can block legitimate urgent fixes if an unrelated flaky test is in the same suite. Mitigate by also enabling `--shard` so a flaky test in shard N does not block shard M deploys; or use `test.fixme()` as a short-term quarantine bypass while the flakiness is investigated.

[official]

---

#### Pattern 282 — Per-Project Worker Allocation: Isolate Heavy Workers From Lightweight Test Projects

Playwright 1.52 added `testProject.workers` allowing each project in a multi-project `playwright.config.ts` to declare its own worker count, while the global `workers` setting acts as a ceiling. Without per-project workers, all projects compete for the same worker pool — a slow browser-based E2E project occupies workers that unit-like API projects could use, or conversely a CPU-heavy API stress project starves the E2E project. With per-project workers you can declare `workers: 4` for the API project and `workers: 1` for the serialised authentication-flow project, and Playwright will honour those bounds without exceeding the global cap. This pattern is especially useful in CI environments where different test categories have very different resource profiles. Run `npx playwright test --list --project=<name>` to audit the worker assignment before committing.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  workers: process.env.CI ? 4 : undefined, // global ceiling

  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium-e2e',
      use: { browserName: 'chromium' },
      testMatch: 'tests/e2e/**/*.spec.ts',
      workers: 2, // never starve the others
    },
    {
      name: 'api-integration',
      use: { browserName: 'chromium' },
      testMatch: 'tests/api/**/*.spec.ts',
      workers: 4, // parallelise freely — no real browser needed
    },
    {
      name: 'auth-setup',
      use: { browserName: 'chromium' },
      testMatch: 'tests/setup/auth.setup.ts',
      workers: 1, // must run serially to write shared storageState
    },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff note:** Over-specifying workers per project can starve other projects if the global ceiling is too low — always model `sum(project.workers) <= global.workers + slack`. If workers is left undefined on a project, Playwright uses the global allocation without restriction.

[official]

---

#### Pattern 283 — `trace: 'retain-on-failure-and-retries'` — Compare Passing and Failing Traces for Flaky Root-Cause Analysis

Playwright's `retain-on-failure-and-retries` trace mode records a separate trace ZIP for every single test run — including retry attempts — and retains ALL of them when at least one attempt fails. With `on-first-retry` you only get one trace covering the first retry, which loses the "what was different between the retry that passed and the one that failed" signal. With `retain-on-failure-and-retries` you can open both the failing trace and the passing retry trace side-by-side in the Trace Viewer and compare network timing, DOM snapshots, and action sequences directly. This is the single most actionable workflow for diagnosing intermittent race conditions in E2E tests. The cost is disk: a 3-retry flaky test produces 3 ZIP files per run. Offset the cost with CI artifact retention policies (e.g. keep only the latest 10 runs).

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  retries: 2,
  use: {
    // Retain all retry traces when any attempt fails —
    // lets you load both the failed trace and the passing retry
    // in Trace Viewer and diff the network/action sequences.
    trace: 'retain-on-failure-and-retries',
  },
  reporter: [
    ['html', { open: 'never' }],
  ],
});

// In CI (GitHub Actions) — upload all trace artifacts:
// - name: Upload Playwright traces
//   if: failure()
//   uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
//   with:
//     name: playwright-traces
//     path: test-results/
//     retention-days: 7
```

**Tradeoff note:** This mode writes significantly more data than `on-first-retry`. For suites with hundreds of tests and `retries: 2`, disk usage can reach several GB per run. Use `--shard` to distribute and limit per-shard trace accumulation, and configure CI artifact expiry to 7 days.

[official]

---

#### Pattern 284 — `test.step()` Timeout: Detect Step-Level Hangs Without Waiting for Full Test Timeout

Before Playwright 1.50, a deadlocked step (waiting for a DOM element that will never appear, polling a queue that stalls) consumed the entire test timeout before failure. The new `timeout` option on `test.step()` lets you assign a tighter per-step budget so that a stalled step fails quickly and the test reports exactly which step timed out — a much stronger diagnostic signal than "test timed out after 30s". This is especially valuable for multi-step checkout or wizard flows where each step has a known SLA: if the "submit order" step takes longer than 5 seconds something is wrong, regardless of how much budget the overall test has remaining. The `TimeoutError` thrown by a timed-out step propagates normally — it triggers the `test.afterEach` cleanup and is recorded in the trace.

```typescript
// checkout.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('complete checkout flow with per-step budgets', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('navigate to cart', async () => {
    await page.goto('/cart');
    await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-summary')).toBeVisible();
  }, { timeout: 5_000 }); // must load within 5 s

  await test.step('enter payment details', async () => {
    await page.fill('[name="card-number"]', '4111111111111111');
    await page.fill('[name="expiry"]', '12/28');
    await page.fill('[name="cvv"]', '123');
  }, { timeout: 3_000 }); // filling should be near-instant

  await test.step('place order', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('order-confirmation')).toBeVisible();
  }, { timeout: 10_000 }); // payment gateway — allow 10 s
});
```

**Tradeoff note:** Setting overly tight step timeouts on steps that legitimately vary (e.g. third-party payment redirect) introduces false timeouts that look like flakiness. Only apply `timeout` where you have a firm SLA expectation. For slow-but-valid steps, use `test.slow()` to triple the overall test budget rather than per-step limits.

[official]

---

#### Pattern 285 — `test.step.skip()` as In-Progress Quarantine: Mark Known-Broken Steps Without Disabling the Whole Test

`test.step.skip()` (added in Playwright 1.50) executes the surrounding test but silently skips the marked step. This is strictly stronger than commenting-out or deleting the step because: (a) the rest of the test continues to run and validate neighbouring functionality; (b) the skipped step is visible in the HTML report with a "skipped" badge — preventing the "why was this step removed?" question in code review; and (c) it is trivially reversible — remove the `.skip` prefix to re-enable. Use it when a downstream service is temporarily broken in the staging environment but the rest of the checkout flow should still be validated. Never leave `test.step.skip()` in main for more than one sprint — treat it as a flakiness quarantine token that must be accompanied by a tracking issue.

```typescript
// payment-flow.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('payment flow — 3DS challenge step under investigation', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('initiate payment', async () => {
    await page.goto('/pay');
    await page.fill('[name="card-number"]', '4000002760003184'); // 3DS card
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();
  });

  // Temporarily quarantined: 3DS iframe intermittently absent on staging
  // Tracking: https://github.com/acme/app/issues/4821
  await test.step.skip('complete 3DS challenge', async () => {
    const challengeFrame = page.frameLocator('[title="3DS Challenge"]');
    await challengeFrame.getByRole('button', { name: 'Authenticate' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('payment-success')).toBeVisible();
  });

  // Still validates post-payment page state even when step is skipped
  await test.step('verify order appears in history', async () => {
    await page.goto('/orders');
    await expect(page.getByTestId('order-row').first()).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff note:** `test.step.skip()` skips silently from a correctness perspective — it does not make the test report as "failed" or "skipped" at the suite level; only the step badge changes. This means a test with a skipped critical step can pass CI, giving false confidence. Use a lint rule or CI check (`grep -r 'step.skip' tests/`) to fail the build if any skipped steps exist past a tracking-issue deadline.

[official]

---

#### Pattern 286 — Vitest `retry: { count, delay, condition }` Object — Surgical Retry That Only Fires on Infrastructure Errors

Vitest 4.1 promoted `retry` from a plain integer to an object supporting `count`, `delay`, and `condition`. Without a `condition`, retries fire on every error including `AssertionError` — which means a logic bug in your production code is silently retried and may produce a false green (the assertion passes on retry because of a race in the test itself). Providing `condition: /timeout|ECONNREFUSED|ECONNRESET/i` restricts retries to genuine infrastructure flakiness — network drops, container cold-starts, DB connection pool exhaustion — while letting logic-level `AssertionError`s fail immediately. The `delay` property adds a back-off between attempts, which is critical when retrying on `ECONNREFUSED` (the service may be mid-restart). Functions in `condition` only work in test files, not `vitest.config.ts`, because config is serialised for worker transport.

```typescript
// user-service.integration.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { fetchUser } from '../src/user-service';

describe('UserService integration', () => {
  test(
    'fetches user by id',
    {
      retry: {
        count: 3,
        delay: 500, // ms between attempts — allow container to settle
        // Only retry on infrastructure-level errors; fail fast on assertion errors
        condition: (error) => {
          const msg = error.message ?? '';
          return /ECONNREFUSED|ECONNRESET|socket hang up|timeout/i.test(msg);
        },
      },
    },
    async () => {
      const user = await fetchUser('usr_123');
      expect(user.id).toBe('usr_123');
      expect(user.email).toMatch(/@example\.com$/);
    }
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff note:** `condition` functions cannot appear in `vitest.config.ts` (serialisation constraint) — only inline in test files or in a `setup.ts` referenced by `setupFiles`. For project-wide infrastructure retry, use a RegExp condition in `vitest.config.ts`; for nuanced per-test logic use inline function conditions. Mixing both is valid: config provides the broad pattern, individual tests override with stricter conditions.

[official]

---

#### Pattern 287 — Playwright `toContainClass()` — Assert Individual CSS Classes Without Full-Class-String Fragility

Before Playwright 1.52, asserting that an element has a particular CSS class required `toHaveClass(/\bselected\b/)` (a regex with word-boundary anchors) or an exact match against the full class string — both are brittle when the component adds utility classes that come and go. The new `toContainClass('selected')` assertion checks only that the named class is present among all classes on the element, regardless of class order or additional classes. This eliminates an entire category of flakiness caused by CSS-in-JS libraries, Tailwind JIT purge ordering, or framework animation state classes that intermittently appear. The assertion is retry-aware and uses Playwright's web-first waiting semantics — it will wait up to `expect.timeout` for the class to appear, not just check a snapshot.

```typescript
// dashboard.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('active nav item has selected state', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  const dashboardLink = page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Dashboard' });

  // toContainClass waits for the class to appear and ignores other classes:
  // passes regardless of whether the element is
  // "nav-item selected text-blue-600 font-bold" or just "nav-item selected"
  await expect(dashboardLink).toContainClass('selected');
  await expect(dashboardLink).toContainClass('nav-item');

  // Navigate away — verify deselection
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Settings' }).click();
  await expect(dashboardLink).not.toContainClass('selected');
});
```

**Tradeoff note:** `toContainClass` only checks the `class` attribute on the element itself — it does not match `:class` bindings on shadow DOM hosts or check computed applied styles. For visual state that is driven by CSS custom properties rather than class toggling, use `toHaveCSS()` instead. `toContainClass` accepts an array of class names to assert multiple classes in one call: `toContainClass(['selected', 'nav-item'])`.

[official]

---

#### Pattern 288 — Playwright IndexedDB in `storageState`: Reuse Firebase Auth Tokens Across Tests Without Re-Login Flakiness

Before Playwright 1.51, `storageState` captured cookies and `localStorage`, but IndexedDB was excluded — meaning any authentication system that stored tokens in IndexedDB (notably Firebase Auth, which stores the refresh token in an IDB key starting with `firebase:authUser`) required a full login flow on every test, introducing network-dependent flakiness and slowness. Playwright 1.51 extended `storageState` to include IndexedDB. The global-setup authentication pattern now captures IDB state alongside cookies, saving it to `playwright/.auth/user.json`; individual test fixtures then restore it via `storageState`. The result: zero login network calls during test execution, eliminating the most common source of auth-related flakiness (stale session, rate-limited auth endpoint, token clock skew).

```typescript
// tests/global-setup.ts
import { chromium } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const authFile = path.join(__dirname, '../playwright/.auth/user.json');

async function globalSetup() {
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  const page = await browser.newPage();

  // Perform actual login — runs ONCE per test suite
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/login');
  await page.fill('[name="email"]', process.env.TEST_USER_EMAIL!);
  await page.fill('[name="password"]', process.env.TEST_USER_PASSWORD!);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
  await page.waitForURL('**/dashboard');

  // Save FULL state including IndexedDB (where Firebase stores the auth token)
  await page.context().storageState({ path: authFile });
  await browser.close();
}

export default globalSetup;

// playwright.config.ts — use the saved state in all tests
// use: { storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json' }
```

**Tradeoff note:** IndexedDB serialisation produces larger `storageState` files than cookie-only auth — Firebase tokens alone add ~4 KB, but some apps store large graph cache blobs in IDB that can reach megabytes. Check the file size after capture; if it exceeds ~500 KB, consider filtering which IDB databases to include (Playwright currently serialises all IDB stores in the context). Commit the auth file to a `.gitignore`'d path and regenerate in CI with a dedicated setup step.

[official]

#### Pattern 289 — Playwright Aria Snapshot Strict Child Matching with `/children` and `/url` — Prevent Phantom-Link Flakiness

Playwright 1.52 extended `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` with two new structural qualifiers: `/children: true` forces an exact child-count match (no unexpected elements allowed) and `/url: "https://..."` asserts a link's `href` value. Without `/children`, an aria snapshot passes even when the component renders extra hidden elements or adds debugging badges in staging — so "unexpected extra item" flakiness only surfaces at the wrong time. With `/children: true` the snapshot fails immediately when any unlisted child appears, and the diff shows exactly which element was added. The `/url` qualifier eliminates flakiness from redirect normalisation: a link that goes to `/checkout` in dev and `/checkout?ref=cta` in CI both match when you assert the base path with a regex.

```typescript
// navigation.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('main nav structure is stable across environments', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  const nav = page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Main' });

  // /children: true — fails if any unlisted item appears (e.g. debug badge)
  // /url — assert the actual href, not just the link text
  await expect(nav).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - navigation "Main":
      /children: true
      - link "Home":
        /url: "/"
      - link "Products":
        /url: "/products"
      - link "Pricing":
        /url: "/pricing"
      - link "Sign in":
        /url: "/login"
  `);
});
```

**Tradeoff note:** `/children: true` makes snapshots brittle when the component legitimately adds new nav items — every addition requires a snapshot update. Use it only for highly stable structural elements (main navigation, footer links) where unapproved additions should always fail the test. For dynamic lists (shopping cart, notification list) omit `/children` and assert only the presence of specific items.

[official]

---

#### Pattern 290 — Vitest `pool: 'forks'` + `singleFork: true` for Singleton-Process Integration Tests That Cannot Share a Worker

Vitest's default `threads` pool runs test files inside worker threads sharing the same OS process. Singleton resources that bind to OS-level state — TCP ports, Unix domain sockets, filesystem watchers via `fs.watch`, native bindings that store process-global handles — cannot be safely shared between concurrent worker threads even with module isolation. Switching to `pool: 'forks'` gives each test file its own OS process with a fully isolated address space. When you also have a test file that must own a port for the duration of an entire integration suite (e.g. a test HTTP server on port 3456), combine with `singleFork: true` inside that project to ensure all tests in the project run in one dedicated fork process sequentially, preventing port-binding races between files.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      // Fast unit tests — default threads pool is fine
      {
        test: {
          name: 'unit',
          include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
          pool: 'threads',
        },
      },
      // Integration tests that bind real TCP ports
      {
        test: {
          name: 'integration',
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
          pool: 'forks',
          poolOptions: {
            forks: {
              // All files in this project share a single fork process —
              // guarantees exclusive port ownership
              singleFork: true,
            },
          },
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff note:** `singleFork: true` serialises all integration test files — no parallelism within the project. Use it only when the resource being owned (port, IPC socket, GPU context) genuinely cannot be shared. For everything else, stay on `pool: 'forks'` without `singleFork` so files run in parallel across isolated OS processes.

[official]

---

#### Pattern 291 — Playwright `testResult.annotations` Per-Retry — Attach Diagnostic Context to Each Individual Retry Attempt

Playwright 1.52 exposed `testResult.annotations` on each test result object (previously only available at the test level). Each retry produces a separate `TestResult`, and you can now attach retry-specific annotations — URLs, server-side trace IDs, log snippets — directly to the attempt that produced them. Without per-retry annotations, a reporter showing "flaky test (passed on retry 2)" cannot explain why retry 1 and retry 2 had different outcomes. With per-retry annotations the HTML report and any custom reporter gain access to the correlation ID that links back to server logs for each specific attempt, enabling instant cross-system debugging.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — custom reporter that uses per-retry annotations
import type { Reporter, TestResult, TestCase } from '@playwright/test/reporter';

class CorrelationReporter implements Reporter {
  onTestEnd(test: TestCase, result: TestResult) {
    if (result.status === 'failed' || result.status === 'flaky') {
      // result.annotations contains annotations added during THIS retry only
      const correlationId = result.annotations.find(
        (a) => a.type === 'correlation-id'
      );
      if (correlationId) {
        console.log(
          `[${result.status.toUpperCase()}] ${test.title} ` +
          `(retry #${result.retry}) — server trace: ${correlationId.description}`
        );
      }
    }
  }
}

// In a fixture — attach the server trace ID for this specific attempt:
// test.info().annotations.push({
//   type: 'correlation-id',
//   description: response.headers['x-request-id'],
// });
```

**Tradeoff note:** Annotations added via `test.info().annotations.push()` during a test run appear on that attempt's `TestResult.annotations`. Annotations added via `test.info().annotate()` at the test level appear on ALL results for the test. Be explicit about which scope you need — per-retry annotations should use `push()` directly; test-wide annotations (e.g. JIRA issue link) should use the test-level API so they appear consistently regardless of which retry you are viewing.

[official]

---

#### Pattern 292 — HAR File Replay for Non-Deterministic Third-Party API Responses That Cause Snapshot Flakiness

Third-party APIs (weather, exchange rates, AI completions, analytics enrichment) return non-deterministic responses — the same request produces different payloads depending on time, region, or upstream state. Tests that assert on the full response body (or snapshots that include response data) flake whenever the upstream changes. Playwright's `page.routeFromHAR()` with `update: false` replays a pre-recorded network exchange, giving the test an exact copy of the response that was valid at recording time. Record with `update: true` in a dedicated refresh job (weekly CI run or on-demand), commit the HAR file, and all tests replay deterministically. The HAR matching is strict on URL and HTTP method; for POST bodies add `updateMode: 'minimal'` to record only the minimal matching set.

```typescript
// weather-widget.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const harPath = path.join(__dirname, 'fixtures/weather-api.har');

test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  // update: false — replay recorded responses; never hits real API
  await page.routeFromHAR(harPath, {
    update: false,
    url: '**/api.weather.example.com/**',
    // Fallback: if a URL isn't in the HAR, block it rather than letting
    // it hit the real endpoint and producing a non-deterministic response
    notFound: 'abort',
  });
});

test('weather widget renders temperature from API', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  // This assertion is now deterministic — uses HAR-replayed 22°C response
  await expect(page.getByTestId('temperature')).toHaveText('22°C');
});

// To refresh the HAR: PLAYWRIGHT_UPDATE_HAR=true npx playwright test weather-widget.spec.ts
```

**Tradeoff note:** HAR files can grow large for APIs with many unique URLs or large response bodies. Use `url` glob patterns in `routeFromHAR()` to scope replay to only the third-party domains you care about — let first-party API calls through normally. Rotate HAR files on a schedule to avoid asserting on stale domain formats.

[official]

---

#### Pattern 293 — Vitest `experimental.fsModuleCache` — Eliminate Cold-Start Flakiness in Large Monorepo Module Graphs

Vitest's `experimental.fsModuleCache` option persists the Vite module transformation cache to disk between test runs. In large monorepos with deep TypeScript module graphs, the first run after a `node_modules` reinstall or a clean CI workspace transforms thousands of files from scratch — and the CPU contention during this burst transformation frequently causes timeout-related flakiness as test workers start racing before their imported modules are fully initialised. Enabling `fsModuleCache` gives subsequent runs (including CI retry runs on the same runner cache volume) a warm module graph, dramatically reducing the burst transform window. The cache is keyed by source file content hash, so stale cache entries from old module versions are automatically invalidated.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    experimental: {
      // Persist transformed modules to disk — eliminates cold-start burst
      // that causes timeout flakiness on first run in CI
      fsModuleCache: true,
    },
    // Combine with a slightly higher test timeout on cold-start runs
    // (detectable via process.env.CI_COLD_START) as belt-and-suspenders
    testTimeout: process.env.CI_COLD_START ? 30_000 : 10_000,
  },
});

// In GitHub Actions — cache the Vitest module cache:
// - name: Cache Vitest module transforms
//   uses: actions/cache@v4
//   with:
//     path: node_modules/.vitest-cache
//     key: vitest-cache-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
```

**Tradeoff note:** The cache directory (`node_modules/.vitest-cache` by default) must be included in CI cache keys that include `package-lock.json` hash — otherwise a dependency update produces a stale cache that causes subtle test failures. Purge the cache directory when upgrading Vitest itself; the serialisation format is not stable across major versions.

[official]

---

#### Pattern 294 — Playwright `page.clock.setFixedTime()` After `goto()` for Date-Display Assertions Without Full Timer Takeover

`page.clock.install()` replaces the entire browser clock (Date, setTimeout, setInterval, requestAnimationFrame, performance.now) — which is correct for timer-driven tests but breaks any component that schedules animations or debounced handlers using `setTimeout`, causing them to stall waiting for fake-timer advancement. When your only goal is to freeze `Date.now()` / `new Date()` for date-display assertions (showing "Today", "5 days ago", "2026-05-14"), use `page.clock.setFixedTime()` instead. `setFixedTime()` only overrides `Date` and `performance.now` — it leaves `setTimeout` and `setInterval` on the real clock so animations and debounce continue to fire normally. Call it AFTER `goto()` so page scripts that run at navigation time use the frozen date.

```typescript
// billing.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('invoice due date shows "Overdue" when past today', async ({ page }) => {
  // Navigate first so page scripts run with the real clock
  await page.goto('/billing/invoice/INV-001');

  // Now freeze Date to a known value AFTER page scripts have executed.
  // setFixedTime only freezes Date — setTimeout/requestAnimationFrame
  // continue running normally so UI transitions do not stall.
  await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2026-01-20T10:00:00Z'));

  // Trigger the UI to re-evaluate the date (e.g. re-render or refresh)
  await page.reload();

  // Invoice due 2026-01-15 is now 5 days in the past — expect "Overdue" badge
  await expect(page.getByTestId('due-status')).toHaveText('Overdue');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('overdue-days')).toHaveText('5 days overdue');
});
```

**Tradeoff note:** If the component subscribes to a `setInterval` that updates its own relative-time display ("3 minutes ago" -> "4 minutes ago"), `setFixedTime` will not advance that interval — the display will be frozen at the initial render time even though the interval fires. In that case you need `page.clock.install()` + `page.clock.tick()` to advance time explicitly. Use `setFixedTime` for purely Date-constructor-based rendering; use `install()` + `tick()` for interval-driven relative-time components.

[official]

---

#### Pattern 295 — Vitest `globalsCleanup: 'on'` + `protectProperties()` for Polyfill-Safe Global Isolation

Vitest's `globalsCleanup: 'on'` automatically restores `globalThis` properties that were added or mutated during a test run, preventing global pollution from leaking between test files. Without it, a test that assigns `globalThis.fetch = vi.fn()` or installs a polyfill permanently mutates the shared environment for all subsequent files loaded in the same worker. However, `globalsCleanup: 'on'` must NOT restore globals that were intentionally installed at environment-setup time (TextEncoder, structuredClone, IntersectionObserver mock). The `protectProperties()` API registers a list of global property names that should be excluded from cleanup — treating them as permanent fixture state rather than per-test mutations.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    globals: true,
    // Automatically restore any globalThis mutations after each test file
    globalsCleanup: 'on',

    testEnvironmentOptions: {
      // These polyfills are installed in setupFiles and must survive cleanup
      protectProperties: [
        'TextEncoder',
        'TextDecoder',
        'structuredClone',
        'IntersectionObserver',
        'ResizeObserver',
        'matchMedia',
      ],
    },

    setupFiles: ['./test-setup/polyfills.ts'],
  },
});

// test-setup/polyfills.ts — installs globals once; they are protected from cleanup
import { vi } from 'vitest';

globalThis.IntersectionObserver = vi.fn().mockImplementation(() => ({
  observe: vi.fn(),
  unobserve: vi.fn(),
  disconnect: vi.fn(),
}));

globalThis.matchMedia = vi.fn().mockImplementation((query: string) => ({
  matches: false,
  media: query,
  addEventListener: vi.fn(),
  removeEventListener: vi.fn(),
  dispatchEvent: vi.fn(),
}));
```

**Tradeoff note:** `globalsCleanup: 'on'` does not reset properties that existed BEFORE the test ran — it only removes or reverts properties that were assigned during the test. This means a test that mutates an existing global property (e.g. `globalThis.fetch.mockReturnValue(...)`) must still manually restore it with `vi.restoreAllMocks()`. The combination of `globalsCleanup` and `restoreAllMocks` covers both categories: new property additions and mutations to existing properties.

[official]

---

### Community Gotchas (Cycle 36)  [community]

**Gotcha 114 — `failOnFlakyTests: true` Fires Even When Flakiness Is in a `test.describe.serial()` Retry — You Did Not Write Flaky Logic, But the Gate Fires Anyway**  [community]
`failOnFlakyTests` counts any test that passed after a retry as "flaky", including tests inside `test.describe.serial()` groups that are retried as a unit due to an unrelated sibling test failing. If test B in a serial group is a known-bad test (wrong env variable) and causes the group to retry, test A may fail the gate as "flaky" even though test A's logic is perfectly deterministic. WHY this surprises teams: they added `failOnFlakyTests` to catch actual unstable tests but now the gate fires on clean tests every time the serial group is retried. Fix: extract the known-bad test from the serial group, or use `test.fixme()` on the bad test to prevent it from triggering a group retry. The gate is correctly reporting a symptom — the root cause is the serial group retry mechanic surfacing flakiness from a sibling.

**Gotcha 115 — Vitest `retry: { condition: fn }` Works in Test Files But Config-Level `condition` Silently Falls Back to Unconditional Retry**  [community]
Vitest serialises `vitest.config.ts` into a JSON-compatible message sent to worker threads. Function values in the config are NOT serialisable and are silently dropped during worker initialisation. If you write `retry: { count: 3, condition: (err) => /timeout/.test(err.message) }` in `vitest.config.ts`, workers receive `retry: { count: 3 }` — the `condition` is absent and ALL errors are retried, including `AssertionError`. WHY this is dangerous: tests that fail due to real logic bugs silently pass on retry, masking production issues. The Vitest documentation notes functions work only "in test files" but the failure mode (silent drop, not error) is not prominently warned. Fix: put conditions in test files or `setupFiles`; use RegExp strings in config (they ARE serialisable).

**Gotcha 116 — `page.routeFromHAR()` With `notFound: 'fallthrough'` Allows Real Network Calls in CI — Response Differs From Local, Test Flakes**  [community]
`notFound: 'fallthrough'` (the default) passes unmatched HAR URLs through to the real network. In local development this is convenient — unrecorded endpoints hit real staging services and the test still works. In CI, the same unrecorded endpoint either fails (network egress blocked) or hits a different environment (CI uses a different staging URL via env vars) and returns a different response. The test passes locally and flakes in CI. WHY this is subtle: the HAR appears to be the source of truth, but a missing entry silently falls through to a live endpoint that varies by environment. Fix: always use `notFound: 'abort'` in CI and `notFound: 'fallthrough'` in local-dev by checking `process.env.CI`. Add a HAR validation step to CI that lists all unmatched routes.

**Gotcha 117 — Vitest `experimental.fsModuleCache` Survives a `vitest` Version Bump — Old Cache Entries Cause `Cannot find module` Flakiness on Next Run**  [community]
The `fsModuleCache` stores serialised module transform results keyed by source hash. When you upgrade Vitest to a version that changes its internal transform pipeline or module ID resolution, old cache entries produced by the previous version have incompatible internal IDs but still appear to be cache hits (same source hash). The result is `Cannot find module './src/utils'` or incorrect module exports that cause test-level `TypeError` failures — not on every test (some modules are freshly transformed), but on the subset whose old cache entries have stale ID references. WHY this is insidious: the failures look like import errors, not cache corruption. Fix: include the Vitest version in the CI cache key (`vitest-cache-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}-${{ hashFiles('node_modules/vitest/package.json') }}`), and run `rm -rf node_modules/.vitest-cache` as part of every Vitest major/minor upgrade migration script.

**Gotcha 118 — Playwright `toContainClass()` Passes When the Class Is Inherited Visually From a Parent, But `toContainClass` Only Checks the Element's Own `class` Attribute**  [community]
`toContainClass('text-red-500')` asserts the `class` attribute of the element returned by the locator — not any inherited or computed CSS property. If the design system applies `text-red-500` to a `<section>` wrapper and the locator targets a `<span>` inside that section, the text IS red visually due to CSS inheritance, but `toContainClass` fails because the `class` attribute on `<span>` does not contain `text-red-500`. Conversely, `toContainClass` CAN pass even when the element is visually hidden by a parent `display: none` — the class is present on the DOM node even when not rendered. WHY this causes flakiness: tests written assuming "class present = visually correct" pass on a happy path but fail when the design system moves the class up the DOM tree in a refactor. Fix: for visual assertions use `toHaveCSS('color', 'rgb(239, 68, 68)')` — it validates the computed style, not the raw class attribute.

### Pattern 296 — Playwright `test.abort()` From Route Handlers for Unrecoverable Test-Environment Violations  [official]

`test.abort(message)` immediately marks a running test as failed and stops execution. The key use-case for flakiness elimination is calling it from `page.route()` handlers when a test inadvertently hits a production endpoint, a shared staging resource, or a route that should never be called in test context. Without `test.abort()`, the route handler silently fulfills or blocks the request and the test continues — often passing when it should have been flagged as incorrectly wired. Surfacing the violation immediately via `test.abort()` prevents the "test passes in CI but corrupts shared staging state" class of flakiness.

```typescript
// tests/checkout.spec.ts — abort immediately when a route that MUST be mocked fires a real request
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout flow uses mocked payment API', async ({ page }) => {
  // GUARD: if the real payment endpoint is ever called, abort the test immediately.
  // This prevents silent state corruption in the shared payment provider sandbox.
  await page.route('**/api.stripe.com/**', (route) => {
    test.abort(
      'GUARDRAIL: test hit real Stripe API. ' +
      'All payment routes must be mocked via page.route() before triggering checkout.'
    );
    return route.abort();
  });

  // CORRECT mock: intercept the internal payment proxy (not the real Stripe endpoint)
  await page.route('**/api/payments/charge', (route) =>
    route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify({ chargeId: 'ch_test_001', status: 'succeeded' }),
    })
  );

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4111111111111111');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
  await page.getByLabel('CVV').fill('123');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();

  // If the Stripe guard fires above, test.abort() runs before we reach this line.
  // The test is reported as failed with the guardrail message — not a mysterious timeout.
  await expect(page.getByTestId('order-confirmation')).toBeVisible();
});

// Second test — demonstrates pattern for multiple forbidden routes
test('order history loads without hitting analytics provider', async ({ page }) => {
  // Guard against accidental analytics calls that depend on non-deterministic timing
  await page.route('**/segment.io/**', (route) => {
    test.abort('GUARDRAIL: Segment analytics called — should be blocked in test environment.');
    return route.abort();
  });

  await page.route('**/api/orders', (route) =>
    route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify({ orders: [{ id: 'ord-001', total: 4999 }] }),
    })
  );

  await page.goto('/orders');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('order-row')).toHaveCount(1);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `test.abort()` fails the test rather than warning — appropriate for shared-state guardrails, too aggressive for optional third-party analytics calls that may fire legitimately in some flows. Use `route.abort()` silently for truly optional external calls (tracking pixels, CDN font preloads); reserve `test.abort()` for calls that would mutate shared test infrastructure.

**When NOT to use:** Inside `beforeAll` hooks — `test.abort()` is only valid inside `test()` / `it()` bodies and fixtures. From `beforeAll`, throw a `new Error()` instead.

[official]

### Pattern 297 — Playwright `page.clock.fastForward()` for Inactivity-Timeout and Session-Expiry Flakiness  [official]

Tests that verify inactivity timeouts (e.g., "auto-logout after 15 minutes of no activity") or session-expiry UI cannot use real timers — a 15-minute wait in CI is both impractical and flaky due to runner load variability. `page.clock.fastForward(ms)` jumps the browser clock forward by the specified milliseconds, firing all pending `setTimeout` and `setInterval` callbacks in sequence, without any real time passing. The call is synchronous from the test's perspective and deterministic regardless of CI load.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('auto-logout modal appears after 15 minutes of inactivity', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install the clock BEFORE any page scripts run to intercept all timer registration.
  // Must be called before page.goto() — after navigation, timers may already be registered
  // with the real clock and will not be captured.
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-01-15T10:00:00Z') });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Confirm user is logged in before simulating inactivity.
  await expect(page.getByTestId('user-menu')).toBeVisible();

  // Fast-forward 14 minutes — no warning modal should appear yet.
  await page.clock.fastForward(14 * 60 * 1_000);
  await expect(page.getByTestId('inactivity-warning')).not.toBeAttached();

  // Fast-forward the remaining 1 minute (+ 1 second buffer) — warning modal should appear.
  await page.clock.fastForward(61 * 1_000);
  await expect(page.getByTestId('inactivity-warning')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByText(/your session is about to expire/i)).toBeVisible();

  // Dismiss the warning — session should be extended.
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /stay signed in/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('inactivity-warning')).not.toBeAttached();

  // Fast-forward another 15 full minutes — logout should now occur.
  await page.clock.fastForward(15 * 60 * 1_000 + 1_000);
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/login/);
});

test('subscription renewal reminder appears 30 days before expiry', async ({ page }) => {
  // Set a fixed date at exactly 31 days before subscription expiry.
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z') });
  await page.route('**/api/user/subscription', (route) =>
    route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      body: JSON.stringify({ expiresAt: '2026-02-01T00:00:00Z', plan: 'pro' }),
    })
  );

  await page.goto('/account');
  // At day 0 (Jan 1) — no reminder; 31 days remain.
  await expect(page.getByTestId('renewal-banner')).not.toBeAttached();

  // Jump to exactly 30 days before expiry — reminder should now appear.
  await page.clock.fastForward(1 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1_000);
  await page.reload();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('renewal-banner')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('renewal-banner')).toContainText('30 days');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `page.clock.install()` intercepts ALL browser-side timers — including ones used by third-party libraries (analytics debounce, scroll lazy-loading, A/B test schedulers). If the SPA depends on any timer-driven UI initialization, advance the clock in small increments via `page.clock.tick()` rather than a single large `fastForward()` to avoid skipping UI state transitions. Use `page.clock.setFixedTime()` (Pattern 294) when you only need to freeze `Date.now()` without intercepting timers.

[official]

### Pattern 298 — Playwright `tracing.startHar()` / `stopHar()` for Post-Hoc Network Flakiness Investigation  [official]

Playwright v1.60 exposed HAR recording as a first-class tracing API via `tracing.startHar()` and `tracing.stopHar()`. Unlike `page.routeFromHAR()` (which replays a pre-recorded HAR), this pattern records a HAR during a live test run and saves it as a test artifact. The HAR captures every request URL, method, status, headers, body, timing, and redirect chain — the complete network picture that is lost with standard `trace: 'on-first-retry'`. When a test fails with an ambiguous 401 or a 503, the HAR artifact provides the exact sequence of network events without requiring a manual repro.

```typescript
// fixtures/har-recording.ts — auto-use fixture for HAR capture on failure
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

export const test = base.extend<{ harRecording: void }>({
  harRecording: [
    async ({ context }, use, testInfo) => {
      const harOutputPath = path.join(
        testInfo.outputDir,
        `network-${testInfo.title.replace(/\s+/g, '-')}.har`
      );

      // Start HAR recording for this test's browser context.
      // url filter: only capture requests to our own API — skip CDN/font/analytics noise.
      await context.tracing.startHar(harOutputPath, {
        url: /\/api\//,   // capture only API-pattern requests
        content: 'omit',  // omit large response bodies to keep HAR size manageable
      });

      await use();

      // Stop and save the HAR. The artifact is attached regardless of pass/fail.
      await context.tracing.stopHar();

      // Attach to the test report — visible in HTML reporter on any failure.
      await testInfo.attach('network-har', {
        path: harOutputPath,
        contentType: 'application/json',
      });
    },
    { auto: true },
  ],
});

// tests/checkout.spec.ts — inherits auto-use HAR fixture
test('completes checkout and receives order confirmation', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('buyer@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4111111111111111');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();

  // If this assertion flakes (e.g., intermittent 503 on /api/orders), the HAR artifact
  // in the test report shows the exact request that failed — no manual repro needed.
  await expect(page.getByTestId('order-confirmation')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 10_000 });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** HAR files include request headers which may contain auth tokens. Use `content: 'omit'` and review HAR sanitisation before committing them to artifact storage shared with external parties. Do not enable HAR recording globally for large suites — target it at integration/E2E tests where network diagnosis is valuable.

**When NOT to use:** Unit tests with fully mocked network (MSW/`vi.mock()`). HAR recording requires a real `BrowserContext` — it is only applicable in Playwright E2E test suites.

[official]

### Pattern 299 — Vitest `aroundEach` Hook for Guaranteed Pre/Post Symmetry in DB Transaction Tests  [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduced `aroundEach` and `aroundAll` hooks that wrap test execution in a single generator function, ensuring setup and teardown are co-located and the teardown runs even if the test throws. The primary use-case over `beforeEach`/`afterEach` is database transaction tests: the transaction `BEGIN` and `ROLLBACK` are structurally coupled — if `ROLLBACK` in `afterEach` is accidentally removed or runs out of order due to a hook exception, the DB state leaks between tests. With `aroundEach`, the `yield` point is the test execution, and code after `yield` always runs.

```typescript
// test-utils/db-around.ts — reusable aroundEach wrapper for DB transaction isolation
import { aroundEach } from 'vitest';
import { getTestDb } from './db-client';

/**
 * Registers an aroundEach hook that wraps each test in a BEGIN/ROLLBACK transaction.
 * Call once per describe block to apply to all tests below it.
 * Unlike beforeEach/afterEach, teardown (ROLLBACK) runs even if the test throws.
 */
export function withTransactionRollback(): void {
  aroundEach(async function* () {
    const db = await getTestDb();

    // BEGIN — every test starts in a fresh transaction.
    await db.query('BEGIN');
    try {
      // Yield control to the test. The test sees the DB with BEGIN applied.
      yield;
    } finally {
      // ROLLBACK always runs — even if test.fn throws. Zero state leakage.
      await db.query('ROLLBACK');
      db.release();
    }
  });
}

// orders.integration.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { withTransactionRollback } from '../test-utils/db-around';
import { OrderRepository } from '../src/repositories/OrderRepository';
import { getTestDb } from '../test-utils/db-client';

describe('OrderRepository — DB integration', () => {
  // Register the aroundEach hook for this describe block only.
  withTransactionRollback();

  it('creates an order and returns the generated ID', async () => {
    const db = await getTestDb();
    const repo = new OrderRepository(db);

    const order = await repo.create({
      userId: 'user-test-001',
      items: [{ sku: 'SKU-A', qty: 2, price: 1500 }],
    });

    expect(order.id).toMatch(/^ord-/);
    expect(order.status).toBe('pending');

    const rows = await db.query('SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id = $1', [order.id]);
    expect(rows.rowCount).toBe(1);
    // After this test: ROLLBACK — the row above never reaches committed state.
  });

  it('throws when SKU does not exist in inventory', async () => {
    const db = await getTestDb();
    const repo = new OrderRepository(db);

    await expect(
      repo.create({ userId: 'user-test-002', items: [{ sku: 'NONEXISTENT', qty: 1, price: 0 }] })
    ).rejects.toThrow('SKU not found');
    // Even after a thrown error, ROLLBACK still runs via the finally block.
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `aroundEach` runs in the Vitest worker process. It does NOT wrap across worker process boundaries — tests using `pool: 'forks'` get a separate OS process per test file, but the transaction must be in the same process as the test code. Ensure your DB connection is initialized inside the generator, not as a module-level singleton.

**Named alternative:** `beforeEach`/`afterEach` with `try/finally` in `afterEach`; Playwright fixture teardown `use()` pattern (which uses the same generator semantics under the hood).

[official]

### Pattern 300 — Playwright Locator Stability Audit Using ARIA Roles for Fragile-Selector Migration  [community]

Tests that use positional CSS selectors (`ul > li:nth-child(3) > button`) or class-based selectors (`[class*="btn-primary"]`) break intermittently when designers add, remove, or reorder DOM elements. An audit script that enumerates interactive elements and categorizes their locator stability — HIGH (ARIA role + accessible name), MEDIUM (`data-testid`), LOW (CSS selector or XPath) — identifies the fragile selectors before they cause flakiness. Running this audit as a pre-merge CI check on test file changes surfaces new fragile selectors at authoring time.

```typescript
// scripts/audit-test-locators.ts — static analysis of test files for fragile selectors
// Run: npx ts-node scripts/audit-test-locators.ts tests/
import * as fs from 'fs';
import * as path from 'path';
import { glob } from 'glob';

interface LocatorRisk {
  file: string;
  line: number;
  locator: string;
  stability: 'high' | 'medium' | 'low';
  reason: string;
}

// Patterns indicating LOW-stability locators (high flakiness risk)
const LOW_STABILITY_PATTERNS: Array<{ re: RegExp; reason: string }> = [
  { re: /nth-child\(/g,          reason: 'positional nth-child — breaks on DOM reorder' },
  { re: /nth-of-type\(/g,        reason: 'positional nth-of-type — breaks on DOM reorder' },
  { re: /\.locator\('[^']*:nth/g, reason: 'CSS nth pseudo-class in locator string' },
  { re: /getByText\('[\w\s]{1,4}'\)/g, reason: 'very short text selector — ambiguous match' },
  { re: /\.locator\('(?:div|span)\./g, reason: 'generic element + class selector — brittle' },
];

// Patterns indicating HIGH-stability locators (low flakiness risk)
const HIGH_STABILITY_PATTERNS: Array<RegExp> = [
  /getByRole\(/,
  /getByLabel\(/,
  /getByTestId\(/,
  /getByPlaceholder\(/,
  /getByAltText\(/,
];

async function auditDirectory(dir: string): Promise<LocatorRisk[]> {
  const files = await glob(`${dir}/**/*.{spec,test}.ts`);
  const risks: LocatorRisk[] = [];

  for (const file of files) {
    const content = fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf-8');
    const lines = content.split('\n');

    lines.forEach((line, index) => {
      for (const { re, reason } of LOW_STABILITY_PATTERNS) {
        if (re.test(line)) {
          risks.push({
            file: path.relative(process.cwd(), file),
            line: index + 1,
            locator: line.trim().slice(0, 100),
            stability: 'low',
            reason,
          });
        }
        re.lastIndex = 0; // Reset global regex state
      }
    });
  }

  return risks;
}

auditDirectory(process.argv[2] ?? 'tests').then((risks) => {
  if (risks.length === 0) {
    console.log('Locator audit passed — no fragile selectors detected.');
    process.exit(0);
  }

  console.error(`Found ${risks.length} low-stability locator(s) — high flakiness risk:`);
  risks.forEach(({ file, line, locator, reason }) => {
    console.error(`  ${file}:${line}  [${reason}]`);
    console.error(`    ${locator}`);
  });
  process.exit(1);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Static analysis misses runtime-constructed locators (`page.locator(\`[data-id="${id}"]\`)`) and cannot determine whether a `getByText()` call is genuinely ambiguous without running the test against a real browser. Use as a first-pass gate to prevent obviously fragile patterns; supplement with Playwright's built-in locator highlight in `npx playwright codegen` for complex cases.

[community]
