### Pattern 301 — Vitest `vi.defineHelper()` for Stack-Trace-Accurate Custom Assertion Wrappers  [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduced `vi.defineHelper()`, which wraps a function so that test failure stack traces point to the call site in the test body, not to the line inside the helper. Before this, custom assertion wrappers (`assertUserShape()`, `expectValidOrder()`) caused confusing "Error at helpers/assertions.ts:23" traces — engineers had to mentally map back to where the helper was called. With `vi.defineHelper()`, the trace shows the exact test file line that called the helper, drastically reducing triage time for intermittent failures in shared assertion utilities.

```typescript
// test-utils/assertions.ts — custom assertion helpers wrapped with vi.defineHelper()
import { vi, expect } from 'vitest';

interface Order {
  id: string;
  status: 'pending' | 'confirmed' | 'shipped' | 'delivered';
  total: number;
  items: Array<{ sku: string; qty: number }>;
}

// WITH vi.defineHelper() — stack trace points to the TEST LINE that called assertValidOrder()
export const assertValidOrder = vi.defineHelper(function assertValidOrder(
  order: unknown
): asserts order is Order {
  // All expect() calls here report failures at the caller's call site, not here.
  expect(order, 'order must be an object').toBeTypeOf('object');
  expect(order).not.toBeNull();
  const o = order as Partial<Order>;
  expect(o.id, 'order.id must match /^ord-/').toMatch(/^ord-/);
  expect(
    ['pending', 'confirmed', 'shipped', 'delivered'],
    'order.status must be a valid status'
  ).toContain(o.status);
  expect(o.total, 'order.total must be positive').toBeGreaterThan(0);
  expect(o.items, 'order.items must be non-empty array').toBeInstanceOf(Array);
  expect(o.items!.length, 'order.items must have at least one item').toBeGreaterThan(0);
});

export const assertApiResponse = vi.defineHelper(function assertApiResponse(
  response: { status: number; body: unknown }
): void {
  expect(response.status, 'API response must be 2xx').toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(200);
  expect(response.status, 'API response must be 2xx').toBeLessThan(300);
  expect(response.body, 'API response body must not be null').not.toBeNull();
});

// order-service.test.ts — test using the helper
import { describe, it } from 'vitest';
import { assertValidOrder, assertApiResponse } from '../test-utils/assertions';
import { OrderService } from '../src/OrderService';

describe('OrderService', () => {
  it('creates a valid order', async () => {
    const result = await OrderService.create({
      userId: 'user-001',
      items: [{ sku: 'WIDGET-A', qty: 2 }],
    });
    // Stack trace on failure: "order-service.test.ts:18" — not "assertions.ts:12"
    assertValidOrder(result);
    assertApiResponse({ status: 201, body: result });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vi.defineHelper()` requires Vitest 4.1+. In older versions, use `expect.extend()` to register custom matchers (they also point to the caller's call site). The `vi.defineHelper()` approach is preferable for assertion FUNCTIONS (not matchers) because it works with TypeScript's `asserts` narrowing keyword. See Gotcha 121 — async helpers do not benefit from `vi.defineHelper()` stack injection.

[official]

---

### Pattern 302 — Vitest `detectAsyncLeaks: true` for Surfacing Timer and Handle Leaks Before They Cascade  [official]

`detectAsyncLeaks: true` in Vitest 4.1 uses Node.js async hooks to track every async resource (timers, network handles, file descriptors, worker threads) created during a test and reports any that remain active when the test ends. Without this flag, a leaked `setInterval` in test A fires during test B's execution and corrupts B's assertion mocks — this is reported as B's failure, not A's leak. With `detectAsyncLeaks`, the leak is reported immediately after test A with the exact source location of the leaked resource.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — enable async leak detection
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Report any timer, handle, or async resource that outlives its test.
    // Requires Vitest 4.1+. Uses Node.js async_hooks — minor performance overhead.
    detectAsyncLeaks: process.env.CI === 'true',

    // Pair with these for complete isolation:
    clearMocks: true,
    resetMocks: true,
    restoreMocks: true,
  },
});

// Example: demonstrating leak detection output
import { vi, test, expect } from 'vitest';

// BAD — this test leaks a polling interval that fires during subsequent tests.
// detectAsyncLeaks reports: "Async resource leaked in 'user status polling — leaking version'"
// Type: Timeout | Created at: example.test.ts:11
test('user status polling — leaking version', () => {
  const onChange = vi.fn();
  // This interval is NOT cleared — it fires every 100ms after this test ends.
  // Without detectAsyncLeaks, the next test's mock gets called unexpectedly.
  setInterval(() => onChange('update'), 100);
  expect(onChange).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  // Missing: return handle; then clearInterval(handle) in afterEach
});

// GOOD — properly cleaned up; no leak reported.
test('user status polling — fixed version', () => {
  const onChange = vi.fn();
  const interval = setInterval(() => onChange('update'), 100);
  expect(onChange).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  clearInterval(interval); // Cleanup before test exits — leak detector reports nothing.
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `detectAsyncLeaks` uses Node.js `async_hooks`, which adds CPU overhead to each async operation. On suites with 10,000+ tests using heavy async I/O, enable it in CI only (`process.env.CI === 'true'`). Some third-party libraries create intentional long-lived async resources — suppress specific known-safe resource types if false positives occur.

[official]

---

### Pattern 303 — Jest `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` for Top-Level `await` Singleton Reset  [official]

Jest 30 added `jest.isolateModulesAsync()`, the async counterpart to `jest.isolateModules()`. It is required when a module uses top-level `await` (ES2022 module initialization) to create a singleton (database pool, cache client, external API connection). `jest.resetModules()` synchronously clears the module registry but does not wait for async module initialization to complete — re-importing a top-level `await` module after `resetModules()` gives back a partially-initialized instance, which causes intermittent `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` that look like flakiness.

```typescript
// src/db/pool.ts — module with top-level await singleton (ES2022)
export const pool = await (async () => {
  const { Pool } = await import('pg');
  const client = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });
  await client.connect();
  return client;
})();

// __tests__/pool.test.ts — using jest.isolateModulesAsync() to get fresh singletons
import { describe, it, expect } from '@jest/globals';

describe('DB pool — environment-dependent initialization', () => {
  it('creates pool with production settings when NODE_ENV=production', async () => {
    await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
      process.env.NODE_ENV = 'production';
      process.env.DATABASE_URL = 'postgresql://prod-host:5432/mydb';

      // Dynamic import inside isolateModulesAsync — runs top-level await fresh.
      // eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-var-requires
      const { pool } = await import('../src/db/pool');

      expect(pool).toBeDefined();
      expect(pool.totalCount).toBe(20); // prod pool size = 20
      await pool.end();
    });
  });

  it('creates pool with test settings when NODE_ENV=test', async () => {
    await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
      process.env.NODE_ENV = 'test';
      process.env.DATABASE_URL = 'postgresql://localhost:5432/testdb';

      const { pool } = await import('../src/db/pool');

      expect(pool.totalCount).toBe(2); // test pool size = 2
      await pool.end();
    });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` creates a completely new module registry for the duration of the callback. Modules with side effects (registering global handlers, modifying `process` properties) execute those side effects again on every isolated import. Audit the module for global side effects before using this pattern — or combine with explicit side-effect cleanup after each `isolateModulesAsync()` block.

**Named alternative:** Vitest `vi.resetModules()` + `vi.importActual()` / `vi.importMock()` for the equivalent ESM module isolation in Vitest; `pool: 'forks'` for process-level isolation (heavier but more complete).

[official]

---

### Pattern 304 — Playwright `page.ariaSnapshot()` for Semantic DOM State Capture on Failure  [official]

Playwright v1.59 exposed `page.ariaSnapshot()` (and `locator.ariaSnapshot()`) as a programmatic API separate from the snapshot assertion `toMatchAriaSnapshot()`. During flakiness investigation, calling `page.ariaSnapshot()` and attaching the result to the test report provides a semantic rendering of the page state at the point of failure, without the pixel-level noise of a screenshot. Two consecutive flaky runs with different `ariaSnapshot()` outputs immediately reveal whether the DOM structure changed (e.g., a list item appeared/disappeared) rather than requiring visual diffing.

```typescript
// fixtures/aria-diagnostic.ts — auto-use fixture that attaches aria snapshot on failure
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend<{ ariaDiagnostic: void }>({
  ariaDiagnostic: [
    async ({ page }, use, testInfo) => {
      await use();

      // Only attach the aria snapshot when the test fails or times out.
      if (testInfo.status === 'failed' || testInfo.status === 'timedOut') {
        try {
          const snapshot = await page.ariaSnapshot();
          await testInfo.attach('aria-snapshot-on-failure', {
            body: snapshot,
            contentType: 'text/plain',
          });

          // Also capture a scoped snapshot for the primary content area.
          const mainContent = page.getByRole('main');
          if (await mainContent.count() > 0) {
            const mainSnapshot = await mainContent.ariaSnapshot();
            await testInfo.attach('aria-snapshot-main-on-failure', {
              body: mainSnapshot,
              contentType: 'text/plain',
            });
          }
        } catch {
          // ariaSnapshot may fail if the page is closed — ignore gracefully.
        }
      }
    },
    { auto: true },
  ],
});

// tests/navigation.spec.ts — uses the aria diagnostic fixture automatically
test('main navigation renders correct menu items', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  const nav = page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Main' });

  // When this assertion flakes (feature flag adds/removes menu items non-deterministically),
  // the attached aria-snapshot-on-failure shows EXACTLY which items were present.
  await expect(nav).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
    - navigation "Main":
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - link "Home"
        - listitem:
          - link "Products"
        - listitem:
          - link "About"
  `);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `ariaSnapshot()` requires that the page has semantic HTML and ARIA attributes. Applications that render all content in non-semantic `<div>` elements produce flat, uninformative snapshots. The diagnostic value is proportional to accessibility quality — adopting this pattern creates a quality-incentive to improve semantic HTML.

[official]

---

### Pattern 305 — Vitest `retry: { count, delay, condition }` Object Form With RegExp Condition for Surgical Retries  [official]

Vitest 4.1 extended the `retry` config option from a plain number to an object with `count`, `delay`, and `condition` fields. The `condition` field accepts a RegExp string (not a function — functions are not serializable across worker message passing and are silently dropped; see Gotcha 115) that is matched against the error message. Only failures whose error message matches the pattern trigger a retry — all other failures (including `AssertionError` from wrong assertions) fail immediately. This is the most precise retry mechanism available in Vitest.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — surgical retry with RegExp condition
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Default: no retry for unit test project — assertion failures must not be retried
    retry: 0,

    projects: [
      // Integration tests: retry only known-transient errors
      {
        extends: true,
        test: {
          name: 'integration',
          include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
          retry: {
            count: 2,
            // IMPORTANT: Use a string RegExp pattern — NOT a function.
            // Functions are stripped during worker message serialisation (Gotcha 115).
            // This pattern matches: network timeouts, connection resets, DB pool exhaustion.
            condition: 'ETIMEDOUT|ECONNRESET|ECONNREFUSED|pool.*exhausted|socket hang up',
            delay: 500, // wait 500ms between retries to let the transient condition clear
          },
        },
      },
      // E2E tests: retry only flaky WebSocket disconnects and DevTools timeouts
      {
        extends: true,
        test: {
          name: 'e2e',
          include: ['e2e/**/*.spec.ts'],
          retry: {
            count: 3,
            condition: 'WebSocket.*disconnected|devtools.*timeout|Target closed',
            delay: 1_000,
          },
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});

// orders.integration.test.ts — demonstrating retry behaviour
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { OrderService } from '../src/OrderService';

describe('OrderService integration', () => {
  it('creates order and persists to DB', async () => {
    // If DB connection pool is temporarily exhausted, this test retries up to 2 times.
    // A wrong assertion ("expected 5000, received 4999") does NOT retry — fails immediately.
    const order = await OrderService.create({ userId: 'u-1', amount: 5000 });
    expect(order.id).toMatch(/^ord-/);
    expect(order.amount).toBe(5000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Using a RegExp condition means new transient error messages that do not match the pattern will NOT be retried. Maintain the condition list as part of the test infrastructure review process and expand it when new known-transient patterns are identified. See Gotcha 123 for the `lastIndex` bug when using global-flag RegExp strings.

[official]

---

### Pattern 306 — Playwright `trace: 'retain-on-failure-and-retries'` for Multi-Retry Trace Comparison  [official]

Playwright's `trace: 'retain-on-failure-and-retries'` mode records a separate trace for EACH test attempt (including passing retries) and saves all of them when any attempt fails. The default `on-first-retry` saves only the trace for the first retry attempt — if the test fails on attempt 1, passes on attempt 2, and fails again on attempt 3, only attempt 1's trace is saved. With `retain-on-failure-and-retries`, all three traces are saved and available for side-by-side comparison in the Playwright trace viewer — the passing attempt reveals what environment state was different from the failing attempts.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — multi-retry trace comparison
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  retries: process.env.CI ? 3 : 0,

  use: {
    // Save traces for ALL retry attempts on any failure.
    // Files: test-results/<test-name>/trace-attempt-0.zip,
    //                                  trace-attempt-1.zip, etc.
    trace: process.env.CI ? 'retain-on-failure-and-retries' : 'on-first-retry',
  },

  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    },
  ],
});

// Investigation workflow:
// 1. Download the artifact ZIP containing all attempt traces.
// 2. Run: npx playwright show-trace trace-attempt-0.zip  # failing attempt
// 3. Run: npx playwright show-trace trace-attempt-1.zip  # passing attempt for comparison
// The network panel diff between failing and passing traces immediately shows
// which API call returned a different status code, which DB query took longer,
// or which element was missing in the failing attempt.
```

**Tradeoff:** With `retries: 3` and `retain-on-failure-and-retries`, each flaky test produces up to 4 trace ZIP files (one per attempt). On a suite with 200 tests and 10% flakiness rate, a CI run can generate 80+ trace ZIPs. Set a GitHub Actions artifact retention policy (7 days) to avoid storage accumulation.

[official]

---

### Pattern 307 — Vitest `pool: 'forks'` + `singleFork: true` for Port-Binding Integration Tests  [official]

Integration tests that bind to specific TCP ports (web servers, database proxies, Redis, gRPC services) fail intermittently with `EADDRINUSE` when multiple Vitest workers attempt to bind the same port simultaneously in the default `threads` pool. `singleFork: true` within `pool: 'forks'` runs all tests in a SINGLE fork process sequentially, guaranteeing only one server is bound at a time. This trades parallelism for deterministic port ownership.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — single-fork for port-binding integration tests
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      // Fast unit tests: threads pool, fully parallel
      {
        test: {
          name: 'unit',
          include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
          pool: 'threads',
        },
      },

      // Port-binding integration tests: single fork, sequential
      // No EADDRINUSE because only one test runs at a time.
      {
        test: {
          name: 'integration-server',
          include: ['src/**/*.server.test.ts'],
          pool: 'forks',
          poolOptions: {
            forks: {
              // All test files run in the SAME OS process — sequential, no port race.
              singleFork: true,
            },
          },
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});

// Example: server integration test using a fixed port safely
import { describe, it, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from 'vitest';
import { createServer } from 'http';

const PORT = 4001; // Fixed port — safe because singleFork ensures only one test runs at a time

describe('HTTP server integration', () => {
  let server: ReturnType<typeof createServer>;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    server = createServer((req, res) => {
      res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
      res.end(JSON.stringify({ status: 'ok', path: req.url }));
    });
    await new Promise<void>((resolve) => server.listen(PORT, resolve));
  });

  afterAll(async () => {
    await new Promise<void>((resolve, reject) =>
      server.close((err) => (err ? reject(err) : resolve()))
    );
  });

  it('responds to GET / with status 200', async () => {
    const res = await fetch(`http://localhost:${PORT}/`);
    expect(res.status).toBe(200);
    const body = await res.json() as { status: string };
    expect(body.status).toBe('ok');
  });

  it('echoes the request path', async () => {
    const res = await fetch(`http://localhost:${PORT}/api/ping`);
    const body = await res.json() as { path: string };
    expect(body.path).toBe('/api/ping');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `singleFork: true` eliminates parallelism for the affected project — 50 integration tests that each take 200ms become a 10-second sequential run instead of a 400ms parallel run. Acceptable for integration tests with real port binding; not acceptable for large unit test suites. Reserve `singleFork` for tests that genuinely cannot be parallelized.

[official]

---

### Pattern 308 — Playwright `toContainClass()` for Stable Single-Class Assertions  [official]

Playwright's `toHaveClass()` asserts the FULL class attribute string. When a design system or state management layer adds utility classes to an element (e.g., `class="nav-item selected animation-fade"`), `expect(el).toHaveClass('nav-item selected')` fails because `animation-fade` was not expected. This produces intermittent failures when utility classes are added/removed by framework internals during component rendering, making the assertion look flaky even though the feature under test (the `selected` state) is correct. `toContainClass('selected')` asserts that one specific class is present, regardless of other classes on the element.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('selected navigation item has "selected" class applied', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  const dashboardLink = page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Dashboard' });

  // BAD: full class string assertion — breaks when Tailwind adds hover utilities
  // await expect(dashboardLink).toHaveClass('nav-item selected');
  // Failure: Expected "nav-item selected hover:text-blue-600 focus:outline-none", received different

  // GOOD: single-class assertion — passes regardless of other utility classes
  await expect(dashboardLink).toContainClass('selected');

  // Navigate to a different page — Dashboard link should lose the 'selected' class
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Settings' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Settings' })).toContainClass('selected');
  await expect(dashboardLink).not.toContainClass('selected');
});

test('form input shows error state class on invalid submission', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/signup');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign up' }).click(); // submit empty form

  const emailInput = page.getByLabel('Email');

  // Only the error class matters — other dynamic classes (focus ring, animation) are irrelevant
  await expect(emailInput).toContainClass('error');
  await expect(emailInput).toContainClass('border-red-500');

  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Email is required');

  // Fix the error — error class should be removed
  await emailInput.fill('valid@example.com');
  await emailInput.blur();
  await expect(emailInput).not.toContainClass('error');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `toContainClass('selected')` passes even if BOTH `selected` and `deselected` classes are present simultaneously (a bug in production code). For state-transition assertions where mutual exclusivity matters, combine: `await expect(el).toContainClass('selected')` AND `await expect(el).not.toContainClass('deselected')`. Single-class assertions are less strict — add complementary negative assertions when correctness requires it.

[official]

---

### Pattern 309 — Playwright `storageState({ indexedDB: true })` for Firebase and Auth0 Token Persistence  [official]

Playwright v1.51 extended `context.storageState()` to include IndexedDB contents via the `indexedDB: true` option. Modern auth libraries (Firebase Auth, Auth0 SPA SDK, Supabase) store session tokens in IndexedDB rather than `localStorage` or cookies, because IndexedDB survives browser restarts and iframe sandbox restrictions. Tests that reuse a `storageState` snapshot created WITHOUT `indexedDB: true` start every run without auth — producing a 401 or redirect-to-login that varies depending on whether the per-test context is fresh or reused from a cached state.

```typescript
// global.setup.ts — create auth snapshot INCLUDING IndexedDB
import { test as setup, expect } from '@playwright/test';

setup('authenticate and capture full storage state', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(process.env.TEST_USER_EMAIL!);
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.TEST_USER_PASSWORD!);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();

  // Wait for a post-login element that only appears after Firebase has persisted the token.
  // Firebase writes to IndexedDB asynchronously AFTER the login response —
  // snapshotting immediately after navigation captures a partially-written state.
  await expect(page.getByTestId('user-avatar')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 15_000 });

  // Additional wait: give Firebase 500ms to finish writing the IndexedDB token entry.
  // This is a known timing dependency — Firebase token persistence is async.
  await page.waitForTimeout(500);

  // Snapshot WITH IndexedDB — captures Firebase auth tokens that would otherwise be missing.
  await page.context().storageState({
    path: 'playwright/.auth/user.json',
    indexedDB: true,  // Requires Playwright v1.51+
  });
});

// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  globalSetup: './global.setup.ts',
  projects: [
    { name: 'setup', testMatch: /global\.setup\.ts/ },
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json' },
      dependencies: ['setup'],
    },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Including IndexedDB in `storageState` increases the snapshot file size significantly for auth libraries that store large token objects (some Firebase snapshots reach 50–100 KB vs 2 KB for cookie-only snapshots). Commit the snapshot file to the repo only if your CI pipeline can securely handle auth credentials in source control; otherwise generate it fresh on each CI run.

[official]

---

### Pattern 310 — Vitest `vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldClearNativeTimers: true })` for Module-Level Timer Contamination  [official]

When `vi.useFakeTimers()` is called without `shouldClearNativeTimers: true`, any timers registered BEFORE the call (including timers in module-level code of imported singletons — e.g., `setInterval` in a caching layer) continue running on the real clock alongside the fake timer timeline. These real timers fire at wall-clock time during fake-timer tests, injecting callbacks at unpredictable positions and producing non-deterministic test outcomes. `shouldClearNativeTimers: true` cancels all active real timers when fake timers are installed.

```typescript
// src/services/CacheManager.ts — module with a module-level interval timer
export class CacheManager {
  private static gcInterval: ReturnType<typeof setInterval>;

  static startGarbageCollection(intervalMs = 30_000): void {
    CacheManager.gcInterval = setInterval(() => {
      CacheManager.purgeExpired();
    }, intervalMs);
  }

  static purgeExpired(): void { /* ... */ }
  static stopGarbageCollection(): void { clearInterval(CacheManager.gcInterval); }
}

// At module load: start GC — creates a real timer BEFORE any test runs
CacheManager.startGarbageCollection(30_000);

// cache-manager.test.ts — test using fake timers
import { vi, test, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { CacheManager } from '../src/services/CacheManager';

describe('CacheManager', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.useFakeTimers({
      // CRITICAL: clear ALL active real timers (including the module-level GC interval above).
      // Without this, the GC interval fires at wall-clock 30s DURING a fake-timer test,
      // contaminating the fake timeline with an unexpected purgeExpired() call.
      shouldClearNativeTimers: true,
      toFake: ['setTimeout', 'setInterval', 'clearTimeout', 'clearInterval', 'Date'],
    });
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    vi.useRealTimers();
    // Restart real GC after each test to avoid leaving the singleton broken.
    CacheManager.startGarbageCollection(30_000);
  });

  test('purges expired cache entries after 30 seconds', async () => {
    const purgeSpy = vi.spyOn(CacheManager, 'purgeExpired');

    // Restart GC on the fake clock — module-level real interval was cleared by shouldClearNativeTimers
    CacheManager.startGarbageCollection(30_000);

    // Advance fake clock 30s — GC fires exactly once on the fake timeline.
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(30_000);

    // Exactly 1 call — no contamination from the real module-level interval.
    expect(purgeSpy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `shouldClearNativeTimers: true` cancels ALL active real timers at fake-timer installation time — including timers from legitimate background processes (health-check pings, metrics reporters, connection keepalives). For long-lived suites that span multiple `describe` blocks, ensure real timers are restarted in `afterEach` for any singletons that depend on them.

[official]

---

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 38)  [community]

**Gotcha 119 — Vitest `aroundEach` With Missing `yield` Silently Skips Test Body — All Tests Pass Vacuously**  [community]
The `aroundEach` generator MUST call `yield` exactly once — this is the point where the test body executes. If the generator exits without yielding (e.g., an early return in an error-handling branch), the test body NEVER runs and Vitest reports the test as passing (no assertions = no failures). WHY this is dangerous: a defensive `if (!db) return;` before `yield` silently skips ALL tests when the DB connection fails — every test goes green, CI ships broken code. Fix: always `yield` unconditionally in `aroundEach`; if the resource is unavailable, `throw` an error (which will fail the test visibly) rather than returning early.

**Gotcha 120 — Playwright `page.clock.install()` After `page.goto()` Does Not Intercept Pre-Navigation Timers**  [official]
`page.clock.install()` MUST be called before `page.goto()` (or before any page script has run). If called after the first navigation, timers registered before the installation call continue to use the real clock — `fastForward()` and `tick()` will not advance them. Teams that move `page.clock.install()` into a `beforeEach` that runs AFTER a navigation in a global `beforeAll` fixture find that 30–50% of tests are unaffected by clock manipulation while the rest are correctly controlled — producing wildly inconsistent flakiness rates depending on test order. WHY: the Playwright docs state this requirement clearly on the Clock API page, but fixture-composition order violations frequently violate it silently. Fix: install the clock in the fixture that also does the first navigation, keeping both in the same scope.

**Gotcha 121 — `vi.defineHelper()` Does Not Improve Stack Traces for Async Helpers — Only Synchronous Wrappers Benefit**  [community]
`vi.defineHelper()` works by replacing the function's source reference in the stack trace using V8's `Error.captureStackTrace`. This mechanism is synchronous — when an async function `await`s before throwing, the original call stack is unwound and V8 cannot walk it back to the `vi.defineHelper()` wrapper call site. Teams that wrap async helpers with `vi.defineHelper()` are surprised that the stack trace still points inside the helper body on `await`-boundary failures. WHY: async stack frames are reconstructed from Promise continuation chains, not from synchronous call stacks. Fix: use `vi.defineHelper()` for synchronous assertion helpers; for async helpers, use `expect.extend()` which uses a different stack-injection mechanism that works with async matchers.

**Gotcha 122 — Playwright `test.abort()` Does Not Immediately Terminate Route Handler Execution — Code After `abort()` Runs**  [official]
`test.abort(message)` marks the test as failed and schedules test teardown, but it does NOT immediately terminate the current JavaScript execution context in the route handler. Any code after `test.abort()` in the handler still runs. Teams that call `test.abort()` and then perform additional async operations (API calls, DB writes) in the same handler are surprised that those operations complete before the test exits. WHY this matters for flakiness: if those post-abort operations have side effects in shared state, they can corrupt the next test. Fix: immediately `return` after `test.abort()` to prevent any post-abort logic from running.

**Gotcha 123 — Vitest `retry: { condition: 'pattern' }` String RegExp Global Flag Causes `lastIndex` State Bug — Every Other Evaluation Returns `false`**  [community]
Vitest converts the `condition` string to a `new RegExp(condition, 'g')` with the global flag enabled. With the global flag, `RegExp.test()` maintains state between calls via `lastIndex`. If the same RegExp object is reused across multiple error evaluations (which Vitest does internally for the serialised condition), every other call returns `false` after the first match due to `lastIndex` not being reset. WHY this trips teams: the condition works for the first 1–2 retry evaluations per run then silently stops matching, causing the 2nd and 3rd retries to skip even though the error message matches the pattern. Fix: write precise conditions with anchors (`'^ETIMEDOUT$'`) or word boundaries (`'\\bETIMEOUT\\b'`); avoid patterns that could accidentally match mid-string in a way that advances `lastIndex` unexpectedly.

| DB integration test leaves dirty rows — downstream tests fail | `afterEach` ROLLBACK not guaranteed on test exception | Pattern 299 (Vitest `aroundEach` with `BEGIN/ROLLBACK` in `try/finally`) | Separate `beforeEach(BEGIN)` / `afterEach(ROLLBACK)` — ROLLBACK can be skipped on failure |
| Test failure says "locator not found" — locator uses brittle nth-child | Fragile positional selector breaks on DOM reorder | Pattern 300 (locator stability audit — migrate to ARIA role + name locators) | `page.locator('ul > li:nth-child(3) > button')` — breaks on any list reorder |

### Pattern 311 — Playwright `locator.describe()` for Trace-Readable Locator Annotations  [official]

Introduced in Playwright v1.53, `locator.describe(label)` attaches a human-readable string to any locator. That label replaces the raw CSS selector in the Trace Viewer action timeline and in the HTML report. When diagnosing a flaky test, a trace entry that says `click "Subscribe button"` is immediately actionable; one that says `click :nth-match(button, 4)` is not. For codebases using getByTestId or complex nth-match selectors, `describe()` turns opaque trace entries into self-documenting action logs without requiring any change to the selectors themselves.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('user can subscribe to newsletter', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/pricing');

  // Raw locator is hard to read in traces: 'getByTestId("btn-sub")'
  // .describe() replaces it in Trace Viewer with "Subscribe button"
  const subscribeBtn = page.getByTestId('btn-sub').describe('Subscribe button');
  const emailInput = page.getByPlaceholder('your@email.com').describe('Email input');
  const confirmationBanner = page.locator('[data-testid="sub-confirm"]')
    .describe('Subscription confirmation banner');

  await subscribeBtn.click();
  await emailInput.fill('test@example.com');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Confirm' }).describe('Confirm button').click();

  // Trace shows: "expect 'Subscription confirmation banner' to be visible"
  // instead of: "expect [data-testid="sub-confirm"] to be visible"
  await expect(confirmationBanner).toBeVisible({ timeout: 5_000 });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `describe()` returns the same locator — the description is purely cosmetic metadata. It cannot substitute for actually fixing a brittle selector. If a test is flaky because `getByTestId('btn-sub')` matches two elements intermittently, describing it will make the flakiness easier to spot in traces but will NOT fix it. Fix the selector with a more specific locator first; add `describe()` second as trace hygiene.

[official]

---

### Pattern 312 — Playwright `testProject.workers` for Per-Project Concurrency Override Without Separate CI Jobs  [official]

Playwright v1.52 added `workers` as a `testProject`-level property, allowing fine-grained concurrency control per project within a single `playwright.config.ts`. Previously, reducing concurrency for resource-contending test categories required either a separate CI job or serialising the entire suite. With per-project workers you can run stable component tests at 8 workers while constraining E2E tests that share staging infrastructure to 2 workers — all in one `npx playwright test` invocation, without touching CI pipeline YAML.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — per-project worker limits (requires Playwright v1.52+)
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Global default — used if a project does not specify workers
  workers: process.env.CI ? '50%' : undefined,
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,

  projects: [
    // Fast component-level tests: maximise parallelism
    {
      name: 'component',
      testMatch: '**/*.component.spec.ts',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
      workers: process.env.CI ? 8 : 4,  // per-project override (v1.52+)
    },

    // E2E tests against shared staging: limit to avoid DB/port contention
    {
      name: 'e2e-staging',
      testMatch: '**/*.e2e.spec.ts',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'], baseURL: process.env.STAGING_URL },
      workers: 2,  // Only 2 concurrent workers -> avoids shared-session flakiness
    },

    // Critical-path tests: serial to guarantee order-sensitive state mutations
    {
      name: 'critical-path',
      testMatch: '**/critical/*.spec.ts',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
      workers: 1,  // Sequential — eliminates all concurrency-driven flakiness
    },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Setting `workers: 1` at the project level is semantically equivalent to `test.describe.serial()` for every test in that project — it eliminates parallelism entirely. This trades speed for determinism. Reserve `workers: 1` for test categories that genuinely share mutable state (session tokens, staging DB rows, port bindings); do not default to it as a "safe setting" for all projects or CI run times will balloon.

[official]

---

### Pattern 313 — Vitest `retry: { count, delay, condition }` with a TypeScript Predicate Function for Surgical Retry  [official]

Vitest 4.1 upgraded the `retry` option from a plain number to a full options object accepting a `condition` predicate — either a RegExp or a synchronous function `(error: Error) => boolean`. Using a typed TypeScript function instead of a RegExp string avoids the `lastIndex` state bug (Gotcha 123) and enables multi-property error inspection (error class + message + HTTP status code). This narrows retries to specific transient failures: `ECONNRESET`, `ETIMEDOUT`, database lock timeouts — while still immediately failing on `AssertionError` (which signals a real logic defect, not a transient infrastructure failure).

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { fetchOrderStatus } from '../api/order-client';

// Type-safe retry condition — only retry specific network/infra transient errors.
// ALL other error types (AssertionError, TypeError, etc.) fail immediately.
const isTransientInfraError = (error: Error): boolean => {
  const transientCodes = ['ECONNRESET', 'ETIMEDOUT', 'ECONNREFUSED', 'ENOTFOUND'];
  // Check Node.js system error code (e.g. errors from HTTP client)
  if ('code' in error && transientCodes.includes((error as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code ?? '')) {
    return true;
  }
  // Also retry on HTTP 503/504 gateway errors surfaced as Error messages
  if (error.message.includes('503') || error.message.includes('504')) {
    return true;
  }
  return false;
};

describe('OrderClient — integration', () => {
  it(
    'fetches live order status from staging gateway',
    {
      retry: {
        count: 3,            // Max 3 retries
        delay: 500,          // 500ms between retries (avoids hammering a recovering service)
        condition: isTransientInfraError,  // Only retry transient network errors
      },
    },
    async () => {
      const status = await fetchOrderStatus('ORD-999');
      // AssertionError here will NOT be retried — it is a real logic failure
      expect(status).toBe('confirmed');
    }
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `condition` function runs synchronously in the Vitest runner process — it cannot `await` async operations. If you need async retry logic (e.g., wait for a health endpoint before retrying), compose the condition with the `delay` option and implement backoff in the condition closure via a mutable retry counter. Also note: `condition` functions cannot be serialised to `vitest.config.ts` — they must be defined inline in the test file or imported from a test utility.

[official]

---

### Pattern 314 — Jest `retryTimes` with `waitBeforeRetry` and `retryImmediately` for Staged Integration Retry  [official]

Jest 30 extended `jest.retryTimes()` with two new options: `waitBeforeRetry` (milliseconds to pause before each retry) and `retryImmediately` (retry as soon as the test fails, rather than after all tests in the file run). Together these options enable a staged retry policy: immediate first retry catches transient in-process failures (mock not yet initialised), while the `waitBeforeRetry` delay on subsequent retries allows remote services time to recover. The combination avoids both hammering a struggling endpoint and waiting an arbitrary global delay before the faster in-process retry.

```typescript
// payment-gateway.test.ts — staged retry for integration tests
import { describe, test, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from '@jest/globals';
import { PaymentGatewayClient } from '../src/payment-gateway';
import { startMockGateway, stopMockGateway } from '../test-utils/mock-gateway';

// Staged retry policy:
// - retryImmediately: true  -> first retry runs immediately (catches in-process flakiness)
// - waitBeforeRetry: 300    -> subsequent retries wait 300ms (allows remote recovery)
// - logErrorsBeforeRetry    -> log each error before retrying (traceability in CI logs)
jest.retryTimes(3, {
  retryImmediately: true,
  waitBeforeRetry: 300,
  logErrorsBeforeRetry: true,
});

let client: PaymentGatewayClient;

beforeAll(async () => {
  const port = await startMockGateway();
  client = new PaymentGatewayClient({ baseURL: `http://localhost:${port}` });
});

afterAll(async () => {
  await stopMockGateway();
});

describe('PaymentGatewayClient', () => {
  test('charges a card and returns transaction ID', async () => {
    const result = await client.charge({ amount: 2500, currency: 'USD' });
    expect(result).toMatchObject({ status: 'succeeded', transactionId: expect.any(String) });
  });

  test('refunds a transaction within 100ms', async () => {
    const charge = await client.charge({ amount: 1000, currency: 'EUR' });
    const refund = await client.refund({ transactionId: charge.transactionId });
    expect(refund.status).toBe('refunded');
    expect(refund.refundedAt).toBeDefined();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `retryImmediately: true` combined with `waitBeforeRetry` creates an asymmetric policy: retry 1 is immediate, retries 2+ wait. If `waitBeforeRetry` is set too high (e.g., 5000ms) and the average test count is large, the total CI time impact grows quickly. Keep `waitBeforeRetry` below 1000ms for unit/integration tests; reserve longer delays for tests that explicitly test rate-limited external services.

[official]

---

### Pattern 315 — Playwright `page.requests()` Post-Test Network Audit for Flakiness Diagnosis  [official]

Playwright v1.60 added `page.requests()` which returns up to the last 100 network requests made by the page during the current test. Unlike `page.route()` (which intercepts and requires upfront registration), `requests()` is a passive accessor — no setup required. For flaky tests that fail with ambiguous errors (element not found, unexpected redirect, wrong data), inspecting `page.requests()` after the failure reveals whether the right API calls were made, in what order, and what status codes they returned. This turns opaque E2E failures into diagnosable network traces without modifying the test body.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Auto-use fixture: dump recent network requests on test failure
// Install in playwright.config.ts via test.use({ ... }) or in a fixtures file
test.beforeEach(async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  // Attach network request log to test report on failure
  testInfo.onTestFailed(async () => {
    const requests = page.requests();
    const summary = requests.map(
      r => `${r.method()} ${r.url()} -> ${r.response()?.status() ?? 'no response'}`
    );
    await testInfo.attach('network-requests', {
      body: summary.join('\n'),
      contentType: 'text/plain',
    });
  });
});

test('dashboard loads user orders after login', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('alice@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.TEST_PASSWORD!);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();

  await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('orders-table')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 8_000 });
  // On failure, testInfo.onTestFailed dumps all requests to the HTML report:
  // GET /api/session -> 200
  // GET /api/orders?userId=42 -> 200
  // GET /assets/icons.svg -> 404  <- suspicious 404 that caused a rendering block
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `page.requests()` holds at most the last 100 requests per page. For single-page applications with heavy polling (WebSockets, SSE fallback, analytics pings), the buffer may overflow and the relevant API call might be evicted before `onTestFailed` runs. In those cases, add `page.route('**/api/**', ...)` with a pass-through handler that logs matched requests to a test-scoped array before the 100-entry limit applies.

[official]

---

### Pattern 316 — Vitest `onTestFailed` with `retryCount` Guard for Retry-Aware Diagnostic Dumps  [official]

Vitest's `onTestFailed` hook fires after every failed attempt including retried ones. Without a retry guard, diagnostic dumps (DB state exports, log file copies) accumulate one artifact per retry attempt — inflating CI storage and making it unclear which attempt corresponds to the actual failure. Combining `onTestFailed` with `taskResult.retryCount` allows the hook to emit diagnostics only on the FINAL failure (when retries are exhausted), keeping the artifact set clean.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, onTestFailed } from 'vitest';
import { db, dumpOrderTable } from '../test-utils/db';
import { writeFileSync } from 'fs';
import { join } from 'path';

const MAX_RETRIES = 3; // must match vitest.config.ts `retry: 3`

describe('OrderRepository — concurrent insertion', () => {
  it('inserts 100 concurrent orders without duplicate IDs', { retry: MAX_RETRIES }, async () => {
    // Register diagnostic dump ONLY on final failure (retry count exhausted)
    onTestFailed(async (taskResult) => {
      if ((taskResult.retryCount ?? 0) >= MAX_RETRIES) {
        // Last attempt — dump DB state for post-mortem investigation
        const snapshot = await dumpOrderTable();
        const outPath = join('test-artifacts', `order-dump-final-${Date.now()}.json`);
        writeFileSync(outPath, JSON.stringify(snapshot, null, 2));
        console.error(`[FINAL FAILURE] DB dump written to ${outPath}`);
      } else {
        console.warn(`[Retry ${(taskResult.retryCount ?? 0) + 1}/${MAX_RETRIES}] Test failed — will retry`);
      }
    });

    const insertions = Array.from({ length: 100 }, (_, i) =>
      db.orders.insert({ customerId: `cust-${i}`, amount: 100 })
    );
    const results = await Promise.all(insertions);
    const ids = results.map(r => r.id);
    const uniqueIds = new Set(ids);

    expect(uniqueIds.size).toBe(100); // All 100 IDs must be unique — concurrent insert check
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `retryCount` field on `TaskResult` is `0`-indexed from Vitest's perspective in some versions. Validate against your Vitest version that `retryCount === MAX_RETRIES` is the correct terminal condition — some versions use `retryCount === MAX_RETRIES - 1` for the last attempt. Add a debug log on every `onTestFailed` invocation initially to confirm the counter behaviour before relying on the guard in production CI.

[official]

---

### Pattern 317 — Playwright `page.clearConsoleMessages()` + `page.clearPageErrors()` for Per-Test Error Accumulation Control  [official]

`page.consoleMessages()` and `page.pageErrors()` buffer up to 200 entries each, persisting across actions within a test. In tests that navigate multiple pages or trigger multiple async operations, earlier benign console warnings can obscure the specific error that preceded a flaky failure. Calling `page.clearConsoleMessages()` and `page.clearPageErrors()` at known checkpoints — immediately after a successful navigation, or after a stable assertion — resets both buffers, making the post-failure snapshot contain only messages from the relevant test phase.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout flow completes without JS errors', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  // Phase 1: login
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('buyer@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.TEST_PASSWORD!);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
  await page.waitForURL('/shop');

  // Clear buffers after successful login — login-phase noise won't appear in checkout diagnostics
  page.clearConsoleMessages();
  page.clearPageErrors();

  // Phase 2: add to cart and checkout
  await page.getByTestId('product-1').getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();

  // On failure, attach ONLY errors from the checkout phase
  testInfo.onTestFailed(async () => {
    const errors = page.pageErrors();
    const consoleErrs = page.consoleMessages().filter(m => m.type() === 'error');
    if (errors.length || consoleErrs.length) {
      const body = [
        ...errors.map(e => `PAGE ERROR: ${e.message}`),
        ...consoleErrs.map(m => `CONSOLE ERROR: ${m.text()}`),
      ].join('\n');
      await testInfo.attach('checkout-phase-errors', { body, contentType: 'text/plain' });
    }
  });

  await expect(page.getByText('Order confirmed')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 10_000 });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Clearing buffers too aggressively — e.g., after every `click()` — means that errors from earlier actions are discarded even when they ARE the root cause of a later assertion failure. Find the right granularity by test phase (login phase, feature phase, assertion phase), not by individual action. A good default is: clear once at the start of the feature under test, after confirming the setup phase completed cleanly.

[official]

---

### Pattern 318 — MSW v2 `http.passthrough()` for Selective Interception Isolation  [community]

A common source of MSW-based flakiness is handler registration order: MSW executes handlers in registration order, and the first matching handler wins. When a test adds a per-test override via `server.use()`, and the handler does NOT call `passthrough()` for non-matching paths, all unregistered endpoints receive `onUnhandledRequest: 'error'` responses — crashing tests that legitimately need those endpoints. Using `http.passthrough()` as an explicit no-op handler for unintercepted paths prevents accidental blanket interception while still making the important endpoint deterministic.

```typescript
import { http, HttpResponse, passthrough } from 'msw';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { beforeAll, afterAll, afterEach, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { loadUserProfile } from '../api/user';

const server = setupServer(
  // Default: all unmatched requests pass through (do not error in unit tests)
  http.all('*', () => passthrough()),
);

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'warn' }));
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

it('loads user profile from API', async () => {
  // Per-test override: intercept ONLY /api/users/:id; all other endpoints passthrough
  server.use(
    http.get('https://api.example.com/users/:id', ({ params }) => {
      return HttpResponse.json({
        id: params.id,
        name: 'Alice Tester',
        plan: 'pro',
      });
    }),
    // Analytics endpoint: intentionally let it passthrough — no mock needed
    http.post('https://analytics.example.com/events', () => passthrough()),
  );

  const profile = await loadUserProfile('42');
  expect(profile.name).toBe('Alice Tester');
  expect(profile.plan).toBe('pro');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `http.passthrough()` only works when MSW has a real network target to pass through to — it requires a real server or a downstream interceptor. In pure unit test environments (Node.js without a running server), `passthrough()` for non-local URLs will result in real network requests if the base handler is `passthrough`. Combine with `onUnhandledRequest: 'warn'` (not `'error'`) during initial handler development, then tighten to `'error'` once handler coverage is verified.

[community]

---

### Pattern 319 — Explicit `AbortController` Signal Propagation to Prevent Open-Handle Flakiness  [community]

Tests that launch async operations (fetch calls, streaming readers, WebSocket connections) without propagating an `AbortSignal` tied to the test lifecycle leave open handles after the test body completes. These handles prevent Node.js from exiting cleanly, triggering Jest/Vitest's `--detectOpenHandles` warning and causing intermittent failures in the next test when the abandoned operation resolves or rejects against a partially torn-down environment. The fix is to create an `AbortController` per test, pass its signal to every async boundary, and call `abort()` in `afterEach`.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { streamOrderEvents } from '../api/order-stream';

describe('OrderStream — open handle prevention', () => {
  let controller: AbortController;

  beforeEach(() => {
    // Fresh controller per test — each test owns its own cancellation token
    controller = new AbortController();
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    // Cancel any in-flight operations started by this test
    // Prevents open-handle warnings and cross-test contamination
    controller.abort('test teardown');
  });

  it('emits order-created events within 2 seconds', async () => {
    const events: string[] = [];

    // Pass signal to every async boundary that accepts one
    await streamOrderEvents({
      signal: controller.signal,
      onEvent: (event: { type: string }) => events.push(event.type),
    });

    // Trigger an order creation to fire the event
    await fetch('/api/orders', {
      method: 'POST',
      body: JSON.stringify({ item: 'sku-A' }),
      signal: controller.signal,  // Same signal — both cancel together
    });

    // Wait for the event with a time-bounded condition
    await vi.waitFor(() => {
      expect(events).toContain('order-created');
    }, { timeout: 2000, interval: 50 });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Aborting via `afterEach` fires even when the test passes — the abort call is a no-op on already-completed operations, so there is no correctness risk. The one gotcha: some older libraries (pre-Node 18 fetch polyfills) do not honour `AbortSignal` reliably and may throw a `DOMException: AbortError` instead of resolving cleanly, surfacing as a false failure. Wrap signal-sensitive calls in a `try/catch` that silently ignores `AbortError` if the operation succeeded before the abort was called.

[community]

---

### Pattern 320 — Snapshot Serialiser Registration Order as Flakiness Source  [community]

Jest and Vitest process custom snapshot serialisers in LIFO registration order: the last `expect.addSnapshotSerializer()` call wins for any given value. When multiple test files register serialisers at module scope (e.g., `emotion/jest-emotion`, `@testing-library/jest-dom`, and a custom date serialiser) and Vitest runs them in parallel workers, the effective serialiser order varies between runs. A snapshot that matches on run N may produce a different string representation on run N+1 if the serialiser order changed, causing non-deterministic snapshot failures that look like visual regressions but are actually serialisation artifacts.

```typescript
// vitest.setup.ts — register ALL serialisers in a single, deterministic file
// loaded via setupFiles in vitest.config.ts BEFORE any test file runs
import { expect } from 'vitest';

// Register in explicit priority order (last registered = lowest priority).
// Priority: most specific first -> least specific last

// 1. Custom date serialiser (most specific — only matches Date objects)
expect.addSnapshotSerializer({
  test: (val): val is Date => val instanceof Date,
  print: (val: Date) => `Date<${(val as Date).toISOString()}>`,
});

// 2. Custom Error serialiser (specific to Error class)
expect.addSnapshotSerializer({
  test: (val): val is Error => val instanceof Error,
  print: (val: Error) => `Error<${(val as Error).message}>`,
});

// 3. Broad serialisers (e.g. Emotion CSS-in-JS) registered LAST — lowest priority
// import { createSerializer } from '@emotion/jest';
// expect.addSnapshotSerializer(createSerializer());

// vitest.config.ts must load this file via:
// test: { setupFiles: ['./vitest.setup.ts'] }
export {};
```

**Tradeoff:** Centralising serialiser registration in `setupFiles` removes the ability for individual test files to add file-local serialisers — any serialiser added inside a test file still applies LIFO against the globally registered set. If a test file legitimately needs a unique serialiser (e.g., a GraphQL AST serialiser only relevant to one test suite), add it to `setupFiles` with a guard condition rather than inlining it in the test file.

[community]

---

### Pattern 321 — `process.env` Mutation in Tests Without Restore Causing Cross-Test Contamination  [community]

Tests that mutate `process.env` directly (`process.env.FEATURE_FLAG = 'true'`) without restoring the original value in `afterEach` contaminate every subsequent test in the same worker process. This is particularly dangerous in Vitest's default `threads` pool where multiple test files share the same Node.js worker: a feature flag set by `api.test.ts` persists into `auth.test.ts` running in the same worker, producing failures that only appear in parallel or in specific execution orders. The correct pattern is to use Vitest's `vi.stubEnv()` API which auto-restores after each test via `vi.unstubAllEnvs()`.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, beforeEach, afterEach, vi } from 'vitest';
import { resolveFeatureFlag } from '../utils/feature-flags';

describe('FeatureFlags — environment-driven', () => {
  // vi.stubEnv(): replaces process.env.X safely; vi.unstubAllEnvs() restores all stubs
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.stubEnv('FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT', '');  // reset to known blank state before each test
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    vi.unstubAllEnvs();  // belt-and-suspenders restore — nothing leaks to next test
  });

  it('enables new checkout when FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT=true', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT', 'true');
    expect(resolveFeatureFlag('new_checkout')).toBe(true);
  });

  it('disables new checkout when FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT is blank', () => {
    // FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT was reset to '' by beforeEach — no cross-test contamination
    expect(resolveFeatureFlag('new_checkout')).toBe(false);
  });

  it('is case-insensitive for TRUE/FALSE variants', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT', 'TRUE');
    expect(resolveFeatureFlag('new_checkout')).toBe(true);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vi.stubEnv()` / `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` only works within Vitest's process model. In Jest, use `jest.replaceProperty(process, 'env', { ...process.env, FEATURE_FLAG: 'true' })` or a manual save-and-restore pattern. Neither approach works when the environment variable is read at import time (module initialisation) — in that case, use `vi.resetModules()` + dynamic `await import(...)` inside the test body to force re-evaluation of the module with the new env value.

[community]

---

### Pattern 322 — Playwright `locator.filter()` to Eliminate Ambiguous Locator Flakiness  [official]

A common source of Playwright flakiness is a locator that matches multiple elements: `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })` matches every Delete button in the DOM when multiple rows are rendered. When tests rely on DOM order for disambiguation (the Nth element or a parent scope), reordering caused by server-side sorting, pagination, or race conditions changes which element is matched. `locator.filter()` adds a secondary constraint without changing the primary selector, making the locator deterministic regardless of DOM order.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('deletes the correct order from the list', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/orders');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('orders-table')).toBeVisible();

  // BAD: relies on DOM order — breaks when server returns orders in different sort order
  // await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' }).nth(2).click();

  // GOOD: use filter() to scope the button to the specific row by content
  // This is order-independent — works regardless of where ORD-456 appears in the list
  const targetRow = page.getByTestId('order-row').filter({
    has: page.getByText('ORD-456'),  // Row containing order ID ORD-456
  });
  const deleteBtn = targetRow.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' });

  // Verify the locator resolves to exactly ONE element before clicking
  await expect(deleteBtn).toHaveCount(1);
  await deleteBtn.click();

  // Confirm the row was removed from the DOM
  await expect(targetRow).toHaveCount(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `locator.filter({ has: ... })` performs a DOM subtree scan for each element in the parent locator set — for very large lists (1000+ rows), this can add meaningful latency to the locator resolution. Use `filter()` by data-attribute or text content for correctness; if performance becomes a concern, prefer server-side test data setup that guarantees uniqueness of the target element rather than client-side disambiguation.

[official]

---

### Pattern 323 — Vitest `pool: 'vmForks'` for Deterministic ESM Module Isolation Across Test Files  [official]

Vitest's default `threads` pool shares the V8 heap across test files in the same worker, meaning module-level singletons initialised during the first test file persist into subsequent files unless `vi.resetModules()` is called explicitly. `pool: 'vmForks'` spawns each test file in its own OS process with a fully isolated V8 instance — equivalent to Jest's default process-per-file isolation. This eliminates an entire class of shared-state flakiness that is nearly impossible to diagnose in the `threads` pool: singleton mutations, require cache contamination, and prototype chain pollution from `vi.spyOn` calls that escape `vi.restoreAllMocks()`.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — vmForks pool for complete module isolation
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // vmForks: separate OS process per test file, full V8 isolate.
    // Eliminates module-level singleton leakage that 'threads' cannot prevent.
    // Slower than 'threads' (~50ms spawn per file) but correct for stateful singletons.
    pool: 'vmForks',

    poolOptions: {
      vmForks: {
        // Reuse forked processes up to 10 times — amortises spawn overhead
        forkTTL: 10,
        env: { NODE_ENV: 'test' },
      },
    },

    testTimeout: 10_000,
    hookTimeout: 10_000,
  },
});
```

```typescript
// Example: module-level singleton that would contaminate 'threads' pool, safe in 'vmForks'
// src/services/MetricsCollector.ts
export class MetricsCollector {
  private static readonly instance = new MetricsCollector();
  private readonly events: string[] = [];

  static getInstance(): MetricsCollector { return MetricsCollector.instance; }
  record(event: string): void { this.events.push(event); }
  getAll(): string[] { return [...this.events]; }
}

// metrics.test.ts — order-independent in vmForks; order-dependent in threads pool
import { it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { MetricsCollector } from '../src/services/MetricsCollector';

it('records checkout event', () => {
  MetricsCollector.getInstance().record('checkout');
  // In vmForks: each test file gets a fresh process — no stale events from prior files
  // In threads: stale ['checkout'] from previous test file persists in the shared worker
  expect(MetricsCollector.getInstance().getAll()).toEqual(['checkout']);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Each test file spawn adds ~50–80ms overhead in `vmForks`. A suite of 500 test files incurs ~25–40 seconds of pure spawn overhead. Profile before migrating wholesale: apply `vmForks` only to test files that interact with module-level singletons (databases, metrics collectors, global event buses) and keep pure-function unit tests in the faster `threads` pool using Vitest's `projects` configuration to split by file pattern.

[official]

---

### Pattern 324 — GitHub Actions `concurrency` Group with `cancel-in-progress` to Eliminate Stale CI Flakiness  [community]

When a developer pushes two commits in quick succession, GitHub Actions may run two CI pipelines simultaneously against the same branch. If both pipelines share staging resources (a single test database, a fixed-port mock server, test user accounts), they interfere with each other and produce flakiness that appears as a transient infrastructure problem but is actually a CI scheduling problem. The `concurrency` group with `cancel-in-progress: true` terminates the older pipeline the moment a newer push is detected, ensuring only one pipeline runs per branch at a time and staging resources are never double-booked.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — concurrency group prevents simultaneous pipeline interference
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: ['main', 'release/**']
  pull_request:
    branches: ['main']

# Cancel in-progress pipelines on the same branch when a new push arrives.
# Prevents two pipelines from sharing staging DB / mock server simultaneously.
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '20', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Run tests
        run: npx playwright test --retries=2 --fail-on-flaky-tests
        env:
          CI: true
          STAGING_DB_URL: ${{ secrets.STAGING_DB_URL }}
          TEST_USER_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TEST_USER_PASSWORD }}
```

**Tradeoff:** `cancel-in-progress: true` cancels the previous pipeline immediately — any tests already in progress on that pipeline are aborted mid-run. If your team relies on per-commit test results in the GitHub PR status checks (e.g., for code review automation), cancelled pipelines show as "cancelled" rather than "passed" or "failed", which can confuse PR automation rules. Consider setting `cancel-in-progress: false` for the `main` branch (where full results are always required) and `true` only for PR branches where developer iteration speed matters more.

[community]

### Pattern 325 — Playwright Auto-Use Fixture Combining `locator.describe()` + `page.ariaSnapshot()` for Self-Annotating Flaky Test Reports  [official]

Combining Playwright v1.53's `locator.describe()` with a custom auto-use fixture that attaches ARIA snapshots and structured error logs on failure produces a self-annotating test report. Every flaky failure emits a structured attachment showing the ARIA tree of the surrounding DOM and any JS errors that preceded the failure. This is the highest-signal diagnostic artifact for element-targeting flakiness because it shows both what the test was looking for and what the DOM actually contained at the moment of failure — without requiring the developer to re-run the test locally.

```typescript
// fixtures/auto-annotate.ts — auto-use fixture for flaky element identification
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend<{ autoAnnotate: void }>({
  autoAnnotate: [async ({ page }, use, testInfo) => {
    // Register failure handler before yielding to the test body
    testInfo.onTestFailed(async () => {
      try {
        // Attach ARIA snapshot of the main content area on failure
        const ariaTree = await page.locator('main').ariaSnapshot();
        await testInfo.attach('aria-snapshot-on-failure', {
          body: ariaTree,
          contentType: 'text/plain',
        });

        // Attach JS errors and console errors from the failing phase
        const pageErrs = page.pageErrors().map(e => e.message);
        const consoleErrs = page.consoleMessages()
          .filter(m => m.type() === 'error')
          .map(m => m.text());

        if (pageErrs.length || consoleErrs.length) {
          await testInfo.attach('errors-on-failure', {
            body: [...pageErrs, ...consoleErrs].join('\n'),
            contentType: 'text/plain',
          });
        }
      } catch {
        // Page already closed (crash) — skip attachment silently
      }
    });

    await use();
  }, { auto: true }],  // auto: true — runs for every test without explicit request
});

// tests/checkout.spec.ts — use extended test; fixture activates automatically
// import { test, expect } from '../fixtures/auto-annotate';

test('order confirmation appears after payment', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');

  // describe() labels appear in both Trace Viewer and aria-snapshot attachment
  const payBtn = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).describe('Pay now button');
  const confirmBanner = page.getByTestId('order-confirm').describe('Order confirmation banner');

  await payBtn.click();

  // On intermittent failure, HTML report includes:
  // 1. ARIA snapshot of <main> showing DOM state at failure time
  // 2. Console/page errors from the post-clear checkpoint
  await expect(confirmBanner).toBeVisible({ timeout: 8_000 });
  await expect(confirmBanner).toContainText('Your order has been placed');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `page.ariaSnapshot()` on the full document can produce several hundred kilobytes for complex SPAs. Scoping to `page.locator('main').ariaSnapshot()` limits the snapshot to the content area, reducing attachment size by 60–80% while retaining the relevant diagnostic context. If `main` does not exist in your DOM (e.g., admin tooling with non-semantic layout), substitute `page.locator('#app').ariaSnapshot()` or `page.locator('body').ariaSnapshot()` with a size warning in the fixture comment.

[official]

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 39)  [community]

**Gotcha 124 — `vi.stubEnv()` Does Not Affect Variables Read at Module Import Time — Only Runtime Reads**  [community]
`vi.stubEnv('API_URL', 'https://staging.example.com')` replaces the value in `process.env` for the test body, but modules that read `process.env.API_URL` at the top level (e.g., `const BASE_URL = process.env.API_URL ?? 'http://localhost'`) evaluate that expression once at import time — BEFORE `vi.stubEnv()` is called. WHY this causes flakiness: the first test to import the module wins; subsequent tests that call `vi.stubEnv()` on the same variable appear to work (the env changes) but the module's internal constant retains the original value, producing inconsistent API call targets across tests. Fix: use `vi.resetModules()` + dynamic `await import(...)` inside the test body to force re-evaluation of the module with the new environment value.

**Gotcha 125 — Playwright `locator.filter({ hasText })` Matches Inner Text Including Child Elements — Unexpected Over-Matching**  [official]
`page.locator('.order-row').filter({ hasText: 'ORD-456' })` matches any `.order-row` whose subtree contains the text "ORD-456" — including rows that contain a child label, tooltip, or footnote mentioning "ORD-456" alongside a different order ID in the main cell. WHY this causes flakiness: on pages that display order references in multiple UI layers (data cell + status tooltip), `hasText` matches more rows than intended, and `.click()` fires on the wrong element intermittently depending on render order. Fix: use `filter({ has: page.getByTestId('order-id').getByText('ORD-456') })` to scope the match to the exact element that renders the order ID.

**Gotcha 126 — Jest `retryTimes` with `retryImmediately: true` Skips `afterEach` Between Retries — Shared State Is Not Reset**  [official]
`retryImmediately: true` re-runs the test body immediately on failure, BEFORE `afterEach` hooks execute. WHY this matters: if a test mutates shared state (appending to a database table, incrementing a counter in a singleton, creating a file) and relies on `afterEach` to reset that state before the next run, the immediate retry starts in a dirty state — producing failures that look like the test ran twice simultaneously or that the initial mutation was duplicated. Fix: move cleanup from `afterEach` into the test body itself using a `try/finally` block, or use `retryImmediately: false` combined with `waitBeforeRetry: 0` to achieve a fast retry after `afterEach` without skipping teardown.

**Gotcha 127 — Vitest `vmForks` Pool Cannot Share `globalSetup` Module-Level Variables Across Forks**  [official]
`globalSetup` files configured via `globalSetup` in `vitest.config.ts` run ONCE before all tests. But in `vmForks`, each test file gets its own OS process — global setup results written to module-level variables (e.g., `global.__SERVER_PORT = await startServer()`) are NOT visible in the child forks. WHY teams are surprised: they migrate from `threads` to `vmForks` and find that `global.__SERVER_PORT` is `undefined` inside every test file even though `globalSetup` ran successfully. Fix: write `globalSetup` output to a temp file or environment variable (`process.env.TEST_SERVER_PORT = String(port)`), not to module-level globals, so each fork can read it via `process.env` or `fs.readFileSync`.

**Gotcha 128 — GitHub Actions `cancel-in-progress` with Matrix Sharding Cancels Some Shards Mid-Run — Partial Merge Fails**  [community]
When using matrix sharding (`matrix: { shard: [1, 2, 3, 4] }`) with `cancel-in-progress: true`, a new push cancels only the PENDING shard jobs — jobs already started continue to completion. If 2 of 4 shards complete before cancellation and 2 are cancelled, the merge-results step fails because two shard result files are missing. WHY this is deceptive: the overall workflow shows as "cancelled" rather than "failed", masking the fact that the merge step would have produced an incomplete test report. Fix: set `cancel-in-progress: true` at the top-level workflow trigger only; add a merge-step guard that skips and reports "superseded" when the workflow was cancelled (`if: cancelled() == false`).

| Trace Viewer shows raw CSS selectors — hard to correlate with flaky locator | No locator description | Pattern 311 (`locator.describe('label')` — annotates traces and HTML reports) | Bare `getByTestId('btn-sub')` in traces without semantic label |
| E2E and component tests interfere with each other on CI despite same runner | No per-project concurrency control | Pattern 312 (Playwright `testProject.workers` — per-project parallelism limit) | Global `workers` setting — serialises all projects or over-parallelises all equally |
| `retry: 3` retries `AssertionError` — real bug silently passes on retry | Unconditional retry number masks logic failures | Pattern 313 (Vitest `retry: { condition: fn }` typed predicate for surgical retry) | `retry: 3` plain number — retries every error type including `AssertionError` |
| Integration test with external gateway fails sporadically on first run | Missing staged retry policy | Pattern 314 (Jest `retryTimes` with `retryImmediately` + `waitBeforeRetry`) | Global `waitBeforeRetry: 2000` — slows all retries including fast in-process ones |
| Flaky E2E test: ambiguous error with no API calls visible | No post-failure network audit | Pattern 315 (Playwright `page.requests()` — last 100 requests buffer on failure) | `page.route('**', ...)` upfront interception — changes test behaviour |
| `onTestFailed` dumps DB state on every retry — CI storage fills up | No retry-count guard in `onTestFailed` | Pattern 316 (Vitest `onTestFailed` with `taskResult.retryCount` terminal guard) | Unconditional dump on every `onTestFailed` — multiple artifacts per test |
| Checkout-phase error buried in login-phase console messages | Buffer not cleared between test phases | Pattern 317 (Playwright `page.clearConsoleMessages()` at phase checkpoints) | Relying on 200-entry buffer through all navigation phases |
| MSW `onUnhandledRequest: 'error'` breaks tests needing analytics endpoint | No `passthrough()` for non-intercepted routes | Pattern 318 (MSW v2 `http.passthrough()` for selective endpoint interception) | Blanket `http.all('*', ...)` error handler — blocks legitimate unregistered endpoints |
| `--detectOpenHandles` warns after async stream test | No `AbortSignal` propagation — fetch/stream left open | Pattern 319 (per-test `AbortController` with `afterEach` `controller.abort()`) | No cancellation at test teardown — stream resolves against torn-down environment |
| Snapshot tests flip between two serialisation formats non-deterministically | Serialisers registered in non-deterministic order across parallel files | Pattern 320 (centralise all serialiser registration in `setupFiles`) | Registering serialisers at module scope inside individual test files |
| `process.env.FEATURE_FLAG` set in test A bleeds into test B | No `vi.stubEnv()` + `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` isolation | Pattern 321 (Vitest `vi.stubEnv()` / `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` per test) | `process.env.X = 'value'` mutation without restore |
| `getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })` clicks wrong row when list reorders | Positional locator disambiguation breaks on sort order change | Pattern 322 (Playwright `locator.filter({ has: page.getByText('ORD-456') })`) | `.nth(2)` locator — breaks on server-side sort change |
| Module singleton retains state from previous test file in Vitest threads pool | Shared V8 heap — module cache not isolated between files | Pattern 323 (Vitest `pool: 'vmForks'` for full OS-process isolation per test file) | `vi.resetModules()` in every `beforeEach` — easy to miss, does not reset all globals |
| Two CI pipelines on same branch share staging DB simultaneously | Concurrent pipelines competing for shared resources | Pattern 324 (GitHub Actions `concurrency` group with `cancel-in-progress: true`) | No concurrency group — allows unlimited simultaneous pipeline runs per branch |
| Flaky failure report has screenshot only — no DOM structure info | No ARIA snapshot or structured locator annotation | Pattern 325 (auto-use fixture: `page.ariaSnapshot()` + `locator.describe()` on failure) | Screenshot-only reports — pixel diff does not show DOM structure changes |
