### Pattern 428 — Playwright `page.waitForLoadState('networkidle')` with Explicit Timeout Override for SPA Stability  [official]

Single-page applications often issue background API calls (analytics, telemetry, prefetch requests) continuously after initial load, meaning `networkidle` (no network requests for 500ms) never resolves in the default timeout — causing the test to hang until the 30s test timeout fires. Setting an explicit, short timeout on `waitForLoadState('networkidle')` and catching the resulting `TimeoutError` allows the test to continue after a "best-effort idle" period rather than hanging: if the page is substantially loaded (critical API calls complete, primary content visible), the test can proceed even if background telemetry calls prevent true idle.

```typescript
// tests/helpers/wait-for-content.ts
import { Page } from '@playwright/test';

/**
 * Wait for the page to reach a stable state, with graceful degradation
 * if continuous background requests prevent true networkidle.
 */
export async function waitForContentReady(page: Page): Promise<void> {
  // First, wait for the critical domcontentloaded — always fast
  await page.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded');

  try {
    // Attempt networkidle with a short budget — SPA may never fully idle
    await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle', { timeout: 3000 });
  } catch {
    // Networkidle timeout is acceptable — fall through to content check
    // This is expected behavior for apps with continuous background polling
  }

  // Verify primary content is rendered regardless of network state
  await page.waitForFunction(() => {
    const mainContent = document.querySelector('[data-testid="main-content"]');
    return mainContent !== null && mainContent.children.length > 0;
  }, { timeout: 10_000 });
}

// tests/dashboard.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { waitForContentReady } from './helpers/wait-for-content';

test('dashboard renders user stats', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await waitForContentReady(page); // Stable regardless of telemetry requests

  await expect(page.getByTestId('user-stats-card')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByText(/Total orders/)).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Replacing `networkidle` with a content-visibility check (`waitForFunction`) requires identifying a reliable DOM sentinel that is only present after critical data has loaded — this sentinel must be kept in sync with UI changes. If the sentinel is too generic (e.g., any `div` inside `main`), the test may proceed before API data has populated the page. If it is too specific (e.g., a particular data value), it becomes a brittle assertion. The ideal sentinel is a structural element (loading spinner gone, skeleton screen replaced) that reflects infrastructure-level readiness rather than data-level content.

### Pattern 429 — Jest `testEnvironmentOptions` for Per-Suite URL and Globals Without Full Environment Swap  [official]

Jest's `testEnvironmentOptions` key in a test file's `@jest-environment` docblock (or in `jest.config.ts` per-project overrides) injects environment-level configuration without swapping the entire environment from `jsdom` to `node` or vice versa. The most flakiness-relevant use is setting `testURL` / `url` to control `window.location.href` — code that reads URL parameters, pathname, or origin at module load time will see a stable, predictable URL rather than the default `http://localhost/`, which may differ from the URL expected by auth guards, router initialization, or analytics initialization code.

```typescript
/**
 * @jest-environment jsdom
 * @jest-environment-options {"url": "https://app.example.com/dashboard?tab=orders", "referrer": "https://app.example.com/"}
 */
// tests/router-guard.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from '@jest/globals';
import { parseCurrentRoute } from '../src/router';
import { initAnalytics } from '../src/analytics';

describe('router guard with explicit URL context', () => {
  it('parses pathname from predictable URL', () => {
    // window.location.pathname === '/dashboard' — stable across test runs
    const route = parseCurrentRoute();
    expect(route.path).toBe('/dashboard');
    expect(route.params.tab).toBe('orders');
  });

  it('analytics init uses correct origin', () => {
    // Prevents flakiness from default localhost origin in analytics beacon URL
    const analytics = initAnalytics();
    expect(analytics.beaconOrigin).toBe('https://app.example.com');
  });
});
```

```typescript
// Alternative: per-project in jest.config.ts for environment-wide URL
// jest.config.ts
export default {
  projects: [
    {
      displayName: 'dashboard-tests',
      testMatch: ['**/dashboard/**/*.test.ts'],
      testEnvironment: 'jsdom',
      testEnvironmentOptions: {
        url: 'https://app.example.com/dashboard',
        customExportConditions: ['browser'],
      },
    },
  ],
};
```

**Tradeoff.** `testEnvironmentOptions.url` sets the URL at environment initialization — it cannot be changed mid-test without `Object.defineProperty(window, 'location', ...)` hacks, which bypass `jsdom`'s navigation model. For tests that simulate navigation between routes, use a routing library's memory history abstraction (React Router `createMemoryRouter`, Vue Router memory mode) rather than mutating `window.location`. Also note that `jsdom`'s URL parsing has known divergences from browser URL parsing for edge cases (data URLs, malformed origins) — validate that `testEnvironmentOptions.url` produces the expected `window.location` object shape for the URL format used.

### Pattern 430 — Playwright `route.fulfill` with `status` and `headers` for Precise Contract-Mocking of Error Responses  [official]

`route.fulfill({ status, headers, body })` intercepts a network request and returns a fully specified HTTP response without forwarding to a real server. While `route.fulfill({ json: {...} })` is sufficient for happy-path mocks, flaky tests often arise from underspecified error-path mocks that omit the HTTP status code, `Content-Type` header, or error body format expected by client-side error handlers. Precisely specifying all three dimensions (status, headers, body) ensures the application's error-handling path behaves identically in tests as it does against the real API, preventing error-handler flakiness caused by mock responses that differ structurally from real error payloads.

```typescript
// tests/error-handling.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  // Intercept the product API and return a precise 429 Too Many Requests response
  await page.route('**/api/v1/products**', async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 429,
      headers: {
        'Content-Type': 'application/problem+json',  // RFC 7807 problem details
        'Retry-After': '60',
        'X-RateLimit-Limit': '100',
        'X-RateLimit-Remaining': '0',
        'X-RateLimit-Reset': String(Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + 60),
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        type: 'https://api.example.com/errors/rate-limited',
        title: 'Too Many Requests',
        status: 429,
        detail: 'Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60 seconds.',
        retryAfter: 60,
      }),
    });
  });
});

test('rate limit banner displays retry countdown', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  // The error handler reads Retry-After header to compute countdown
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /rate limit/i })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByText(/retry in 60 seconds/i)).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Retry' })).toBeDisabled();
});

test('rate limit clears after countdown completes', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.clock.install({ time: Date.now() });
  await page.goto('/products');

  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /rate limit/i })).toBeVisible();

  // Advance clock past retry window — banner should clear
  await page.clock.fastForward(61_000);
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).not.toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Precisely specified `route.fulfill` mocks are coupled to the exact response format the application expects — if the real API changes its error schema (e.g., moves from a custom error format to RFC 7807 Problem Details), tests using the old mock format will continue to pass even though the real integration has broken. Mitigate this by writing a parallel contract test that validates the real API's error response schema matches the mock shape, or by using Playwright's `page.routeFromHAR` (Pattern 417) to record real error responses rather than constructing them manually.

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 50)  [community]

**Gotcha 165 — Playwright `context.grantPermissions` Scope Leaks to All Pages in the Context Including Subsequent Tests Using the Same Context**  [community]
`context.grantPermissions(['geolocation'])` modifies permissions at the BrowserContext level and persists for the lifetime of that context. WHY this causes flakiness: in Playwright test setups where a single browser context is shared across multiple tests (a common optimization to reduce auth setup cost), a test that grants geolocation permission leaves that permission active for all subsequent tests in the same context — even tests that should be running without permissions to verify that permission-denied error paths work correctly. A test that checks "location access denied" behavior will pass when run first (no permissions granted) but fail when run second (permissions already granted by the previous test). Fix: always call `context.clearPermissions()` in a `afterEach` hook when using `grantPermissions`, or use a per-test context (Playwright's default `{ scope: 'test' }` context fixture) rather than a shared context — the default context is torn down after each test and starts clean.

**Gotcha 166 — Vitest `vi.stubGlobal` Restoration Is Skipped When the Test Throws Before `vi.unstubAllGlobals` — Subsequent Tests Observe the Stubbed Global**  [community]
`vi.stubGlobal('fetch', mockFetch)` replaces the global `fetch` function with a mock and registers an undo operation. WHY restoration is skipped: if the test body throws an uncaught error before `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` is called (or before `afterEach` runs it), and the test framework catches the error but skips the `afterEach` hook due to a configuration error or hook ordering bug, the global `fetch` remains stubbed for subsequent tests. Tests that rely on real `fetch` behavior (or a different mock) will silently use the stale stub. This is subtly different from spy-based mocks — `vi.spyOn` restores the original via the auto-restore mechanism, but `vi.stubGlobal` requires explicit restoration. Fix: always configure `restoreAllMocks: true` and `unstubAllGlobals: true` in `vitest.config.ts` under the `test` key — this ensures restoration happens at the framework level regardless of test body exceptions.

**Gotcha 167 — Jest `fakeTimers` with `modern` Implementation Delays Promise Microtask Resolution — `await Promise.resolve()` Does Not Flush Between Timer Ticks**  [community]
In Jest's `modern` fake timer implementation (the default since Jest 27), `jest.runAllTimers()` processes the fake timer queue synchronously — but Promise microtasks scheduled via `Promise.resolve().then(...)` are not flushed between timer callback invocations. WHY this causes unexpected ordering: code that does `setTimeout(() => { someVar = 1; Promise.resolve().then(() => callback(someVar)); }, 0)` expects `callback` to be called with `1`, but in a synchronous `runAllTimers()` call, the microtask queue is only flushed after the entire timer queue has been drained — so `callback` may observe a stale `someVar` if it was updated by a later timer in the queue. Fix: use `jest.runAllTimersAsync()` (available since Jest 29.5) which interleaves `await Promise.resolve()` flushes between timer callbacks, preserving the real event-loop ordering of microtasks relative to timer callbacks. This is the most common source of "my fake-timer test works locally but fails on the async code path" reports.

**Gotcha 168 — Playwright `page.waitForResponse(urlOrPredicate)` String Matching Uses `includes`, Not Exact Match — Partial URL Strings Match Unintended Requests**  [community]
`page.waitForResponse('/api/users')` resolves on the first response whose URL includes the string `/api/users`. WHY this causes flakiness in apps with URL hierarchies: a call to `waitForResponse('/api/users')` will resolve on the first matching response, which could be `/api/users/profile`, `/api/users/123/orders`, or `/api/users?page=2` — not necessarily the root `/api/users` list endpoint the test was intended to wait for. When the application issues multiple API calls in parallel on page load, the order in which these responses arrive is non-deterministic — `waitForResponse('/api/users')` may resolve on a child endpoint response rather than the list endpoint, causing the subsequent assertion (`expect(res.json()).toEqual([...])`) to fail because the response body is a single user object, not an array. Fix: always pass a predicate function instead of a string: `page.waitForResponse(res => res.url() === 'https://app.example.com/api/users' && res.request().method() === 'GET')` — exact URL match eliminates partial-path ambiguity.

**Gotcha 169 — Vitest Browser Mode Test Timeout Is Not Inherited by `page` Fixtures — Long-Running Page Operations Exceed Default 5s Action Timeout**  [community]
In Vitest 4.x browser mode, the `test.timeout` setting (default 5000ms in browser mode, configurable via `browser.timeout`) applies to the test body's total execution time. However, individual Playwright-style page actions within browser mode fixtures (e.g., `await page.click(...)`, `await expect(locator).toBeVisible()`) use Playwright's internal action timeout — which defaults to 5 seconds and is independent of Vitest's test timeout. WHY this creates confusing double-timeout flakiness: a developer sets `test.timeout(30_000)` expecting the test to have 30 seconds, but a `page.click()` on a slow element still times out after 5 seconds with a Playwright `TimeoutError` — the Vitest timeout is not propagated to Playwright's action timeout. Fix: explicitly pass `{ timeout: 25_000 }` to long-running page actions (`page.click(selector, { timeout: 25_000 })`), or configure `playwright.config.ts` `actionTimeout` globally. In browser mode where there is no separate `playwright.config.ts`, set the action timeout on the `page` object in a `beforeEach`: `page.setDefaultTimeout(testInfo.timeout - 1000)` — this keeps the Playwright action timeout slightly under the Vitest test timeout, allowing Playwright's timeout error to surface before Vitest's outer timeout fires.

## Quick Reference Additions (Cycle 50)

| Symptom | Likely Root Cause | Pattern/Fix | Anti-Pattern to Avoid |
|---------|-------------------|-------------|----------------------|
| Screenshot test passes on Linux CI but fails on macOS with 2–5% pixel diff | OS-level font antialiasing and GPU compositing differences inflate per-platform pixel diffs | Pattern 416 (per-project `toHaveScreenshot.threshold` calibrated per OS) | Single global threshold for all platforms — too tight for macOS/Windows, too loose for Linux |
| Flaky test suite when API is under load — occasional 500s and timeouts break E2E | Tests hit the real network — external API instability causes non-deterministic failures | Pattern 417 (Playwright `routeFromHAR` strict replay — hermetic network recording) | Live network in E2E tests — all instability and latency non-determinism propagates |
| Single slow step (PDF generation, video encode) consumes entire test timeout | No per-step time budget — one slow operation starves cleanup and diagnostic steps | Pattern 418 (Playwright test step `timeout` option for bounded async step budget) | Relying only on test-level timeout — one slow step can silence all remaining diagnostics |
| Test uses `await sleep(500)` waiting for async side effect to complete | Fixed sleep is brittle — fast CI passes, slow CI fails; too long wastes time | Pattern 419 (Vitest `vi.waitFor` with interval + timeout for deterministic polling) | `sleep()`/`setTimeout` waiting — flaky on machines with variable timing |
| Parallel tests collide on the same DB schema — random FK constraint failures | No worker-level resource namespacing — all workers share one schema | Pattern 420 (Playwright `workerInfo.workerIndex` for per-worker schema suffix) | Shared DB schema across workers — cross-worker writes cause non-deterministic constraint errors |
| Config singleton reads `process.env` at import time — env change not picked up by next test | Module-level `process.env` reads are cached after first `require` | Pattern 421 (Jest `isolateModules` for per-test module registry scope) | `jest.resetModules()` globally — flushes entire cache, breaks unrelated module dependencies |
| Non-deterministic UUIDs in snapshots and assertions — test fails on ID mismatch | `crypto.randomUUID()` or `Math.random()` called in production code during test | Pattern 422 (Playwright `BrowserContext.addInitScript` for pre-load global stub injection) | `page.evaluate()` post-load stub injection — production code already called the real API |
| Integration test suite has cross-file DB schema conflicts when run concurrently | No file-level serialization — concurrent files collide on shared schema names | Pattern 423 (Vitest `sequence.concurrent: false` + `maxConcurrency` for bounded intra-file parallelism) | Full concurrency without file-level isolation — relies on correct workerIndex mapping which can race |
| `expect(apiResult).toEqual(...)` requires hand-written retry loop for async API assertions | `expect()` has no built-in retry for non-locator values | Pattern 424 (Playwright `expect.poll` for retry-assertion on API call results) | Manual `while` retry loop with `sleep` — non-deterministic timing, hard to maintain |
| Order-dependent flakiness in a large test file — unclear which sibling is the contaminator | Multiple tests share a file; the contaminating pair is unknown | Pattern 425 (Jest `--testNamePattern` + `--randomize` for surgical flakiness bisection) | `it.only()` file edits — source file changes required, not safe to commit to bisect loop |
| Fixed-size API key pool exhausted — test gets `undefined` key when `workerIndex` exceeds pool | `workerIndex` is unbounded in dynamic worker spawn mode | Pattern 426 (Playwright `testInfo.parallelIndex` for bounded pool slot allocation) | Using unbounded `workerIndex` as pool index — exceeds pool size when workers are recycled or reused |
| Browser mode tests have no screenshot on failure — debugging requires local reproduction | No automatic failure capture in browser mode — failure context is lost after the run | Pattern 427 (Vitest `onTestFailed` + `page.screenshot()` + attachment for auto-capture) | Manual `try/catch` screenshot in each test — duplicated code, missed by new tests |
| SPA test hangs for 30s waiting for `networkidle` — background analytics calls never stop | Continuous background polling prevents `networkidle` state | Pattern 428 (Playwright `waitForLoadState('networkidle')` with short timeout + content-visibility sentinel) | Waiting on `networkidle` with full test timeout — background telemetry causes guaranteed timeout |
| Tests fail because `window.location.href` is `http://localhost/` but code expects a real origin | Default jsdom URL does not match the app's expected origin for auth guards and analytics | Pattern 429 (Jest `testEnvironmentOptions.url` for per-suite stable URL context) | `Object.defineProperty(window, 'location', ...)` mid-test URL mutation — bypasses jsdom navigation model |
| Error-path tests pass but error handler silently ignores the mock response — wrong status code | `route.fulfill({ json: {...} })` without `status` defaults to 200 — error handler never triggers | Pattern 430 (Playwright `route.fulfill` with full `status` + `headers` + `body` for error contract mocking) | `{ json: errorBody }` without status — application receives 200 with error body, error branch not taken |

## Cycle 51 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 431 — Playwright `page.requestGC()` for Memory Leak Detection in Long-Running Tests  [official]

Long-running E2E tests that accumulate DOM nodes, event listeners, or large response payloads can exhaust browser memory, causing heap-pressure flakiness that only manifests after many tests have run in the same worker. Playwright v1.48 introduced `page.requestGC()` which triggers a browser-level garbage collection cycle, allowing tests to verify that large objects held through `WeakRef` are actually released after a work unit completes. Because GC is non-deterministic, `requestGC()` is not a guarantee but a strong suggestion — combine it with `WeakRef` dereferencing checks to get a reliable signal.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('large response body is not retained after processing', async ({ page }) => {
  // Register a WeakRef to track the large object's lifecycle
  await page.goto('/data-export');
  await page.click('[data-testid="load-large-dataset"]');
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Loaded');

  // Ask the browser to collect garbage
  await page.requestGC();

  // Verify via page.evaluate that the app's internal cache was cleared
  const cacheSize = await page.evaluate(() =>
    (window as any).__appCache?.size ?? 0
  );
  expect(cacheSize).toBe(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.requestGC()` is advisory — V8 may defer collection if the heap pressure heuristic disagrees. Tests that pass locally may still fail on memory-constrained CI runners if the heap is close to the GC threshold. Use this pattern to catch obvious leaks in development, but do not rely on it as a hard memory budget assertion in CI without also monitoring `performance.memory.usedJSHeapSize` trends across the test suite.

### Pattern 432 — Playwright `page.requests()` Snapshot for Network Audit After Action  [official]

Race conditions between network requests and assertions are a primary source of E2E flakiness. Rather than wrapping every action in `Promise.all([page.waitForResponse(...), action()])`, Playwright v1.56 provides `page.requests()` which returns the 100 most recent requests made by the page as an array — enabling post-action auditing without the setup overhead of response interceptors. This is particularly useful when verifying that analytics events, beacon calls, or background sync requests were fired exactly once after a user action.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout fires exactly one analytics event', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');
  await page.click('[data-testid="checkout-btn"]');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order Confirmed' })).toBeVisible();

  // Snapshot recent requests — access immediately before GC collection
  const requests = await page.requests();
  const analyticsHits = requests.filter(r =>
    r.url().includes('/analytics/event') && r.method() === 'POST'
  );

  expect(analyticsHits).toHaveLength(1);
  const body = JSON.parse(analyticsHits[0].postData() ?? '{}');
  expect(body.event).toBe('purchase_complete');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The returned requests array holds only the 100 most recent requests and the underlying objects are collected to prevent unbounded memory growth — the Playwright docs explicitly warn to "access returned requests immediately." In tests with high request volume (SPAs with polling or frequent background sync), the analytics request may have been pushed out of the 100-request window. For such cases, `page.waitForResponse()` with an exact predicate (Pattern 168) is safer than `page.requests()` post-action auditing.

### Pattern 433 — Vitest `vi.defineHelper()` for Clean Stack Traces in Custom Assertion Utilities  [official]

Shared assertion helpers extracted into utility files are a common source of misleading flakiness diagnostics — when an assertion inside a helper fails, the stack trace points into the helper's internal implementation rather than the test line that called it. Vitest 4.1 introduces `vi.defineHelper()` which wraps any sync or async function so that on failure, V8's `Error.captureStackTrace` is instructed to trim the helper's stack frames, making the error point directly to the calling test. This eliminates the "assertion failed in `assertUserShape` at line 14 of test-utils.ts" noise that makes flakiness triage slower.

```typescript
import { vi, expect } from 'vitest';

// Define once in test-utils.ts
export const assertApiResponse = vi.defineHelper(
  async (actual: unknown, expected: Record<string, unknown>) => {
    expect(actual).toBeDefined();
    expect(actual).toMatchObject(expected);
    // Additional structural checks
    expect((actual as any).timestamp).toBeTypeOf('number');
    expect((actual as any).requestId).toMatch(/^req_[a-z0-9]{16}$/);
  }
);

// In the test — stack traces point HERE on failure, not into assertApiResponse
test('user profile endpoint returns expected shape', async () => {
  const response = await fetchUserProfile('user_123');
  await assertApiResponse(response, { id: 'user_123', role: 'admin' });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `vi.defineHelper()` only cleans up stack traces for errors thrown inside the helper — if the helper itself has a JavaScript runtime error (e.g., `TypeError: Cannot read property 'x' of undefined`) rather than an assertion error, the stack trace may still include internal frames depending on the V8 version. Additionally, helpers defined with `vi.defineHelper()` must not be used outside of test contexts (they rely on Vitest's internal error capture mechanism), so mixing them with production utility code in the same file can cause confusing import-time errors in non-test builds.

### Pattern 434 — Vitest `aroundEach` for Database Transaction Rollback Without `afterEach` Leaks  [official]

The classic `beforeEach`/`afterEach` pair for database transaction wrapping has a well-known failure mode: if the test throws, the `afterEach` hook may not run (or runs but the transaction is already in an error state), leaving committed or partially-committed data that contaminates subsequent tests. Vitest 4.1's `aroundEach` hook receives a `runTest` callback and wraps the test body inside a single function, guaranteeing that the post-test logic (rollback) executes even if the test throws — because it runs in the same call frame.

```typescript
import { describe, aroundEach } from 'vitest';
import { db } from '../lib/db';

describe('order service', () => {
  aroundEach(async (runTest) => {
    // Begin transaction before test
    await db.query('BEGIN');
    try {
      await runTest();       // Run the test — may throw
    } finally {
      // Rollback always runs — even if runTest() threw
      await db.query('ROLLBACK');
    }
  });

  test('creates order with correct total', async () => {
    await db.query(
      'INSERT INTO orders (user_id, total) VALUES ($1, $2)',
      ['user_1', 99.99]
    );
    const order = await db.query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1', ['user_1']);
    expect(order.rows[0].total).toBe('99.99');
  });

  test('rejects order with negative total', async () => {
    await expect(
      db.query('INSERT INTO orders (user_id, total) VALUES ($1, $2)', ['user_1', -1])
    ).rejects.toThrow('check_total_positive');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `aroundEach` requires that `runTest()` is always called exactly once — forgetting to call it silently skips the test body, while calling it twice causes undefined behavior (the test runs twice, and state mutations from the first run contaminate the second). Unlike `beforeEach`/`afterEach`, there is no framework-level enforcement of the `runTest` call, making code review the only gate. Lint rules or ESLint plugins that enforce `runTest` invocation do not yet exist as of Vitest 4.1.

---

### Pattern 435 — Playwright `tracing.group()` for Structuring Traces Around Logical Operations  [official]

In Playwright traces that capture dozens or hundreds of network calls and DOM events, identifying which actions belong to which logical operation is time-consuming. Playwright v1.49 introduced `tracing.group(name, callback)` which visually groups actions in the trace viewer under a collapsible label. This dramatically reduces triage time for flaky tests — instead of scanning raw timestamps to find "which network call fired during the sidebar render", the trace shows a labeled `sidebar:render` group containing only the relevant actions.

```typescript
import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard renders sidebar and main content independently', async ({ page, context }) => {
  await context.tracing.start({ screenshots: true, snapshots: true });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  await context.tracing.group('sidebar:initialize', async () => {
    await page.waitForSelector('[data-testid="sidebar"]');
    await page.click('[data-testid="sidebar-toggle"]');
  });

  await context.tracing.group('main-content:load', async () => {
    await page.waitForResponse(res =>
      res.url().includes('/api/dashboard/widgets') && res.status() === 200
    );
    await page.waitForSelector('[data-testid="widget-grid"]');
  });

  await context.tracing.stop({ path: 'traces/dashboard-test.zip' });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `tracing.group()` adds metadata overhead to the trace ZIP — each group creates an additional trace entry with timing boundaries. For tests that already generate large traces (many screenshots + snapshots), heavy nesting of groups can increase trace file size by 5–15%. In suites where trace storage cost is a concern (cloud storage billed by size), limit group usage to the outermost logical boundaries rather than fine-grained sub-operations.

### Pattern 436 — Playwright `test.describe.configure({ retries })` for Per-Suite Retry Budgets  [official]

Global retry settings in `playwright.config.ts` apply a uniform retry budget to all tests regardless of their inherent stability — stable unit-style tests get unnecessarily retried, while fragile integration suites may need a higher budget. Playwright's `test.describe.configure({ retries: N })` allows per-suite retry configuration directly in the spec file, overriding the global setting. This enables a tiered retry strategy: 0 retries for deterministic unit-like specs, 2 retries for integration suites, and 3 for E2E smoke tests that interact with live staging infrastructure.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Stable unit-like API contract tests — no retries
test.describe('API contract: user service', () => {
  test.describe.configure({ retries: 0 });

  test('GET /users returns 200', async ({ request }) => {
    const res = await request.get('/api/users');
    expect(res.status()).toBe(200);
  });
});

// Flaky integration suite — allow 3 retries
test.describe('E2E: checkout flow (live staging)', () => {
  test.describe.configure({ retries: 3 });

  test('complete purchase with card payment', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.fill('[data-testid="card-number"]', '4242424242424242');
    await page.click('[data-testid="pay-now"]');
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /order confirmed/i })).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Per-suite retry configuration creates a maintenance risk when tests are reorganized — moving a test from a high-retry `describe` block to a zero-retry block changes its retry behavior silently. Teams that rely on code search to identify all "fragile" tests may miss that the retry budget was previously compensating for environmental instability rather than test logic issues. Document the reason for non-default retry counts in a comment next to `test.describe.configure()` to preserve intent across refactors.

### Pattern 437 — Vitest `--detect-async-leaks` for CI-Time Async Handle Leak Detection  [official]

Leaked `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, open server handles, or unresolved database connections cause two distinct flakiness modes: tests that hang indefinitely waiting for the event loop to drain, and tests that observe callbacks from a previous test's leaked timer firing mid-assertion. Vitest 4.1's `--detect-async-leaks` flag (configurable as `detectAsyncLeaks: true` in `vitest.config.ts`) uses `node:async_hooks` to track all async resources opened during a test and reports those still open at test end, including their source location.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    detectAsyncLeaks: true,  // Enable async resource leak detection
    // When a leak is found, the test is marked failed with a diagnostic:
    // "Async leak detected: Timeout at src/services/cache.ts:42"
  },
});

// Demonstrates a leaky pattern that detectAsyncLeaks will catch:
test('cache service initializes', async () => {
  const cache = new CacheService({ ttl: 5000 });
  await cache.connect();
  // Missing: await cache.disconnect() — timer still running after test
  expect(cache.isConnected()).toBe(true);
  // detectAsyncLeaks will report the leaked setInterval from CacheService
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `detectAsyncLeaks` reports every unclosed async resource — including intentional singleton connections (e.g., a shared database pool initialized in `beforeAll` and torn down in `afterAll`). Tests in the middle of the suite will be reported as leaking the shared connection even though it is properly managed at the suite level. Mitigate by scoping the pool initialization to worker-scoped fixtures rather than `beforeAll`, ensuring the fixture's teardown phase closes the handle before the worker exits.

### Pattern 438 — Playwright `await using` Async Disposables for Automatic Route Cleanup  [official]

Playwright v1.59 extended many APIs to return `Disposable` or `AsyncDisposable` objects supporting the TC39 `await using` syntax (TypeScript 5.2+). For route handlers, this eliminates a common source of test pollution where `page.route()` registrations from one test leak into the next — the route handler stays active because the test forgot to call `page.unroute()` or `page.unrouteAll()`. With `await using`, disposal is guaranteed at block exit regardless of whether the test throws.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('product list shows error banner on API failure', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  // Route handler is automatically removed when 'using' block exits (even on throw)
  await using _route = await page.route('**/api/products', route =>
    route.fulfill({ status: 503, body: 'Service Unavailable' })
  );

  await page.reload();
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /unavailable/i })).toBeVisible();

  // _route.dispose() is called automatically here — even if the expect above threw
});

// Subsequent test is NOT affected by the 503 route from above
test('product list loads successfully', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');
  await expect(page.getByRole('list', { name: 'products' })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `await using` requires TypeScript 5.2+ with `"lib": ["es2022", "esnext.disposable"]` in `tsconfig.json`. Projects on older TypeScript or targeting JavaScript outputs that strip type annotations need to ensure the Babel/SWC transform chain includes the disposables plugin (`@babel/plugin-proposal-explicit-resource-management`). In environments where the transform is missing, `await using` silently becomes a regular `await` — route cleanup is skipped without any compile-time or runtime error, reintroducing the leak.

---

### Pattern 439 — Playwright `testInfo.retry`-Conditional Server-Side State Reset  [official]

When an E2E test fails and Playwright retries it, the server-side state from the failed attempt (partially-created records, in-flight transactions, locked resources) may persist and cause the retry to fail for a different reason than the original failure. `testInfo.retry` (available in tests, hooks, and fixtures) allows a conditional cleanup block that only runs on retry attempts — avoiding the overhead of full state reset on the first attempt while guaranteeing a clean slate for retries.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { resetUserState } from '../helpers/api';

test.beforeEach(async ({ request }, testInfo) => {
  // Only clean up on retries — avoid unnecessary API calls on first run
  if (testInfo.retry > 0) {
    console.log(`Retry ${testInfo.retry}: resetting server state for clean slate`);
    await resetUserState(request, 'test-user@example.com');
    // Clear any created orders/sessions from the failed attempt
    await request.delete('/api/test/cleanup', {
      data: { testId: testInfo.testId, runId: testInfo.parallelIndex }
    });
  }
});

test('user completes onboarding flow', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/onboarding');
  await page.fill('[data-testid="name"]', 'Test User');
  await page.click('[data-testid="continue"]');
  await page.fill('[data-testid="email"]', 'test-user@example.com');
  await page.click('[data-testid="submit"]');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Welcome!' })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Retry-conditional cleanup introduces asymmetry between the first run and retries — if a bug causes a test to always fail, the first failure leaves dirty state and the retry runs cleanup before the second attempt, potentially masking whether the cleanup itself is correct. Validate the cleanup path in isolation (a dedicated test for the cleanup helper) before relying on it for retry hygiene. Also be aware that `testInfo.retry` is 0-indexed: `retry === 0` means "first attempt", not "first retry".

---

### Pattern 440 — Jest `runAllTimersAsync()` for Microtask-Correct Timer Draining  [official]

Jest's `jest.runAllTimers()` drains the fake timer queue synchronously, which means Promise microtasks scheduled inside timer callbacks are not flushed between timer invocations — only after the entire queue is empty. This creates a subtle ordering mismatch in code that chains `setTimeout` with `Promise.resolve()` or `async/await`, causing tests to observe intermediate state that would never appear in production. `jest.runAllTimersAsync()` (Jest 29.5+) interleaves `await Promise.resolve()` flushes between timer callbacks, faithfully reproducing the event-loop ordering of microtasks relative to macrotasks.

```typescript
import { jest, test, expect } from '@jest/globals';

jest.useFakeTimers();

test('async debounce fires callback with final value', async () => {
  const calls: string[] = [];

  async function debounced(value: string) {
    await Promise.resolve(); // Simulate async processing
    calls.push(value);
  }

  // Schedule two debounced calls 50ms apart
  setTimeout(() => debounced('first'), 100);
  setTimeout(() => debounced('second'), 150);

  // runAllTimers() would NOT flush microtasks between the two callbacks
  // runAllTimersAsync() DOES — calls array is populated in correct order
  await jest.runAllTimersAsync();

  expect(calls).toEqual(['first', 'second']);
  // With runAllTimers(), calls might be [] if microtasks weren't flushed
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `runAllTimersAsync()` is slower than `runAllTimers()` because it yields to the microtask queue between each timer callback — in test suites with hundreds of timer-heavy tests, this can add measurable overhead (typically 10–50ms per test depending on the number of timers). Do not blindly replace `runAllTimers()` with `runAllTimersAsync()` — only upgrade tests that specifically involve `async/await` or `Promise` chains inside timer callbacks. Using `runAllTimersAsync()` for purely synchronous timer tests adds latency without benefit.

---

### Pattern 441 — Playwright `page.clock.setSystemTime()` for Date-Sensitive UI Tests Without Real Delays  [official]

Components that render differently based on the current date (expiry warnings, relative timestamps, "trial ends in N days" banners) are chronically flaky when tested against the real system clock — the test passes at 11:59 PM and fails at midnight because the "1 day remaining" copy rolls over. Playwright's `page.clock` API (v1.45+) provides `setSystemTime(date)` to freeze the browser's `Date`, `performance.now()`, and timer APIs at a specific moment, allowing fully deterministic date-sensitive assertions.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('shows expiry warning when trial ends in 3 days', async ({ page }) => {
  // Freeze time at a specific date — trial expires on 2026-05-17
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-05-14T10:00:00Z') });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // This banner only appears when expiry is within 7 days
  await expect(
    page.getByRole('alert', { name: /trial expires in 3 days/i })
  ).toBeVisible();

  // Advance to expiry day — banner should change to "expires today"
  await page.clock.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-05-17T10:00:00Z'));
  await page.reload();
  await expect(
    page.getByRole('alert', { name: /trial expires today/i })
  ).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.clock.install()` must be called before `page.goto()` to intercept time APIs that are read during module initialization (e.g., a singleton that captures `new Date()` at import time). Calling `clock.install()` after `goto()` is a documented gotcha — modules that cached `Date.now()` at load time retain the real timestamp, creating split-state where some code paths use frozen time and others use real time. Always install the clock as the very first action in a time-sensitive test, before any navigation.

---

### Pattern 442 — Vitest `vi.setTimerTickMode('nextTimerAsync')` for Automatic Async Timer Advancement  [official]

Integration tests that involve multiple async timer callbacks (e.g., polling loops, exponential backoff retry logic, heartbeat timers) require tedious manual `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(N)` calls to drive each tick. Vitest 4.1's `vi.setTimerTickMode('nextTimerAsync')` switches the fake timer engine to automatically advance to the next pending timer after each macrotask, removing the need for manual timer advancement in tests that need to "let the async machine run" rather than control each tick individually.

```typescript
import { vi, test, expect } from 'vitest';

vi.useFakeTimers();

test('retry client retries 3 times then throws', async () => {
  vi.setTimerTickMode('nextTimerAsync');

  const mockFetch = vi.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('Network error'))
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('Network error'))
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('Network error'))
    .mockResolvedValueOnce({ status: 200, data: 'ok' });

  const client = new RetryClient({ maxRetries: 3, backoffMs: 100 });

  // With nextTimerAsync mode, timers advance automatically — no manual advanceTimersByTime calls
  const result = await client.fetch('/api/resource', mockFetch);

  expect(result.data).toBe('ok');
  expect(mockFetch).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(4); // 3 failures + 1 success
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `nextTimerAsync` mode is powerful but can cause infinite loops if the code under test schedules a new timer inside every timer callback (e.g., a polling loop implemented as recursive `setTimeout`). In this case, `nextTimerAsync` will drive the polling loop forever, hanging the test until the test timeout fires. Always ensure there is a clear termination condition (the promise resolves or rejects) before using `nextTimerAsync` with recursive timer patterns. For infinite polling, use `vi.setTimerTickMode('manual')` and advance time up to a fixed horizon.

---

### Pattern 443 — Google's "Four Synchronization Checks" Framework for Locator Wait Logic  [community]

Community experience (echoed by Google's testing blog and Wayne Roseberry's flakiness research) has codified four synchronization primitives that cover the vast majority of async wait scenarios in browser tests: (1) does element X exist right now, (2) does element X not-exist right now, (3) does element X come to exist within timeout T, (4) does element X disappear within timeout T. Playwright's web-first assertions map cleanly onto all four — but tests frequently misuse immediate-mode checks (`isVisible()` returning a boolean) where polling-mode assertions (`expect(locator).toBeVisible()`) are required, causing flakiness on slower machines.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('four synchronization checks — correct Playwright idioms', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/app');

  // Check 1: Exists RIGHT NOW — use only after an event that guarantees presence
  const exists = await page.locator('[data-testid="modal"]').isVisible();
  // ⚠️  Only safe immediately after a direct trigger with auto-wait

  // Check 2: Does NOT exist right now — same caveat
  const dismissed = await page.locator('[data-testid="modal"]').isHidden();

  // Check 3: Comes to exist within timeout — ALWAYS prefer this pattern
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Confirm' })).toBeVisible({
    timeout: 5_000,
  });

  // Check 4: Disappears within timeout — after dismiss action
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Close' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Confirm' })).not.toBeVisible({
    timeout: 3_000,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The polling assertions (checks 3 and 4) retry the condition on an interval (default 100ms) until timeout — this means a test that genuinely should pass immediately may take up to 100ms of unnecessary polling before asserting. In test suites with thousands of such assertions, this adds cumulative overhead. Use `{ timeout: 0 }` (or a very short timeout like 50ms) when you are certain the state is synchronously established, and the full polling timeout for truly async conditions.

Tag: [community]

---

### Pattern 444 — Isolating Singleton `process.env` Readers with Jest `isolateModulesAsync()`  [official]

Modules that read `process.env` at import time (rather than inside function calls) create test order-dependency: the first test that imports the module caches the environment, and subsequent tests that mutate `process.env` before re-importing see the cached value. Jest's `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` (the async variant of `jest.isolateModules()`) creates a fresh module registry for its callback scope, ensuring each test gets a clean import with the current environment values — critical for testing modules whose behavior changes based on feature flags read at module initialization.

```typescript
import { jest, test, expect } from '@jest/globals';

test('feature flag OFF — returns legacy behavior', async () => {
  process.env.FEATURE_NEW_PRICING = 'false';

  const { getPricingEngine } = await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
    // Fresh import — module reads FEATURE_NEW_PRICING = 'false'
    return import('../lib/pricing');
  });

  const engine = getPricingEngine();
  expect(engine.type).toBe('legacy');
});

test('feature flag ON — returns new pricing engine', async () => {
  process.env.FEATURE_NEW_PRICING = 'true';

  const { getPricingEngine } = await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
    // Fresh import — module reads FEATURE_NEW_PRICING = 'true'
    return import('../lib/pricing');
  });

  const engine = getPricingEngine();
  expect(engine.type).toBe('new-tiered');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `isolateModulesAsync()` creates a new module registry for every call — if the module under test has a large transitive dependency tree (e.g., imports 20+ modules transitively), the isolated import can be significantly slower than a cached import (2–10x on cold runs). For test suites that must run dozens of feature-flag permutations, consider dependency injection (pass the env value as a constructor argument) rather than module-level reads — this avoids the registry overhead entirely while achieving the same test isolation goal.

---

### Pattern 445 — Playwright `testProject.workers` for Flakiness-Isolated Per-Project Worker Limits  [official]

When multiple Playwright test projects (e.g., `chromium`, `firefox`, `mobile-safari`) share the same worker pool, a worker that encounters an unrecoverable browser crash is discarded and replaced — but this replacement consumes a slot from the global worker budget, potentially starving other projects and causing timing-sensitive tests to fail due to resource contention. Playwright v1.52's `testProject.workers` allows each project to have an independent worker count, isolating resource pressure so that a crashing Firefox worker does not affect the Chromium project's timing characteristics.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  workers: process.env.CI ? 4 : undefined,  // Global default

  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium-stable',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
      workers: 4,  // Independent worker budget — Firefox crashes don't steal slots
    },
    {
      name: 'firefox-experimental',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Firefox'] },
      workers: 2,  // Lower budget — Firefox has higher crash/recovery rate on CI
      retries: 2,  // Additional retries to absorb browser-level instability
    },
    {
      name: 'mobile-safari',
      use: { ...devices['iPhone 15'] },
      workers: 1,  // Sequential — WebKit on Linux CI has resource contention issues
    },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Setting `workers` per-project means the total worker count can exceed the `global workers` limit — if `chromium-stable` uses 4 workers and `firefox-experimental` uses 2 and `mobile-safari` uses 1, up to 7 workers may be running simultaneously, which can overwhelm CI runners with limited CPU or memory. Set per-project worker counts conservatively on CI and profile memory usage before enabling high per-project concurrency. The per-project isolation benefit is only meaningful when projects are run simultaneously (`--project=*`); when running a single project, the global worker count is used.

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 51)  [community]

**Gotcha 170 — Vitest `aroundEach` Without Calling `runTest()` Silently Skips the Test Body — The Test is Reported as Passed**  [community]
Vitest 4.1's `aroundEach(async (runTest) => { ... })` hook requires the test author to explicitly call `await runTest()` inside the callback to execute the test body. WHY this causes invisible flakiness: if `runTest()` is accidentally omitted (e.g., a refactor removes the call while leaving the `aroundEach` shell), the test body never executes — but Vitest reports the test as "passed" because the `aroundEach` callback itself completed without throwing. This creates a false-green test that provides no coverage guarantees and will not surface real regressions. Unlike `beforeEach`/`afterEach` which always run the test regardless of hook logic, `aroundEach` delegates test execution entirely to the callback author. Fix: add an ESLint custom rule or code review checklist item to verify that every `aroundEach` callback contains a `runTest()` invocation; the Vitest team has indicated a warning for missing `runTest()` is planned for a future release.

**Gotcha 171 — Playwright `page.requests()` Returns a Stale Snapshot — Requests Added After the Call Are Not Included**  [community]
`page.requests()` captures a snapshot of the 100 most recent requests at the moment it is called, not a live view. WHY this causes test flakiness: a test that calls `page.requests()` immediately after a user action, then asserts that a specific request was made, may find the request missing from the snapshot if the request is still in-flight at the time of the call — the response has not yet arrived, so Playwright has not yet fully recorded the request's lifecycle. Tests that pass on fast local machines (where the action + request + response roundtrip completes in under 5ms) can fail on slower CI environments where the request is still pending when `requests()` is called. Fix: use `page.waitForResponse(predicate)` to wait for the specific response before calling `page.requests()`, ensuring the request is fully resolved before snapshotting.

**Gotcha 172 — Jest `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` Does Not Reset Mocks Set Before the Isolated Scope — `jest.spyOn` Calls Outside the Callback Persist**  [community]
`jest.isolateModulesAsync()` creates a fresh module registry inside its callback, but it does not reset spy state on modules imported outside the callback. WHY this causes cross-test contamination: if a previous test used `jest.spyOn(someModule, 'fetchData')` to mock a method, that spy is still active in the outer module registry. When the next test uses `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` to re-import the same module, it gets a fresh registry copy — but any shared utility module (like a logger or config singleton) that both the isolated module and outer tests share remains contaminated by the spy. The isolated import does not undo side effects on objects that were passed by reference across registry boundaries. Fix: call `jest.restoreAllMocks()` in `afterEach` and `jest.clearAllMocks()` in `beforeEach`, even when using `isolateModulesAsync` — the mock reset lifecycle is orthogonal to the module registry isolation lifecycle.

**Gotcha 173 — Playwright `page.clock.install()` After `page.goto()` Does Not Retroactively Freeze Time for Already-Executed JavaScript**  [community]
`page.clock.install({ time: frozenTime })` patches `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `performance.now()` in the browser context. WHY installing after navigation causes split-state flakiness: JavaScript that ran during `page.goto()` — including module-level code, framework initialization, and component constructors — executed before the clock was installed and captured real `Date.now()` values. When the clock is subsequently frozen, those already-captured timestamps are stale real-time values while new `Date.now()` calls return the frozen time. Code that computes "elapsed time" as `Date.now() - capturedAt` will see enormous elapsed values (real wall-clock time minus a frozen anchor), causing expiry checks, TTL calculations, and debounce guards to behave incorrectly. Fix: always call `page.clock.install()` before `page.goto()` — it is the first action in every time-sensitive test.

**Gotcha 174 — Vitest `detectAsyncLeaks` False-Positives From Shared Worker-Scoped Fixtures — Singleton Connections Reported as Leaks Between Tests**  [community]
Vitest 4.1's `detectAsyncLeaks` uses `node:async_hooks` to track async resources opened per-test. WHY it generates false-positives for worker-scoped fixtures: a database connection pool or Redis client initialized in a `worker`-scoped fixture (created once per worker, shared across all tests in that worker) keeps an async handle open for the entire worker lifetime. `detectAsyncLeaks` sees this handle as "opened during test A but not closed before test A ended" and reports it as a leak — even though the handle is intentionally long-lived and will be properly torn down in the worker-scoped fixture's cleanup phase. This generates noisy "Async leak detected" failures for every test that uses the shared fixture, masking genuine leaks in non-fixture code. Fix: move long-lived shared resources into worker-scoped fixtures rather than `beforeAll` hooks — Vitest's leak detector is aware of fixture lifecycle and does not report worker-scoped fixture handles as leaks (this behavior is documented in the Vitest 4.1 release notes as the canonical migration path from `beforeAll` to worker-scoped fixtures).
