## Cycle 53 — 2026-05-14
<!-- sources: WebFetch live — playwright.dev/docs/test-retries, playwright.dev/docs/best-practices, playwright.dev/docs/release-notes, playwright.dev/docs/test-timeouts, jestjs.io/docs/timer-mocks, vitest.dev/guide/browser, vitest.dev/guide/snapshot, vitest.dev/config, testing.googleblog.com/2020/12/test-flakiness-one-of-main-challenges.html, testing.googleblog.com/2016/05/flaky-tests-at-google-and-how-we.html, martinfowler.com/articles/nonDeterminism.html -->

### Pattern 446 — Playwright `test.describe.configure({ retries })` for Cascading Retry Tiers

Playwright's global `retries` value in `playwright.config.ts` applies uniformly across all tests, but within a suite you can override with `test.describe.configure({ retries: N })`. This lets you express retry semantics at the suite level: a heavily state-dependent auth suite can get 3 retries while a stateless unit-style route-handler spec gets 0, giving teams a fine-grained retry budget without splitting configuration files.

```typescript
// tests/auth/login.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Auth flows depend on external token refresh — allow more retries
test.describe.configure({ retries: 3 });

test.describe('OAuth login flow', () => {
  test('redirects to provider on unauthenticated access', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/dashboard');
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/auth\/login/);
  });

  test('exchanges code for session cookie', async ({ page, request }) => {
    // Exchange step can hit token-service latency spikes
    const response = await request.post('/api/auth/callback', {
      data: { code: 'test_code', state: 'csrf_token' },
    });
    expect(response.ok()).toBe(true);
    await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="user-menu"]')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Per-describe retries compound with global retries — a describe-level `retries: 3` inside a config with `retries: 1` does NOT add to 4; the describe value overrides the global for tests within that block. Misunderstanding this leads to teams thinking tests get extra coverage when the global budget is silently consumed. Always document the retry tier rationale inline and keep retry counts ≤ 3 to prevent masking genuine regressions. [official]

---

### Pattern 447 — Jest `jest.runOnlyPendingTimers()` for Recursive Timer Safety

`jest.runAllTimers()` executes all timers synchronously including any newly-created timers during execution, causing infinite loops when recursive `setTimeout` patterns (polling loops, debounce re-schedules, heartbeat intervals) are present. `jest.runOnlyPendingTimers()` executes only the timers that are currently queued at the moment of the call — it does not execute timers created as a side effect of executing the current queue, stopping one generation at a time.

```typescript
// src/poller.ts
export function startPoller(
  fetchFn: () => Promise<void>,
  intervalMs: number,
): () => void {
  let handle: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>;
  const schedule = () => {
    handle = setTimeout(async () => {
      await fetchFn();
      schedule(); // recursive re-schedule — would cause jest.runAllTimers() infinite loop
    }, intervalMs);
  };
  schedule();
  return () => clearTimeout(handle);
}

// src/poller.test.ts
import { startPoller } from './poller';

jest.useFakeTimers();

test('poller calls fetchFn each interval without infinite loop', async () => {
  const fetchFn = jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined);
  startPoller(fetchFn, 1000);

  expect(fetchFn).not.toHaveBeenCalled();

  // Safe: only fires the currently-queued timer, not newly-created re-schedules
  jest.runOnlyPendingTimers();
  await Promise.resolve(); // flush microtasks after async fetchFn

  expect(fetchFn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);

  jest.runOnlyPendingTimers();
  await Promise.resolve();

  expect(fetchFn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Because `runOnlyPendingTimers()` processes one generation at a time, testing behavior after N intervals requires N explicit calls, making the test more verbose than `advanceTimersByTime(N * interval)`. However, it is the only safe option for recursive patterns — `runAllTimers()` with an uncapped recursion depth will throw "Aborting after running 100000 timers". Set `jest.useFakeTimers({ timerLimit: 50 })` for an earlier bailout during development to catch runaway recursion faster. [official]

---

### Pattern 448 — Playwright `page.waitForResponse()` Before Asserting on `page.requests()` Snapshot

`page.requests()` returns a snapshot of the most recent 100 requests at the moment of the call. If a test fires a user action that triggers a network request but immediately calls `page.requests()` before the response arrives, the request may appear in the snapshot without its completed state — or in worst-case timing scenarios on slow CI runners, the request may not yet be registered at all. The fix is to await `page.waitForResponse(predicate)` before reading the snapshot, ensuring the full request lifecycle (sent → received → recorded) is complete.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('analytics event is sent after form submission', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.fill('[data-testid="email"]', 'user@example.com');

  // Start waiting BEFORE the action that triggers the request
  const analyticsPromise = page.waitForResponse(
    (res) => res.url().includes('/api/analytics') && res.status() === 200,
  );

  await page.click('[data-testid="submit-btn"]');

  // Await the response BEFORE reading the snapshot — fully resolved lifecycle
  const analyticsResponse = await analyticsPromise;
  expect(analyticsResponse.ok()).toBe(true);

  // Now safe: all matching requests are fully registered in the snapshot
  const allRequests = page.requests();
  const analyticsRequests = allRequests.filter((r) =>
    r.url().includes('/api/analytics'),
  );
  expect(analyticsRequests).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(JSON.parse(await analyticsRequests[0].postData() ?? '{}')).toMatchObject({
    event: 'checkout_submit',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `waitForResponse` with a URL predicate can return a different request than intended if multiple requests match (e.g., paginated analytics batching). Use a precise predicate that checks both URL and response body shape, or consider `page.waitForRequest()` followed by `waitForResponse(request)` to tie the wait to the exact request object. Avoid setting `waitForResponse` timeout too short on CI — 30 s is safer than the 5 s default for analytics endpoints with batching delays. [official]

---

### Pattern 449 — Vitest Async Snapshot Concurrency Guard with Local `expect`

When concurrent tests (using `test.concurrent`) write to the same `.snap` file, Vitest's default `expect` from the global scope cannot distinguish which test owns which snapshot slot — snapshot collisions cause flaky assertion failures where Test A's actual value is matched against Test B's stored baseline. Vitest's fix is to use the `expect` instance from the per-test `TestContext` (`context.expect`) which carries the correct test identity for snapshot routing.

```typescript
import { describe, test, expect as globalExpect } from 'vitest';

// WRONG — concurrent tests share global expect; snapshot slot collision
describe.concurrent('formatters (wrong)', () => {
  test('formats currency', async () => {
    globalExpect(formatCurrency(1234.56, 'USD')).toMatchSnapshot(); // collision-prone
  });
  test('formats percent', async () => {
    globalExpect(formatPercent(0.856)).toMatchSnapshot(); // collision-prone
  });
});

// CORRECT — use context.expect for concurrent snapshot safety
describe.concurrent('formatters (correct)', () => {
  test('formats currency', async ({ expect }) => {
    expect(formatCurrency(1234.56, 'USD')).toMatchSnapshot();
  });

  test('formats percent', async ({ expect }) => {
    expect(formatPercent(0.856)).toMatchSnapshot();
  });

  test('formats date relative', async ({ expect }) => {
    const base = new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z');
    expect(formatRelativeDate(base, base)).toMatchSnapshot();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Switching from global `expect` to context `expect` requires refactoring every `test.concurrent` body that uses snapshots — large suites may have dozens of call sites. An ESLint rule checking for `toMatchSnapshot` called on non-context `expect` inside `describe.concurrent` blocks catches this mechanically. Note that `toMatchInlineSnapshot` is also affected: inline snapshots in concurrent tests must also use context `expect`. [official]

---

### Pattern 450 — Jest `jest.useFakeTimers({ doNotFake: ['performance'] })` for Accurate Performance Measurements

`jest.useFakeTimers()` by default replaces all timer-related globals including `performance.now()`, `performance.mark()`, and `performance.measure()`. When the code under test uses the Performance API to record timing spans (e.g., a custom profiler, an OpenTelemetry instrumentation wrapper, or a React profiler callback), faking `performance` causes all spans to report 0ms duration — making performance-sensitive assertions permanently trivially true and hiding regressions where an operation genuinely takes too long. `doNotFake: ['performance']` exempts `performance` from replacement while still controlling `setTimeout`/`setInterval`.

```typescript
import { measureOperation } from './profiler';

// vitest.config.ts  (or jest.config.ts)
// fakeTimers: { doNotFake: ['performance'] }   ← applied globally

describe('operation profiler', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    jest.useFakeTimers({
      doNotFake: ['performance'], // keeps real performance.now()
    });
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    jest.useRealTimers();
  });

  test('records span duration above minimum threshold', async () => {
    const spans: PerformanceEntry[] = [];
    performance.setResourceTimingBufferSize(200);

    // This uses performance.mark() internally — would be broken if faked
    await measureOperation('heavy-compute', async () => {
      await Promise.resolve(); // simulate async work
    });

    const entries = performance.getEntriesByName('heavy-compute');
    expect(entries).toHaveLength(1);
    // duration is real — not spoofed to 0ms by timer mocks
    expect(entries[0].duration).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Keeping real `performance.now()` means that test assertions on duration thresholds can fail on heavily-loaded CI machines where everything runs slower. Use `toBeGreaterThan(0)` and `toBeLessThan(hardUpperBound)` rather than exact durations — this validates the profiler is recording correctly without asserting specific wall-clock values that are environment-dependent. For strict performance regression tests, use a dedicated benchmarking tool (Vitest bench, Playwright tracing) rather than unit-test duration assertions. [official]

---

### Pattern 451 — Playwright `page.clock.install()` Called Before `page.goto()` for Split-State-Free Time Testing

`page.clock.install({ time: frozenTime })` patches `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `performance.now()` in the browser context. If called after `page.goto()`, all JavaScript that executed during navigation (module initializers, framework bootstrap, component constructors) already captured real `Date.now()` values. Those stale real timestamps interact with the frozen clock to produce enormous computed durations in expiry checks, TTL calculations, and debounce guards. Installing the clock before navigation ensures every timestamp in the page shares the same frozen anchor.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('session expiry banner appears after 30 minutes of inactivity', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  const frozenNow = new Date('2026-03-15T10:00:00Z');

  // CRITICAL: install clock BEFORE goto — all JS in the page uses frozen time
  await page.clock.install({ time: frozenNow });
  await page.goto('/app');

  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="session-banner"]')).not.toBeVisible();

  // Advance 29 minutes — banner should still be hidden
  await page.clock.fastForward('29:00');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="session-banner"]')).not.toBeVisible();

  // Advance 1 more minute — crosses 30-minute threshold
  await page.clock.fastForward('01:00');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="session-banner"]')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="session-banner"]')).toContainText(
    'Your session will expire',
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Installing the clock before navigation prevents any real-time-based health checks, service worker caching decisions, or browser-native timing APIs from working naturally. If the page's startup sequence requires real time (e.g., a WebSocket heartbeat that needs at least 100ms to establish), use `page.clock.pauseAt(frozenNow)` and `page.clock.resume()` after the warmup rather than `install()` — `pauseAt` freezes time at a specific moment but allows explicit advancement without affecting the clock state before the pause. [official]

---

### Pattern 452 — Vitest `vi.spyOn` with `using` Keyword for Auto-Restored Spies

Vitest 3.2+ supports ECMAScript explicit resource management (`using` keyword). `vi.spyOn` returns a disposable whose `[Symbol.dispose]()` method calls `mockRestore()`. Declaring spies with `using` guarantees restoration at the end of the containing block scope, even when the test throws — eliminating the need for `afterEach(() => vi.restoreAllMocks())` boilerplate and preventing cross-test mock contamination when a test fails midway.

```typescript
import { describe, test, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import * as emailService from './email-service';
import { notifyUser } from './notify';

describe('notifyUser', () => {
  test('sends email on successful notification', async () => {
    // 'using' auto-restores the spy when block exits, even on throw
    using sendEmailSpy = vi.spyOn(emailService, 'sendEmail').mockResolvedValue({
      messageId: 'test-id-123',
      accepted: ['user@example.com'],
    });

    await notifyUser({ userId: 'u1', channel: 'email', message: 'Hello' });

    expect(sendEmailSpy).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(sendEmailSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ to: 'user@example.com' }),
    );
    // spy auto-restored here — no afterEach needed
  });

  test('falls back to push when email fails', async () => {
    using sendEmailSpy = vi.spyOn(emailService, 'sendEmail').mockRejectedValue(
      new Error('SMTP timeout'),
    );
    const pushSpy = vi.spyOn(emailService, 'sendPush').mockResolvedValue(undefined);

    await notifyUser({ userId: 'u1', channel: 'email', message: 'Hello' });

    expect(sendEmailSpy).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(pushSpy).toHaveBeenCalledOnce(); // fallback triggered
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `using` keyword requires TypeScript ≥ 5.2 with `"target": "ES2022"` and `"lib": ["ES2022", "ES2022.Disposable"]` in `tsconfig.json`. Projects on older TypeScript versions or Babel transpilation without the disposable plugin cannot use this pattern and must continue with `afterEach(() => vi.restoreAllMocks())`. Note also that `using` is block-scoped — spies declared at the top of a test function persist only until that function returns; spies that must outlive the declaring block (e.g., created in a helper and used across multiple statements) still require manual management. [official]

---

### Pattern 453 — Playwright `webServer.wait` Regex for CI Service Readiness Detection

Playwright's `testConfig.webServer.wait` accepts a regex pattern that is matched against the server's stdout/stderr output to determine readiness. When `waitForURL` is unavailable (the service does not expose an HTTP health endpoint) or unreliable (the health endpoint returns 200 before the service is actually ready to accept test traffic), `wait` provides a deterministic readiness signal — test execution begins only after the exact startup log line appears, eliminating arbitrary `sleep` statements or polling loops in CI pipeline YAML.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run start:test-server',
    port: 3001,
    timeout: 120_000,
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,

    // Wait for this exact log line before running any tests (v1.57+)
    // Matches: "Server listening on port 3001 — ready"
    wait: /Server listening on port \d+ — ready/,
  },
  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:3001',
  },
});
```

```typescript
// Alternative: use for services with DB migration output
export default defineConfig({
  webServer: {
    command: 'node server/index.js',
    url: 'http://localhost:4000/health',
    // Also wait for the migration log — health endpoint returns 200 too early
    wait: /All migrations completed successfully/,
    timeout: 180_000,
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Matching on log output is brittle if the server changes its startup message format — a minor dependency upgrade that rewrites a log string will cause all tests to timeout waiting for a pattern that never appears. Prefer `waitForURL` to a health endpoint when available; use `wait` regex as a supplement when the service emits a known startup sequence that is part of a stable public API (e.g., a framework's boot message). Pin the regex to a non-version-specific portion of the log string (`/migrations completed/` rather than `/migrations completed in v\d+.\d+/`). [official]

---

### Pattern 454 — Jest `jest.runAllTimersAsync()` for Microtask-Correct Timer Draining

`jest.runAllTimers()` executes all pending timers synchronously but does not flush the microtask queue between timer callbacks. When timer callbacks contain `await` expressions or return Promises (e.g., a retry loop that calls `await fetch()` then reschedules with `setTimeout`), the microtask queue is never flushed between timer invocations — async callbacks appear to run synchronously with no awaited work completing. `jest.runAllTimersAsync()` (Jest 29.5+) interleaves microtask flushes between each timer callback, matching the real event-loop execution order.

```typescript
import { exponentialBackoffRetry } from './retry';

jest.useFakeTimers();

test('exponential backoff retries 3 times with correct delays', async () => {
  const apiCall = jest
    .fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('503'))
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('503'))
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('503'))
    .mockResolvedValue({ data: 'ok' });

  const retryPromise = exponentialBackoffRetry(apiCall, {
    maxRetries: 3,
    baseDelayMs: 1000,
    multiplier: 2,
  });

  // runAllTimersAsync flushes microtasks between each timer callback
  // — each awaited fetch() rejection is properly awaited before the next timer fires
  await jest.runAllTimersAsync();

  const result = await retryPromise;
  expect(result).toEqual({ data: 'ok' });
  expect(apiCall).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(4); // 3 failures + 1 success
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `runAllTimersAsync()` is inherently async — the test must `await` it, which requires the test function to be `async`. Tests that previously used synchronous `jest.runAllTimers()` need refactoring. More importantly, `runAllTimersAsync()` still suffers from the same infinite-loop risk as `runAllTimers()` for recursive timers — use `jest.runOnlyPendingTimersAsync()` (also Jest 29.5+) when the code under test reschedules itself to process one generation at a time while still flushing microtasks. [official]

---

### Pattern 455 — Playwright Serial Mode with `test.describe.serial()` for Stateful Multi-Step Flows

Playwright tests run in parallel by default, but multi-step flows that build shared state (a wizard with 5 pages, a checkout funnel, a setup/teardown sequence for slow external resources) benefit from `test.describe.serial()` to enforce execution order within the describe block. When running serially, Playwright retries the entire group from the first failing test — ensuring state built by earlier steps is present for later ones.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// All tests in this block run sequentially in declaration order
// If step 2 fails, step 3 is not attempted; on retry, step 1 runs again first
test.describe.serial('new user onboarding wizard', () => {
  test('step 1: creates account', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/signup');
    await page.fill('[name="email"]', 'wizard-test@example.com');
    await page.fill('[name="password"]', 'SecureP@ss1');
    await page.click('[data-testid="create-account-btn"]');
    await expect(page).toHaveURL('/onboarding/step-1');
  });

  test('step 2: completes profile', async ({ page }) => {
    // Relies on session from step 1 — only safe because of serial mode
    await page.goto('/onboarding/step-1');
    await page.fill('[name="displayName"]', 'Test User');
    await page.selectOption('[name="timezone"]', 'America/New_York');
    await page.click('[data-testid="next-btn"]');
    await expect(page).toHaveURL('/onboarding/step-2');
  });

  test('step 3: connects integration', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/onboarding/step-2');
    await page.click('[data-testid="skip-integration-btn"]');
    await expect(page).toHaveURL('/dashboard');
    await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="welcome-banner"]')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Serial mode prevents parallelism for the entire describe block, reducing CI throughput for long flows. Each test in a serial block runs in a fresh browser context (Playwright's worker isolation is preserved), so state that must persist between steps needs to be externalized (session cookies via `storageState`, API-created records, shared files) rather than relying on in-memory page state from the previous test. Serial mode is the right tool for externally-stateful flows, not a substitute for proper test isolation in stateless scenarios. [official]

---

### Pattern 456 — Martin Fowler's Resource Pool Size-1 Trick for Immediate Leak Detection

Fowler's "Eradicating Non-Determinism in Tests" identifies resource leaks (unclosed DB connections, open file handles, unreleased sockets) as a primary source of test-suite-level flakiness that is invisible per-test but catastrophic across large suites. The diagnostic technique: configure all resource pools with `maxSize: 1` in the test environment. The first test that fails to release its resource causes the next test to block on acquisition — the leak becomes a deterministic hard failure traceable to the exact test that leaked, rather than a mysterious intermittent timeout 50 tests later.

```typescript
// test-setup/db-pool.ts  (test-environment-specific DB pool config)
import { Pool } from 'pg';

export const testPool = new Pool({
  connectionString: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL,
  // Size-1 forces immediate failure on leak — the leaking test hangs,
  // not some unrelated later test
  max: 1,
  // Short acquire timeout makes the hang surfaceable immediately
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 2000,
  // Idle timeout forces connection release between tests
  idleTimeoutMillis: 500,
});

// vitest.config.ts  (or jest.config.ts)
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    globalSetup: ['./test-setup/db-pool.ts'],
    // detectAsyncLeaks will catch the held connection as an async resource
    detectAsyncLeaks: true,
  },
});
```

```typescript
// leaky test — pool size 1 makes this fail immediately, not 50 tests later
test('fetches user record (leaky version)', async () => {
  const client = await testPool.connect();
  // BUG: no client.release() call — pool exhausted after this test
  const result = await client.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1', [1]);
  expect(result.rows[0].email).toBe('test@example.com');
  // Missing: client.release()
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Size-1 pools serialize all database access, eliminating any concurrency between test-level queries. On large suites with many DB-touching tests, this can dramatically increase total runtime (from 30 s to 5 min if hundreds of tests each need a sequential DB round-trip). Use size-1 only during leak-hunting mode, or configure it specifically for the CI environment where you suspect leaks. For normal CI runs, use a pool sized proportionally to `--workers` count and rely on `detectAsyncLeaks` for detection. [community]

---

### Pattern 457 — Vitest `test.todo()` + `test.fails()` as Structured Flakiness Annotation

When a known-flaky test cannot be fixed immediately, teams often comment it out or delete it — losing the coverage signal and the engineering context. Vitest provides two alternatives: `test.todo('description')` marks tests as acknowledged-not-yet-written (no code runs) and `test.fails()` asserts that a test is expected to fail — if it starts passing, the test harness reports it as "unexpectedly succeeded," preventing silent flakiness fixes from going unnoticed. Using `test.fails()` on a quarantined test ensures the team is notified when the underlying issue is resolved.

```typescript
import { test, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { loadUserProfile } from './user-profile';

// Documents known flakiness with context — test still runs and validates it still fails
test.fails(
  'loadUserProfile handles concurrent cache invalidation without race condition',
  async () => {
    // This test reliably reproduces a race condition between cache.invalidate()
    // and cache.get() in high-concurrency scenarios. Tracked: JIRA-4892
    // When this test starts PASSING, JIRA-4892 is likely resolved — investigate.
    const promises = Array.from({ length: 20 }, (_, i) =>
      loadUserProfile(`user-${i % 3}`),
    );
    const results = await Promise.all(promises);
    // Should all return valid profiles — currently fails with 'undefined' for some
    for (const result of results) {
      expect(result).toMatchObject({ id: expect.any(String), email: expect.any(String) });
    }
  },
);

// Documents planned coverage without polluting test output with skips
test.todo('loadUserProfile retries on 429 with exponential backoff (JIRA-4901)');
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.fails()` marks the test as expected to fail — if CI configuration treats "expected failure" as a green signal, the test provides no regression gate while still consuming test runtime. Teams must periodically review `test.fails()` annotations (a scheduled "flakiness review" sprint item) to ensure quarantined tests are either fixed or formally removed. Do not use `test.fails()` as a permanent state — set a maximum quarantine duration (e.g., 2 sprints) after which the test must either be fixed or promoted to `test.skip()` with full bug-ticket documentation. [official]

---

### Pattern 458 — Google's Four Synchronization Primitives Mapped to Playwright Locators

Google's Testing Blog identifies four fundamental synchronization checks that any resilient E2E test framework must support: (1) element exists now, (2) element does not exist now, (3) element appears within N ms, (4) element remains absent within N ms. Playwright's locator API expresses all four directly via web-first assertions, replacing manual polling loops with deterministic assertion retries that respect the configured `expect.timeout`.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('demonstrates all four synchronization primitives', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/notifications');

  // 1. Element EXISTS now — immediate check, no retry needed
  //    (but toBeVisible() retries internally, handling race with DOM insertion)
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="inbox-panel"]')).toBeVisible();

  // 2. Element does NOT exist now — absence assertion with retry
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="unread-badge"]')).not.toBeVisible();

  // 3. Element APPEARS within N ms — triggers an async action, waits up to timeout
  await page.click('[data-testid="load-new-btn"]');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="new-notification"]')).toBeVisible({
    timeout: 10_000, // wait up to 10s for new notification to appear
  });

  // 4. Element REMAINS ABSENT within N ms — stability assertion
  //    ensure no error toast appears for 3 seconds after a benign action
  await page.click('[data-testid="mark-all-read-btn"]');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="error-toast"]')).not.toBeVisible({
    timeout: 3_000,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** All four locator assertions use Playwright's internal polling mechanism (retrying every 100 ms by default), so they consume real time waiting for the timeout to expire when asserting absence. For assertions of type 2 and 4, if you expect an element to be absent immediately, add `{ timeout: 500 }` rather than relying on the 5-second default — a false absence that eventually clears will appear to pass but wastes 4.5 seconds of CI time per test. Playwright's `toHaveCount(0)` is an alternative for absence that also retries. [community]

---

### Pattern 459 — Playwright `test.slow()` vs `testInfo.setTimeout()` for Dynamic Timeout Extension

`test.slow()` triples the current timeout (both test timeout and expect timeout), making it a blunt instrument. `testInfo.setTimeout(newMs)` sets an absolute timeout, which is safer when you know the exact budget needed. In fixtures or `beforeEach` hooks that perform slow operations (large database seeds, container warmup), use `testInfo.setTimeout(testInfo.timeout + extraMs)` to add time rather than replace the total — this preserves any per-test timeout overrides already applied by the test body.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// fixture that seeds a large dataset
const slowTest = test.extend<{ largeDataset: void }>({
  largeDataset: async ({ page }, use, testInfo) => {
    // Add 45s for seeding on top of whatever timeout the test declared
    testInfo.setTimeout(testInfo.timeout + 45_000);

    await page.request.post('/api/test/seed-large-dataset', {
      data: { records: 10_000 },
    });

    await use();

    await page.request.delete('/api/test/cleanup-dataset');
  },
});

slowTest(
  'paginated table renders all 10,000 records across pages',
  async ({ page, largeDataset }) => {
    // test body's 30s timeout + fixture's 45s addon = 75s total
    await page.goto('/admin/records');
    await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="record-count"]')).toContainText(
      '10,000 records',
    );
  },
);
```

**Tradeoff.** `testInfo.setTimeout()` inside a fixture sets the timeout for the entire test (fixture setup + test body + teardown). If the additive calculation is done in `beforeEach` instead of a fixture, the teardown time is not included in the extension — a slow teardown can still timeout. Prefer fixtures over `beforeEach` for slow setup/teardown that requires timeout extension, as fixture teardown runs within the same timeout budget as fixture setup. [official]

---

### Pattern 460 — Vitest `globalSetup` + `teardown` Export for One-Time Expensive Fixture Initialization

Vitest's `globalSetup` configuration accepts a module path whose default export receives the project config and whose named export `teardown` runs after all workers complete. This is the correct home for truly global resources (database container spin-up, shared OAuth server, S3 mock bucket creation) that would be prohibitively expensive to initialize per-worker or per-test. Unlike `beforeAll` in a test file, `globalSetup` runs in the main Vitest process, outside of worker isolation, with access to full process environment.

```typescript
// test-setup/global.ts
import { startTestDatabase } from './database';
import type { GlobalSetupContext } from 'vitest/node';

let dbContainer: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof startTestDatabase>>;

export default async function setup(config: GlobalSetupContext) {
  // Runs once in the main process — expensive container init happens here
  dbContainer = await startTestDatabase({
    image: 'postgres:16-alpine',
    port: 5433,
  });

  // Expose connection string to all workers via provide()
  config.provide('TEST_DATABASE_URL', dbContainer.connectionString);
  process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL = dbContainer.connectionString;
}

export async function teardown() {
  // Runs after all workers complete — cleanup expensive resources here
  await dbContainer?.stop();
}

// test-setup/inject.ts  (consumed in tests via inject())
import { inject } from 'vitest';

export const getTestDbUrl = () => inject('TEST_DATABASE_URL');
```

**Tradeoff.** `globalSetup` runs in the main process and cannot access Vitest test utilities (`vi`, `expect`, `describe`) — it is pure setup/teardown infrastructure code. Values provided via `config.provide()` are serialized across the worker boundary using `structuredClone`, so only JSON-serializable values can be passed (connection strings, port numbers, config objects — not class instances or functions). If workers need access to non-serializable shared resources, use a sidecar pattern: expose the resource via a local HTTP endpoint or IPC channel rather than direct object sharing. [official]

---

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 53)  [community]

**Gotcha 175 — `jest.runAllTimers()` Causes Infinite Loop with Recursive `setTimeout` — Reports "Aborting after running 100000 timers"**  [community]
`jest.runAllTimers()` exhaustively drains the timer queue including any timers created by executing the current queue. WHY this causes indefinite infinite-loop failures: polling patterns and heartbeat loops that use `setTimeout` recursively to reschedule themselves after each tick will produce an unbounded queue — the method runs timer → timer registers successor → runs successor → successor registers another → and so on until the 100,000-timer hard limit throws an abort error. The failure message `"Aborting after running 100000 timers"` is cryptic to developers unfamiliar with the cause; they often add longer timeouts or increase `timerLimit` rather than switching to `runOnlyPendingTimers()`. Fix: use `jest.runOnlyPendingTimers()` for any timer under test that has recursive self-rescheduling behavior — it processes exactly one generation and stops, preventing unbounded queue growth.

**Gotcha 176 — Vitest `test.concurrent` with Global `expect` Causes Snapshot Slot Collisions — Random Failures on Re-Run**  [community]
`describe.concurrent` runs tests simultaneously in the same worker, but Vitest's global `expect` associates snapshot keys with the current running test ID. When two tests call `expect(value).toMatchSnapshot()` concurrently using the global `expect`, Vitest may associate both snapshots with the same test ID, causing one test's actual value to overwrite the other's stored baseline on the first write. WHY this produces intermittent failures: on the first run both snapshots are written (coincidentally) in the correct order; on subsequent runs the race condition resolves differently and one test's stored baseline no longer matches its actual value. Fix: always destructure `expect` from the test `context` parameter (`test('name', async ({ expect }) => { ... })`) inside any `describe.concurrent` block that uses snapshot assertions.

**Gotcha 177 — Playwright `webServer.url` Health Check Returns 200 Before Service Is Actually Ready — Tests Start Against Uninitialized Service**  [community]
Many web frameworks expose a `/health` endpoint that responds with `200 OK` as soon as the HTTP server is bound to the port — before database connections are established, migrations complete, or background job queues are initialized. WHY this causes intermittent test failures: `webServer.url` polling sees the 200 response and signals Playwright to start tests, but the first test to hit a DB-backed endpoint gets a connection error or "migrations not applied" error. On fast machines this gap is 200ms; on slow CI runners with cold storage it can be 30s — meaning local tests pass but CI is consistently flaky. Fix: use `webServer.wait` regex combined with `webServer.url` — the regex matches a log line emitted only after full initialization, and the URL check provides a lightweight liveness gate.

**Gotcha 178 — Fowler's Quarantine Numeric Limit Violated — Quarantine Queue Grows Unboundedly and Masks Genuine Regressions**  [community]
Martin Fowler recommends enforcing a hard numeric limit (e.g., ≤ 8 tests) on the quarantine suite and a time limit (e.g., max 1 week quarantined) before a test must be either fixed or deleted. WHY ignoring this creates a confidence collapse: organizations that use `test.skip()` or `.only` flags without enforcement gradually quarantine dozens or hundreds of tests. The quarantine suite becomes a graveyard — the team stops investigating failures because "it's probably a flaky test," genuinely broken features slip through, and the value of the CI green signal collapses. Fix: track quarantined tests in a dedicated label/tag (e.g., Vitest `{ tags: ['quarantine'] }`) and add a CI gate that fails if the quarantine count exceeds the limit or any test has been quarantined longer than the allowed window.

**Gotcha 179 — `page.clock.fastForward()` Does Not Advance `performance.now()` When `doNotFake: ['performance']` Is Set — Clock-Dependent Profilers Break**  [community]
Using `page.clock.install()` with a custom `doNotFake` option excludes named globals from time patching. WHY this creates subtle split-clock flakiness: `page.clock.fastForward('30:00')` advances all patched clocks (`Date.now()`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`) but leaves `performance.now()` on real wall-clock time. Application code that blends both time sources (e.g., an animation timer that uses `performance.now()` for frame interpolation but `Date.now()` for session expiry) will experience timestamp divergence — the session expiry code thinks 30 minutes passed while the animation code thinks only 2ms passed (the real elapsed time). This causes animation-timing assertions to fail despite session-expiry assertions passing. Fix: do not mix `page.clock.install()` with `doNotFake` for performance-sensitive UI tests; instead use a real clock for performance.now()-dependent animation tests and the fake clock for session/expiry tests in separate test files.

## Quick Reference Additions (Cycle 53)

| Symptom | Likely Root Cause | Pattern/Fix | Anti-Pattern to Avoid |
|---------|-------------------|-------------|----------------------|
| CI hangs with "Aborting after running 100000 timers" in Jest | Recursive `setTimeout` reschedule + `jest.runAllTimers()` — unbounded queue | Pattern 447 (`runOnlyPendingTimers()` for one-generation timer drain) | `jest.runAllTimers()` with recursive timer patterns |
| Playwright `page.requests()` snapshot missing in-flight request | `page.requests()` snapped before request lifecycle completed | Pattern 448 (`waitForResponse()` before reading `page.requests()` snapshot) | Immediate `page.requests()` call right after triggering action |
| Concurrent Vitest snapshot tests have random failures on re-run | Global `expect` snapshot slot collision in `describe.concurrent` | Pattern 449 (context `expect` from test parameter for concurrent snapshot safety) | `import { expect } from 'vitest'` global inside `describe.concurrent` |
| Performance spans all report 0ms duration with Jest fake timers | `performance.now()` faked by `jest.useFakeTimers()` — all durations zeroed | Pattern 450 (`doNotFake: ['performance']` to preserve real Performance API) | Default `jest.useFakeTimers()` when code uses `performance.now()` for durations |
| Session expiry test passes locally but fails in CI — enormous computed durations | `page.clock.install()` called after `page.goto()` — split-state timestamps | Pattern 451 (install clock before `goto` — all JS uses frozen anchor) | `page.clock.install()` after navigation |
| Cross-test spy contamination when test throws before `afterEach` restore | `afterEach(() => vi.restoreAllMocks())` skipped on throw | Pattern 452 (`using` keyword auto-restore on block exit, even on throw) | Manual `afterEach` spy restore — skipped when test throws |
| CI tests start before DB migrations complete — service reports ready too early | `webServer.url` health endpoint returns 200 before full init | Pattern 453 (`webServer.wait` regex matching post-migration log line) | `webServer.url`-only readiness check for services with two-phase init |
| Async retry loop test fails because intermediate `await` results not committed | `jest.runAllTimers()` does not flush microtasks between timer callbacks | Pattern 454 (`jest.runAllTimersAsync()` interleaves microtask flushes) | `jest.runAllTimers()` for async timer callbacks |
| Multi-step wizard test fails at step 3 because step 2 state not present | Tests run in parallel — step 2's state not built before step 3 starts | Pattern 455 (`test.describe.serial()` for ordered stateful multi-step flows) | Assuming test declaration order = execution order without serial mode |
| DB connection leak causes 50th test to hang — leak invisible on individual test | Leaked connection exhausts pool — starvation happens in an unrelated test | Pattern 456 (Pool `max: 1` + `detectAsyncLeaks` for immediate leak attribution) | Large pool that silently absorbs leaks until exhaustion |
| Quarantined flaky test starts passing — team unaware, issue resolved unnoticed | `test.skip()` with no coverage recovery mechanism | Pattern 457 (`test.fails()` for expected-failure annotation — passes are surfaced as unexpected success) | Commenting out or deleting flaky tests — coverage gap never recovered |
| Absence assertion accepts intermittently-present toast — wrong timeout | `not.toBeVisible()` with 5s default timeout — slow CI renders toast after assertion | Pattern 458 (short timeout for absence assertions, long timeout for appearance assertions) | Default `expect.timeout` for all assertion types |
| Fixture slow seed times out before test body runs | `test.slow()` triples current timeout — additive adjustment unavailable | Pattern 459 (`testInfo.setTimeout(testInfo.timeout + N)` in fixture for additive extension) | `test.slow()` when timeout extension must be proportional to existing budget |
| Database container initialized per-worker — 8 container starts slow CI by 4 min | `beforeAll` in test file initializes per-worker — not shared globally | Pattern 460 (Vitest `globalSetup` + `teardown` for one-time expensive resource init) | `beforeAll` in root describe for global infrastructure — runs once per worker, not once globally |

## Cycle 54 — 2026-05-14

### New Patterns

**Pattern 461: Playwright `test.describe.configure({ retries })` Per-Describe Retry Tiering** [official]
Different test scopes tolerate different amounts of flakiness. Network-dependent tests benefit from higher retry counts while pure unit-style Playwright tests rarely need more than one retry. Using per-describe retry overrides lets you apply aggressive retries only where environmental non-determinism is expected without polluting the global retry budget.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Pure interaction tests — deterministic, no retries needed
test.describe('Form validation', () => {
  test.describe.configure({ retries: 0 });
  test('shows error on empty submit', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/signup');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toBeVisible();
  });
});

// Network-dependent tests — external API may be slow
test.describe('Checkout flow', () => {
  test.describe.configure({ retries: 3 });
  test('completes payment via Stripe', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242 4242 4242 4242');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByText('Order confirmed')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 15_000 });
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Per-describe retries can mask genuine regressions inside the group if the retry count is too high. Audit retry counts at each release — if a group is consistently hitting retry > 0, treat it as a flakiness debt signal rather than an acceptable baseline.

---

**Pattern 462: Jest `jest.useFakeTimers({ timerLimit })` to Prevent Runaway Recursive Timer Loops** [official]
The default behavior of `jest.runAllTimers()` continues processing timers until the queue is empty, which is infinite for self-rescheduling timers. Setting `timerLimit` acts as a circuit breaker: the test fails with a clear error rather than hanging or silently consuming CPU for minutes.
```typescript
beforeEach(() => {
  jest.useFakeTimers({ timerLimit: 200 });
});

afterEach(() => {
  jest.useRealTimers();
  jest.clearAllTimers();
});

test('polling loop does not run away under fake timers', () => {
  const onPoll = jest.fn();

  // Simulates a polling heartbeat that reschedules every 500ms
  function startPoller() {
    const tick = () => {
      onPoll();
      setTimeout(tick, 500);
    };
    setTimeout(tick, 500);
  }

  startPoller();
  // Advance 5 seconds worth of ticks — safe because timerLimit prevents runaway
  jest.advanceTimersByTime(5_000);
  expect(onPoll).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(10);
});
```
Tradeoff: A `timerLimit` that is too low will cause legitimate timer chains to abort prematurely. Start at 200 and raise only if specific tests require deeper chains. Document the reason for any limit above 500 in a comment next to the `useFakeTimers` call.

---

**Pattern 463: Playwright Worker Restart on Retry via `testInfo.retry` + Fixture Teardown Guard** [official]
When Playwright retries a test it discards the worker process and browser, but custom fixtures retain their setup state unless explicitly guarded. Checking `testInfo.retry` inside fixture teardown lets you perform extra cleanup (flush caches, reset rate-limit counters) only on retried runs without paying the cost on every clean run.
```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const test = base.extend<{ cleanSession: void }>({
  cleanSession: [async ({ page }, use, testInfo) => {
    // On retry, wipe any server-side session caches that may have been poisoned
    if (testInfo.retry > 0) {
      await page.request.delete('/api/test/session-cache');
    }
    await use();
    // Aggressive teardown only on failure to preserve evidence on first pass
    if (testInfo.status !== testInfo.expectedStatus) {
      await page.screenshot({ path: `screenshots/retry-${testInfo.retry}.png` });
    }
  }, { auto: true }],
});

test('dashboard loads user data', async ({ page, cleanSession }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('user-greeting')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Auto-fixtures that fire delete/reset requests add latency on every retried test. Scope the cleanup to only the specific resources that are known to poison retries — avoid blanket "reset everything" teardown that defeats the purpose of worker reuse.

---

**Pattern 464: Vitest `--no-isolate` + Explicit Module Reset for Performance-Critical Suites** [official]
Vitest's per-file VM isolation is the default and prevents cross-test module contamination, but it imposes a non-trivial per-file overhead for large module graphs. For test files whose modules have no cross-test side effects, disabling isolation and calling `vi.resetModules()` in `beforeEach` achieves near-identical isolation guarantees at a fraction of the startup cost.
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — apply selectively via project configuration
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      {
        // Isolated (default) — for tests that mutate module-level state
        include: ['src/**/*.spec.ts'],
        isolate: true,
      },
      {
        // Fast path — for pure-function utility tests with no module side effects
        include: ['src/utils/**/*.fast.spec.ts'],
        isolate: false,
        globals: true,
      },
    ],
  },
});
```
```typescript
// src/utils/parser.fast.spec.ts
import { beforeEach, describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';

beforeEach(() => {
  // Manual module reset replaces VM isolation overhead
  vi.resetModules();
});

describe('parseAmount', () => {
  it('handles locale-specific decimals', async () => {
    const { parseAmount } = await import('./parser');
    expect(parseAmount('1.234,56', 'de-DE')).toBe(1234.56);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `--no-isolate` with manual `vi.resetModules()` is only safe for modules that do not register global listeners, timers, or process hooks at import time. Any module that calls `process.on()`, `setInterval()`, or patches `globalThis` at the module level will leak across tests. Audit imports before applying this pattern.

---

**Pattern 465: Jest `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()` for Deterministic `requestAnimationFrame` Testing** [official]
`requestAnimationFrame` callbacks are driven by the browser's rendering pipeline in real environments, but in Jest's JSDOM they are queued as fake timer entries. `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()` advances fake time by exactly 16ms (one ~60fps frame), firing any enqueued `rAF` callbacks in order without needing to know the exact frame timing.
```typescript
import { jest } from '@jest/globals';
import { scheduleAnimation } from './animator';

beforeEach(() => {
  jest.useFakeTimers();
});

afterEach(() => {
  jest.useRealTimers();
});

test('animates element opacity over 3 frames', () => {
  const el = document.createElement('div');
  el.style.opacity = '0';
  document.body.appendChild(el);

  scheduleAnimation(el, { from: 0, to: 1, frames: 3 });

  expect(el.style.opacity).toBe('0'); // not yet started

  jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame(); // frame 1
  expect(parseFloat(el.style.opacity)).toBeCloseTo(0.33, 1);

  jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame(); // frame 2
  expect(parseFloat(el.style.opacity)).toBeCloseTo(0.66, 1);

  jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame(); // frame 3
  expect(parseFloat(el.style.opacity)).toBeCloseTo(1.0, 1);
});
```
Tradeoff: Each `advanceTimersToNextFrame()` call is always exactly 16ms regardless of the system's actual rendering rate. Code that reads `performance.now()` expecting a variable frame delta will behave differently under fake timers — combine with `doNotFake: ['performance']` or avoid performance-delta-sensitive logic in unit tests.

---

**Pattern 466: Playwright `page.clock.install()` Before Navigation for Single-Anchor Time State** [official]
Playwright's `page.clock` API intercepts browser-level time functions (`Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `performance.now`). Installing the clock after the page has already loaded creates a split-anchor state: timers registered during the initial page load use real time, while timers registered after clock installation use the fake anchor. Installing before `goto` ensures the entire page lifecycle uses one consistent time anchor.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('session expires after 30 minutes of inactivity', async ({ page }) => {
  // CORRECT: install clock before any navigation
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-01-01T10:00:00Z') });
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Simulate 30 minutes of inactivity
  await page.clock.fastForward('30:00');

  // Session expiry banner should appear
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /session expired/i }))
    .toBeVisible();

  // Verify the displayed expiry time uses the fake clock anchor
  await expect(page.getByTestId('expiry-time'))
    .toContainText('10:30:00');
});
```
Tradeoff: Installing the clock before navigation means the page's own bootstrap timers (e.g., telemetry pings, lazy-load triggers) also run under the fake clock and may behave differently than in production. If such timers interfere, use `page.clock.pauseAt()` to pause time at a specific instant and explicitly tick forward only when needed.

---

**Pattern 467: Playwright `webServer.wait` Regex for Two-Phase Service Readiness** [official]
Many Node.js servers emit an HTTP `200 OK` as soon as the port is bound, but critical initialization (DB migrations, connection pool warm-up, background workers) completes seconds later. Playwright's `webServer.wait` regexp matches against server stdout/stderr, allowing tests to wait for a log line that is only emitted after full initialization rather than trusting the HTTP health check alone.
```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  webServer: {
    command: 'node dist/server.js',
    url: 'http://localhost:3000/health',
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
    // Wait for the log line that signals migrations + pool warm-up completed
    wait: /Server ready — migrations applied, pool warmed/,
    timeout: 120_000,
  },
  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000',
  },
});
```
```typescript
// server.ts — emit the matching log line only after full init
async function bootstrap() {
  await runMigrations();
  await warmConnectionPool();
  app.listen(3000, () => {
    // This line matches the webServer.wait regex
    console.log('Server ready — migrations applied, pool warmed');
  });
}
bootstrap();
```
Tradeoff: The `wait` regex is matched against stdout/stderr in real time, so if the log line is buffered or emitted by a child process, Playwright may miss it. Always pipe child-process output to the parent's stdio (use `stdio: 'inherit'` in `child_process.spawn`) and ensure log lines are not suppressed in CI environments via `LOG_LEVEL` settings.

---

**Pattern 468: Vitest `fsModuleCache` Persistent Disk Cache for Large Module Graphs** [official]
For monorepos with deep module graphs, Vitest re-transforms all dependencies on every cold start. Enabling `experimental.fsModuleCache` persists the Vite transform cache to disk so that incremental reruns only transform changed modules. This directly reduces flakiness-induced retry costs by making re-runs faster and more consistent in timing.
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    experimental: {
      // Persist transformed module cache to disk — survives process restarts
      fsModuleCache: true,
    },
    // Combine with dir restriction to avoid scanning unrelated workspace packages
    dir: 'src',
    pool: 'threads', // threads pool typically faster than forks for large graphs
  },
});
```
```typescript
// CI pipeline — ensure cache is preserved across runs
// .github/workflows/test.yml
// - uses: actions/cache@v4
//   with:
//     path: node_modules/.vitest
//     key: vitest-cache-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
//     restore-keys: |
//       vitest-cache-
```
Tradeoff: The disk cache grows unboundedly until cleared. On CI, tie the cache key to a hash of `package-lock.json` or `pnpm-lock.yaml` so the cache is busted when dependencies change. A stale cache from a broken dependency upgrade can cause tests to run against wrong module versions, producing phantom failures that are hard to diagnose.

**Pattern 469: Vitest Test Sharding with Blob Reporter for Distributed Flakiness Triage** [official]
When a test suite is sharded across CI workers, a flaky test that only manifests on shard 3 can be invisible when reviewing individual shard results. Using Vitest's blob reporter on each shard and the `--merge-reports` command on the aggregation step produces a unified result set where per-shard flakiness patterns become visible.
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — used on each shard worker
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    reporters: ['blob'],
    outputFile: '.vitest-reports/results.json',
    // Each shard runs 1/N of the test files
    // Set via CLI: --shard=1/4, --shard=2/4, etc.
  },
});
```
```bash
# CI: run all shards in parallel
npx vitest run --shard=1/4 --reporter=blob --outputFile=.vitest-reports/shard-1.json
npx vitest run --shard=2/4 --reporter=blob --outputFile=.vitest-reports/shard-2.json
npx vitest run --shard=3/4 --reporter=blob --outputFile=.vitest-reports/shard-3.json
npx vitest run --shard=4/4 --reporter=blob --outputFile=.vitest-reports/shard-4.json

# Aggregate and report
npx vitest merge-reports .vitest-reports/ --reporter=html
```
Tradeoff: Blob reports require all shard outputs to be available before the merge step, which adds a synchronization point in the pipeline. If any shard times out and does not produce its blob file, the merge step will either fail or produce an incomplete report. Add a fallback that uploads partial results even on shard timeout.

**Pattern 470: Jest `jest.runAllTimersAsync()` for Microtask-Correct Async Timer Chains** [official]
`jest.runAllTimers()` is synchronous — it drains the timer queue but does not yield to the microtask queue between timer callbacks. Code that uses `await` inside `setTimeout` callbacks requires microtask flushes between each timer execution. `jest.runAllTimersAsync()` runs timers and interleaves `Promise.resolve()` flushes, ensuring `await`-using timer callbacks complete correctly.
```typescript
import { jest } from '@jest/globals';

jest.useFakeTimers();

async function retryWithBackoff(fn: () => Promise<void>, attempts = 3): Promise<void> {
  for (let i = 0; i < attempts; i++) {
    try {
      await fn();
      return;
    } catch {
      await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 1000 * 2 ** i));
    }
  }
  throw new Error('All retries exhausted');
}

test('retryWithBackoff retries on failure then succeeds', async () => {
  const action = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('fail'))
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('fail'))
    .mockResolvedValueOnce(undefined);

  const promise = retryWithBackoff(action);

  // runAllTimersAsync interleaves microtask flushes — await chain inside setTimeout resolves
  await jest.runAllTimersAsync();

  await promise;
  expect(action).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.runAllTimersAsync()` is only available from Jest 29.5+. In older projects use `jest.runAllTimers()` combined with manual `await Promise.resolve()` flushes — but this requires knowing exactly how many microtask rounds the implementation needs, making it fragile. Upgrade to Jest 29.5+ as the pragmatic fix.

---

**Pattern 471: Playwright `test.describe.serial()` for Stateful Multi-Step Wizard Tests** [official]
E2E tests for multi-step flows (checkout wizards, onboarding sequences) carry implicit state dependencies — step 3 requires step 2's server-side state to exist. Running these tests in parallel with the default `parallel` mode causes step 3 to start before step 2's server writes are committed. `test.describe.serial()` enforces sequential execution and retries the entire group together on failure, preserving the state chain.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' });

let orderId: string;

test('step 1 — add items to cart', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');
  await page.getByTestId('product-42').getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-count')).toHaveText('1');
});

test('step 2 — proceed to checkout and enter shipping', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  await page.getByLabel('Address').fill('123 Main St');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('shipping-confirmed')).toBeVisible();
});

test('step 3 — complete payment and capture order ID', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout/payment');
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242 4242 4242 4242');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();
  const idText = await page.getByTestId('order-id').textContent();
  orderId = idText ?? '';
  expect(orderId).toMatch(/^ORD-\d{6}$/);
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.describe.serial()` forfeits parallelism for the group. If step 1 takes 10s and step 3 takes 10s, the entire group takes 30s sequentially even if CI has idle workers. Reserve serial mode for tests that are genuinely stateful; refactor stateless E2E tests to use isolated auth fixtures so they can run in parallel.

---

**Pattern 472: Playwright `failOnFlakyTests` CI Gate to Enforce Zero-Flakiness Policy** [official]
Enabling `failOnFlakyTests: true` in `playwright.config.ts` causes the Playwright test runner to exit with a non-zero status code whenever any test passes on retry after an initial failure. This turns the CI green signal into a meaningful guarantee: a green build means no test needed a retry to pass, not just "eventual success after several attempts."
```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Zero-flakiness policy: fail CI if any test needed a retry to pass
  failOnFlakyTests: process.env.CI === 'true',
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,
  reporter: [
    ['html', { open: 'never' }],
    ['junit', { outputFile: 'test-results/results.xml' }],
  ],
  use: {
    trace: 'retain-on-failure',
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: `failOnFlakyTests` is only appropriate when the team has committed to investigating every flaky failure within the sprint. If the quarantine queue is already non-empty, enabling this flag immediately breaks CI. Phase it in: first tag known-flaky tests with `{ annotation: [{ type: 'flaky' }] }`, exclude them from the gate, then progressively fix and remove annotations until the gate covers the entire suite.

---

**Pattern 473: Playwright `retain-on-failure-and-retries` Trace Mode for Multi-Retry Comparison** [official]
When a test is retried, the default `retain-on-failure` trace mode captures only the last (final) run's trace. Using `retain-on-failure-and-retries` captures a separate trace file for every attempt, enabling side-by-side comparison of what differed between the flaky attempt and the eventual pass — often revealing the exact race condition or animation frame that caused the initial failure.
```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  retries: 2,
  use: {
    // Capture trace for every attempt on failure — enables multi-retry diff
    trace: 'retain-on-failure-and-retries',
    // Record video for visual diff alongside trace
    video: 'retain-on-failure',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
  },
  reporter: [
    ['html', { open: 'never', outputFolder: 'playwright-report' }],
  ],
});
```
Tradeoff: Capturing three trace files per flaky test run (initial + 2 retries) multiplies artifact storage requirements. On a suite with 50 flaky tests, each producing ~5MB traces, a CI run can generate 750MB of trace data. Apply this mode only in CI runs dedicated to flakiness investigation, not in the primary merge pipeline. Use `--shard` to route known-flaky tests to a separate job that always uses this trace mode.

---

**Pattern 474: Fowler's Pool-Size-1 Trick for Immediate Resource Leak Attribution** [community]
Martin Fowler recommends configuring any pooled resource (DB connections, HTTP agents, worker threads) to a maximum size of 1 during tests. With a pool of size 1, the first leaked resource immediately starves the next test that needs that resource — the failure is attributed to the test that leaked it, not the 50th unrelated test that happens to exhaust the pool later. This converts a deferred, intermittent failure into an immediate, deterministic one.
```typescript
// test-setup/db.ts
import { Pool } from 'pg';

let pool: Pool;

export function getPool(): Pool {
  if (!pool) {
    pool = new Pool({
      connectionString: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL,
      // Size 1: any leaked connection is immediately visible in the next test
      max: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'test' ? 1 : 10,
      // Short idle timeout surfaces slow leaks faster
      idleTimeoutMillis: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'test' ? 1_000 : 30_000,
      connectionTimeoutMillis: 3_000,
    });
  }
  return pool;
}
```
```typescript
// Typical test using the size-1 pool
afterEach(async () => {
  // This must run — if a test throws before releasing, the next test hangs here
  // revealing the leaking test rather than a random downstream test
  await getPool().query('ROLLBACK');
});
```
Tradeoff: Pool size 1 serializes all DB operations within a test, including those that would safely run concurrently in production. Tests that rely on parallel query execution to simulate real concurrency (e.g., optimistic locking conflict tests) must be refactored to use two separate pool instances or be run in a dedicated test project with a larger pool.

---

**Pattern 475: Google's Four Synchronization Primitives Mapped to Playwright Assertions** [community]
The Google Testing Blog identifies four fundamental synchronization patterns that, when applied consistently, eliminate the majority of timing-related flakiness. Each maps directly to a Playwright web-first assertion: existence now, absence now, existence within time, and absence within time. Encoding these four checks as typed test helpers enforces consistent timeout and polling semantics across the entire test suite.
```typescript
import { Page, Locator, expect } from '@playwright/test';

/**
 * Google's Four Synchronization Primitives — Playwright mapping
 *
 * 1. Object exists at this moment (no wait)
 * 2. Object does not exist at this moment (no wait)
 * 3. Object exists within max time (with polling)
 * 4. Object does not exist within max time (with polling)
 */

// Primitive 1: synchronous existence (element already in DOM and visible)
export async function assertPresentNow(locator: Locator): Promise<void> {
  await expect(locator).toBeVisible({ timeout: 0 });
}

// Primitive 2: synchronous absence (element already gone)
export async function assertAbsentNow(locator: Locator): Promise<void> {
  await expect(locator).not.toBeVisible({ timeout: 0 });
}

// Primitive 3: existence within timeout (element will appear within window)
export async function waitForPresence(
  locator: Locator,
  maxMs = 10_000,
): Promise<void> {
  await expect(locator).toBeVisible({ timeout: maxMs });
}

// Primitive 4: absence within timeout (element will disappear within window)
export async function waitForAbsence(
  locator: Locator,
  maxMs = 5_000,
): Promise<void> {
  // Short default — absence assertions rarely need long windows
  await expect(locator).not.toBeVisible({ timeout: maxMs });
}
```
Tradeoff: The synchronous primitives (1 and 2) with `timeout: 0` will fail immediately if the element is in an intermediate rendering state. Reserve them for assertions that follow an explicit `await` call that already waited for the state change — never use them as the first assertion after triggering an action.

---

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G180 — `jest.runAllTimers()` Hangs CI with "Aborting after running 100000 timers" When `setInterval` Is Used Without Cleanup**  [community]
`jest.runAllTimers()` processes the entire timer queue including any intervals registered via `setInterval`, which reschedule themselves indefinitely. WHY this causes CI freezes rather than fast failures: `setInterval` callbacks push new entries back into the timer queue faster than the 100,000-entry limit is reached, consuming CPU for tens of seconds before the abort fires — and on some CI machines the abort never fires because memory is exhausted first. The root cause is that `setInterval` is not semantically compatible with `runAllTimers()`. Fix: switch to `jest.advanceTimersByTime(N)` to advance time by a known bounded window, and call `jest.clearAllTimers()` in `afterEach` to tear down any lingering intervals.

**Gotcha G181 — Vitest `describe.concurrent` + `vi.spyOn` Without `using` Keyword Leaves Spies Restored Out of Order**  [community]
In `describe.concurrent` blocks, tests share the same worker and execute simultaneously. Manual `afterEach(() => vi.restoreAllMocks())` runs concurrently with still-executing tests in sibling concurrent blocks. WHY this causes intermittent assertion failures: the spy is restored in the middle of another test's execution — that test suddenly calls the real implementation instead of the mock, producing a failure that appears completely unrelated to the spy. Fix: use the TypeScript 5.2+ `using` keyword — `using spy = vi.spyOn(...)` — which ties the spy's restoration to the lexical block exit of each individual test, not to a shared `afterEach` that races with concurrent siblings.

**Gotcha G182 — Playwright `page.clock.install()` After `page.goto()` Produces Split-Time State: Some Timers Use Real Anchor, Others Use Fake Anchor**  [community]
JavaScript frameworks (React, Vue, Svelte) install their own timers during hydration (e.g., for error boundary retry loops, suspense timeouts, scheduler ticks). These timers are scheduled using real `Date.now()` as their base. WHY this creates ghost flakiness: when `page.clock.install()` is called after hydration, the framework's already-queued timers have expiry times in the past relative to the fake clock anchor, so they fire immediately on any `clock.tick()` call — causing spurious re-renders or error boundaries to trigger that would never fire in production. Fix: always call `page.clock.install()` before `page.goto()` so the framework's bootstrap lifecycle is fully bracketed inside the fake clock context.

**Gotcha G183 — Vitest `fsModuleCache` Stale Cache Causes Phantom Test Failures After Dependency Upgrade**  [community]
`experimental.fsModuleCache` writes transformed module content to `node_modules/.vitest/` keyed by file path and mtime. WHY this causes phantom failures after upgrades: when a dependency is upgraded, only the package's own files change mtime — transitive files that were previously compiled and cached may retain their old transform output. Vitest does not deep-invalidate the cache for all files that import a changed module, so tests that use the upgraded API surface may run against stale compiled code. Fix: add a `postinstall` script that runs `rm -rf node_modules/.vitest` after every `npm install`, and tie the CI cache key to a hash of the lockfile so the remote cache is busted whenever dependencies change.

**Gotcha G184 — Playwright `failOnFlakyTests` Breaks CI for Quarantined Tests That Were Expected to Be Flaky**  [community]
`failOnFlakyTests: true` applies to every test in the suite including those that are intentionally annotated as known-flaky. WHY this breaks CI unexpectedly after enabling: any test that passes on retry — even one the team already knows is flaky and is tracking — causes the build to fail, creating a situation where the CI is simultaneously "passing" and "breaking" for the same known-flaky test. Fix: tag known-flaky tests with `{ annotation: [{ type: 'known-flaky', description: 'TICKET-123' }] }` and pair `failOnFlakyTests` with a custom reporter that reads annotations and exempts tagged tests from the flakiness gate. The exemption should be time-boxed: the reporter should also fail the build if a `known-flaky` annotation references a ticket that was closed more than 2 weeks ago.
