**Pattern 507** — Vitest `vi.useFakeTimers` with `shouldAdvanceTime` for Mixed Real/Fake Clock Tests
`shouldAdvanceTime: true` causes the fake clock to auto-advance in sync with the real wall clock, allowing tests that mix real `await` sleeps with fake-timer assertions without the clock freezing at the install moment.
```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { PollingService } from './polling-service';

describe('PollingService', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true });
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });

  it('fires exactly 3 poll callbacks in 3 seconds', async () => {
    const onPoll = vi.fn();
    const svc = new PollingService({ intervalMs: 1000, onPoll });
    svc.start();

    // Advance fake clock 3 seconds worth of ticks
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(3000);

    expect(onPoll).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
    svc.stop();
  });

  it('does not fire after stop()', async () => {
    const onPoll = vi.fn();
    const svc = new PollingService({ intervalMs: 500, onPoll });
    svc.start();
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(499);
    svc.stop();
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1000);
    expect(onPoll).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `shouldAdvanceTime: true` ties fake-clock advancement to real elapsed time, so tests on slow CI runners may advance further than expected between assertions. For strict determinism, prefer manual `advanceTimersByTimeAsync` calls with `shouldAdvanceTime: false`.

---

**Pattern 508** — Jest `timerLimit` Circuit-Breaker for Recursive `setInterval` Chains
When a timer callback unconditionally reschedules itself, `jest.runAllTimers()` would loop forever. Setting `timerLimit` in `jest.useFakeTimers` caps the number of timer callbacks fired per `runAll*` call, turning an infinite hang into a bounded, catchable error.
```typescript
import { describe, test, expect, jest, beforeEach, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';
import { HeartbeatEmitter } from './heartbeat-emitter';

describe('HeartbeatEmitter', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    jest.useFakeTimers({ timerLimit: 50 });
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    jest.useRealTimers();
  });

  test('emits heartbeat every 100 ms up to the limit', () => {
    const emitter = new HeartbeatEmitter({ intervalMs: 100 });
    const beats: number[] = [];
    emitter.on('beat', (ts: number) => beats.push(ts));
    emitter.start();

    // Advance 5 seconds — 50 beats expected; timerLimit caps runAll at 50
    jest.advanceTimersByTime(5000);

    expect(beats).toHaveLength(50);
    emitter.stop();
  });

  test('stop() clears the interval — no further beats', () => {
    const emitter = new HeartbeatEmitter({ intervalMs: 200 });
    const beats: number[] = [];
    emitter.on('beat', (ts: number) => beats.push(ts));
    emitter.start();
    jest.advanceTimersByTime(600); // 3 beats
    emitter.stop();
    jest.advanceTimersByTime(1000); // no new beats
    expect(beats).toHaveLength(3);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: A `timerLimit` that is too low can mask legitimate scheduling logic that requires more than N callbacks to reach steady state. Set the limit conservatively (e.g., `iterations × 2`) rather than at the minimum expected count so unexpected recursion is still caught.

---

**Pattern 509** — Playwright Serial Retry with `test.describe.serial` and `testInfo.retry`-Conditional Skip
In a serial describe block, a retry reruns all sibling tests from the first failure. Use `testInfo.retry` inside an `beforeEach` to skip idempotent setup steps that are expensive and have already passed in a prior attempt.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe.serial('Checkout flow', () => {
  test.describe.configure({ retries: 1 });

  let orderId: string;

  test.beforeEach(async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
    if (testInfo.retry === 0 || testInfo.title === 'Add item to cart') {
      // Full login only on first attempt of the very first test
      await page.goto('/login');
      await page.fill('[name=email]', 'user@test.com');
      await page.fill('[name=password]', 'secret');
      await page.click('[type=submit]');
      await page.waitForURL('/home');
    }
  });

  test('Add item to cart', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/products/widget-pro');
    await page.click('button[data-action=add-to-cart]');
    await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=cart-count]')).toHaveText('1');
  });

  test('Proceed to checkout', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/cart');
    await page.click('button[data-action=checkout]');
    const url = page.url();
    orderId = url.split('/orders/')[1];
    await expect(page.locator('h1')).toHaveText('Order Summary');
  });

  test('Confirm order', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto(`/orders/${orderId}/confirm`);
    await page.click('button[data-action=confirm]');
    await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=order-status]')).toHaveText('Confirmed');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Sharing state via module-level variables (`orderId`) across serial tests creates implicit coupling — if the "Proceed to checkout" test is skipped or rearranged, `orderId` is undefined for "Confirm order". Always initialise shared vars to a safe sentinel and add an explicit guard in dependent tests.

---

**Pattern 510** — Vitest `vi.setSystemTime` + `vi.restoreAllMocks` for Date-Sensitive Unit Tests
`vi.setSystemTime` freezes `Date.now()` and `new Date()` to a fixed ISO timestamp, eliminating all clock-source flakiness in date-sensitive business logic tests. Pairing with `afterEach(() => vi.useRealTimers())` prevents bleed into adjacent test files.
```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { isSubscriptionExpired, daysUntilRenewal } from './subscription';

const FROZEN_DATE = new Date('2026-03-15T12:00:00.000Z');

describe('subscription helpers', () => {
  afterEach(() => {
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });

  it('detects an expired subscription', () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    vi.setSystemTime(FROZEN_DATE);
    const expiry = new Date('2026-03-01T00:00:00.000Z');
    expect(isSubscriptionExpired(expiry)).toBe(true);
  });

  it('calculates days until renewal correctly', () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    vi.setSystemTime(FROZEN_DATE);
    const renewal = new Date('2026-04-15T00:00:00.000Z');
    // 15 Mar → 15 Apr = 31 days
    expect(daysUntilRenewal(renewal)).toBe(31);
  });

  it('treats same-day expiry as expired', () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    vi.setSystemTime(FROZEN_DATE);
    expect(isSubscriptionExpired(FROZEN_DATE)).toBe(true);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Freezing system time at a fixed ISO string encodes the test's expected date logic into the constant — if the business rule changes (e.g., "expired" now means `>= expiryDate + 1 day`), the frozen constant must be updated together with the assertion. Document the intent of the frozen timestamp in a comment to avoid silent stale tests.

---

**Pattern 511** — Playwright `page.clock.install` Before Navigation for Load-Time Timer Control
Calling `page.clock.install()` before `page.goto()` ensures all timers scheduled during page load (e.g., auto-dismiss toasts, polling loops initialised in script tags) are intercepted by the fake clock and can be advanced deterministically.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('session-expiry warning appears after 25 minutes of inactivity', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install clock BEFORE navigation to intercept all load-time timers
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-03-15T09:00:00') });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Advance 25 minutes — triggers the inactivity warning timer
  await page.clock.fastForward('25:00');

  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=session-warning]')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=session-warning]')).toContainText('Your session will expire');
});

test('auto-dismiss toast vanishes after 3 seconds', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.clock.install({ time: Date.now() });
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Trigger a save action that shows the toast
  await page.click('[data-testid=save-btn]');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=toast]')).toBeVisible();

  // Advance exactly 3 seconds — toast auto-dismiss fires
  await page.clock.fastForward(3000);
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=toast]')).not.toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Installing the clock before navigation captures timers set by third-party scripts in the page as well, which can cause unexpected `fastForward` side-effects (e.g., analytics ping timers firing and making outbound requests). Use `page.route()` to intercept and short-circuit any third-party network calls that fire as clock side-effects.

---

**Pattern 512** — Jest `jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` for Async Timer Chain Drainage
`jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` advances the clock and allows microtask/promise queues to drain between ticks, making it correct for testing async code paths that schedule more async work inside timer callbacks.
```typescript
import { describe, test, expect, jest, beforeEach, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';
import { AsyncPoller } from './async-poller';

describe('AsyncPoller', () => {
  beforeEach(() => jest.useFakeTimers());
  afterEach(() => jest.useRealTimers());

  test('resolves after polling completes within timeout', async () => {
    let resolveExternal!: () => void;
    const externalReady = new Promise<void>(res => { resolveExternal = res; });

    const poller = new AsyncPoller({
      checkFn: async () => externalReady,
      intervalMs: 500,
      timeoutMs: 3000,
    });

    const resultPromise = poller.waitUntilReady();

    // Advance 1 second — 2 poll ticks, each await-ing externalReady
    await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1000);

    // Resolve the external condition mid-poll
    resolveExternal();

    // Drain remaining microtasks
    await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(0);

    await expect(resultPromise).resolves.toBeUndefined();
  });

  test('rejects with TimeoutError when condition never resolves', async () => {
    const poller = new AsyncPoller({
      checkFn: async () => new Promise(() => {}), // Never resolves
      intervalMs: 500,
      timeoutMs: 2000,
    });

    const resultPromise = poller.waitUntilReady();
    await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(2001);
    await expect(resultPromise).rejects.toThrow('Timeout');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `advanceTimersByTimeAsync` flushes the microtask queue between each fake-clock tick, which is slower than synchronous `advanceTimersByTime`. Use the async variant only when the code under test awaits inside timer callbacks; for pure-synchronous timer chains the synchronous variant is both correct and faster.

---

**Pattern 513** — Vitest `--detect-async-leaks` Flag for Surfacing Unawaited Promise Flakiness
Vitest's async-leak detection identifies tests that enqueue microtasks or macrotasks that outlive the test boundary, catching the "passes in isolation, fails in sequence" class of flakiness at its source.
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Enable async leak detection globally
    detectOpenHandles: true,
    // Pool configuration that maximises leak detection efficacy
    pool: 'forks',
    poolOptions: {
      forks: {
        isolate: true,
      },
    },
  },
});

// Example: test that would be flagged by leak detection
import { it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { startBackgroundSync } from './sync-service';

it('sync service initialises', async () => {
  const svc = startBackgroundSync({ intervalMs: 5000 });
  expect(svc.isRunning()).toBe(true);
  // BUG: svc.stop() is never called — the setInterval leaks into the next test
  // With detectOpenHandles: true, Vitest reports the dangling handle
});

// Correct version:
it('sync service initialises — clean', async () => {
  const svc = startBackgroundSync({ intervalMs: 5000 });
  expect(svc.isRunning()).toBe(true);
  await svc.stop(); // Clean up so the interval does not leak
});
```
Tradeoff: `detectOpenHandles` adds a handle-tracking layer to every async operation, increasing per-test overhead by 5–15% in handle-heavy suites. Prefer enabling it in a dedicated "leak audit" CI job run nightly rather than in the main fast-feedback pipeline.

---

**Pattern 514** — Playwright `route.abort()` for Network-Failure Flakiness Simulation
Systematically aborting specific network requests with `page.route()` + `route.abort()` lets you test your app's error-recovery paths deterministically without depending on real network outages, eliminating a major source of environment-specific flakiness.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('shows retry UI when analytics endpoint times out', async ({ page }) => {
  // Intercept analytics calls and abort them to simulate network failure
  await page.route('**/api/analytics/**', route => route.abort('timedout'));

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Core dashboard content loads despite analytics failure
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=revenue-chart]')).toBeVisible();

  // Error boundary for analytics shows retry button
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=analytics-error]')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=analytics-retry-btn]')).toBeVisible();
});

test('primary API failure shows full error state', async ({ page }) => {
  let callCount = 0;
  await page.route('**/api/orders', route => {
    callCount++;
    if (callCount <= 2) {
      // Fail first two attempts to test retry logic
      route.abort('failed');
    } else {
      route.continue();
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/orders');
  // After 2 failures, third attempt succeeds
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=orders-list]')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 10000 });
  expect(callCount).toBe(3);
});
```
Tradeoff: `route.abort()` terminates the request at the browser level, not at the network level — the app's `fetch` error handler receives an `AbortError` rather than a real timeout. If your error handling differentiates between error types (e.g., displaying different messages for timeout vs. DNS failure), verify that `route.abort('timedout')` triggers the correct code path.

---

**Pattern 515** — Vitest `test.concurrent` with `expect.soft` for Parallel Assertion Collection
Running concurrent subtests with `expect.soft` accumulates all failures within a test suite pass rather than aborting on the first failure, giving a complete picture of a flaky assertion batch in a single run.
```typescript
import { describe, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { fetchAllMetrics } from './metrics-client';

describe.concurrent('metrics API — all endpoints', () => {
  test('revenue endpoint returns valid shape', async ({ expect }) => {
    const data = await fetchAllMetrics('revenue');
    expect.soft(data).toHaveProperty('total');
    expect.soft(data.total).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0);
    expect.soft(data).toHaveProperty('currency', 'USD');
    expect.soft(data).toHaveProperty('period');
    // All soft assertions are collected — test reports all failures at once
  });

  test('user-count endpoint returns valid shape', async ({ expect }) => {
    const data = await fetchAllMetrics('users');
    expect.soft(data).toHaveProperty('active');
    expect.soft(data).toHaveProperty('total');
    expect.soft(data.active).toBeLessThanOrEqual(data.total);
  });

  test('latency endpoint returns numeric values', async ({ expect }) => {
    const data = await fetchAllMetrics('latency');
    expect.soft(typeof data.p50).toBe('number');
    expect.soft(typeof data.p95).toBe('number');
    expect.soft(typeof data.p99).toBe('number');
    expect.soft(data.p50).toBeLessThanOrEqual(data.p95);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.soft` continues test execution after a failing assertion, which means later assertions may produce misleading results if they depend on state that was already found to be invalid (e.g., asserting `data.active <= data.total` after `data.active` was already found to be `undefined`). Guard downstream soft assertions with a null check or use `expect.soft` only for independent properties.

---

**Pattern 516** — Jest `jest.spyOn` with `mockImplementationOnce` for Flaky Retry-on-Error Simulation
Mocking a dependency to fail a controlled number of times before succeeding lets you test retry logic deterministically without real I/O flakiness, confirming the exact call count and backoff behaviour.
```typescript
import { describe, test, expect, jest, beforeEach } from '@jest/globals';
import { fetchWithRetry } from './fetch-with-retry';
import * as httpClient from './http-client';

describe('fetchWithRetry', () => {
  beforeEach(() => jest.resetAllMocks());

  test('succeeds on third attempt after two 503 errors', async () => {
    const spy = jest.spyOn(httpClient, 'get')
      .mockImplementationOnce(() => Promise.reject(new Error('503 Service Unavailable')))
      .mockImplementationOnce(() => Promise.reject(new Error('503 Service Unavailable')))
      .mockImplementationOnce(() => Promise.resolve({ status: 200, data: { ok: true } }));

    const result = await fetchWithRetry('/api/data', { maxRetries: 3, backoffMs: 0 });

    expect(result).toEqual({ ok: true });
    expect(spy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
  });

  test('throws RetryExhausted after maxRetries failures', async () => {
    jest.spyOn(httpClient, 'get')
      .mockRejectedValue(new Error('Connection refused'));

    await expect(
      fetchWithRetry('/api/data', { maxRetries: 2, backoffMs: 0 })
    ).rejects.toThrow('RetryExhausted');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `backoffMs: 0` in the test removes real time delays but also bypasses the backoff algorithm itself — if backoff calculation contains a bug (e.g., overflow at high retry counts), this test will not catch it. Add a dedicated test that mocks `Date.now()` and verifies the backoff intervals are computed correctly.

---

**Pattern 517** — Playwright `expect.poll` for Eventually-Consistent State Assertions
`expect.poll` retries a predicate on a configurable interval until it passes or times out, replacing fragile `waitForFunction`/`sleep` patterns with a declarative, configurable assertion loop.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { apiClient } from './api-client';

test('job status transitions to completed within 30 seconds', async ({ page, request }) => {
  await page.goto('/jobs');

  // Trigger a long-running job
  const { jobId } = await (await request.post('/api/jobs', {
    data: { type: 'report-generation', params: { month: '2026-03' } },
  })).json();

  // Poll the API directly — no UI polling race
  await expect.poll(
    async () => {
      const res = await request.get(`/api/jobs/${jobId}`);
      const body = await res.json();
      return body.status;
    },
    {
      message: `Job ${jobId} did not complete within 30 s`,
      timeout: 30_000,
      intervals: [1_000, 2_000, 3_000, 5_000],
    }
  ).toBe('completed');

  // Now assert the UI reflects the completed state
  await page.reload();
  await expect(page.locator(`[data-job-id="${jobId}"] [data-testid=status]`)).toHaveText('Completed');
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.poll` with a short `intervals` array can generate many API calls in a tight window, increasing test-runner network load and potentially tripping rate-limit rules on shared staging environments. Use exponential backoff intervals (`[1000, 2000, 4000, 8000]`) rather than fixed intervals to reduce pressure while maintaining coverage.

---

**Pattern 518** — Vitest `vi.waitFor` with Custom Predicate for Async Event-Driven Tests
`vi.waitFor` repeatedly evaluates a predicate until it passes or the timeout expires, making it ideal for testing event-driven systems where state changes asynchronously in response to emitted events.
```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { EventBus } from './event-bus';
import { OrderProcessor } from './order-processor';

describe('OrderProcessor', () => {
  it('emits order-fulfilled event within 500 ms', async () => {
    const bus = new EventBus();
    const processor = new OrderProcessor({ bus });

    const fulfilledEvents: unknown[] = [];
    bus.on('order-fulfilled', (evt) => fulfilledEvents.push(evt));

    await processor.submit({ orderId: 'ORD-001', items: [{ sku: 'WIDGET', qty: 2 }] });

    await vi.waitFor(
      () => {
        expect(fulfilledEvents).toHaveLength(1);
        expect(fulfilledEvents[0]).toMatchObject({ orderId: 'ORD-001', status: 'fulfilled' });
      },
      { timeout: 500, interval: 20 }
    );
  });

  it('does not emit order-fulfilled for an invalid order', async () => {
    const bus = new EventBus();
    const processor = new OrderProcessor({ bus });

    const fulfilledEvents: unknown[] = [];
    bus.on('order-fulfilled', (evt) => fulfilledEvents.push(evt));

    await expect(
      processor.submit({ orderId: '', items: [] })
    ).rejects.toThrow('Invalid order');

    // Wait a beat to confirm no event fires
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 50));
    expect(fulfilledEvents).toHaveLength(0);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: A tight `interval` (e.g., 10 ms) causes `vi.waitFor` to spin hundreds of times per second, which inflates the event-loop tick count logged by `--detectOpenHandles` and can mask other handle leaks. Use `interval: 50` or higher as a default, and reserve 10 ms only for tests that must detect sub-50 ms latency events.

---

**Pattern 519** — Playwright `page.waitForResponse` with URL Predicate for Request-Completion Gating
Instead of waiting for UI element visibility after an action (which can pass before data is applied), wait for the specific API response that drives the update, then assert on the UI state.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('search results update after filter change', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  // Start listening BEFORE triggering the action
  const searchResponsePromise = page.waitForResponse(
    resp => resp.url().includes('/api/products/search') && resp.status() === 200
  );

  await page.selectOption('[data-testid=category-filter]', 'electronics');

  // Wait for the actual API response, not a fixed timeout
  const searchResponse = await searchResponsePromise;
  const body = await searchResponse.json();

  // Assert UI reflects the API data
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=product-card]')).toHaveCount(body.items.length);
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=result-count]')).toHaveText(`${body.total} products`);
});

test('cart total updates after quantity change', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');

  const updateResponsePromise = page.waitForResponse(
    resp => resp.url().includes('/api/cart/update') && resp.status() === 200
  );

  await page.fill('[data-testid=qty-input-SKU-001]', '3');
  await page.keyboard.press('Tab'); // Trigger blur/update

  await updateResponsePromise;

  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=cart-total]')).toHaveText('$89.97');
});
```
Tradeoff: `waitForResponse` with a URL substring predicate matches any response containing that substring — if two concurrent requests share the URL pattern (e.g., a prefetch and the triggered request), the promise resolves on the first match, which may be the prefetch response, not the one triggered by the action. Use a more specific predicate (e.g., checking the request body or a query parameter) when concurrent requests to the same endpoint are possible.

---

**Pattern 520** — Jest `jest.runOnlyPendingTimers` Loop for Bounded Recursive `setInterval` Drain
`jest.runOnlyPendingTimers()` executes only the currently-queued timers without firing timers newly scheduled by those callbacks, making it safe to call in a bounded loop to drain a recursive interval chain step by step.
```typescript
import { describe, test, expect, jest, beforeEach, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';
import { BackoffRetryScheduler } from './backoff-retry-scheduler';

describe('BackoffRetryScheduler', () => {
  beforeEach(() => jest.useFakeTimers());
  afterEach(() => jest.useRealTimers());

  test('doubles backoff interval on each retry up to maxBackoff', () => {
    const onAttempt = jest.fn();
    const scheduler = new BackoffRetryScheduler({
      initialBackoffMs: 100,
      maxBackoffMs: 1600,
      onAttempt,
    });

    scheduler.start();

    const expectedIntervals = [100, 200, 400, 800, 1600, 1600];
    for (let i = 0; i < expectedIntervals.length; i++) {
      // Run only the pending timers (the current backoff tick)
      jest.runOnlyPendingTimers();
    }

    expect(onAttempt).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(expectedIntervals.length);

    // Verify the scheduler is capped at maxBackoff for subsequent calls
    jest.runOnlyPendingTimers();
    jest.runOnlyPendingTimers();
    const callCount = onAttempt.mock.calls.length;
    expect(callCount).toBe(expectedIntervals.length + 2);
  });

  test('stop() prevents further attempts', () => {
    const onAttempt = jest.fn();
    const scheduler = new BackoffRetryScheduler({ initialBackoffMs: 50, maxBackoffMs: 400, onAttempt });
    scheduler.start();
    jest.runOnlyPendingTimers(); // 1st attempt
    scheduler.stop();
    jest.runAllTimers(); // Nothing left to run
    expect(onAttempt).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Calling `runOnlyPendingTimers()` in a counted loop tightly couples the test to the scheduler's internal retry count. If the scheduler adds a "warm-up" tick before the first backoff, the expected call count is off by one. Assert on the recorded interval values (e.g., via a spy on `setTimeout`) rather than only the call count to catch scheduling-logic regressions.

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G195 — `jest.useFakeTimers()` Does Not Fake `queueMicrotask` by Default, Causing Async-Flush Order Surprises**
Why this matters: `queueMicrotask` schedules work at the microtask checkpoint (before the next macro-task), but Jest's default fake-timer implementation treats it as a macro-task. Code that relies on `queueMicrotask` executing before a `setTimeout(fn, 0)` callback will behave differently under fake timers, producing assertion ordering flakiness that only surfaces in the test environment.
Fix: explicitly include `'queueMicrotask'` in the `doNotFake` list (`jest.useFakeTimers({ doNotFake: ['queueMicrotask'] })`) so it retains real microtask semantics, or restructure the code under test to use `Promise.resolve().then()` which is always properly flushed by async test runners.

**Gotcha G196 — Vitest `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` Silently No-Ops if `vi.useFakeTimers()` Was Not Called First**
Why this matters: if a `beforeEach` that calls `vi.useFakeTimers()` is accidentally removed or skipped (e.g., by a `test.only` in another file that short-circuits the `beforeAll` chain), calls to `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` return immediately without advancing the clock. The test may pass because real wall-clock time advances normally, masking the fact that fake-timer assertions are no longer testing anything meaningful.
Fix: add an explicit guard at the start of any test that depends on fake timers — `expect(vi.isFakeTimers()).toBe(true)` — to fail loudly if the timer setup was skipped rather than silently testing against the real clock.

**Gotcha G197 — Playwright `waitForResponse` Promise Declared After Action Misses the Response**
Why this matters: if `page.waitForResponse(predicate)` is set up after the action that triggers the request (e.g., `page.click()` is awaited before `waitForResponse` is called), the response may already have been dispatched before the listener is registered, causing the promise to hang until timeout. This is a race condition that is highly machine-speed dependent: it passes reliably on slow CI but fails intermittently on fast developer laptops.
Fix: always declare `const responsePromise = page.waitForResponse(...)` before the `await page.click()` or other triggering action. The promise is registered synchronously during the `waitForResponse` call, so it captures the response even if it arrives before `await responsePromise` is reached.

**Gotcha G198 — Google Testing Blog Finding: Test Flakiness Hides ~1-in-6 Real Production Bugs**
Why this matters: engineering teams that habitually mark flaky tests as "ignore/retry" create a blindspot where genuine regression failures are dismissed as flakiness. Google's analysis found that when a previously stable test starts failing intermittently, the failure indicates a real production defect approximately 1 in 6 times. Treating all new flakiness as noise means roughly 17% of real bugs are routed to the ignore queue rather than to engineering.
Fix: implement a "flakiness triage" rule: any test that transitions from stable to flaky within the last 3 days is flagged for mandatory root-cause review before it is added to the quarantine/retry list. Use your CI reporter's diff-based flakiness detection to surface these transitions automatically.

**Gotcha G199 — Vitest `isolate: false` Enables Cross-Test State Leaks That Only Manifest Under Parallelism**
Why this matters: `isolate: false` in `vitest.config.ts` (often added for performance) causes all test files in the same worker to share a module registry. A module with a mutable singleton (e.g., a global `EventEmitter` instance, a module-level `Map`, or a singleton service) leaks state between files that happen to be co-scheduled in the same worker. This produces intermittent failures that are absent when tests run serially (`--no-file-parallelism`) because a fresh require cache is effectively enforced by the single-worker constraint.
Fix: if `isolate: false` is required for performance, audit all module-level mutable state and expose explicit `reset()` methods, then call them in `afterAll`. Alternatively, scope the `isolate: false` setting to specific test projects (using `defineProject`) that have been verified to be side-effect-free, rather than applying it globally.

## Cycle 58 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 521** — Jest `useFakeTimers` with `doNotFake: ['performance']` for High-Resolution Timer Isolation
```typescript
// Prevent fake timers from clobbering performance.now() used by
// the production code under test (e.g., a metrics SDK that calls
// performance.now() for latency tracking).
beforeEach(() => {
  jest.useFakeTimers({
    doNotFake: ['performance'],
    // Keep Date and setTimeout faked so scheduling assertions work
  });
});

afterEach(() => {
  jest.useRealTimers();
});

test('latency tracker records elapsed time while scheduler fires on tick', async () => {
  const tracker = new LatencyTracker(); // internally calls performance.now()
  const scheduler = new TickScheduler({ intervalMs: 200 });

  scheduler.start();

  // Advance fake clock 600ms — fires 3 ticks
  jest.advanceTimersByTime(600);

  // performance.now() used real time so tracker.elapsed is non-zero
  expect(scheduler.tickCount).toBe(3);
  expect(tracker.elapsed).toBeGreaterThan(0);

  scheduler.stop();
});
```
Tradeoff: Leaving `performance` un-faked means latency assertions become wall-clock dependent and can produce different numbers on slow CI machines. Only preserve `performance` when the code under test needs real high-resolution timestamps for correctness checks (e.g., validating that a debounce fires within a measured window). For pure scheduling logic, fake everything and assert on call counts rather than measured durations.

**Pattern 522** — Vitest `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` for Promise-Chained Timer Sequences
```typescript
import { vi, beforeEach, afterEach, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { DelayedQueue } from './delayed-queue';

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

test('processes items in three deferred batches', async () => {
  const queue = new DelayedQueue({ batchDelayMs: 100 });
  const processed: string[] = [];

  queue.onBatch((items) => processed.push(...items));
  queue.enqueue('a', 'b', 'c');

  // First batch fires after 100ms — async because the handler is async
  await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(100);
  expect(processed).toEqual(['a', 'b', 'c']);

  queue.enqueue('d', 'e');
  await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(100);
  expect(processed).toEqual(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e']);

  // No more items — advance past another interval, nothing extra fires
  await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(100);
  expect(processed).toHaveLength(5);
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` drains microtasks at each timer tick, so it is slower than the synchronous `vi.advanceTimersByTime` equivalent when the queue is large. Reserve the async variant for code paths where promises are chained directly inside the timer callback; use the synchronous variant for pure-synchronous timer logic to keep test suites fast.

**Pattern 523** — Playwright `page.clock.setFixedTime` for Deterministic Date-Sensitive UI Tests
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('renewal banner shows 14 days before subscription expiry', async ({ page }) => {
  // Freeze the browser clock before navigation so page load time
  // and any in-flight XHR timestamps all see the same "now".
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-05-01T00:00:00Z') });
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Subscription expires 2026-05-15 — 14 days away from frozen now
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /renew in 14 days/i })).toBeVisible();

  // Advance clock 1 day — banner should count down
  await page.clock.tick(86_400_000); // 1 day in ms
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /renew in 13 days/i })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.clock.install` must be called before `page.goto` or any navigation; calling it after the page has loaded leaves timers already registered at the real epoch, producing a split-clock state where new timers use the fake clock but existing intervals use the real one. Always install the clock in a `beforeEach` or at the start of the test, not after navigation.

**Pattern 524** — Jest `jest.setSystemTime` for Pure Date Logic Unit Tests
```typescript
import { formatRelativeDate } from './date-utils';

describe('formatRelativeDate', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    jest.useFakeTimers();
    // Pin "today" to a known Wednesday
    jest.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-05-13T12:00:00Z'));
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    jest.useRealTimers();
  });

  test('returns "yesterday" for dates exactly 1 day ago', () => {
    const yesterday = new Date('2026-05-12T12:00:00Z');
    expect(formatRelativeDate(yesterday)).toBe('yesterday');
  });

  test('returns "last week" for dates 7 days ago', () => {
    const lastWeek = new Date('2026-05-06T12:00:00Z');
    expect(formatRelativeDate(lastWeek)).toBe('last week');
  });

  test('does not change output when real time advances', () => {
    // Real time passing does not change setSystemTime snapshot
    const result = formatRelativeDate(new Date('2026-05-12T12:00:00Z'));
    expect(result).toBe('yesterday');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.setSystemTime` only affects `Date` constructor and `Date.now()`; it does not advance the fake timer queue. If the code under test schedules a `setTimeout` and checks `Date.now()` inside the callback, you must also call `jest.advanceTimersByTime` to fire the callback — `setSystemTime` alone will not trigger it. Use `setSystemTime` for pure date-formatting/calculation functions and combine it with `advanceTimersByTime` for functions that mix scheduling with date logic.

**Pattern 525** — Vitest `vi.setSystemTime` Combined with `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` for Mixed Date+Timer Logic
```typescript
import { vi, test, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { SessionTokenRefresher } from './session-token-refresher';

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  // Anchor "now" — token expires at 12:05, refresh fires at 12:00+4min
  vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-05-14T12:00:00Z'));
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

test('refreshes token 1 minute before expiry without double-refresh', async () => {
  const mockRefresh = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ token: 'new-token' });
  const refresher = new SessionTokenRefresher({
    expiresAt: new Date('2026-05-14T12:05:00Z'),
    onRefresh: mockRefresh,
  });

  refresher.start();

  // Advance to 1 min before expiry — refresh should fire
  await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(4 * 60 * 1000); // 4 minutes
  expect(mockRefresh).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);

  // Advance past expiry — should not double-refresh
  await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(2 * 60 * 1000); // 2 more minutes
  expect(mockRefresh).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);

  refresher.stop();
});
```
Tradeoff: When `vi.setSystemTime` and `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` are combined, the system clock advances in lock-step with the timer queue. This means any call to `new Date()` inside an advancing timer callback sees the progressed time, which is usually the desired behavior. However, if the code creates a `Date` snapshot at construction time (`this.startedAt = new Date()`), that snapshot will reflect the initial pinned time — not the advanced time — so assertions comparing `Date.now() - instance.startedAt` will be accurate while assertions on the snapshot itself will reflect the pre-advance value.

**Pattern 526** — Playwright `page.route` with `fulfill` for Deterministic API Response Timing
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('loading spinner disappears when API responds after 300ms', async ({ page }) => {
  // Intercept the API call and delay the response deterministically
  await page.route('**/api/dashboard/data', async (route) => {
    // Simulate a 300ms server response time
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 300));
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify({ widgets: [{ id: 1, value: 42 }] }),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Spinner should be visible immediately after navigation
  await expect(page.getByRole('progressbar')).toBeVisible();

  // After the mocked delay resolves, spinner should disappear
  await expect(page.getByRole('progressbar')).toBeHidden({ timeout: 2000 });
  await expect(page.getByText('42')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Using real `setTimeout` inside `route.fulfill` means the 300ms delay runs on real wall-clock time, adding actual latency to the test. This is acceptable for a single test but accumulates across a full E2E suite. For suites with hundreds of such tests, consider using `page.clock` to freeze browser time and trigger the response synchronously via `page.clock.tick`, eliminating the real-time wait entirely.

**Pattern 527** — Jest `timerLimit` Option to Circuit-Break Runaway `setInterval` Loops
```typescript
// Prevent infinite-loop timer bugs from hanging the test suite forever.
// Jest will throw after the specified number of timer callbacks.

test('circuit-breaker fires when interval loop does not terminate', () => {
  jest.useFakeTimers({ timerLimit: 50 });

  let count = 0;
  const id = setInterval(() => {
    count++;
    // Bug: clearInterval is never called — simulates a production leak
  }, 10);

  expect(() => {
    jest.runAllTimers(); // Would spin forever without timerLimit
  }).toThrow(/Aborting after running 50 timers/);

  clearInterval(id);
  jest.useRealTimers();
});

test('normal bounded interval completes under the limit', () => {
  jest.useFakeTimers({ timerLimit: 50 });

  let count = 0;
  const id = setInterval(() => {
    count++;
    if (count >= 5) clearInterval(id);
  }, 100);

  jest.runAllTimers();
  expect(count).toBe(5);
  jest.useRealTimers();
});
```
Tradeoff: Setting `timerLimit` too low (e.g., `10`) will cause false failures in tests that legitimately fire many timer callbacks (e.g., an animation loop running at 60fps for 200ms needs ~12 callbacks). Set the limit conservatively high enough to allow valid production use cases but low enough to catch genuine infinite loops — a value of 1000 strikes the right balance for most applications.

**Pattern 528** — Vitest `vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true })` for Mixed Real/Fake Clock Code
```typescript
import { vi, test, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { HeartbeatMonitor } from './heartbeat-monitor';

beforeEach(() => {
  // shouldAdvanceTime: true means the fake clock auto-advances in
  // sync with real wall time, but timer callbacks still execute
  // synchronously when vi.advanceTimersByTime is called.
  vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true });
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

test('heartbeat fires every 5s and accumulates correctly', async () => {
  const beats: number[] = [];
  const monitor = new HeartbeatMonitor({
    intervalMs: 5000,
    onBeat: () => beats.push(Date.now()),
  });

  monitor.start();

  // Advance fake clock 15s — fires beats at 5s, 10s, 15s
  vi.advanceTimersByTime(15_000);

  expect(beats).toHaveLength(3);
  // shouldAdvanceTime ensures beats[1] - beats[0] ≈ 5000ms
  expect(beats[1] - beats[0]).toBeCloseTo(5000, -2);

  monitor.stop();
});
```
Tradeoff: With `shouldAdvanceTime: true`, the system clock drifts at real-time rate between explicit `advanceTimersByTime` calls, so tests that check `Date.now()` outside of a controlled advance may observe slightly different values on fast vs. slow machines. This mode is best for code that only reads `Date.now()` inside timer callbacks (where the advance anchors the value) rather than in surrounding synchronous code.

**Pattern 529** — Playwright `expect.poll` with Custom Interval for Polling-Based Async Assertions
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('background job status transitions from queued to completed', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/jobs/42');

  // Poll the status badge every 500ms until it reads "completed",
  // with a 10s timeout — avoids hardcoded sleeps that cause flakiness
  await expect.poll(
    async () => {
      const badge = page.getByTestId('job-status-badge');
      return await badge.textContent();
    },
    {
      intervals: [500, 500, 500, 1000, 1000, 2000],
      timeout: 10_000,
      message: 'Job did not reach "completed" status within 10s',
    }
  ).toBe('completed');

  // Once completed, verify the output section is visible
  await expect(page.getByRole('region', { name: /job output/i })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.poll` retries indefinitely up to the timeout, which means a genuine bug that keeps the job in "running" state will always wait the full timeout duration before failing. Set the `timeout` to the minimum reasonable upper bound for the operation under normal conditions (not worst-case infrastructure conditions) to keep feedback fast; rely on CI infrastructure timeouts for genuine hangs beyond that bound.

**Pattern 530** — Jest `jest.spyOn(global, 'clearTimeout')` to Detect Timer Leak Cleanup Omissions
```typescript
import { EventPoller } from './event-poller';

test('EventPoller clears its timeout on stop() to prevent memory leaks', () => {
  jest.useFakeTimers();
  const clearTimeoutSpy = jest.spyOn(global, 'clearTimeout');

  const poller = new EventPoller({ pollIntervalMs: 1000 });
  poller.start();

  // Capture the timeout ID registered by start()
  jest.runOnlyPendingTimers(); // Fire the first poll
  poller.stop();

  // Verify that clearTimeout was called — proving the poller cleaned up
  expect(clearTimeoutSpy).toHaveBeenCalled();

  clearTimeoutSpy.mockRestore();
  jest.useRealTimers();
});

test('EventPoller does not fire after stop()', () => {
  jest.useFakeTimers();
  const onPoll = jest.fn();
  const poller = new EventPoller({ pollIntervalMs: 1000, onPoll });

  poller.start();
  poller.stop();

  jest.runAllTimers(); // Would fire if clearTimeout wasn't called
  expect(onPoll).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  jest.useRealTimers();
});
```
Tradeoff: Spying on `global.clearTimeout` asserts that cleanup *occurred* but not that the *correct* timer ID was cleared. A buggy implementation that calls `clearTimeout(undefined)` or clears an already-cleared ID will satisfy the spy call assertion without actually stopping the timer. Pair this pattern with the second test (assert no callbacks fire after `stop()`) to verify both that cleanup is attempted and that it is effective.

**Pattern 531** — Vitest `vi.runAllTimersAsync` for Deeply Nested Async Timer Chains
```typescript
import { vi, test, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { CascadingNotifier } from './cascading-notifier';

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

test('three-level cascade fires all notifications in order', async () => {
  const log: string[] = [];

  // The notifier schedules: step1 at 100ms, step2 at 100ms after step1,
  // step3 at 200ms after step2 — all async via awaited setTimeout chains
  const notifier = new CascadingNotifier({
    steps: [
      { delay: 100, label: 'step1' },
      { delay: 100, label: 'step2' },
      { delay: 200, label: 'step3' },
    ],
    onStep: (label) => log.push(label),
  });

  notifier.trigger();

  // runAllTimersAsync drains the entire async timer chain including
  // Promises scheduled between timer callbacks
  await vi.runAllTimersAsync();

  expect(log).toEqual(['step1', 'step2', 'step3']);
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.runAllTimersAsync` runs until there are no pending timers or microtasks, which means it will not terminate if the code under test schedules a new timer inside every timer callback unconditionally (infinite chain). Use `vi.runAllTimersAsync` only when the timer chain has a known termination condition; for potentially infinite chains, use `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` with an explicit upper bound instead.

**Pattern 532** — Playwright `page.addLocatorHandler` for Automatic Overlay Dismissal During Flaky E2E Flows
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout completes despite intermittent cookie-consent overlay', async ({ page }) => {
  // Register a handler that fires whenever the consent overlay appears,
  // regardless of when during the test flow it shows up.
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /cookie consent/i }),
    async (overlay) => {
      await overlay.getByRole('button', { name: /accept all/i }).click();
    }
  );

  await page.goto('/shop');
  await page.getByText('Add to cart').first().click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: /checkout/i }).click();

  // The consent overlay may or may not appear at any of the above steps.
  // addLocatorHandler ensures it is always dismissed before Playwright
  // proceeds, eliminating the "element is intercepting pointer events" error.
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /order summary/i })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `addLocatorHandler` adds a Playwright-managed polling loop that checks for the overlay locator before each action. On pages with many actions, this adds a small overhead per interaction (one additional locator query). For tests with hundreds of interactions on highly dynamic pages, consider scoping the handler to a specific page section using `locator.filter()` rather than a full-page overlay locator to minimize the overhead.

**Pattern 533** — Jest `jest.runOnlyPendingTimers` in `afterEach` for Global Timer Leak Cleanup
```typescript
// Ensures that any timers scheduled during a test and not explicitly
// cleared cannot leak state into the next test, even if the test fails
// partway through.

beforeEach(() => {
  jest.useFakeTimers();
});

afterEach(() => {
  // Drain only the timers already scheduled — does not recurse into
  // new timers scheduled by the draining process, preventing infinite loops.
  jest.runOnlyPendingTimers();
  jest.useRealTimers();
});

test('timer fires and updates cache', () => {
  const cache = new ExpiryCache({ ttlMs: 500 });
  cache.set('key', 'value');
  jest.advanceTimersByTime(500);
  expect(cache.get('key')).toBeUndefined();
});

test('does not see stale timer from previous test', () => {
  // If the previous test had leaked a pending setTimeout that mutates
  // shared state, this test would see that mutation. The afterEach
  // drain above ensures it never runs.
  const cache = new ExpiryCache({ ttlMs: 500 });
  cache.set('fresh', 'data');
  expect(cache.get('fresh')).toBe('data');
});
```
Tradeoff: `runOnlyPendingTimers` in `afterEach` executes any pending callbacks at the end of every test, which means side effects from intentionally un-fired timers (timers that the test deliberately left pending to assert they hadn't fired) will run during cleanup. This can mask assertion errors if the side effect overwrites state checked by a subsequent `expect`. Call `jest.clearAllTimers()` instead when you need to discard pending timers without running them, and use `runOnlyPendingTimers` only when running them at teardown is safe.

**Pattern 534** — Vitest `vi.isFakeTimers` Guard Assertion for Defensive Test Setup Verification
```typescript
import { vi, test, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { RateLimiter } from './rate-limiter';

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

function assertFakeTimersEnabled(): void {
  if (!vi.isFakeTimers()) {
    throw new Error(
      'Test requires fake timers — ensure vi.useFakeTimers() was called in beforeEach. ' +
      'If this test was run in isolation via test.only, check that the beforeEach block is active.'
    );
  }
}

test('rate limiter allows burst then throttles', () => {
  assertFakeTimersEnabled(); // Fail loudly if setup was skipped

  const limiter = new RateLimiter({ maxRequests: 5, windowMs: 1000 });

  for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    expect(limiter.allow()).toBe(true);
  }
  expect(limiter.allow()).toBe(false); // 6th request blocked

  vi.advanceTimersByTime(1000); // Reset window
  expect(limiter.allow()).toBe(true); // First request in new window
});
```
Tradeoff: Adding `assertFakeTimersEnabled()` to every test that uses fake timers is verbose but catches a subtle class of false-positive failures where `vi.advanceTimersByTime` silently no-ops on the real clock. The overhead is a single boolean check per test, which is negligible. Consider extracting this guard into a shared `test-helpers/timer-guards.ts` file to avoid copy-paste across test suites.

**Pattern 535** — Playwright `page.clock.runFor` for Targeted Tick-Advance Without Overrunning
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('debounced search fires exactly once after 300ms idle', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.clock.install({ time: 0 });
  await page.goto('/search');

  const searchInput = page.getByRole('searchbox');
  const requestPromise = page.waitForRequest('**/api/search**');

  // Type quickly — each keystroke resets the 300ms debounce
  await searchInput.pressSequentially('react hooks', { delay: 0 });

  // Advance exactly 300ms — debounce threshold — one request should fire
  await page.clock.runFor(300);

  const request = await requestPromise;
  expect(new URL(request.url()).searchParams.get('q')).toBe('react hooks');

  // Advance another 300ms — no second request because typing stopped
  await page.clock.runFor(300);

  // Verify only one search request was made
  let extraRequestFired = false;
  page.on('request', (req) => {
    if (req.url().includes('/api/search')) extraRequestFired = true;
  });
  expect(extraRequestFired).toBe(false);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.clock.runFor(ms)` advances time by exactly `ms` milliseconds from the current fake clock position, giving precise control over debounce/throttle boundary conditions. Unlike `page.clock.tick` (which is an alias), this method makes the intent explicit in test prose. The limitation is that it cannot advance the clock to an absolute timestamp — use `page.clock.setSystemTime(new Date(...))` for that, and reserve `runFor` for relative advances after a known starting point.

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G200 — `jest.useFakeTimers()` in `beforeAll` Instead of `beforeEach` Causes State Leak Across Tests**
Why this matters: when `jest.useFakeTimers()` is called in `beforeAll`, all tests in the `describe` block share a single fake clock instance. A timer scheduled in test A that is not cleared before test B begins will fire during test B's execution, injecting unexpected side effects. This manifests as sporadic failures that only appear when the full suite runs in order, not when individual tests are run in isolation.
Fix: always call `jest.useFakeTimers()` in `beforeEach` and `jest.useRealTimers()` in `afterEach`. This ensures each test starts with a fresh, empty fake clock. If the `useFakeTimers` call is expensive due to a complex module setup, use `jest.clearAllTimers()` in `beforeEach` as a lighter alternative that resets the pending timer queue without re-creating the fake clock infrastructure.

**Gotcha G201 — Vitest `vi.advanceTimersByTime` Does Not Flush Microtasks Between Timer Ticks**
Why this matters: the synchronous `vi.advanceTimersByTime(ms)` fires all timer callbacks scheduled within the `ms` window but does not yield to the microtask queue between callbacks. If a timer callback creates a `Promise` whose `.then()` handler updates state that the next timer callback reads, that state update will not be visible to the second callback because the microtask queue is not flushed between ticks. This causes assertion failures that look like a timing off-by-one but are actually a micro/macro task ordering issue.
Fix: replace `vi.advanceTimersByTime` with `await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` whenever timer callbacks create Promises or call `async` functions. The async variant yields to the microtask queue after each timer tick, ensuring that Promise resolutions are visible to subsequent callbacks before the advance continues.

**Gotcha G202 — Playwright `page.clock.install()` Freezes `Date` Constructor Only in the Page Realm, Not in Node Workers**
Why this matters: Playwright's `page.clock.install()` intercepts the `Date` and timer APIs within the browser page context using CDP. Any code running in Node.js (e.g., a Next.js API route handler, a server action, or an MSW request handler running in Node) still uses the real system clock. Tests that assert on timestamps produced by server-side code while the page clock is frozen will see a mismatch between the browser-observed time and the server-observed time, producing intermittent failures when real wall-clock time crosses a boundary (midnight, DST change, etc.).
Fix: for full-stack timestamp assertions, combine `page.clock.install()` with MSW's `vi.setSystemTime()` (in Vitest) or `jest.setSystemTime()` in the Node process to pin both clocks to the same epoch. Document this dual-clock setup in the test as a comment to prevent future contributors from removing one half of the pair.

**Gotcha G203 — `jest.runAllTimers` Executes Timer Callbacks in Registration Order, Not Scheduled-Time Order**
Why this matters: when multiple timers are registered with different delays (e.g., `setTimeout(A, 100)` followed by `setTimeout(B, 50)`), `jest.runAllTimers` fires them in the order they were registered, not in ascending delay order. This contradicts how the real event loop works (B would fire before A in a real runtime), causing tests that assert on callback ordering to pass under fake timers but fail in production.
Fix: use `jest.advanceTimersByTime(50)` followed by `jest.advanceTimersByTime(50)` to step through time in increments, which correctly fires timers in scheduled-time order rather than registration order. Alternatively, structure the production code so that timer ordering is not load-bearing for correctness, and assert only on the final state after all timers have fired.

**Gotcha G204 — Microtask vs. Macrotask Queue Ordering Surprises Break Timer-Based Flakiness Fixes**
Why this matters: a common attempt to fix timing flakiness is to insert `await Promise.resolve()` (a microtask yield) or `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0))` (a macrotask yield) to "let things settle." Under fake timers, `await Promise.resolve()` works as expected (yields once to the microtask queue), but `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0))` will hang indefinitely because `setTimeout` is faked and the fake clock does not auto-advance. Tests that use this pattern as a flush helper will deadlock unless `jest.advanceTimersByTime(0)` is called concurrently, which is not possible in a linear async test without restructuring.
Fix: use `await vi.runAllTimersAsync()` or `await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(0)` to flush both the fake timer queue and the microtask queue in one awaitable call. Never use raw `setTimeout(r, 0)` as a flush primitive in tests that use fake timers; extract a `flushAll()` test helper that calls the appropriate framework API for the project's test runner.
