## Cycle 59 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 536** — Playwright `page.clock.setFixedTime` for Date-Only Assertions Without Pausing Timers
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard header shows today\'s date in correct locale format', async ({ page }) => {
  // setFixedTime pins Date.now() and new Date() without installing fake timers.
  // Intervals, setTimeout, and requestAnimationFrame continue to fire normally.
  await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2026-05-14T09:00:00Z'));

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Wait for the header to render — real timers still run, so animations complete
  const dateHeader = page.getByTestId('dashboard-date-header');
  await expect(dateHeader).toBeVisible();

  // Assert the rendered date string matches the pinned clock value
  await expect(dateHeader).toHaveText('Wednesday, May 14, 2026');

  // Verify a "days until deadline" counter computed from Date.now()
  const countdown = page.getByTestId('deadline-countdown');
  await expect(countdown).toContainText('16 days remaining');
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.clock.setFixedTime` is the lightest-weight clock control method: it affects only `Date.now()` and `new Date()`, leaving the timer queue and animation loop intact. This means components that rely on real `setTimeout` for animations or polling will still run, avoiding the frozen-page side effects that `page.clock.install() + pauseAt()` can introduce. The limitation is that it cannot be used to test timer-specific logic (debounce, interval polling); for those cases, `page.clock.install()` is required. Prefer `setFixedTime` by default and escalate to `install` only when the test must control timer execution.

**Pattern 537** — Playwright `page.clock.pauseAt` + `fastForward` for Session-Timeout Flakiness
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('session timeout warning appears after 14 minutes of inactivity', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install the fake clock before navigation so all timer APIs are intercepted
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-05-14T10:00:00Z') });
  await page.goto('/app');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Log in' }).click();

  // Pause the clock at a known reference point
  await page.clock.pauseAt(new Date('2026-05-14T10:00:00Z'));

  // FastForward jumps time and fires all due timers in one shot —
  // equivalent to "closing the laptop lid" for 14 minutes
  await page.clock.fastForward('14:00');

  // Session timeout modal should now be visible
  const timeoutModal = page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Session expiring soon' });
  await expect(timeoutModal).toBeVisible();
  await expect(timeoutModal.getByRole('button', { name: 'Stay logged in' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `fastForward` fires all timers that are due in the specified window without executing intermediate callbacks one by one, which is faster than calling `runFor` in a loop but means intermediate state transitions are skipped. Use `fastForward` when you only care about the final state after a long idle period (e.g., session timeout, token expiry). Use `page.clock.runFor` when intermediate timer callbacks (e.g., progress updates, polling retries) must also be verified. Always call `install` before navigation to avoid the undefined behaviour caused by out-of-order clock initialisation.

**Pattern 538** — Vitest `vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake })` Selective Faking to Preserve `performance` API
```typescript
import { vi, describe, it, expect, afterEach } from 'vitest';

// Only fake the specific APIs needed — leave performance.now() real
// so Web Vitals measurements in the same process remain accurate.
vi.useFakeTimers({
  toFake: ['setTimeout', 'clearTimeout', 'setInterval', 'clearInterval', 'Date'],
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.clearAllTimers();
});

describe('polling service', () => {
  it('retries exactly 3 times with 2-second back-off before giving up', async () => {
    const fetchMock = vi.fn()
      .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('network error'))
      .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('network error'))
      .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('network error'));

    const { pollUntilSuccess } = await import('../src/polling-service');
    const promise = pollUntilSuccess(fetchMock, { retries: 3, backoffMs: 2000 });

    // Step through each back-off window precisely
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(2000);
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(2000);
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(2000);

    await expect(promise).rejects.toThrow('Max retries exceeded');
    expect(fetchMock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: the `toFake` allowlist prevents `performance.now()` from being intercepted, which matters when the module under test or its transitive imports use the Performance API for telemetry or profiling. Without `toFake`, `vi.useFakeTimers()` intercepts every timer API including `performance`, causing telemetry assertions to always see `0`. The cost is that the allowlist must be maintained as new timer APIs are added to the module; consider centralising the `vi.useFakeTimers` call in a shared test setup file so the list is authoritative for the whole suite.

**Pattern 539** — Jest `advanceTimersByTimeAsync` for Promise-Chained Retry Logic
```typescript
import { jest, describe, test, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';

beforeEach(() => {
  jest.useFakeTimers();
});

afterEach(() => {
  jest.useRealTimers();
  jest.restoreAllMocks();
});

describe('exponential-backoff fetch wrapper', () => {
  test('resolves on second attempt after 500 ms back-off', async () => {
    const networkSpy = jest
      .fn()
      .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('timeout'))
      .mockResolvedValueOnce({ status: 200, data: 'ok' });

    const { fetchWithRetry } = await import('../src/fetch-with-retry');
    const resultPromise = fetchWithRetry('https://api.example.com/data', { maxRetries: 2, backoffMs: 500 });

    // advanceTimersByTimeAsync fires the scheduled retry AND flushes the
    // microtask queue so the resolved Promise propagates before the assertion
    await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(500);

    const result = await resultPromise;
    expect(result.data).toBe('ok');
    expect(networkSpy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` (introduced in Jest 29.5) combines clock advancement with microtask queue flushing in a single awaitable call, eliminating the brittle pattern of interleaving `jest.advanceTimersByTime(ms)` with manual `await Promise.resolve()` flushes. The async variant is slower than its synchronous counterpart because it must yield to the event loop after each timer tick, but this cost is negligible for integration-level retry tests. Always `await` the call; omitting `await` causes the microtask flush to be skipped silently, re-introducing the very race condition the async API is designed to prevent.

**Pattern 540** — Vitest `vi.runAllTimersAsync` for Deeply Nested Interval Chains
```typescript
import { vi, it, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { createHeartbeatService } from '../src/heartbeat';

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

it('heartbeat service sends 5 pings over a 10-second window and then stops', async () => {
  const sendPing = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ ack: true });
  const service = createHeartbeatService(sendPing, { intervalMs: 2000, maxPings: 5 });

  service.start();

  // runAllTimersAsync exhausts the entire timer queue, including timers created
  // inside timer callbacks (nested setInterval re-registrations), and flushes
  // microtasks between each callback execution.
  await vi.runAllTimersAsync();

  expect(sendPing).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5);
  expect(service.isStopped()).toBe(true);
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.runAllTimersAsync` is the correct tool when timer callbacks themselves schedule new timers (e.g., a heartbeat that re-registers the next interval after each ping). The synchronous `vi.runAllTimers` will exhaust only the timers registered at call time; timers added by those callbacks may not be processed. The risk is infinite loops: if a timer callback unconditionally schedules another timer, `runAllTimersAsync` will loop forever. Guard against this by setting a `loopLimit` option in `vi.useFakeTimers({ loopLimit: 50 })` so Vitest throws a descriptive error instead of hanging the test process.

**Pattern 541** — Playwright `page.clock.resume` for Real-Time Segment After Controlled Pause
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('live-clock widget ticks forward after a controlled pause', async ({ page }) => {
  const startTime = new Date('2026-05-14T12:00:00Z');
  await page.clock.install({ time: startTime });
  await page.goto('/live-dashboard');

  // Pause at a known point to make assertions on the frozen state
  await page.clock.pauseAt(startTime);
  const clockWidget = page.getByTestId('live-clock');
  await expect(clockWidget).toHaveText('12:00:00');

  // Resume lets real time (relative to the fake epoch) flow again
  await page.clock.resume();

  // Wait for two real seconds — the fake clock also advances ~2 seconds
  await page.waitForTimeout(2000);

  // Widget should have ticked at least 1 second forward
  const displayed = await clockWidget.textContent();
  const [h, m, s] = displayed!.split(':').map(Number);
  expect(h * 3600 + m * 60 + s).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(43202); // 12:00:02
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.clock.resume` restarts the fake clock at the same rate as real time, so this pattern is only appropriate when you need to verify that a UI updates continuously over a short real-time window (e.g., a live countdown, a ticking clock). The test duration is bounded by real wall-clock time, which makes it slower and environment-dependent compared to purely synthetic advances. Limit its use to a few seconds of real-time observation; for longer scenarios, use `page.clock.fastForward` followed by a static assertion.

**Pattern 542** — MSW + Vitest Fake Timers: Coordinating Network Delay Simulation
```typescript
import { vi, it, expect, beforeAll, afterAll, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { http, delay, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { fetchUserProfile } from '../src/api/user';

const server = setupServer(
  http.get('/api/user/:id', async () => {
    // MSW delay() uses real timers internally — do NOT use fake timers with it.
    // Instead, model latency via request processing time in test logic.
    await delay(0); // passthrough: resolve on next macrotask
    return HttpResponse.json({ id: '1', name: 'Alice' });
  })
);

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

it('shows loading spinner while request is in-flight, then renders profile', async () => {
  // Do NOT call vi.useFakeTimers() here — MSW uses real timers for delay().
  // For timeout assertions, use vi.useFakeTimers only in tests that do not use MSW delay().
  const renderResult = render(<UserProfile userId="1" />);

  expect(renderResult.getByRole('progressbar')).toBeInTheDocument();

  await waitFor(() => {
    expect(renderResult.getByText('Alice')).toBeInTheDocument();
  });

  expect(renderResult.queryByRole('progressbar')).not.toBeInTheDocument();
});
```
Tradeoff: MSW's `delay()` helper uses real `setTimeout` under the hood; activating `vi.useFakeTimers()` in the same test will cause `delay()` calls to hang indefinitely because the fake clock never auto-advances. The correct split is: use real timers for tests that involve MSW network simulation, and use fake timers only in pure unit tests that do not touch MSW. Document this constraint in the test file's module-level comment to prevent future contributors from accidentally combining the two.

**Pattern 543** — `jest.spyOn(global, 'setTimeout')` for Timer Registration Verification
```typescript
import { jest, describe, test, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';

beforeEach(() => {
  jest.useFakeTimers();
  jest.spyOn(global, 'setTimeout');
});

afterEach(() => {
  jest.useRealTimers();
  jest.restoreAllMocks();
});

describe('notification scheduler', () => {
  test('schedules a retry with exactly 5000 ms delay on first failure', () => {
    const { scheduleNotification } = require('../src/notification-scheduler');

    scheduleNotification({ message: 'Deploy complete', retryOnFailure: true });

    // First call registers the initial notification send
    expect(setTimeout).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);

    // Simulate a send failure by advancing and checking retry registration
    jest.runOnlyPendingTimers();

    // A retry setTimeout should now be registered with the correct delay
    expect(setTimeout).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);
    expect(setTimeout).toHaveBeenLastCalledWith(expect.any(Function), 5000);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.spyOn(global, 'setTimeout')` combined with `jest.useFakeTimers` lets you assert not just that a timer fired but that it was registered with the correct delay and handler. This is valuable for scheduler modules where the retry delay is a business-critical value. The limitation is that spy call counts include timers registered by framework internals (React's scheduler, MSW internals, etc.) if those run in the same process, making `toHaveBeenCalledTimes` assertions fragile in integration tests. Restrict this pattern to pure unit tests where the module under test is isolated from framework timer usage.

**Pattern 544** — Vitest `vi.setSystemTime` + `vi.useFakeTimers` for DST-Safe Date Arithmetic Tests
```typescript
import { vi, describe, it, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';

beforeEach(() => {
  // Combine fake timers with a pinned system time to test DST boundary behaviour.
  // Pin to the moment just before US Eastern Spring Forward (2026-03-08 02:00 → 03:00).
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-03-08T06:59:00Z')); // 01:59 EST
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

describe('appointment scheduler — DST transition', () => {
  it('correctly computes a "1 hour from now" slot across the spring-forward boundary', () => {
    const { getNextAvailableSlot } = require('../src/appointment-scheduler');

    const slot = getNextAvailableSlot({ durationMinutes: 60 });

    // In EST, 01:59 + 60 min = 03:59 (not 02:59, because 02:xx does not exist on this date)
    expect(slot.localHour).toBe(3);
    expect(slot.localMinute).toBe(59);
    expect(slot.tzOffset).toBe(-4 * 60); // EDT offset after spring forward
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.setSystemTime` changes the value returned by `Date.now()`, `new Date()`, and `performance.timeOrigin`, while `vi.useFakeTimers` intercepts scheduling APIs. Together they allow testing date-arithmetic edge cases (DST transitions, leap seconds, year-end rollovers) deterministically. The pitfall is that Node.js itself does not change its internal timezone rules at test time; only the JavaScript-visible clock is affected. Tests that rely on `Intl.DateTimeFormat` or `toLocaleString` will still use the host machine's actual timezone database, so CI runners with UTC-only settings may produce different locale strings than developer machines. Always assert on UTC-normalised values when possible, and reserve locale assertions for dedicated i18n test suites with explicit `TZ=America/New_York` environment variables.

**Pattern 545** — Playwright `page.clock.install` + `setSystemTime` for Server-Rendered Timestamp Consistency
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('invoice page displays the same creation timestamp in header and PDF preview', async ({ page }) => {
  const pinnedTime = new Date('2026-05-14T14:30:00Z');

  // Install the browser-side fake clock before navigation
  await page.clock.install({ time: pinnedTime });

  // Set the Node-process clock for any SSR or server-action timestamp calls
  // (requires the test environment to support this — e.g., via a test-mode env var)
  await page.request.post('/__test/set-system-time', {
    data: { isoTimestamp: pinnedTime.toISOString() },
  });

  await page.goto('/invoices/new');

  const headerTimestamp = page.getByTestId('invoice-created-at');
  const pdfPreviewTimestamp = page.getByTestId('pdf-preview-timestamp');

  await expect(headerTimestamp).toHaveText('May 14, 2026, 2:30 PM UTC');
  await expect(pdfPreviewTimestamp).toHaveText('May 14, 2026, 2:30 PM UTC');
});
```
Tradeoff: full-stack timestamp consistency requires pinning the clock in both the browser context (`page.clock.install`) and the server/SSR context. The cleanest approach is a test-mode HTTP endpoint that calls `process.env.TEST_FIXED_TIME` or a similar mechanism to freeze the server clock. Without this dual-pin, SSR-rendered timestamps and client-rendered timestamps will diverge whenever real wall-clock time crosses a formatting boundary (second rollover, etc.), producing intermittent assertion failures. Document the test-mode endpoint clearly and protect it behind a `NODE_ENV === 'test'` guard to prevent misuse in production.

**Pattern 546** — Jest `timerLimit` Circuit-Breaker for Runaway Interval Detection
```typescript
import { jest, describe, test, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';

beforeEach(() => {
  // Set a low timerLimit to catch infinite-loop timers before they hang CI.
  // The default is 100 000; a limit of 200 is sufficient for well-behaved modules.
  jest.useFakeTimers({ timerLimit: 200 });
});

afterEach(() => {
  jest.useRealTimers();
});

describe('polling loop circuit-breaker', () => {
  test('throws when a polling loop registers more than 200 iterations', () => {
    // A buggy polling implementation that never clears its interval
    const { startRunawayPoller } = require('../src/buggy-poller');
    startRunawayPoller();

    // jest.runAllTimers() will throw "Aborting after running 200 timers, to prevent infinite loops"
    // This converts a CI hang into a fast, descriptive failure.
    expect(() => jest.runAllTimers()).toThrow(/Aborting after running 200 timers/);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: setting `timerLimit` to a small value converts infinite-timer bugs from hanging test processes (which time out after the CI job timeout, wasting 10–60 minutes of runner time) into fast, descriptive failures. The risk is false positives: legitimate modules that register many timers (e.g., complex animation libraries) will trip the limit. Calibrate the limit per describe block rather than globally, and set it to approximately 2× the maximum expected timer registrations for the module under test. Keep the global default high (or absent) to avoid breaking unrelated tests.

**Pattern 547** — Vitest `vi.advanceTimersByTime` + Manual Microtask Flush for Synchronous Tests
```typescript
import { vi, describe, it, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

describe('cache invalidation — synchronous mode', () => {
  it('evicts stale entry after TTL expires (synchronous test style)', async () => {
    const { createTTLCache } = await import('../src/ttl-cache');
    const cache = createTTLCache({ ttlMs: 1000 });
    cache.set('key', 'value');

    // Advance time synchronously to cross the TTL boundary
    vi.advanceTimersByTime(1001);

    // Synchronous timer advance does NOT flush microtasks — if the eviction
    // logic uses a Promise internally, flush manually before asserting.
    await Promise.resolve(); // one microtask tick
    await Promise.resolve(); // second tick for chained .then() handlers

    expect(cache.get('key')).toBeUndefined();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: the synchronous `vi.advanceTimersByTime` is faster than its async counterpart and avoids the overhead of yielding to the event loop between every tick. It is appropriate for modules whose timer callbacks are purely synchronous. When a timer callback calls `async` functions or returns Promises, the synchronous advance will complete without waiting for those Promises to settle, making subsequent assertions see stale state. The fix is either to switch to `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` (preferred) or to insert explicit `await Promise.resolve()` flushes. Document the chosen approach in the test file so reviewers understand why the pattern differs from the async variant.

**Pattern 548** — Playwright `expect.poll` as a Fake-Timer-Free Async Poller
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('metric counter increments to 100 within 10 seconds of job completion', async ({ page, request }) => {
  await page.goto('/jobs/123/status');

  // Trigger the background job
  await request.post('/api/jobs/123/start');

  // expect.poll retries the assertion up to the timeout without fake timers —
  // it uses real time, so it is immune to fake-clock interference.
  await expect.poll(
    async () => {
      const counter = page.getByTestId('processed-count');
      const text = await counter.textContent();
      return parseInt(text ?? '0', 10);
    },
    {
      intervals: [500, 1000, 2000, 2000, 2000],
      timeout: 10_000,
      message: 'Expected processed-count to reach 100 within 10 seconds',
    }
  ).toBe(100);
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.poll` is the correct primitive for waiting on real async state changes (job completion, cache population, background queue drain) because it uses real timers and is therefore immune to fake-clock state. Avoid the temptation to use fake timers to speed up this type of test; the speedup is illusory because the underlying process being polled is a real asynchronous operation. The `intervals` array gives fine-grained control over the polling schedule, allowing short initial retries (catching fast completions) with longer back-off to reduce assertion noise during slow operations.

**Pattern 549** — Jest `jest.clearAllTimers` in `afterEach` to Prevent Timer Leak Across Test Files
```typescript
import { jest, describe, test, expect, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';

afterEach(() => {
  // Clear all pending timers even if the test did not register any —
  // this guards against timers leaked from imported module side effects.
  jest.clearAllTimers();
  // Also restore real timers so the next test file starts clean.
  if (jest.isFakeTimers()) {
    jest.useRealTimers();
  }
});

describe('notification badge — timer cleanup', () => {
  test('badge count updates after 3-second poll interval', () => {
    jest.useFakeTimers();
    const { startBadgePoller, getBadgeCount } = require('../src/badge-poller');

    startBadgePoller({ pollIntervalMs: 3000 });
    jest.advanceTimersByTime(3000);

    expect(getBadgeCount()).toBeGreaterThan(0);
    // afterEach will clear the recurring interval, preventing it from bleeding
    // into unrelated tests in the same Jest worker process.
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.clearAllTimers` in `afterEach` is a low-cost safety net that prevents interval leaks from propagating into tests in subsequent `describe` blocks within the same worker process. Without it, a `setInterval` registered in one test can fire during assertion phases of a completely unrelated test, producing confusing failures that only appear when tests run in a specific order. The overhead is a single synchronous call per test, which is negligible. Combine this with `jest.useRealTimers()` in the same `afterEach` block to fully reset the timer environment.

**Pattern 550** — Vitest `loopLimit` + `vi.runAllTimers` for Controlled Recursion Testing
```typescript
import { vi, it, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';

beforeEach(() => {
  // loopLimit prevents recursive timer patterns from hanging the test runner.
  // Set it to the expected maximum number of iterations plus a small buffer.
  vi.useFakeTimers({ loopLimit: 20 });
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

it('auto-refresh stops after 10 cycles and does not loop infinitely', () => {
  const { startAutoRefresh, getRefreshCount } = require('../src/auto-refresh');
  startAutoRefresh({ intervalMs: 1000, maxCycles: 10 });

  // runAllTimers exhausts the queue; loopLimit=20 means it will throw if more
  // than 20 timers fire, catching off-by-one bugs in the stop condition.
  vi.runAllTimers();

  expect(getRefreshCount()).toBe(10);
});
```
Tradeoff: `loopLimit` is Vitest's equivalent of Jest's `timerLimit` — a numeric safety valve that converts infinite-loop timer bugs into thrown errors instead of hung processes. Setting it slightly above the expected iteration count (e.g., `loopLimit: maxCycles + 5`) means a legitimate test never trips the limit, while a module that forgets to clear its interval will fail fast with a clear error message. The tradeoff is that `loopLimit` is shared across all timers registered during the test, including those created by framework internals in integration tests. Restrict this pattern to isolated unit tests where you can reliably count all expected timer registrations.

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G205 — `vi.useFakeTimers` Silently Fakes `performance.now()`, Breaking Web Vitals Assertions**
Why this matters: by default, `vi.useFakeTimers()` intercepts `performance.now()` along with all timer APIs. Code that measures actual render latency, LCP, or CLS using `performance.now()` will see `0` or a frozen value in tests, causing Web Vitals assertions to always pass regardless of real rendering performance. This creates false confidence and masks genuine performance regressions.
Fix: call `vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ['setTimeout', 'clearTimeout', 'setInterval', 'clearInterval', 'Date'] })` to explicitly exclude `performance` from the fake list. Alternatively, add `performance` to a `doNotFake` equivalent by omitting it from the `toFake` array. Document this configuration in a shared `test-setup.ts` file so the exclusion is applied consistently across all test files that run Web Vitals checks.

**Gotcha G206 — `page.clock.install` Called After `page.goto` Leaves Pre-Navigation Timers on the Real Clock**
Why this matters: Playwright's `page.clock.install` must be called before any navigation that loads JavaScript capable of registering timers. If `install` is called after `goto`, any `setTimeout` or `setInterval` calls that ran during page load will have used the real clock. These real-clock timers will still fire at unpredictable real-time points during the test, causing race conditions with subsequent `page.clock.fastForward` or `page.clock.runFor` calls that only control the fake clock.
Fix: always call `await page.clock.install({ time: ... })` before `await page.goto(...)`. If the page must be in a certain state before clock installation (e.g., after a login redirect), use `page.route` to intercept and delay the response, install the clock, then unroute to let the navigation complete. Never assume that post-navigation clock installation is safe even if the page appears static.

**Gotcha G207 — `jest.advanceTimersByTime` Does Not Trigger `setTimeout` Callbacks Scheduled With `0` Delay in Some Environments**
Why this matters: `setTimeout(fn, 0)` is a common idiom for deferring execution to the next event loop tick, but under Jest fake timers, `advanceTimersByTime(0)` fires only timers scheduled with exactly `0` delay — and some environments schedule them with a minimum delay of `1` ms internally. This means `advanceTimersByTime(0)` may silently skip the callback, causing assertions to see the pre-callback state and producing intermittent failures depending on which Jest version and Node.js runtime combination is in use.
Fix: advance by at least `1` ms (`jest.advanceTimersByTime(1)`) when the goal is to flush zero-delay deferred tasks, or use `jest.runAllTimers()` to exhaust the entire pending queue regardless of delay values. Add a comment explaining the `+1` offset to prevent future refactoring back to `0`.

**Gotcha G208 — Vitest `vi.runAllTimers` Does Not Process Timers Created Inside `Promise.then` Handlers**
Why this matters: when a timer callback resolves a Promise and the `.then()` handler schedules a new timer, `vi.runAllTimers` (synchronous) will not process that second timer because it only flushes the macrotask queue at the moment it is called; it does not yield to the microtask queue between passes. The second timer exists only after the microtask queue drains, which the synchronous `runAllTimers` never does. Tests that assert on state produced by this pattern will see stale values.
Fix: replace `vi.runAllTimers()` with `await vi.runAllTimersAsync()`. The async variant alternates between draining the macrotask timer queue and flushing the microtask queue, ensuring that timers created inside `.then()` handlers are discovered and executed. If the synchronous API must be used for performance reasons, separate the Promise chain from the timer scheduling so that all timers are registered synchronously at known points.

**Gotcha G209 — `page.clock.fastForward` With Human-Readable String Format Silently Parses Incorrectly**
Why this matters: `page.clock.fastForward` accepts both milliseconds (number) and human-readable strings like `"01:30"` (1 minute 30 seconds). The string format follows `MM:SS`, not `HH:MM`, which is counterintuitive for developers accustomed to `HH:MM:SS` notation. Passing `"01:00"` intending to advance one hour actually advances only one minute, causing tests that verify long-duration timeout behaviour (session expiry, token refresh) to assert on the wrong state without any error or warning.
Fix: prefer passing milliseconds as numbers (`page.clock.fastForward(3_600_000)` for one hour) rather than using the string format. If the string format is used for readability, add an inline comment documenting the `MM:SS` interpretation: `// "60:00" = 60 minutes = 3600 seconds`. Consider adding a project-level lint rule or custom ESLint plugin that flags string arguments to `page.clock.fastForward` to enforce the numeric form in CI.

## Cycle 60 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 551** — Playwright `testInfo.retry` Guard for State Reset Before Retry
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout flow completes without errors', async ({ page, request }, testInfo) => {
  // On any retry attempt, wipe server-side cart state so the retry
  // starts from a known baseline rather than a partially-completed order.
  if (testInfo.retry > 0) {
    await request.post('/api/test/reset-cart', {
      data: { sessionId: testInfo.testId },
    });
  }

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place Order' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('order-confirmation')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `testInfo.retry > 0` to gate destructive reset calls prevents unnecessary API calls on first-run tests while ensuring retries always start from a clean slate; the downside is that the reset call itself can fail if the test API endpoint is slow or unavailable, turning a transient UI flake into a persistent infrastructure failure that obscures the real cause.

**Pattern 552** — Playwright `test.describe.configure({ retries })` for Scoped Retry Budgets
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Only the tests inside this describe block get 2 retries.
// Tests outside remain at the global retry=0 setting.
test.describe('payment gateway integration', () => {
  test.describe.configure({ retries: 2 });

  test('card tokenisation succeeds', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/pay');
    await page.getByLabel('Card Number').fill('4111111111111111');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay Now' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByText('Payment successful')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 15_000 });
  });

  test('3DS challenge completes', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/pay?method=3ds');
    await page.frameLocator('#challenge-frame').getByRole('button', { name: 'Authenticate' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('auth-success')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 20_000 });
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Scoping retries to an individual `describe` block containing known-flaky third-party integration tests avoids inflating the global retry budget, which would mask genuinely broken tests elsewhere in the suite by giving them undeserved extra chances to pass.

**Pattern 553** — `expect.poll` with Custom `intervals` for Exponential-Backoff API Polling
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('background job reaches "completed" status within 30 s', async ({ request }) => {
  const { jobId } = await request.post('/api/jobs').then(r => r.json());

  // Exponential backoff: check at 500 ms, 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, then every 5 s.
  // Total ceiling controlled by timeout so the test never hangs indefinitely.
  await expect.poll(
    async () => {
      const res = await request.get(`/api/jobs/${jobId}`);
      return (await res.json()).status;
    },
    {
      message: `job ${jobId} did not reach "completed" within 30 s`,
      intervals: [500, 1_000, 2_000, 4_000, 5_000],
      timeout: 30_000,
    },
  ).toBe('completed');
});
```
Tradeoff: Passing a custom `intervals` array to `expect.poll` lets you match your polling cadence to the known latency profile of the job (fast first checks, then slower ones), reducing both total network round-trips and wall-clock test time compared to a fixed 1-second interval; however, if job latency varies widely across environments, a fixed-interval strategy is safer because the exponential backoff may exhaust the short early intervals before the job has had a chance to even start in slow CI environments.

**Pattern 554** — `expect.toPass` with `intervals` for Retry-Until-Pass on Multi-Step Async Flows
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard widget eventually renders with live data', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // toPass retries the entire async block — including navigation side-effects —
  // until every assertion inside passes or the timeout expires.
  await expect(async () => {
    const text = await page.getByTestId('revenue-widget').innerText();
    expect(text).toMatch(/\$[\d,]+/);
    expect(await page.getByTestId('revenue-widget').getAttribute('data-loaded')).toBe('true');
  }).toPass({
    intervals: [1_000, 2_000, 5_000],
    timeout: 20_000,
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.toPass` retries the entire async callback including any `await` calls inside it, which makes it powerful for multi-step checks but also means that slow `await` expressions inside the callback eat into the `timeout` budget with every attempt; for simple single-value polling, `expect.poll` is more efficient because it only awaits the value-producing function, not additional assertions.

**Pattern 555** — Jest `jest.retryTimes` with `logErrorsBeforeRetry` for Flake Diagnosis in CI
```typescript
// auth-service.test.ts
import { authService } from '../src/auth-service';

// Retry up to 3 times and log the failure reason before each retry so CI
// logs capture the error message even when the test eventually passes.
jest.retryTimes(3, { logErrorsBeforeRetry: true });

describe('AuthService.refreshToken', () => {
  it('returns a new token when the refresh endpoint responds within SLA', async () => {
    const token = await authService.refreshToken('expired-token-abc');
    expect(token).toMatch(/^Bearer /);
    expect(token.length).toBeGreaterThan(20);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `logErrorsBeforeRetry: true` preserves the error message from every failed attempt in CI output, which is invaluable for diagnosing the root cause of flakiness rather than just suppressing it; the tradeoff is that retrying failed tests rather than fixing root causes accumulates technical debt — use this pattern as a temporary diagnostic measure while filing a tracking issue, not as a permanent solution.

**Pattern 556** — Jest `retryImmediately` + `waitBeforeRetry` for Rate-Limited External API Tests
```typescript
// payments-api.test.ts
jest.retryTimes(2, {
  retryImmediately: true,
  waitBeforeRetry: 2_000, // wait 2 s between retries to avoid hitting rate limits
});

it('stripe charge creation returns a charge ID', async () => {
  const charge = await stripe.charges.create({
    amount: 500,
    currency: 'usd',
    source: 'tok_visa',
    description: 'Test charge',
  });

  expect(charge.id).toMatch(/^ch_/);
  expect(charge.status).toBe('succeeded');
});
```
Tradeoff: `retryImmediately: true` combined with `waitBeforeRetry: 2000` retries the test right after failure with a 2-second pause, which respects external API rate limits while keeping test-file wall-clock time low; using `waitBeforeRetry` without `retryImmediately` would instead defer all retries until every other test in the file has run, which can make CI logs harder to read and increases the total time before the retry executes.

**Pattern 557** — Jest `randomize: true` + `showSeed` to Surface Order-Dependent Flakiness
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  randomize: true,
  showSeed: true,   // prints the seed so a failing run can be reproduced exactly
  testTimeout: 10_000,
});
```
```typescript
// reproduce a specific failure order in CI:
// npx jest --randomize --seed=12345
```
Tradeoff: Running tests in random order each CI invocation exposes implicit ordering dependencies that would otherwise pass reliably, but it also means that a single failed CI run may be difficult to reproduce locally unless you capture and reuse the printed seed; always pair `randomize: true` with `showSeed: true` and configure your CI to persist the seed value in build artifacts alongside the failure log.

**Pattern 558** — Jest `workerIdleMemoryLimit` to Prevent Memory-Leak-Induced Flakiness
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  // Recycle worker processes that exceed 400 MB to prevent heap exhaustion
  // from accumulating module-level singletons or unclosed database connections.
  workerIdleMemoryLimit: '400MB',
  workerGracefulExitTimeout: 3_000,
  maxWorkers: '50%',
});
```
Tradeoff: Setting `workerIdleMemoryLimit` recycles workers that exceed the threshold before they run the next test file, preventing memory-pressure-induced flakiness like GC pauses mid-assertion or OOM crashes; the cost is that worker recycling involves spawning a new Node.js process, which adds 200–500 ms overhead per recycled worker — in suites with many large test files this can noticeably increase total CI time.

**Pattern 559** — Vitest `test.extend` with `file`-Scoped Database Fixture for Deterministic Isolation
```typescript
import { test as baseTest, expect } from 'vitest';
import { createTestDatabase, dropTestDatabase } from '../test-utils/db';

const test = baseTest.extend<{ dbUrl: string }>({
  // file scope: one database per test file, not one per test.
  // Avoids the overhead of creating/destroying a DB for every test
  // while still isolating files from each other.
  dbUrl: [
    async ({}, { onCleanup }) => {
      const { url, name } = await createTestDatabase();
      onCleanup(async () => {
        await dropTestDatabase(name);
      });
      return url;
    },
    { scope: 'file' },
  ],
});

test('user creation inserts a row', async ({ dbUrl }) => {
  const db = await connectDatabase(dbUrl);
  await db.users.create({ name: 'Alice' });
  expect(await db.users.count()).toBe(1);
  await db.disconnect();
});
```
Tradeoff: File-scoped fixtures amortize expensive setup (database creation, container spin-up) across all tests in a file instead of paying the cost per test, dramatically reducing suite runtime; however, tests within the same file now share state across the DB lifecycle, so any test that leaves uncommitted transactions or dirty rows will corrupt subsequent tests — always wrap individual tests in explicit transactions and roll back in `afterEach`.

**Pattern 560** — Vitest `test.extend` Builder Pattern with `onCleanup` for Temp-File Isolation
```typescript
import { test as baseTest, expect } from 'vitest';
import { writeFile, unlink, mkdtemp } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { join } from 'node:path';
import { tmpdir } from 'node:os';

const test = baseTest
  .extend('tmpDir', async ({}, { onCleanup }) => {
    const dir = await mkdtemp(join(tmpdir(), 'vitest-'));
    onCleanup(async () => {
      await unlink(dir).catch(() => {});
    });
    return dir;
  })
  .extend('configFile', async ({ tmpDir }: { tmpDir: string }, { onCleanup }) => {
    const path = join(tmpDir, 'config.json');
    await writeFile(path, JSON.stringify({ debug: true }));
    onCleanup(async () => {
      await unlink(path).catch(() => {});
    });
    return path;
  });

test('config loader reads debug flag correctly', async ({ configFile }) => {
  const config = await import(configFile, { assert: { type: 'json' } });
  expect(config.default.debug).toBe(true);
});
```
Tradeoff: Chaining `.extend()` calls with individual `onCleanup` registrations per fixture creates a fine-grained, composable cleanup graph where each fixture is responsible for exactly its own resources; the constraint that `onCleanup` can only be called once per fixture means complex cleanup (e.g., close connection and drop database) must be encoded into a single async function or split across separate fixtures — attempting to call `onCleanup` twice in the same fixture silently ignores the second registration.

**Pattern 561** — Playwright Soft Assertions to Collect All Failures Without Early Termination
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('profile page displays all user fields correctly', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/profile/42');

  // Soft assertions accumulate failures rather than aborting on the first one.
  // This gives a complete picture of which fields are broken in a single run.
  const softExpect = expect.configure({ soft: true });

  await softExpect(page.getByTestId('user-name')).toHaveText('Alice Example');
  await softExpect(page.getByTestId('user-email')).toHaveText('alice@example.com');
  await softExpect(page.getByTestId('user-role')).toHaveText('Admin');
  await softExpect(page.getByTestId('avatar-img')).toBeVisible();
  await softExpect(page.getByTestId('last-login')).toContainText('2026');

  // Hard assertion at the end: fails the test with a summary of all soft failures.
  expect(page).toBeDefined(); // triggers the accumulated soft-assertion report
});
```
Tradeoff: Soft assertions reveal the full set of broken fields in one test run, eliminating the common pattern where fixing one assertion just reveals the next; the risk is that soft assertions continue executing code after a meaningful failure (e.g., asserting child elements when a parent element is missing), which can produce misleading secondary errors that obscure the actual root cause — always add a structural hard assertion before soft assertions that depend on a parent element being present.

**Pattern 562** — `test.slow()` to Triple Timeout for Known-Slow Tests Without Config Changes
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('full PDF generation pipeline completes', async ({ page }) => {
  // Marks this test as slow, tripling its effective timeout from the global
  // default (e.g., 30 s -> 90 s) without changing playwright.config.ts.
  // Preserves the global timeout for all other tests.
  test.slow();

  await page.goto('/reports/generate');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Generate PDF' }).click();

  // PDF rendering is I/O-bound; wait up to the tripled timeout.
  await expect(page.getByTestId('download-link')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 60_000 });
  const href = await page.getByTestId('download-link').getAttribute('href');
  expect(href).toMatch(/\.pdf$/);
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.slow()` is a surgical override that avoids inflating the global timeout for every test just to accommodate a handful of known-slow operations; the downside is that it can become a crutch — a test that needs `test.slow()` because of an inherent performance problem in the application should ideally be accompanied by a performance ticket, otherwise the annotation accumulates into a misleading baseline where "slow" is normalised rather than investigated.

**Pattern 563** — Playwright `test.describe.serial` for Stateful Multi-Step Flows That Cannot Be Isolated
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// serial mode: tests run one after another in the same worker.
// If any test fails, subsequent tests in the group are skipped.
// On retry, the entire group reruns from the first test.
test.describe.serial('onboarding wizard — ordered steps', () => {
  test('step 1: account creation', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/onboard/step-1');
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('newuser@example.com');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' }).click();
    await expect(page).toHaveURL('/onboard/step-2');
  });

  test('step 2: profile completion', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.getByLabel('Display Name').fill('New User');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save & Continue' }).click();
    await expect(page).toHaveURL('/onboard/step-3');
  });

  test('step 3: email verification redirect', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send Verification Email' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByText('Check your inbox')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.describe.serial` is appropriate only for flows where each step genuinely depends on the previous step's server-side state (e.g., a wizard that writes to a database at each step); the significant downside is that a flaky step 1 causes steps 2 and 3 to be skipped and reported as "did not run," which inflates the apparent failure scope and makes it harder to distinguish a skip from a genuine independent failure in CI dashboards.

**Pattern 564** — Vitest `vi.stubEnv` for Deterministic Environment Variable Isolation Per Test
```typescript
import { vi, test, expect, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { getFeatureFlag } from '../src/feature-flags';

afterEach(() => {
  // vi.unstubAllEnvs restores the original process.env values set before the test
  // suite started, preventing env mutations from leaking between tests.
  vi.unstubAllEnvs();
});

test('feature flag returns true when env var is "enabled"', () => {
  vi.stubEnv('FEATURE_NEW_DASHBOARD', 'enabled');
  expect(getFeatureFlag('NEW_DASHBOARD')).toBe(true);
});

test('feature flag returns false when env var is absent', () => {
  vi.stubEnv('FEATURE_NEW_DASHBOARD', '');
  expect(getFeatureFlag('NEW_DASHBOARD')).toBe(false);
});

test('feature flag is unaffected by previous test stubs', () => {
  // Do not stub — env var is absent entirely after unstubAllEnvs.
  expect(getFeatureFlag('NEW_DASHBOARD')).toBe(false);
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.stubEnv` + `vi.unstubAllEnvs` is safer than directly mutating `process.env` because Vitest tracks all stubs and can restore them atomically; however, `vi.stubEnv` only patches `process.env` — code that reads environment variables at module load time (before the test runs) will see the original value regardless, requiring `vi.resetModules()` and a dynamic `import()` inside the test body to force re-evaluation.

**Pattern 565** — Jest `fakeTimers.doNotFake` Global Config to Protect `Date.now` Benchmarks
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  fakeTimers: {
    enableGlobally: true,
    // Preserve real Date.now() for performance.mark / performance.measure
    // while still faking setTimeout and setInterval everywhere.
    doNotFake: ['Date', 'performance'],
    timerLimit: 500,
  },
});
```
```typescript
// performance-monitor.test.ts — Date and performance remain real; timers are faked
import { getTimestamp } from '../src/performance-monitor';

it('getTimestamp returns a real wall-clock millisecond value', () => {
  const before = Date.now();
  const ts = getTimestamp();
  const after = Date.now();
  expect(ts).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(before);
  expect(ts).toBeLessThanOrEqual(after);
});
```
Tradeoff: Enabling `fakeTimers` globally in `jest.config.ts` eliminates per-file `jest.useFakeTimers()` boilerplate and ensures timers are always faked, reducing the risk that a developer forgets to fake timers in a new test file; the critical caveat is that `doNotFake` must explicitly list every global that should remain real (including `Date` and `performance` for timing-sensitive code), and omitting a needed entry from `doNotFake` can silently break assertions in tests that rely on real elapsed time.

---

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G210 — `jest.retryTimes` Declared Inside `beforeAll` Is Silently Ignored**
Why this matters: `jest.retryTimes()` must be declared at the top level of a test file or directly inside a `describe` block — placing it inside `beforeAll`, `beforeEach`, or any other lifecycle hook causes the call to be silently ignored by `jest-circus`. Tests will not be retried, and no error or warning is emitted, making this a hard-to-diagnose misconfiguration. Developers who refactor retry setup into a shared `beforeAll` hook discover the problem only when a flaky test fails in CI after appearing to have retry coverage.
Fix: always declare `jest.retryTimes(n, options)` as a direct statement at the top level of the test file (above all `describe` blocks) or as the first statement inside a `describe` block. If you need shared retry configuration across multiple files, set it via `globalSetup` or configure it in `jest.config.ts` using the `retryTimes` project config key rather than through the `jest` object API.

**Gotcha G211 — Vitest `onCleanup` Can Only Be Called Once Per Fixture; Second Call Is Silently Dropped**
Why this matters: Vitest's `onCleanup` registration within a `.extend()` fixture is a one-time registration slot — calling `onCleanup` a second time within the same fixture function does not enqueue a second cleanup callback. The second call is silently dropped without any error or warning. Fixtures that conditionally register different cleanup paths (e.g., "if connection succeeded, close it; if file was created, delete it") will silently skip the cleanup of whichever branch registers second, causing resource leaks that accumulate across test runs.
Fix: encode all cleanup logic into a single `onCleanup` async function using `try/finally` to handle both success and failure paths: `onCleanup(async () => { try { await closeConnection(); } finally { await deleteFile(); } })`. Alternatively, decompose the fixture into two separate fixtures each with their own `onCleanup`, and compose them via fixture dependencies.

**Gotcha G212 — Playwright `expect.toPass` Has a Default Timeout of 0, Making It Effectively Non-Retrying Without Explicit Configuration**
Why this matters: unlike `expect.poll`, which defaults to a 5-second timeout, `expect.toPass` defaults to `timeout: 0`, meaning it executes the callback exactly once with no retry unless you explicitly pass a `timeout` option. Developers who use `expect.toPass` expecting automatic retry behaviour — by analogy with other Playwright web-first assertions — will find their tests pass on the first attempt in fast environments but fail intermittently in CI where async state may not have settled, producing the exact flakiness the pattern was intended to prevent.
Fix: always specify both `timeout` and `intervals` when using `expect.toPass`: `await expect(async () => { ... }).toPass({ intervals: [500, 1_000, 2_000], timeout: 15_000 })`. Consider creating a project-level wrapper (`expectToPass`) that applies your standard retry configuration by default, reducing the risk that individual test authors omit the required options.

**Gotcha G213 — Jest `randomize: true` Without `showSeed` Makes Flaky-Order Failures Impossible to Reproduce**
Why this matters: enabling `randomize: true` in `jest.config.ts` causes tests to execute in a different order each run, which is excellent for detecting order-dependent flakiness. However, if `showSeed: true` is not also set (or the seed is not captured in CI artifacts), a failure that only manifests under a specific test order cannot be reproduced locally. The seed that caused the failure is neither printed to the console nor accessible in the failure report, making investigation dependent on luck or brute-force re-runs.
Fix: always pair `randomize: true` with `showSeed: true` in `jest.config.ts`. Additionally, configure your CI system to capture the seed value from Jest's stdout (it appears as `Randomized with seed: 12345`) and store it as a build artifact or annotate the failed build with it. To reproduce locally: `npx jest --randomize --seed=<captured-seed>`.

**Gotcha G214 — Vitest File-Scoped Fixtures Do Not Have Access to Test Context (`task`, `expect`, `skip`)**
Why this matters: Vitest fixture functions declared with `{ scope: 'file' }` run in file scope, which is outside the per-test context. Attempting to access `task.name`, call `skip()`, or use the context-bound `expect` inside a file-scoped fixture results in a runtime error or returns `undefined`. Developers who copy fixture code from test-scoped fixtures to file-scoped ones and use context properties are surprised to find their fixture crashes on initialisation with cryptic errors like "Cannot read properties of undefined."
Fix: file-scoped fixtures should derive any test-file-specific information (e.g., the current file path for database naming) using `expect.getState().testPath` rather than the fixture context object. Move any logic that depends on per-test context (`task`, `skip`, `annotate`) into test-scoped fixtures that are composed with the file-scoped fixture as a dependency. The hierarchy is strict: file/worker fixtures cannot consume test-scoped context; only test-scoped fixtures can consume file/worker-scoped ones.

## Cycle 61 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 566** — Playwright `route.fulfill` with `json` Option for Deterministic API Responses
```typescript
// tests/dashboard.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard renders user count from API', async ({ page }) => {
  // Intercept before navigation so the page never hits the real endpoint
  await page.route('**/api/users/count', async route => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      json: { count: 42, lastUpdated: '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z' },
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('user-count')).toHaveText('42');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('last-updated')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `route.fulfill({ json })` completely removes real-network latency and response variability, making the test deterministic; however, the mock response must be kept in sync with the actual API contract manually — schema drift between the mock and the live API goes undetected until an integration test or consumer-driven contract test catches it.

**Pattern 567** — Playwright `route.fetch` + `route.fulfill` for Selective Response Patching
```typescript
// tests/pricing.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('out-of-stock badge renders when inventory is zero', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('**/api/products/*', async route => {
    // Execute the real request so auth headers, query params, etc. are preserved
    const response = await route.fetch();
    const body = await response.json();

    // Surgically patch only the field under test
    body.inventory = 0;
    body.available = false;

    await route.fulfill({ response, json: body });
  });

  await page.goto('/products/widget-pro');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="out-of-stock-badge"]')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="add-to-cart"]')).toBeDisabled();
});
```
Tradeoff: Fetching the real response and patching only the relevant fields keeps the rest of the response realistic (including any server-generated tokens or dynamic fields) and avoids full-mock maintenance burden; the tradeoff is that the test still depends on the backend being reachable at test time, which reintroduces partial network flakiness in environments where the upstream service is unavailable.

**Pattern 568** — Playwright `page.waitForResponse` Promise Hoisted Before the Triggering Action
```typescript
// tests/search.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('search results appear after typing', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/search');

  // Create the promise BEFORE the action that triggers the request.
  // If created after, the response may arrive before the promise is set up,
  // causing a race condition that fails intermittently in fast environments.
  const searchResponsePromise = page.waitForResponse(
    resp => resp.url().includes('/api/search') && resp.status() === 200,
  );

  await page.getByPlaceholder('Search…').fill('playwright');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Search' }).click();

  const searchResponse = await searchResponsePromise;
  expect(searchResponse.ok()).toBe(true);

  await expect(page.getByTestId('result-list')).not.toBeEmpty();
});
```
Tradeoff: Hoisting the `waitForResponse` promise before the triggering action guarantees that no response can be missed regardless of how fast the network is; the pattern requires developers to identify every network request that must complete before subsequent assertions, which can be tedious for pages that fire multiple parallel requests — in those cases, `Promise.all([waitForResponse(...), waitForResponse(...)])` is the correct extension.

**Pattern 569** — Playwright Worker-Scoped Fixture for Browser-Level Authentication State
```typescript
// fixtures/auth.ts
import { test as base, BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

type AuthFixtures = { authenticatedContext: BrowserContext };

export const test = base.extend<{}, AuthFixtures>({
  authenticatedContext: [
    async ({ browser }, use) => {
      // Log in once per worker; reuse the context storage state for all tests in the worker.
      const context = await browser.newContext();
      const page = await context.newPage();
      await page.goto('/login');
      await page.fill('[name=email]', process.env.TEST_USER_EMAIL!);
      await page.fill('[name=password]', process.env.TEST_USER_PASSWORD!);
      await page.click('[type=submit]');
      await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
      await use(context);
      await context.close();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

// tests/billing.spec.ts
import { test } from '../fixtures/auth';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('billing page loads for authenticated user', async ({ authenticatedContext }) => {
  const page = await authenticatedContext.newPage();
  await page.goto('/billing');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Billing' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: A worker-scoped auth fixture logs in exactly once per worker process and reuses the authentication cookies for every test in that worker, eliminating repeated login flows that are a major source of CI flakiness and slowness; the risk is that a test that mutates auth state (e.g., changes the user's role or revokes a token) will corrupt the shared context for all subsequent tests in that worker, so tests that modify auth state must use a separate test-scoped context and never share the worker-scoped one.

**Pattern 570** — Playwright `test.describe.configure({ retries })` Scoped to Network-Dependent Describe Block
```typescript
// tests/external-payment.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Only the payment provider block gets retries — the rest of the suite runs once.
// This avoids masking bugs in stable code while tolerating known third-party flakiness.
test.describe('Stripe webhook delivery', () => {
  test.describe.configure({ retries: 2 });

  test('webhook fires within 5 seconds of checkout', async ({ page, request }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.click('[data-testid="pay-button"]');

    // Poll the internal webhook log endpoint — Stripe delivery timing is non-deterministic
    await expect
      .poll(
        async () => {
          const resp = await request.get('/api/test/webhook-log');
          const log = await resp.json();
          return log.events.some((e: { type: string }) => e.type === 'checkout.session.completed');
        },
        { timeout: 8_000, intervals: [500, 1_000, 2_000] },
      )
      .toBe(true);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Scoping retries with `test.describe.configure({ retries })` surgically applies retry budget only to tests that have a known external dependency, avoiding the anti-pattern of setting a global retry count that silently masks logic bugs in fast, stable tests; the downside is that each describe block's retry budget must be audited independently — a developer may forget to add retries to a new third-party-dependent test added outside the configured block.

**Pattern 571** — Vitest `vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ['nextTick', 'queueMicrotask'] })` for Microtask-Level Determinism
```typescript
// src/debounce-queue.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { DebounceQueue } from './debounce-queue';

describe('DebounceQueue', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    // Fake both macro-timers and micro-task queues so Promise resolution
    // order is fully deterministic and not subject to real event-loop timing.
    vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ['setTimeout', 'clearTimeout', 'nextTick', 'queueMicrotask'] });
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });

  it('batches events fired within the debounce window', async () => {
    const handler = vi.fn();
    const queue = new DebounceQueue(handler, 200);

    queue.push('a');
    queue.push('b');
    queue.push('c');

    // Time has not advanced — handler should not have fired yet
    expect(handler).not.toHaveBeenCalled();

    // Advance past the debounce window and flush microtasks
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(250);

    expect(handler).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(handler).toHaveBeenCalledWith(['a', 'b', 'c']);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Including `'nextTick'` and `'queueMicrotask'` in the `toFake` array gives the test complete control over micro-task scheduling, preventing Promise chains inside the implementation from resolving in real time and introducing non-determinism; the critical caveat is that faking `nextTick` can break third-party libraries (including some Node.js internals) that rely on `process.nextTick` for internal housekeeping — scope `toFake` as narrowly as possible and test for unexpected side effects when adding microtask fakes.

**Pattern 572** — Vitest `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` for Async Timer Chains Without Real Waiting
```typescript
// src/polling-service.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { PollingService } from './polling-service';

describe('PollingService', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });

  it('retries fetch on 503 and succeeds on third attempt', async () => {
    const fetcher = vi.fn()
      .mockResolvedValueOnce({ status: 503 })
      .mockResolvedValueOnce({ status: 503 })
      .mockResolvedValueOnce({ status: 200, data: { ready: true } });

    const service = new PollingService(fetcher, { interval: 1_000, maxRetries: 5 });
    const resultPromise = service.pollUntilReady();

    // Advance 3 polling intervals — each await drains the microtask queue
    // so the Promise chain inside PollingService resolves at the right time.
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1_000);
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1_000);
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1_000);

    const result = await resultPromise;
    expect(result).toEqual({ ready: true });
    expect(fetcher).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` is the async counterpart of `vi.advanceTimersByTime` and drains Promise microtasks between each timer tick, making it the correct tool for testing code that mixes `setTimeout` with `await` internally; using the synchronous `vi.advanceTimersByTime` on async code can result in timers advancing without the accompanying Promise resolutions executing, causing assertions to run against incompletely settled state.

**Pattern 573** — Vitest `vi.setTimerTickMode('nextTimerAsync')` for Continuous Async Timer Drain
```typescript
// src/retry-backoff.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { retryWithBackoff } from './retry-backoff';

describe('retryWithBackoff', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    // Auto-advance to the next timer and drain microtasks after each macrotask,
    // so the test body only needs to await the final result rather than manually
    // advancing time for each retry interval.
    vi.setTimerTickMode('nextTimerAsync');
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });

  it('returns the result after 3 retries with exponential backoff', async () => {
    const operation = vi.fn()
      .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('transient'))
      .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('transient'))
      .mockResolvedValueOnce({ success: true });

    const result = await retryWithBackoff(operation, { maxAttempts: 3, baseDelayMs: 100 });

    expect(result).toEqual({ success: true });
    expect(operation).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.setTimerTickMode('nextTimerAsync')` (added in Vitest 4.1.0) eliminates the need to manually call `advanceTimersByTimeAsync` for each delay in retry/backoff tests, dramatically reducing boilerplate; however, the auto-advance behaviour is global for the test and can cause timers unrelated to the code under test (such as those in auto-imported test helpers) to fire unexpectedly, producing subtle false positives — always pair with targeted `vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: [...] })` to limit which global timer functions are intercepted.

**Pattern 574** — Jest `resetMocks: true` + `restoreMocks: true` in Global Config to Prevent Cross-Test Mock Contamination
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  // Automatically clear mock.calls and mock.instances before every test
  clearMocks: true,
  // Automatically reset mock implementation to undefined before every test
  resetMocks: true,
  // Automatically restore jest.spyOn mocks to real implementations before every test
  restoreMocks: true,
});
```
```typescript
// user-service.test.ts
import { fetchUser } from '../src/user-service';
import * as api from '../src/api-client';

it('returns user data on success', async () => {
  jest.spyOn(api, 'get').mockResolvedValue({ id: 1, name: 'Alice' });
  const user = await fetchUser(1);
  expect(user.name).toBe('Alice');
  // No manual cleanup needed — restoreMocks: true handles it before next test
});

it('throws on 404 using real api.get behaviour', async () => {
  // If restoreMocks were false and the previous test leaked its spy,
  // this test would incorrectly use the mock rather than the real implementation.
  await expect(fetchUser(9999)).rejects.toThrow('Not found');
});
```
Tradeoff: Setting all three mock-reset flags globally guarantees that no spy, mock implementation, or call history leaks from one test to another, eliminating a large class of order-dependent flakiness; the cost is a small per-test overhead from resetting mock state before every test, and tests that intentionally share a spy across multiple `it` blocks within a `describe` must be refactored to set up the spy afresh inside each test or in a `beforeEach`.

**Pattern 575** — Jest `waitForUnhandledRejections: true` to Catch Swallowed Async Errors
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  // Give the event loop one extra turn to handle rejectionHandled events,
  // preventing silently swallowed async errors from causing intermittent failures
  // in a subsequent, unrelated test that happens to catch the dangling rejection.
  waitForUnhandledRejections: true,
  testTimeout: 10_000,
});
```
```typescript
// async-event-bus.test.ts
it('emits error event when subscriber throws', async () => {
  const bus = new AsyncEventBus();
  const errors: Error[] = [];

  bus.on('error', err => errors.push(err));
  bus.subscribe('data', async () => {
    throw new Error('subscriber failure');
  });

  bus.emit('data', { payload: 42 });

  // waitForUnhandledRejections ensures the rejection from the async subscriber
  // is observed and attributed to THIS test rather than silently propagating
  // and corrupting the next test's assertion state.
  await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 50));
  expect(errors).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(errors[0].message).toBe('subscriber failure');
});
```
Tradeoff: `waitForUnhandledRejections: true` ensures that a Promise rejection generated in one test is attributed to that test rather than appearing as a mysterious failure in a later test, which is the classic symptom of async rejection leakage; the documented trade-off is that this option adds noticeable per-test overhead because it inserts an extra event-loop tick between every test, making it more impactful on large suites with thousands of fast unit tests than on smaller integration suites.

**Pattern 576** — Jest `workerGracefulExitTimeout` + `detectOpenHandles` for Resource-Leak Diagnosis
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  // Allow workers 3 seconds to close open handles before Jest force-kills them.
  // Default is 500ms, which is too short for database connection pool teardown.
  workerGracefulExitTimeout: 3_000,
  // Print a warning describing which async operations kept the worker alive,
  // enabling targeted investigation rather than blind force-exit.
  detectOpenHandles: true,
  openHandlesTimeout: 2_000,
});
```
```typescript
// database.test.ts — teardown that ensures the pool closes within the grace period
import { pool } from '../src/database';

afterAll(async () => {
  // Without this, the worker stays alive past workerGracefulExitTimeout because
  // the connection pool holds open TCP sockets, detected by --detectOpenHandles
  // as a "TCPSERVERWRAP" or "TCPWRAP" open handle.
  await pool.end();
});

it('returns a user row by id', async () => {
  const result = await pool.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1', [1]);
  expect(result.rows).toHaveLength(1);
});
```
Tradeoff: Combining `workerGracefulExitTimeout` with `detectOpenHandles` gives the test suite both the time and the diagnostics needed to cleanly shut down long-lived resources — increasing the grace period prevents spurious force-kill warnings in slow teardown environments; however, `detectOpenHandles` is implemented by monkey-patching Node.js internals and imposes a measurable performance cost, so it should be enabled during flakiness investigation and disabled in production CI once the root cause has been fixed.

**Pattern 577** — Playwright `serviceWorkers: 'block'` on BrowserContext to Prevent Service Worker Request Interception Shadowing
```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium-no-sw',
      use: {
        ...devices['Desktop Chrome'],
        // Block service workers so that page.route() intercepts are not shadowed
        // by a cached SW response from a previous test run's browser context.
        serviceWorkers: 'block',
      },
    },
  ],
});
```
```typescript
// tests/offline-fallback.spec.ts — route intercepts work reliably without SW interference
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('shows offline fallback when API is unreachable', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('**/api/**', route => route.abort('internetdisconnected'));
  await page.goto('/app');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('offline-banner')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Setting `serviceWorkers: 'block'` on the browser context ensures that `page.route()` interceptions are always the authoritative response for a request, preventing a cached Service Worker from fulfilling requests before Playwright's routing layer sees them — this is essential for deterministic network mocking; the downside is that any feature relying on a Service Worker (push notifications, background sync, offline caching) will not function in this context, so tests verifying SW-specific behaviour must use a separate project configuration with `serviceWorkers: 'allow'`.

**Pattern 578** — Playwright `fullyParallel: true` + `--shard` with Blob Reporter for Balanced CI Sharding
```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Split at the individual test level rather than file level so shards
  // receive balanced workloads regardless of file size distribution.
  fullyParallel: true,
  // Use blob reporter in CI; each shard writes a blob that is merged post-run.
  reporter: process.env.CI ? [['blob', { outputDir: './blob-report' }]] : [['html']],
  workers: process.env.CI ? 2 : undefined,
});
```
```yaml
# .github/workflows/playwright.yml (excerpt)
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
    steps:
      - run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: blob-report-${{ matrix.shard }}
          path: blob-report/
  merge-reports:
    needs: [test]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { pattern: blob-report-*, merge-multiple: true, path: all-blob-reports }
      - run: npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports
```
Tradeoff: `fullyParallel: true` paired with `--shard=X/Y` achieves near-linear CI time reduction with each additional shard because tests are distributed at the individual test level rather than the file level, preventing the "one giant file dominates shard 1" imbalance; the trade-off is that `fullyParallel` can expose previously hidden inter-test state dependencies — tests that accidentally shared browser context state and happened to run sequentially in the same file will now fail non-deterministically when distributed across workers.

**Pattern 579** — Playwright Locator `waitFor` with `state: 'detached'` to Confirm Element Removal Before Proceeding
```typescript
// tests/modal.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('modal closes and form is accessible after dismiss', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/settings');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Open Warning' }).click();

  const modal = page.getByRole('dialog');
  await expect(modal).toBeVisible();

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Dismiss' }).click();

  // Wait for the modal to be fully removed from the DOM before interacting
  // with elements beneath it. Without this, the next click may target the
  // modal's overlay rather than the now-visible form field, causing a
  // flaky "element not interactable" error.
  await modal.waitFor({ state: 'detached' });

  await page.getByLabel('Display name').fill('Alice');
  await expect(page.getByLabel('Display name')).toHaveValue('Alice');
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `locator.waitFor({ state: 'detached' })` explicitly gates subsequent interactions on the complete DOM removal of an overlaying element, eliminating a category of flakiness where Playwright's auto-waiting considers a button "enabled" and "visible" but clicks are still intercepted by a fading-out overlay; the limitation is that CSS transitions that move an element off-screen without actually detaching it from the DOM will not be detected by `'detached'` — in those cases, `expect(modal).not.toBeVisible()` combined with a locator assertion is the appropriate alternative.

**Pattern 580** — Jest `slowTestThreshold` + `openHandlesTimeout` Combined for Proactive Flakiness Budgeting
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  // Flag tests that exceed 3 seconds — slow tests are disproportionately flaky
  // because they sit closer to timeout boundaries and accumulate more timing variance.
  slowTestThreshold: 3,

  // Warn if Jest hasn't exited 2 seconds after all tests complete — this surfaces
  // event loop holds (open DB connections, unresolved timers) before they cause
  // random failures in subsequent test runs.
  openHandlesTimeout: 2_000,

  testTimeout: 15_000,
  detectOpenHandles: process.env.CI === 'true',
});
```
```typescript
// slow-query.test.ts — example of a test that legitimately needs extra time
import { queryAnalytics } from '../src/analytics';

// Explicitly opt out of the project-wide slowTestThreshold warning for
// this test by documenting why it is expected to be slow, rather than
// raising slowTestThreshold globally and masking newly-slow tests.
it(
  'analytics aggregation query completes under 5 seconds',
  async () => {
    const result = await queryAnalytics({ period: '30d' });
    expect(result.totalEvents).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  },
  5_000, // per-test timeout override
);
```
Tradeoff: Using `slowTestThreshold` as an early-warning signal and `openHandlesTimeout` as a post-run health check creates a two-layer flakiness budget — slow tests are flagged for investigation before they start hitting timeouts, and open handles are surfaced before they silently affect subsequent test runs; the tension between these two options is that raising `testTimeout` to suppress false timeout failures can push tests beyond `slowTestThreshold`, generating noise — the correct response is to fix the underlying slowness rather than raise the threshold globally.
