### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G215 — `vi.useFakeTimers` Does Not Reset `Date` by Default; `vi.setSystemTime` Must Be Called Explicitly**
Why this matters: Calling `vi.useFakeTimers()` without specifying `{ toFake: ['Date'] }` (or relying on the default fake list, which does include `Date` in most configurations) does not automatically reset `Date.now()` or `new Date()` to a fixed value — they continue to return real wall-clock time unless `vi.setSystemTime()` is explicitly called. Tests that assert on timestamps generated inside the implementation (e.g., `createdAt` fields, expiry calculations) will produce different values on each run because the real clock advances between runs, causing intermittent assertion mismatches. Developers unfamiliar with the distinction between "timer faking" (controlling `setTimeout` scheduling) and "system time faking" (controlling `Date.now()`) frequently conflate the two.
Fix: always call `vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z'))` after `vi.useFakeTimers()` in any test that asserts on timestamp values, and call `vi.useRealTimers()` in `afterEach` to restore the real clock. For projects where many tests depend on a fixed date, set a global fake time in `globalSetup` via `vi.setSystemTime(FIXED_DATE)` and document the epoch date in the project's test conventions.

**Gotcha G216 — Playwright `page.route` Handlers Registered After `page.goto` Miss Requests That Fire During Navigation**
Why this matters: `page.route()` intercepts only requests that are made after the handler is registered. If a test calls `await page.goto('/app')` first and registers a route handler afterwards, any requests fired during the initial page load — including the first API call triggered by component mount — will have already completed with real network responses before the route handler was in place. Tests that depend on mocked responses for startup requests pass locally (where the real API returns expected data) but fail intermittently in CI (where the API may be unavailable, rate-limited, or return different staging data).
Fix: always register `page.route()` handlers before calling `page.goto()`. For complex setups, use `browserContext.route()` rather than `page.route()` so the handler applies to all pages created by the context, including redirects that create new page objects. If setup must happen after navigation, use `page.reload()` to re-fire the instrumented requests after the handler is in place.

**Gotcha G217 — Jest `--detectOpenHandles` Causes Test-Order-Dependent False Positives When Shared Server Is Closed Too Early**
Why this matters: When a test suite starts a shared HTTP server in `globalSetup` and closes it in `globalTeardown`, enabling `--detectOpenHandles` can cause Jest to report the server as an open handle if worker cleanup races with `globalTeardown` execution. Worker processes that are still running their `afterAll` cleanup when `globalTeardown` fires will see the server close underneath them, causing the worker to report its own open TCP sockets as leaked handles — even though those sockets would have closed correctly had `globalTeardown` waited. This produces inconsistent open handle warnings across runs, with no actual leak present.
Fix: ensure `globalTeardown` waits for a global signal (e.g., a shared flag written to a temp file, or an explicit delay matching `workerGracefulExitTimeout`) before closing shared resources. Alternatively, move shared server lifecycle into a worker-scoped Jest `setup` file (via `setupFilesAfterFramework`) so teardown is co-located with each worker's lifecycle rather than in the global teardown, which runs outside worker scope.

**Gotcha G218 — Vitest `fileParallelism: false` Does Not Make Tests Within a File Sequential; Use `test.sequential` or `describe.sequential`**
Why this matters: Developers who set `fileParallelism: false` expecting that tests within a file will also run sequentially are surprised to discover that the option only disables parallelism between files — individual tests within the same file that perform concurrent async operations can still interleave if the test runner picks up multiple `it` blocks simultaneously. Specifically, Vitest runs tests within a file sequentially by default, but if a test returns a Promise that resolves after the next test has started (e.g., a fire-and-forget async side effect), the overlapping execution creates shared-state flakiness that `fileParallelism: false` does not prevent.
Fix: for tests that must be strictly sequential with no overlap, annotate the `describe` block with `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'sequence' })` (or use the `describe.sequential` shorthand). For individual tests with fire-and-forget side effects, ensure all async work is `await`-ed before the test body returns — dangling Promises that outlive the test function body are the primary source of within-file concurrency bugs.

**Gotcha G219 — Playwright `locator.click()` Auto-Waiting Does Not Guard Against CSS `pointer-events: none` Transitions**
Why this matters: Playwright's actionability checks verify that an element is visible, stable, enabled, and receives pointer events before performing a click. However, during a CSS animation that transitions from `pointer-events: none` to `pointer-events: auto` (or vice versa), the computed style snapshot that Playwright reads may pass the "receives events" check at the moment of the check but fail by the time the synthetic mouse event is dispatched — a race window of a few milliseconds that is consistently reproducible only in headless environments where rendering is accelerated. Tests that click buttons or links appearing via CSS fade-in transitions will pass locally in headed mode and fail intermittently in headless CI.
Fix: add a `locator.waitFor({ state: 'visible' })` call followed by a short `expect.poll` that reads `getComputedStyle(el).pointerEvents` via `page.evaluate` and waits until it equals `'auto'` before clicking. For animation-heavy UIs, set `animations: 'disabled'` in the `use` block of `playwright.config.ts` to eliminate CSS transition timing entirely from the test environment, which is the most reliable long-term fix.

## Cycle 62 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 581** — Playwright `expect.poll` with Custom `intervals` for Non-Uniform Polling Cadence on Expensive Async Checks

```typescript
// expensive-poll.test.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('job queue drains within 30 seconds after submission', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/jobs');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Run batch job' }).click();

  // expect.poll converts a synchronous assertion into a polling loop.
  // The `intervals` array controls wait times BETWEEN probes — use an
  // exponential-ish sequence so fast successes resolve immediately while
  // slow completions are still caught without hammering the server.
  // Default intervals are [100, 250, 500, 1000], which probe too
  // aggressively for jobs that take 10+ seconds and can generate
  // excess server load in CI environments running many workers.
  await expect.poll(
    async () => {
      const cell = page.getByTestId('job-status');
      return cell.textContent();
    },
    {
      message: 'Expected job status to reach "completed" within 30 s',
      timeout: 30_000,
      // Back off: probe at 500 ms, 1 s, 2 s, 5 s, then every 5 s
      intervals: [500, 1_000, 2_000, 5_000, 5_000],
    },
  ).toBe('completed');
});

// contrast: tight polling for fast in-memory operations
test('counter increments within 500 ms', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/counter');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Increment' }).click();

  await expect.poll(
    () => page.getByTestId('count').textContent(),
    { timeout: 500, intervals: [50, 100] },
  ).toBe('1');
});
```
Tradeoff: Tuning `intervals` to match the realistic completion time of the operation under test prevents both false timeouts (when polling too infrequently relative to actual completion) and server overload (when polling too frequently on expensive async work); the tension is that a single hardcoded `intervals` sequence optimised for CI speed may be too aggressive for slow staging environments, so for cross-environment reliability it is better to derive timeout and intervals from environment variables rather than hardcoding them.

---

**Pattern 582** — Playwright `expect.toPass` for Retrying Multi-Step Assertion Blocks Without Structural Changes

```typescript
// multi-step-retry.test.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard summary card reflects newly submitted report', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Submit report via API to bypass UI timing entirely
  await page.request.post('/api/reports', {
    data: { title: 'Q2 Summary', status: 'final' },
  });

  // expect.toPass retries the entire callback block — not just a single
  // assertion — until ALL assertions inside pass or the timeout is reached.
  // This is the correct tool when the test must assert several related
  // values that update together (e.g., count AND last-updated timestamp)
  // and a partial pass/fail would give a misleading error message.
  await expect(async () => {
    const count = await page.getByTestId('report-count').textContent();
    const badge = await page.getByTestId('new-badge').textContent();

    expect(Number(count)).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1);
    expect(badge).toBe('New');
  }).toPass({ timeout: 10_000 });
});

// anti-pattern: using individual locator assertions with await — they do
// not compose into a single retried block and can interleave with DOM updates
test('❌ non-atomic assertions race with DOM updates', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  // These two assertions run in separate auto-wait cycles — the DOM can
  // update between them, causing one to see stale data
  await expect(page.getByTestId('report-count')).toHaveText('1');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('new-badge')).toHaveText('New'); // may race
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.toPass` retries the entire block including any side-effectful async calls (such as `page.request.post` if mistakenly placed inside), so only pure read operations and assertions should live inside the callback — place any write operations before `expect.toPass` to prevent duplicate mutations on retry; using `expect.toPass` for trivially simple single-assertion checks adds no benefit over `expect(locator).toHaveText()` and obscures intent.

---

**Pattern 583** — Playwright `trace: 'on-first-retry'` Combined With `screenshot: 'only-on-failure'` for Zero-Overhead CI Diagnostics

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Retries run only on CI — local runs fail fast for developer feedback
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,

  use: {
    // Traces are recorded ONLY on the first retry of a failing test.
    // Recording on every run would double test runtime; recording on
    // all retries wastes disk space on tests that consistently fail.
    // 'on-first-retry' captures exactly the retry that transitions
    // a test from "failed" to "potentially-flaky" status.
    trace: 'on-first-retry',

    // Screenshots on failure provide a lightweight first-pass diagnosis
    // without the storage overhead of full traces on every failure.
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',

    // Video is the heaviest artefact — restrict to CI and only on retry
    video: process.env.CI ? 'on-first-retry' : 'off',
  },

  reporter: [
    ['html'],
    // JSON reporter enables downstream flakiness aggregation scripts
    // that parse `status: "flaky"` entries across runs
    ['json', { outputFile: 'test-results/results.json' }],
  ],

  projects: [
    { name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },
  ],
});
```
Tradeoff: The `'on-first-retry'` strategy captures diagnostic data for flaky tests (the most actionable category) while keeping trace overhead near zero for reliably-passing tests; the limitation is that for tests which consistently fail on all retries, the trace from the first retry may not represent the actual failure mode encountered in the final attempt — for persistent failures, temporarily switching to `trace: 'on'` locally to capture all attempts is the correct diagnostic approach.

---

**Pattern 584** — Playwright `test.describe.configure({ retries: N })` to Scope Retry Budget to Known-Flaky Third-Party Integration Blocks

```typescript
// payments.spec.ts — integrates with a third-party payment sandbox
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// This describe block retries independently from the project-level retries
// setting. Scoped retries prevent the global retry budget from being consumed
// by one noisy third-party integration while keeping zero retries for all
// other tests in the suite, preserving the signal that a non-retried failure
// is a genuine regression.
test.describe('Stripe payment sandbox integration', () => {
  test.describe.configure({ retries: 3 });

  test('checkout completes with test card 4242424242424242', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242 4242 4242 4242');
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/30');
    await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();

    // Stripe's test sandbox has documented latency variance (50 ms – 3 s)
    // which is the source of flakiness — not our application code
    await expect(page.getByTestId('payment-confirmation')).toBeVisible({
      timeout: 15_000,
    });
  });

  test('declined card shows error message', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4000 0000 0000 0002');
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/30');
    await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();

    await expect(page.getByTestId('payment-error')).toContainText('declined');
  });
});

// First-party tests outside the describe block use the global retries: 0
test('product page loads', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');
  await expect(page).toHaveTitle(/Products/);
});
```
Tradeoff: Scoping retries to the integration boundary makes the test suite's flakiness budget explicit and auditable (a reviewer can immediately see which integrations are noise sources), but the presence of any `test.describe.configure({ retries })` block in the codebase is a signal that the underlying integration lacks a deterministic stub — the long-term resolution is to replace the live sandbox call with `page.route` mocking so that retries can be removed entirely.

---

**Pattern 585** — Vitest `retry` with `condition` Callback to Retry Only on Network-Class Errors

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Global retry count for all tests — conservative because most
    // unit tests should never need a retry; this catches CI network blips
    // during tests that make real HTTP calls to localhost test servers.
    retry: 1,
  },
});
```
```typescript
// integration/api-client.test.ts
import { test, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { fetchUser } from '../src/api-client';

// Per-test retry with a condition function restricts retries to the
// specific error class that is environmentally flaky (ECONNREFUSED on
// a test server that hasn't fully started) while letting assertion
// errors propagate immediately without burning retry attempts.
// condition functions ONLY work in test files, not in vitest.config.ts,
// because they cannot be serialized for worker threads.
test(
  'fetchUser returns user data from test server',
  {
    retry: {
      count: 3,
      delay: 200,  // wait 200 ms between attempts to let server stabilise
      condition: (error) =>
        // Retry on connection errors (server not ready) but not on
        // assertion failures (test logic is wrong)
        error.message.includes('ECONNREFUSED') ||
        error.message.includes('ETIMEDOUT'),
    },
  },
  async () => {
    const user = await fetchUser(1);
    expect(user).toMatchObject({ id: 1, name: expect.any(String) });
  },
);

// helper: test that should never retry — assertion failures are real bugs
test('user shape validation', () => {
  const user = { id: 'bad', name: 123 };
  // No retry config — any failure here is a genuine type error
  expect(typeof user.id).toBe('number');
});
```
Tradeoff: Filtering retries by error class prevents the anti-pattern of retrying assertion failures (which are genuine bugs and should fail fast), but `condition` functions that inspect error messages are brittle — a Node.js version upgrade that changes the `ECONNREFUSED` message format will silently disable retry filtering; using `error instanceof` checks against typed error classes (where available) is more robust than string matching.

---

**Pattern 586** — Jest `fakeTimers.enableGlobally` with `doNotFake: ['nextTick', 'setImmediate']` for Promise-Compatible Timer Control

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  fakeTimers: {
    // Enable fake timers for all tests without requiring per-test
    // jest.useFakeTimers() calls — eliminates the category of flakiness
    // where a developer forgets to enable fake timers in a new test file
    // that calls production code containing setTimeout.
    enableGlobally: true,

    // nextTick and setImmediate drive Promise microtask resolution in
    // many Node.js environments. Faking them causes await expressions
    // to deadlock because the microtask queue never drains.
    // Explicitly exclude them so async/await works normally while
    // setTimeout/setInterval remain under fake timer control.
    doNotFake: ['nextTick', 'setImmediate'],

    // Prevent infinite recursive timer loops (e.g., a setInterval that
    // re-schedules itself) from hanging the test runner.
    timerLimit: 1_000,

    // Fix the initial Date to a known epoch so any new Date() calls
    // inside production code produce deterministic timestamps.
    now: new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z').getTime(),
  },

  testTimeout: 10_000,
});
```
```typescript
// timer-service.test.ts
import { timerService } from '../src/timer-service';

it('debounced save triggers after 500 ms', async () => {
  const saveSpy = jest.fn();
  timerService.onSave(saveSpy);
  timerService.scheduleDebounce(500);

  expect(saveSpy).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  jest.advanceTimersByTime(500);

  // Because nextTick is real, awaiting a resolved Promise here works;
  // without doNotFake: ['nextTick'] this await would hang indefinitely.
  await Promise.resolve();
  expect(saveSpy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
});
```
Tradeoff: `enableGlobally` combined with `doNotFake: ['nextTick', 'setImmediate']` is the most pragmatic configuration for codebases that mix timers and async/await, but it creates a subtle risk: production code that uses `setImmediate` for deferred work will NOT be under fake timer control and may execute at real-wall-clock time, causing test ordering surprises; auditing the production codebase for `setImmediate` calls before enabling this configuration prevents unexpected real-time delays.

---

**Pattern 587** — Jest `randomize: true` + `showSeed: true` for Exposing Order-Dependent Test Failures in CI

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  // Randomize execution order of test files and tests within files.
  // Tests that rely on global state left by a previous test will fail
  // non-deterministically, surfacing hidden order dependencies before
  // they cause CI flakiness in a different file ordering.
  randomize: true,

  // Print the random seed to stdout so a specific failure order can be
  // reproduced exactly with --seed=<value> on the CLI.
  showSeed: true,

  // Companion option: reset module registry between tests to prevent
  // module-level singletons from carrying state across test files.
  resetModules: true,

  // Also clear all mock state so test A's mocked return values cannot
  // affect test B when execution order changes under randomization.
  clearMocks: true,
  resetMocks: true,
  restoreMocks: true,
});
```
```typescript
// To reproduce a specific failing seed on the command line:
// jest --seed=1234567890
//
// In CI, capture and store the seed alongside the test report so that
// a flaky failure can be reproduced locally:
//
// jest --json --outputFile=results.json 2>&1 | tee jest-output.txt
// # The seed line appears as: "Randomized with seed: 1234567890"
// grep "Randomized with seed" jest-output.txt

// shared-state-bug.test.ts — example that breaks under randomization
let lastUser: string;

test('set user', () => {
  lastUser = 'alice'; // writes module-level state
});

test('read user', () => {
  // Fails when this test runs BEFORE 'set user' due to randomization
  expect(lastUser).toBe('alice'); // ← order-dependent
});
```
Tradeoff: `randomize: true` is a highly effective tool for surfacing hidden test-order dependencies but can make the test suite appear flakier in the short term (many previously-hidden failures become visible) — this is the correct outcome, but teams should budget investigation time before enabling it in a mature codebase; the seed-based reproduction mechanism (`--seed=N`) is what makes randomization practical rather than just noisy.

---

**Pattern 588** — Jest `workerIdleMemoryLimit` to Prevent Slow Memory-Leak-Driven Flakiness in Long-Running Worker Processes

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  // Recycle a worker process when its heap exceeds this limit between
  // test files. Without this, a worker that runs 200 test files
  // accumulates V8 heap fragmentation and module cache entries, causing
  // GC pauses that push tests over their timeout thresholds — a form of
  // flakiness that only manifests in full CI runs, never in local
  // subset runs with --testPathPattern.
  workerIdleMemoryLimit: '512MB',

  // Run with enough workers to exploit parallelism but not so many that
  // each worker's memory budget is too small to fit its module cache.
  maxWorkers: '50%',

  // Complement with a generous but bounded test timeout — memory pressure
  // causes GC pauses of 100-500 ms, so tests with 5 s timeouts that
  // take 4.8 s in normal conditions will flap under memory pressure.
  testTimeout: 15_000,

  // Force a module registry reset between files to help limit per-worker
  // heap growth from accumulated require() cache entries.
  resetModules: false, // only enable if your suite can tolerate it — has a perf cost
});
```
```typescript
// diagnostic: measure per-worker heap usage to size the limit correctly
// Add to globalSetup.ts:
export default async function globalSetup() {
  // Baseline heap before any tests run
  const baseline = process.memoryUsage().heapUsed;
  console.log(`[setup] baseline heap: ${Math.round(baseline / 1024 / 1024)} MB`);
}

// Add to globalTeardown.ts:
export default async function globalTeardown() {
  const final = process.memoryUsage().heapUsed;
  console.log(`[teardown] final heap: ${Math.round(final / 1024 / 1024)} MB`);
}
```
Tradeoff: Setting `workerIdleMemoryLimit` too low (e.g., `128MB`) causes workers to recycle between almost every test file, defeating worker-level caching and significantly increasing total runtime via repeated module initialisation; setting it too high (e.g., `4GB`) provides no protection against memory-driven flakiness — the correct value is discovered empirically by running the full suite with `--logHeapUsage` and setting the limit to approximately 1.5× the observed peak per-worker heap.

**Pattern 589** — Playwright `browserContext.route` Over `page.route` for Intercepts That Must Survive Cross-Origin Redirects and Popup Windows

```typescript
// context-level-route.test.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('analytics event is fired even when checkout redirects to payment domain', async ({
  context,
  page,
}) => {
  const analyticsRequests: string[] = [];

  // browserContext.route applies to ALL pages and popup windows created
  // by this context — including pages spawned by redirects to a different
  // origin. page.route() would miss requests from the redirected page
  // because the redirect creates a new navigation target that the
  // page-level route handler does not cover.
  await context.route('**/api/analytics/event', async (route) => {
    const body = route.request().postDataJSON();
    analyticsRequests.push(body.event_name);
    // Fulfill with 204 so the application logic succeeds
    await route.fulfill({ status: 204 });
  });

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to payment' }).click();

  // Navigation redirects to pay.example.com — a different origin.
  // The context-level route handler still captures the analytics call
  // fired from the redirected page.
  await page.waitForURL('**/pay.example.com/**');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Confirm' }).click();

  await expect.poll(() => analyticsRequests).toContain('checkout_confirmed');
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `context.route` is correct for cross-origin and popup scenarios but overrides ALL pages in the context, meaning a route registered in one test that is not properly disposed will affect a subsequent test if the same context is reused via a fixture — always call `await route.dispose()` or use per-test context fixtures (`{ scope: 'test' }`) to prevent route handler accumulation across tests.

---

**Pattern 590** — Playwright `page.waitForResponse` Hoisted Before Action to Capture Responses That Arrive Before the Await Point

```typescript
// hoisted-waitForResponse.test.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('search results load after submitting query', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/search');

  // CORRECT: create the waitForResponse Promise BEFORE triggering the
  // action. If the response arrives before the await is reached (common
  // when the server is fast or the network stack is locally cached),
  // the Promise resolves immediately from the already-captured response
  // rather than timing out looking for a response that already passed.
  const responsePromise = page.waitForResponse(
    (resp) =>
      resp.url().includes('/api/search') && resp.status() === 200,
  );

  await page.getByLabel('Search').fill('playwright');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Search' }).click();

  // Now await the previously-hoisted Promise
  const response = await responsePromise;
  const data = await response.json();
  expect(data.results).toHaveLength(10);
});

// WRONG — the response can arrive and be missed before the await is set up
test('❌ race-prone pattern', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/search');
  await page.getByLabel('Search').fill('playwright');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Search' }).click();

  // By the time this line runs, the response may have already arrived
  const response = await page.waitForResponse('/api/search'); // can time out
  expect((await response.json()).results).toHaveLength(10);
});
```
Tradeoff: Hoisting `waitForResponse` before the triggering action is always correct and eliminates the race condition entirely, but it requires careful placement when multiple responses are expected — if two actions each trigger one API call, the `waitForResponse` for the second call must also be hoisted before the first action if they fire in close succession; alternatively, `page.waitForResponse` accepts a predicate function, so a single hoisted call with a URL-matching predicate can capture the right response even when other requests fire first.

---

**Pattern 591** — Vitest `test.sequential` Inside `describe.concurrent` to Isolate State-Mutating Tests Within a Parallel Suite

```typescript
// user-store.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect, beforeEach, vi } from 'vitest';
import { userStore } from '../src/user-store';

// Run the describe block's tests concurrently for speed — most tests
// read from the store and are safe to parallelise.
describe.concurrent('userStore read operations', () => {
  test('getUser returns null for unknown id', async () => {
    const user = await userStore.getUser('unknown');
    expect(user).toBeNull();
  });

  test('listUsers returns array', async () => {
    const users = await userStore.listUsers();
    expect(Array.isArray(users)).toBe(true);
  });

  // Write operations must run sequentially to prevent the concurrent
  // test runner from interleaving mutations. test.sequential inside
  // describe.concurrent opts individual tests out of the parallel pool
  // without splitting the describe block into two separate blocks,
  // which would require duplicating beforeEach/afterEach setup.
  test.sequential('createUser adds entry and returns new id', async () => {
    const id = await userStore.createUser({ name: 'Alice' });
    expect(typeof id).toBe('string');

    const user = await userStore.getUser(id);
    expect(user?.name).toBe('Alice');

    // Clean up after mutation to avoid polluting concurrent readers
    await userStore.deleteUser(id);
  });

  test.sequential('deleteUser removes entry', async () => {
    const id = await userStore.createUser({ name: 'Bob' });
    await userStore.deleteUser(id);
    const user = await userStore.getUser(id);
    expect(user).toBeNull();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Mixing `test.sequential` inside `describe.concurrent` is more granular than converting the entire describe block to sequential, preserving parallelism for read-only tests; however, sequential tests within a concurrent describe still share the same module context as concurrent tests, so any state a sequential test writes between its own setup and cleanup is temporarily visible to concurrently executing read tests — for truly isolated mutations, a separate `describe` block with its own `beforeEach` teardown is the safer approach.

---

**Pattern 592** — Jest `expect.assertions(N)` Combined With `Promise.allSettled` to Prevent Silent Skips in Async Multi-Branch Tests

```typescript
// async-branches.test.ts
import { userService } from '../src/user-service';

describe('userService.processAll', () => {
  it('processes each user and records success or failure', async () => {
    // Declare upfront how many assertions must run.
    // If processAll short-circuits on the first error and skips the
    // remaining users, the test passes vacuously without this guard —
    // the assertions for skipped users simply never execute.
    expect.assertions(6);

    const users = [
      { id: '1', email: 'valid@example.com' },
      { id: '2', email: 'also-valid@example.com' },
      { id: '3', email: '' }, // invalid — should fail gracefully
    ];

    // Promise.allSettled guarantees ALL promises run to completion
    // regardless of individual failures, which pairs with
    // expect.assertions to ensure we assert on every outcome.
    const results = await Promise.allSettled(
      users.map((u) => userService.process(u)),
    );

    expect(results[0].status).toBe('fulfilled');
    expect((results[0] as PromiseFulfilledResult<unknown>).value).toMatchObject({ id: '1', processed: true });

    expect(results[1].status).toBe('fulfilled');
    expect((results[1] as PromiseFulfilledResult<unknown>).value).toMatchObject({ id: '2', processed: true });

    expect(results[2].status).toBe('rejected');
    expect((results[2] as PromiseRejectedResult).reason.message).toMatch(/invalid email/);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.assertions(N)` is a low-cost, high-signal guard against vacuous test passes caused by early return or exception swallowing, but maintaining the correct count as tests evolve requires discipline — a refactor that adds a branch without updating the assertion count silently re-introduces the vulnerability; pairing it with a TypeScript helper that counts the assertion calls statically (via lint rules or test framework plugins) removes the manual maintenance burden.

---

**Pattern 593** — Playwright `page.addInitScript` for Injecting Deterministic Stubs Before Any Page JavaScript Executes

```typescript
// init-script-stub.test.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('feature flag gate renders correct variant without network dependency', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  // addInitScript runs BEFORE any script on the page, including the app
  // bundle. This is the only reliable way to stub globals that the
  // application reads synchronously during module initialisation (e.g.,
  // window.featureFlags, window.analyticsId, window.__ENV__).
  // page.route() cannot intercept these because they are injected via
  // <script> tags or module evaluation, not HTTP requests.
  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    // Stub the feature flag client before the app reads it
    (window as unknown as Record<string, unknown>).__FEATURE_FLAGS__ = {
      newCheckoutFlow: true,
      experimentalSearch: false,
    };

    // Fix Math.random for deterministic A/B test bucket assignment
    const originalRandom = Math.random;
    let callCount = 0;
    Math.random = () => {
      // First call returns 0.1 (bucket A), subsequent calls use real random
      callCount++;
      return callCount === 1 ? 0.1 : originalRandom();
    };
  });

  await page.goto('/checkout');

  // The app read __FEATURE_FLAGS__.newCheckoutFlow === true at startup,
  // so the new flow is shown without any network call to a flag service.
  await expect(page.getByTestId('new-checkout-banner')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `addInitScript` provides unparalleled determinism for globally-initialised state that cannot be stubbed after page load, but it operates outside the normal Playwright request interception model — changes to the stub are not reflected in network logs or trace files, making debugging harder; always add a comment documenting what is being stubbed and why, and use `page.addInitScript({ path: './stubs/feature-flags.js' })` with an external file for complex stubs to keep test files readable.

---

**Pattern 594** — Jest `setupFilesAfterEnv` Global `afterEach` to Assert Zero Unhandled Promise Rejections Per Test

```typescript
// jest-setup-after-env.ts  (referenced in jest.config setupFilesAfterEnv)
// This file runs after Jest's test framework is initialised, giving
// access to jest.fn(), expect, and lifecycle hooks.

// Collect unhandled rejections that occur during test execution.
// Node.js fires 'unhandledRejection' asynchronously — by the time
// a test's assertions run, a rejection from a fire-and-forget Promise
// may not yet have propagated. Capturing it here and asserting in
// afterEach catches it before the next test starts.
const unhandledRejections: unknown[] = [];

beforeAll(() => {
  process.on('unhandledRejection', (reason) => {
    unhandledRejections.push(reason);
  });
});

afterEach(() => {
  if (unhandledRejections.length > 0) {
    const reasons = unhandledRejections.splice(0);
    throw new Error(
      `Test left ${reasons.length} unhandled rejection(s):\n` +
        reasons.map((r) => String(r)).join('\n'),
    );
  }
});
```
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  setupFilesAfterEnv: ['<rootDir>/jest-setup-after-env.ts'],
  // Built-in option for one-event-loop-turn attribution (complements above)
  waitForUnhandledRejections: true,
});
```
Tradeoff: Asserting on unhandled rejections in `afterEach` surfaces a class of flakiness (fire-and-forget Promises that intermittently reject) that is otherwise completely invisible to test assertion counts, but the implementation uses `process.on('unhandledRejection')` which is a global listener — if multiple test workers share the same Node.js process, rejections from one worker's tests may be attributed to another worker's `afterEach`; this pattern is safe with Jest's default forked workers but may require adjustment when using `--runInBand`.

---

**Pattern 595** — Playwright `locator.filter` Chaining to Avoid Ambiguous Multi-Match Flakiness in Dynamic Lists

```typescript
// list-filter.test.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('user can archive a specific notification by name', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/notifications');

  // WRONG: selecting by role alone returns ALL notification items —
  // if the list order changes (due to real-time updates or server-side
  // sort order variance), nth(0) resolves to a different item on retry.
  // const firstItem = page.getByRole('listitem').nth(0); // ← order-dependent

  // CORRECT: chain .filter() with hasText to narrow the locator to exactly
  // the item with the known text, regardless of its position in the list.
  // This makes the interaction order-independent and resilient to real-time
  // list mutations that reorder items between test steps.
  const targetNotification = page
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ hasText: 'Deployment completed: v1.2.3' });

  // Confirm exactly one match to prevent false passes when multiple
  // items share similar text (e.g., "v1.2.3" matches "v1.2.30")
  await expect(targetNotification).toHaveCount(1);

  await targetNotification.getByRole('button', { name: 'Archive' }).click();

  // Verify removal — the item should detach from the DOM after archiving
  await expect(targetNotification).toHaveCount(0);
});

// complementary pattern: use filter with hasNot to find items lacking a badge
test('shows unread count excluding archived items', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/notifications');

  const unreadItems = page
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ hasNot: page.getByTestId('archived-badge') });

  const count = await unreadItems.count();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('unread-counter')).toHaveText(String(count));
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.filter({ hasText })` produces a semantically stable selector that survives list reordering, but `hasText` performs a substring match by default — a list containing both "Deploy v1.2" and "Deploy v1.2.3" will match both items when filtering for "v1.2"; use a RegExp anchored to the full text (`filter({ hasText: /^Deployment completed: v1\.2\.3$/ })`) to guarantee single-item selection when text uniqueness cannot be guaranteed by the application.

---

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G220 — Jest `expect.assertions(N)` Count Does Not Include Assertions Inside `catch` Blocks That Are Never Reached**
Why this matters: A test that wraps a Promise in a try/catch and places assertions in the catch block will pass vacuously if the Promise resolves successfully — the catch block is never entered, the assertions inside it never execute, and Jest reports the test as passed because no assertion failed. Developers writing "error path" tests frequently omit `expect.assertions(N)` (or set it to 0 incorrectly), meaning the test never validates the error condition it was written to cover. This produces a suite that appears green but provides zero coverage of failure paths, only surfacing when the CI environment happens to trigger the error and the assertion count suddenly mismatches.
Fix: always add `expect.assertions(N)` at the top of any test that contains assertions inside a `catch` block or a `.rejects` chain, where N counts every assertion that must execute including those in the error path. For tests that cover both success and error paths in a single function, split them into separate `it` blocks with their own `expect.assertions` guards so the assertion count is unambiguous and the failure message identifies which path was skipped.

**Gotcha G221 — Vitest `onTestFailed` Hook Registered Inside `beforeEach` Fires for All Subsequent Tests in the Block, Not Just the Next One**
Why this matters: The `onTestFailed` hook (available via the test context object in Vitest) is designed to register a callback that runs when the current test fails. When a developer registers it inside `beforeEach` rather than inside the test body, the hook accumulates across all tests in the describe block — each test that runs after the first registers an additional `onTestFailed` handler, so by the tenth test in a block, nine stale handlers from previous tests fire on failure, producing duplicate log entries, duplicate API calls (e.g., to a bug-reporting service), and occasionally duplicate state mutations that corrupt the test environment for subsequent tests.
Fix: register `onTestFailed` inside the test body using the test context parameter (`test('...', ({ onTestFailed }) => { ... })`), not inside `beforeEach`. This scopes the handler to exactly the test it was registered in. If the same failure handler must apply to all tests in a block, use `afterEach` with a conditional check on `expect.getState().currentTestName` and the overall test result status, which is a stable pattern that does not accumulate.

**Gotcha G222 — Playwright `page.evaluate` Closures Cannot Capture Variables From the Node.js Test Scope By Reference**
Why this matters: `page.evaluate(fn, args)` serialises the function and its arguments via JSON and re-evaluates them in the browser context. Developers who write closures that reference Node.js test-scope variables (e.g., `const token = await getToken(); page.evaluate(() => fetch('/api', { headers: { Authorization: token } }))`) are surprised when `token` is `undefined` inside the browser — the closure variable lookup happens in the browser process where `token` does not exist in scope, not in the Node.js process where it was defined. This produces flaky-looking failures (the variable is defined in Node.js but missing in the browser) that are difficult to diagnose because `console.log(token)` in the Node.js test context prints the correct value.
Fix: always pass external variables as the second argument to `page.evaluate`: `page.evaluate((t) => fetch('/api', { headers: { Authorization: t } }), token)`. Playwright serialises `token` into the argument and makes it available as the function parameter inside the browser. For complex objects, ensure all values are JSON-serialisable — functions, class instances, and Symbols cannot be transferred and will be silently dropped or throw a serialisation error.

**Gotcha G223 — Jest `--runInBand` Hides Flakiness Caused by Worker Isolation Gaps That Only Appear Under Parallel Execution**
Why this matters: `--runInBand` runs all test suites sequentially in a single process, which resolves many classes of flakiness caused by shared Node.js module singletons, global event listeners, and in-memory caches — because there is only one process, there is no possibility of cross-worker state contamination. A test suite that passes reliably under `--runInBand` but fails intermittently in normal (parallel) CI runs has worker-isolation bugs that the single-process mode is masking. Teams that habitually use `--runInBand` in CI to "fix flakiness" are trading test safety for apparent stability, allowing the underlying isolation problems to accumulate undetected.
Fix: use `--runInBand` only as a diagnostic tool to determine whether a failure is isolation-related, not as a permanent CI configuration. For actual fixes, identify the shared resource (module singleton, global event listener, in-memory store) and either reset it in `beforeEach`/`afterEach` using `jest.resetModules()` or `jest.isolateModules()`, or refactor the production code to avoid module-level mutable state. Once isolation is fixed, remove `--runInBand` from CI to restore the parallelism that catches future regressions.

**Gotcha G224 — Playwright `locator.nth(0)` Is Not Stable When a List Is Rendered With Real-Time Server-Sent Events**
Why this matters: `locator.nth(0)` resolves to the first DOM node matching the locator at the moment the call is evaluated, but for lists populated by Server-Sent Events (SSE) or WebSocket pushes, new items are prepended or inserted at arbitrary positions as they arrive. A test that clicks `nth(0)` intending to interact with a specific known item will intermittently interact with a different item if a new event fires and inserts a new item at position 0 between the time the locator resolves and the time the click action is dispatched. This class of flakiness is almost impossible to reproduce locally (where SSE latency is near zero) and appears only in CI where network jitter causes items to arrive during the action window.
Fix: replace positional locators (`nth(0)`, `first()`) with content-based locators that uniquely identify the intended element: `page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: knownItemText })` or `page.getByTestId(specificItemId)`. If the specific item's text or ID is not known at test write time (e.g., it is dynamically generated), capture the data-attribute of the item you intend to interact with before the SSE stream opens and use that attribute for selection. For tests that legitimately need to interact with "the most recent item," use `page.waitForResponse` to gate the action until a specific SSE message confirming item arrival has been received.

**Pattern 596** — Playwright `page.waitForResponse` With URL Predicate to Replace Unreliable `waitForLoadState('networkidle')`
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard loads all widgets before asserting counts', async ({ page }) => {
  // Register waitForResponse BEFORE navigation so no response is missed.
  // waitForLoadState('networkidle') is unreliable for SPAs that maintain
  // a persistent WebSocket or long-poll connection — the network never
  // truly goes idle and the test either times out or proceeds too early.
  const widgetDataPromise = page.waitForResponse(
    (resp) =>
      resp.url().includes('/api/widgets') &&
      resp.request().method() === 'GET' &&
      resp.status() === 200,
  );

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Await the specific response we care about, not a heuristic idle state.
  const widgetResp = await widgetDataPromise;
  const body = await widgetResp.json();
  expect(body.widgets).toHaveLength(4);

  // Now assert the rendered count — the data has definitively arrived.
  await expect(page.getByTestId('widget-count')).toHaveText('4');
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.waitForResponse` synchronises the test to the exact HTTP response that drives the assertion, eliminating the 500 ms–2 s idle-detection window of `waitForLoadState('networkidle')`, but it couples the test to a specific URL pattern — if the endpoint path is versioned (e.g., `/api/v2/widgets`), the predicate must be updated alongside the route change, making this pattern slightly more brittle to backend refactors than a purely DOM-based assertion.

**Pattern 597** — Vitest `vi.useFakeTimers` With `toFake` Allowlist and `vi.setSystemTime` to Prevent `Date` Drift in Snapshot Tests
```typescript
import { afterEach, beforeEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';
import { formatRelativeTime } from './time-utils';

describe('formatRelativeTime', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    // Only fake the timer APIs and Date that are needed.
    // Pinning Date via setSystemTime eliminates snapshot drift from
    // wall-clock changes between CI runs and local developer machines.
    vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ['setTimeout', 'setInterval', 'Date'] });
    vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-01-15T12:00:00.000Z'));
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    // Always restore real timers to prevent fake timer state from leaking
    // into the next test file when Vitest reuses worker threads.
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });

  it('returns "3 days ago" for a timestamp 72 hours before the pinned now', () => {
    const ts = new Date('2026-01-12T12:00:00.000Z').toISOString();
    expect(formatRelativeTime(ts)).toBe('3 days ago');
  });

  it('returns "just now" for a timestamp within 60 seconds of pinned now', () => {
    const ts = new Date('2026-01-15T11:59:30.000Z').toISOString();
    expect(formatRelativeTime(ts)).toBe('just now');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.setSystemTime` pins `Date.now()` to a deterministic value and eliminates snapshot flakiness from wall-clock drift, but any production code that calls `performance.now()` for high-resolution timing will still use the real clock unless `performance` is added to the `toFake` list — omitting it causes subtle assertion failures in code that mixes `Date` and `performance.now()` for elapsed-time measurements.

**Pattern 598** — Jest `jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` for Async Callbacks Scheduled Inside `setTimeout` Without Microtask Flush Ceremony
```typescript
import { afterEach, beforeEach, describe, expect, jest, test } from '@jest/globals';
import { scheduleHealthCheck } from './scheduler';

describe('scheduleHealthCheck', () => {
  let pingMock: jest.Mock;

  beforeEach(() => {
    jest.useFakeTimers();
    pingMock = jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ status: 'ok' });
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    jest.useRealTimers();
    jest.restoreAllMocks();
  });

  test('invokes the ping function after the configured delay', async () => {
    scheduleHealthCheck(pingMock, 5_000);

    // advanceTimersByTimeAsync advances fake time AND flushes any
    // microtask queue entries (resolved Promises) that fire as a result,
    // so async callbacks inside setTimeout resolve correctly without
    // needing a separate `await Promise.resolve()` flush.
    await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(5_000);

    expect(pingMock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
    expect(pingMock).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ url: expect.any(String) }),
    );
  });

  test('does not invoke ping before the delay has elapsed', async () => {
    scheduleHealthCheck(pingMock, 5_000);
    await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(4_999);
    expect(pingMock).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` (introduced in Jest 29.5) flushes both timer callbacks and the microtask queue in lock-step, resolving the classic "forgotten `await flushPromises()`" class of async-timer flakiness, but it requires Jest ≥ 29.5 and does not exist in Vitest — teams sharing test utilities across both runtimes must branch on the runtime or vendor a `flushTimersAndMicrotasks` helper that polyfills the behaviour using `runOnlyPendingTimersAsync` in older Jest versions.

**Pattern 599** — Playwright `browserContext.route` With Stateful Handler to Simulate a Single Transient Network Failure
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('retry banner appears then disappears after transient 503', async ({
  context,
  page,
}) => {
  let callCount = 0;

  // Intercept the first call to /api/feed and return a 503; let all
  // subsequent calls pass through to the real handler. The stateful
  // callCount variable precisely models a one-shot transient failure
  // without requiring a separate mock server process.
  await context.route('**/api/feed', async (route) => {
    callCount++;
    if (callCount === 1) {
      await route.fulfill({ status: 503, body: 'Service Unavailable' });
    } else {
      await route.continue();
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/feed');

  // The UI should show a retry banner after the first failed request.
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /retrying/i })).toBeVisible();

  // After the automatic client-side retry succeeds, the banner clears.
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /retrying/i })).toBeHidden();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('feed-item')).not.toHaveCount(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: a stateful `callCount` closure precisely models one-shot transient failures and validates that the UI correctly surfaces and then clears retry state, but because the handler captures mutable state, running this test with `test.describe.configure({ retries: 2 })` will reset `callCount` only if the handler is registered inside the test body — if it is hoisted to `beforeAll`, `callCount` accumulates across retries and the second retry attempt never triggers the 503, so always register stateful route handlers inside the test body, not in shared setup hooks.

**Pattern 600** — Vitest `expect.poll` With `interval` and `timeout` Overrides for Eventual-Consistency Queue Assertions
```typescript
import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { enqueueJob, getJobStatus } from './job-queue';

describe('job queue eventual consistency', () => {
  it('transitions job to completed within 2 seconds of enqueue', async () => {
    const jobId = await enqueueJob({ type: 'report-export', userId: 'u-42' });

    // expect.poll retries the assertion callback on the given interval
    // until it passes or the timeout expires. This avoids a fixed
    // `await sleep(2000)` that always burns 2 s even when the job
    // completes in 200 ms, and avoids the fragility of a single-shot
    // assertion that fails if the job has not yet completed.
    await expect
      .poll(async () => (await getJobStatus(jobId)).state, {
        interval: 100,   // re-check every 100 ms
        timeout: 2_000,  // fail the test if not passing within 2 s
      })
      .toBe('completed');

    const result = await getJobStatus(jobId);
    expect(result.outputUrl).toMatch(/^https:\/\/storage\./);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.poll` surfaces the eventual state without burning fixed sleep time and produces a clear timeout error with the last received value when the condition is never met, but each poll iteration makes a real async call — if `getJobStatus` is an HTTP request to a test server, 20 iterations over 2 seconds will generate 20 HTTP requests; for rate-limited or quota-constrained APIs, replace `getJobStatus` with a mocked in-process queue accessor to avoid exhausting request budgets during CI runs.

**Pattern 601** — Playwright `locator.waitFor({ state: 'detached' })` to Assert DOM Removal Without Fixed-Sleep Polling
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('toast notification auto-dismisses after 3 seconds', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/home');

  // Trigger the action that produces the toast.
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save changes' }).click();

  const toast = page.getByRole('status', { name: /saved successfully/i });

  // Confirm the toast appeared first — tight timeout to fail fast if
  // the feature is broken outright rather than merely slow.
  await expect(toast).toBeVisible({ timeout: 2_000 });

  // waitFor({ state: 'detached' }) retries until the element is removed
  // from the DOM, avoiding an arbitrary sleep(3500) that is both slower
  // and fragile to animation-duration changes in the production CSS.
  await toast.waitFor({ state: 'detached', timeout: 6_000 });

  // After detachment, verify no residual toast remains anywhere on the page.
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveCount(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.waitFor({ state: 'detached' })` precisely asserts DOM removal and respects Playwright's retry backoff, making it faster than `sleep` and more explicit than `toBeHidden`, but it fails if the toast is hidden via CSS (`display:none` or `visibility:hidden`) rather than actual DOM removal — for applications that hide toasts without detaching them, use `await expect(toast).toBeHidden({ timeout: 6_000 })` instead, which waits for the CSS hidden state.

**Pattern 602** — Jest `jest.isolateModulesAsync` to Reload Singleton Modules With Different Environment Variables Per Test
```typescript
import { describe, expect, jest, test } from '@jest/globals';

describe('FeatureFlags singleton with different env configs', () => {
  test('enables dark-mode flag when FEATURE_DARK_MODE=true', async () => {
    process.env.FEATURE_DARK_MODE = 'true';

    // jest.isolateModulesAsync resets the module registry for the async
    // callback's scope, forcing a fresh require/import of all modules.
    // This is the async counterpart of jest.isolateModules and correctly
    // handles modules that use top-level await in their initialisation.
    let flags: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof import('./feature-flags')>>;
    await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
      flags = await import('./feature-flags');
    });

    expect(flags!.isEnabled('dark-mode')).toBe(true);
    delete process.env.FEATURE_DARK_MODE;
  });

  test('disables dark-mode flag when FEATURE_DARK_MODE is unset', async () => {
    delete process.env.FEATURE_DARK_MODE;

    await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
      const flags = await import('./feature-flags');
      expect(flags.isEnabled('dark-mode')).toBe(false);
    });
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.isolateModulesAsync` provides the strongest module-isolation guarantee in Jest by fully resetting the registry, which reliably prevents singleton state bleed between env-var tests, but it adds measurable overhead (full module-graph re-evaluation per test) — for large dependency trees this can add 200–500 ms per test; consider using `vi.stubEnv` in Vitest or injecting env config via a factory function rather than module-level `process.env` reads to achieve isolation without a full registry reset.

**Pattern 603** — Playwright `expect.soft` Inside `test.step` to Collect All Optional-Section Failures in a Single Run
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('profile page renders all optional sections', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/profile/u-42');

  // test.step groups related assertions and gives each group a name
  // in the HTML report — very useful for long assertion sequences.
  await test.step('required fields', async () => {
    await expect(page.getByTestId('display-name')).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('email')).toBeVisible();
  });

  // expect.soft() records failures but does not abort the test, so all
  // optional sections are evaluated and reported even when one fails.
  // This prevents a single missing optional section from masking all
  // subsequent failures in the same CI run.
  await test.step('optional sections', async () => {
    await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('bio-section')).toBeVisible();
    await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('avatar-image')).toBeVisible();
    await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('social-links')).toBeVisible();
    await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('activity-feed')).toBeVisible();
  });

  // Force the test to fail if any soft assertion above failed, while
  // still having run all checks.
  expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.soft` combined with `test.step` maximises the diagnostic value of a single test run by collecting all failures at once rather than stopping at the first, which is especially valuable in CI where re-runs are expensive, but mixing hard and soft assertions in the same test can obscure severity — a test that fails only on soft assertions may be triaged as lower priority when a hard failure on the same element would have been caught and escalated faster; reserve `expect.soft` exclusively for genuinely optional or cosmetic assertions.

**Pattern 604** — Vitest `vi.spyOn(globalThis, 'fetch')` With Chained `mockImplementationOnce` for Ordered Multi-Step API Sequences
```typescript
import { afterEach, beforeEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';
import { loadUserDashboard } from './dashboard-loader';

describe('loadUserDashboard multi-step fetch sequence', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.spyOn(globalThis, 'fetch');
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    vi.restoreAllMocks();
  });

  it('loads user, then loads preferences, then posts audit log', async () => {
    (globalThis.fetch as ReturnType<typeof vi.spyOn>)
      // First call: GET /api/user/42
      .mockImplementationOnce(async () =>
        new Response(JSON.stringify({ id: 42, name: 'Alice' }), { status: 200 }),
      )
      // Second call: GET /api/user/42/preferences
      .mockImplementationOnce(async () =>
        new Response(JSON.stringify({ theme: 'dark' }), { status: 200 }),
      )
      // Third call: POST /api/audit
      .mockImplementationOnce(async () =>
        new Response(JSON.stringify({ logged: true }), { status: 201 }),
      );

    const result = await loadUserDashboard(42);

    expect(globalThis.fetch).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
    expect(result.user.name).toBe('Alice');
    expect(result.preferences.theme).toBe('dark');
    expect(result.auditLogged).toBe(true);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: chaining `mockImplementationOnce` calls enforces a strict call-order contract that immediately surfaces regressions when a refactor reorders API calls, but it also makes the test brittle to benign reorderings (e.g., swapping user-fetch and preferences-fetch when both are independent) — use `mockImplementation` with a URL-switch pattern (`url.includes('/preferences')`) instead when call order is architecturally irrelevant and only the total call count and response data matter.

**Pattern 605** — Playwright `page.clock.install` to Freeze and Advance Browser-Side Time for Debounce and Throttle Testing
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('search input debounce fires exactly once after 300 ms silence', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  // page.clock.install replaces the browser's native timer APIs (setTimeout,
  // Date, requestAnimationFrame) with a controllable fake clock, analogous
  // to sinon.useFakeTimers but built into Playwright and synchronised with
  // the page lifecycle. Install BEFORE navigation so the page's JS never
  // sees a real clock tick during module initialisation.
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-01-15T09:00:00Z') });
  await page.goto('/search');

  const input = page.getByRole('searchbox');
  await input.fill('query');

  // Advance 200 ms — debounce threshold of 300 ms not yet crossed.
  await page.clock.tickAsync(200);
  await expect(page.getByTestId('result-count')).toHaveText('–');

  // Advance another 200 ms (total 400 ms) — debounce fires.
  await page.clock.tickAsync(200);
  await expect(page.getByTestId('result-count')).not.toHaveText('–');
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.clock.install` provides deterministic control over all browser timer APIs in a single call and avoids the real-time wait that makes debounce/throttle tests slow and flaky, but it replaces `Date` globally in the page context — any production code that uses `Date.now()` for cache expiry or session timeout calculations will behave as if time froze and then jumped, potentially triggering unintended cache-miss or session-expiry side-effects; use `page.clock.setSystemTime` between steps if the production code relies on monotonically advancing time rather than a single frozen instant.

**Pattern 606** — Jest `--randomize` With `--shard` to Detect Order-Dependent Flakiness Across Distributed CI Workers
```typescript
// jest.config.ts — enable randomisation and expose the seed for reproduction
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  // Randomise test execution order within each worker. Combined with
  // --shard in CI, each shard runs a different random subset in a different
  // order, maximising the chance of discovering order-dependent failures
  // without requiring a dedicated "shuffle" run.
  randomize: true,

  // Log the seed so a flaky order-dependent failure can be reproduced
  // locally by passing --seed=<value> to jest. Without this, reproducing
  // a random-order failure requires brute-forcing the shuffle, which is
  // impractical for suites with hundreds of tests.
  showSeed: true,

  // Mandatory companion: isolate every test file in its own worker to
  // prevent randomised order from creating cross-file state bleed via
  // shared module singletons. Without isolation, randomised order can
  // increase flakiness by surfacing cross-file order dependencies
  // in addition to within-file ones.
  isolateModules: true,
};

export default config;

// CI pipeline — each shard runs a different random order automatically:
// jest --shard=1/4 --randomize
// jest --shard=2/4 --randomize
// jest --shard=3/4 --randomize
// jest --shard=4/4 --randomize
```
Tradeoff: `--randomize` with `--shard` turns every CI run into an implicit order-dependency detector at zero extra cost, surfacing order-coupled tests that would otherwise only flake in production-like environments, but adding `randomize: true` to the config also applies randomisation to all local development runs — developers accustomed to a stable test order may find their usual debugging workflow disrupted; gate `randomize` behind a `CI` environment variable check in the config to keep local runs deterministic while preserving CI-level detection.

**Pattern 607** — Playwright `expect.toPass` With Exponential `intervals` for Multi-Step Navigation Flows With Variable Completion Time
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('wizard completes and redirects to confirmation page', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/wizard/start');

  // expect.toPass retries the entire async callback until it passes or
  // times out. This is the correct pattern for multi-step flows where
  // intermediate steps may fail transiently (e.g., a redirect that
  // depends on a distributed background job completing).
  await expect(async () => {
    // Step 1 — verify we are on the wizard, not an error page.
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/wizard\/(start|step-\d+)/);

    // Step 2 — advance the wizard if the Next button is still visible;
    // this step is idempotent if already on a later step.
    const nextBtn = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next' });
    if (await nextBtn.isVisible()) {
      await nextBtn.click();
    }

    // Step 3 — assert the final redirect has happened.
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/wizard\/confirmation/);
    await expect(page.getByTestId('order-id')).toBeVisible();
  }).toPass({
    intervals: [500, 1_000, 2_000, 4_000], // exponential back-off
    timeout: 15_000,
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.toPass` with exponential `intervals` avoids both the fragility of a single-shot assertion and the waste of a fixed sleep for flows whose completion time is bounded but variable, but wrapping DOM-manipulation steps (like `nextBtn.click()`) inside the callback means those steps re-execute on every retry — any step with non-idempotent side effects (form submission, payment initiation) will be triggered multiple times, potentially creating duplicate records; hoist all side-effecting actions outside the `toPass` callback and keep only idempotent observation steps inside it.

**Pattern 608** — Vitest `describe.concurrent` With `vi.stubEnv` for Parallel Environment-Matrix Tests Without Global Pollution
```typescript
import { describe, expect, test, vi } from 'vitest';
import { getApiBaseUrl } from './config';

// test.concurrent runs tests in this block in parallel within the same
// worker thread. vi.stubEnv is per-test-context in Vitest 2.x with
// unstubEnvs: true (default), so each concurrent test sees its own
// isolated env snapshot and cleanup is automatic.
describe.concurrent('getApiBaseUrl environment resolution', () => {
  test('returns staging URL when APP_ENV=staging', async ({ expect }) => {
    vi.stubEnv('APP_ENV', 'staging');
    expect(getApiBaseUrl()).toBe('https://api.staging.example.com');
  });

  test('returns production URL when APP_ENV=production', async ({ expect }) => {
    vi.stubEnv('APP_ENV', 'production');
    expect(getApiBaseUrl()).toBe('https://api.example.com');
  });

  test('returns localhost when APP_ENV is unset', async ({ expect }) => {
    vi.stubEnv('APP_ENV', '');
    expect(getApiBaseUrl()).toBe('http://localhost:3000');
  });

  test('throws for unknown APP_ENV values', async ({ expect }) => {
    vi.stubEnv('APP_ENV', 'canary-unknown');
    expect(() => getApiBaseUrl()).toThrow(/unknown environment/i);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `describe.concurrent` with `vi.stubEnv` in Vitest 2.x achieves parallel execution without env-variable race conditions because Vitest isolates `process.env` mutations per test context, dramatically reducing suite runtime for large env-matrix tests, but this isolation only works when `getApiBaseUrl` reads `process.env` at call time rather than at module-initialisation time — if `APP_ENV` is captured into a module-level constant (`const ENV = process.env.APP_ENV`) during import, `vi.stubEnv` changes after import have no effect and all concurrent tests observe the same module-initialisation-time value.

**Pattern 609** — Playwright `page.routeFromHAR` for Hermetic Third-Party API Playback Without Sandbox Credentials
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import * as path from 'path';

// RECORDING MODE: set UPDATE_HAR=true to capture fresh responses from the
// real network. Commit the resulting HAR file; subsequent CI runs replay it.
// RECORDED: 2026-01-15 against Stripe test-mode account; rotate quarterly.

test('payment widget renders Stripe price from API', async ({ page }) => {
  const harPath = path.join(__dirname, '__hars__', 'stripe-prices.har');

  if (process.env.UPDATE_HAR) {
    // Route all matching requests to the real network and record responses.
    await page.routeFromHAR(harPath, { update: true });
  } else {
    // Play back the recorded HAR — requests are matched by URL and method,
    // responses are served from the HAR file without touching the network.
    // No Stripe API key needed in CI; no rate limits; no third-party latency.
    await page.routeFromHAR(harPath, {
      update: false,
      notFound: 'abort', // fail loudly if a new request is not in the HAR
    });
  }

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('plan-price')).toHaveText('$29/month');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('stripe-badge')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.routeFromHAR` makes tests fully hermetic against third-party API flakiness and eliminates the need for sandbox API credentials in CI, but HAR files capture exact response bodies including tokens, cursor IDs, and cache-control headers that may expire — a HAR recorded against a Stripe test-mode price ID will break if the test-mode product is deleted or the HAR is more than a few months stale; add a `// RECORDED:` comment with the capture date and establish a quarterly rotation schedule enforced by a lint rule that fails CI if the HAR is older than 90 days.

**Pattern 610** — Jest `server.closeAllConnections()` Combined With `--detectOpenHandles` to Eliminate Async Teardown Flakiness
```typescript
import { afterAll, beforeAll, describe, expect, test } from '@jest/globals';
import { createServer } from 'http';
import type { Server } from 'http';
import request from 'supertest';
import { app } from './app';

describe('HTTP integration tests', () => {
  let server: Server;

  beforeAll((done) => {
    server = createServer(app);
    // Port 0 lets the OS assign an ephemeral port, preventing port-conflict
    // flakiness in parallel CI workers that share a host.
    server.listen(0, done);
  });

  afterAll((done) => {
    // server.closeAllConnections() (Node 18.2+) forcibly closes all
    // keep-alive connections that would otherwise keep the server alive
    // past server.close(). Without this, jest --detectOpenHandles reports
    // the server as a leaked handle, Jest exits with code 1, and the next
    // test suite may inherit partially torn-down process state — a source
    // of hard-to-reproduce CI failures that look like test-order flakiness.
    server.closeAllConnections();
    server.close(done);
  });

  test('GET /health returns 200', async () => {
    const { port } = server.address() as { port: number };
    const res = await request(`http://localhost:${port}`).get('/health');
    expect(res.status).toBe(200);
    expect(res.body).toMatchObject({ status: 'ok' });
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `server.closeAllConnections()` followed by `server.close()` guarantees clean teardown on Node 18.2+ and eliminates the most common class of Jest "open handle" warnings, but the method does not exist on Node 16 and earlier — a compatibility shim (`if (server.closeAllConnections) server.closeAllConnections()`) is needed for projects that still support Node 16, and teams should add an `engines` field to `package.json` to document the Node version floor so future contributors do not silently downgrade and reintroduce the teardown race.

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G225 — Playwright `page.clock.install` Must Be Called Before `page.goto` or Browser-Side Timers Initialise With the Real Clock**
Why this matters: `page.clock.install` replaces the browser's native timer implementation by injecting a script into the page context. If `page.goto` runs first, the page's JavaScript has already executed its module-level `setTimeout` and `setInterval` registrations using the real clock; the subsequent `clock.install` replaces the clock object but cannot retroactively re-register already-scheduled timers under the fake implementation, meaning any debounce, throttle, or polling function initialised at page load will fire on the real clock schedule and not respond to `page.clock.tickAsync`. This produces flaky tests where timer-sensitive behaviour is correct on slow CI (real time elapses) but wrong on fast developer machines (test runs too fast for real timers to fire).
Fix: always call `await page.clock.install(options)` before `await page.goto(url)`. For tests that need the clock installed on a page that has already been navigated (e.g., in a shared `beforeEach` fixture that runs after a global navigation), use `page.addInitScript` to inject `window.__clockOptions = { ... }` and bootstrap the fake clock from within the page's init script, which executes before any page JS regardless of navigation order.

**Gotcha G226 — Vitest `vi.mock` Hoisting Means the Factory Cannot Reference Variables Declared in the Same `describe` Block**
Why this matters: Vitest (like Jest) hoists `vi.mock(...)` calls to the top of the file at compile time so that the mock is in place before any `import` statement executes. A factory function passed to `vi.mock` that references a variable declared below it in the source (e.g., `const mockFn = vi.fn(); vi.mock('./module', () => ({ fn: mockFn }))`) will see `mockFn` as `undefined` at the time the factory runs because the variable declaration has not yet executed — the factory is hoisted above it. This produces the confusing error "Cannot access 'mockFn' before initialization" or, worse, silently substitutes `undefined` for the mock function, making the mock appear to do nothing without any runtime error.
Fix: declare any variables that the mock factory references using `vi.hoisted(() => vi.fn())`, which explicitly hoists the variable initialisation alongside the `vi.mock` call: `const mockFn = vi.hoisted(() => vi.fn()); vi.mock('./module', () => ({ fn: mockFn }))`. Alternatively, return a new `vi.fn()` inline from the factory and retrieve a reference to it later with `vi.mocked(module).fn`.

**Gotcha G227 — Jest `fakeTimers` Does Not Fake `queueMicrotask` By Default, Causing Async Flush-Order Surprises**
Why this matters: `jest.useFakeTimers()` replaces macro-task APIs (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `setImmediate`) but leaves micro-task APIs (`Promise`, `queueMicrotask`, `MutationObserver`) on the real event loop unless explicitly included via the `toFake` configuration. Code that schedules work via `queueMicrotask` (used internally by many browser APIs and some polyfills) will execute on the real micro-task queue between fake timer ticks, producing an interleaved execution order that differs from both the "all fake" and "all real" models. Tests asserting on callback invocation order under fake timers will flake depending on whether `queueMicrotask` callbacks fire before or after `setTimeout(fn, 0)` callbacks, and the answer changes across Node.js minor versions because the micro-task and macro-task queues are drained in a Node-version-specific interleaving order.
Fix: audit whether the code under test uses `queueMicrotask` directly or via a dependency. If it does, either add `queueMicrotask` to the `toFake` list (`jest.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ['setTimeout', 'setInterval', 'queueMicrotask'] })`) to bring it under deterministic control, or refactor the production code to use `Promise.resolve().then(fn)` consistently, which is more widely supported under fake timer environments and more predictable across Node.js versions.

**Gotcha G228 — Playwright `route.continue()` Without `await` Causes Intermittent "Request Already Handled" Errors When Two Handlers Match the Same URL**
Why this matters: When two `page.route` or `context.route` handlers match the same URL, Playwright invokes them in registration order and expects each handler to either `fulfill`, `abort`, or `continue` the route before the next handler is called. If a handler calls `route.continue()` without `await`, the route is marked as handled asynchronously, but Playwright's routing pipeline may attempt to invoke the next handler before the `continue` resolves, triggering a "Request already handled" runtime error that fails the test. This is intermittent because the timing depends on microtask scheduling and manifests only when two handlers are registered — a common pattern in tests that combine a global auth-token injector with a per-test response stub.
Fix: always `await route.continue()`, `await route.fulfill()`, and `await route.abort()` in Playwright route handlers. For the auth-token injection use case specifically, use `page.setExtraHTTPHeaders` instead of a `route` handler to avoid the double-handler problem entirely — headers added via `setExtraHTTPHeaders` are applied at the network layer without entering the route handler pipeline.

**Gotcha G229 — Jest `beforeAll` Errors Are Attributed to the First Test in the Block, Not to the Hook, When Using `--testNamePattern` Filtering**
Why this matters: When a `beforeAll` hook throws, Jest attributes the failure to the first test in the describe block rather than to the `beforeAll` hook itself. This is a known diagnostic limitation that causes confusion when using `--testNamePattern` or `--testPathPattern` to run a filtered subset of tests: the filtered run may exclude the first test in a block, causing the `beforeAll` error to be attributed to a different test (whichever happens to be first in the filtered set) or, in some Jest versions, to be swallowed entirely — the suite exits with code 0 even though setup failed. This is especially dangerous in CI pipelines that filter tests by name to run only the tests affected by a change, because a broken `beforeAll` in an unrelated-but-included describe block silently passes.
Fix: wrap `beforeAll` bodies in an explicit try/catch and re-throw with a clear prefix: `beforeAll(async () => { try { await setup(); } catch (e) { throw new Error(\`beforeAll setup failed: \${(e as Error).message}\`); } })`. Additionally, run the full unfiltered suite in the nightly CI job so that `beforeAll` errors are always attributed and visible, reserving filtered runs for fast-feedback developer workflows only where the attribution ambiguity is an acceptable trade-off.
