**Pattern 647** — `vi.stubEnv` in `beforeEach` / `vi.unstubAllEnvs` in `afterEach` for Environment-Sensitive Unit Tests
```typescript
// Unit tests that branch on environment variables (feature flags, API endpoints,
// log levels) are flaky when tests run in a different order than expected because
// a prior test sets process.env.FEATURE_X and forgets to restore it. vi.stubEnv
// isolates environment mutations to the test that declares them.
import { beforeEach, afterEach, describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { buildApiClient } from '../src/api-client';

describe('buildApiClient', () => {
  afterEach(() => {
    // Restore all stubs set during this test, regardless of whether the test
    // passed or threw. This runs even when a test assertion fails.
    vi.unstubAllEnvs();
  });

  it('uses the staging base URL when DEPLOY_ENV=staging', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('DEPLOY_ENV', 'staging');
    vi.stubEnv('API_BASE_URL', 'https://staging-api.example.com');

    const client = buildApiClient();

    expect(client.baseURL).toBe('https://staging-api.example.com');
  });

  it('throws when API_BASE_URL is missing', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('DEPLOY_ENV', 'production');
    // Explicitly remove the variable to test the missing-config branch.
    vi.stubEnv('API_BASE_URL', '');

    expect(() => buildApiClient()).toThrow('API_BASE_URL must be set');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.stubEnv` + `vi.unstubAllEnvs` guarantees environment variables are scoped to the test that sets them, eliminating the most common source of order-dependent flakiness in configuration-heavy codebases; the tradeoff is that `vi.stubEnv` only patches `process.env` — it does not re-execute module-level code that read `process.env` at import time (e.g., `const BASE = process.env.API_BASE_URL ?? ''` evaluated once at module load); for those cases, combine `vi.stubEnv` with `vi.resetModules()` and a dynamic `import()` to force the module to re-evaluate with the stubbed value.

**Pattern 648** — `browserContext.route` With `route.continue` Header Injection for Auth-Token Normalisation Across All Pages
```typescript
// End-to-end tests that open multiple pages within a context (popup windows,
// new tabs, OAuth redirects) require every outgoing request to carry a valid
// auth token. Setting the header at the context level rather than per-page
// prevents flakiness where a popup opens before the per-page route handler is
// registered, causing the popup's first request to be unauthenticated.
import { test, expect, BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

async function injectAuthToken(context: BrowserContext, token: string) {
  await context.route('**/*', async (route) => {
    const headers = {
      ...route.request().headers(),
      Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
    };
    await route.continue({ headers });
  });
}

test('OAuth popup receives auth header on first request', async ({ browser }) => {
  const context = await browser.newContext();
  await injectAuthToken(context, process.env.E2E_AUTH_TOKEN!);

  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Open a popup; the context-level route handler fires immediately on the
  // popup's first request without needing per-page registration.
  const [popup] = await Promise.all([
    context.waitForEvent('page'),
    page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Open analytics' }).click(),
  ]);

  await popup.waitForLoadState('networkidle');
  await expect(popup.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Analytics' })).toBeVisible();

  await context.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: registering the auth header injection at the `browserContext` level ensures all pages and popups in the context receive the token without per-page boilerplate, removing an entire class of flaky 401 failures on popup tests; the tradeoff is that `context.route('**/*', ...)` intercepts every request including static assets, adding one handler invocation per asset load — on asset-heavy pages this increases the number of route callbacks per test, which can measurably slow test execution; scope the route pattern to API endpoints only (`**/api/**`) when static assets do not require the auth header.

**Pattern 649** — `vi.useFakeTimers` With `shouldClearNativeTimers: true` to Neutralise Third-Party SDK Polling
```typescript
// Third-party SDKs (analytics, error reporters, feature-flag clients) often
// start internal polling loops when they are imported. These real timers run
// concurrently with the test's fake clock, fire at unpredictable times during
// teardown, and can trigger log noise, network requests, or state mutations that
// bleed into the next test. Enabling shouldClearNativeTimers cancels those real
// timers when the fake clock is installed.
import { beforeEach, afterEach, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { initAnalytics } from '../src/analytics';

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.useFakeTimers({
    // Cancel all existing real timers set by SDK initialisation code that ran
    // during module load, so they cannot fire during or after the test.
    shouldClearNativeTimers: true,
    // Pin the initial fake time to a known instant.
    now: new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z'),
  });
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

it('analytics client does not flush before the 30-second interval', async () => {
  const flush = vi.fn();
  initAnalytics({ onFlush: flush });

  // Advance time by 29 seconds — the flush should not have fired yet.
  await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(29_000);
  expect(flush).not.toHaveBeenCalled();

  // Advance past the threshold — exactly one flush should occur.
  await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1_001);
  expect(flush).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
});
```
Tradeoff: `shouldClearNativeTimers: true` prevents third-party polling loops from firing during tests, eliminating spurious network calls and teardown-phase state mutations that cause the following test to receive dirty shared state; the tradeoff is destructive — it cancels every real timer in the process, including timers set by test framework internals (e.g., Vitest's own worker heartbeat in some configurations); always verify that `vi.useRealTimers()` in `afterEach` fully restores normal timer behaviour and monitor for "worker process unresponsive" errors that can appear if a framework heartbeat timer is inadvertently cleared.

---

**Pattern 650** — `page.getByRole('status')` to Assert on Live-Region Announcements Without Timing Races
```typescript
// ARIA live regions (role="status", role="alert") are updated asynchronously
// after user actions. Tests that assert immediately after triggering the action
// race against the DOM update. Using Playwright's auto-retrying locator
// combined with toHaveText avoids explicit waits while keeping the assertion
// grounded in the accessible announcement the user actually perceives.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('form submission announces success to screen readers', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/contact');

  await page.getByLabel('Your name').fill('Bob Martinez');
  await page.getByLabel('Message').fill('Hello from the test suite');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send message' }).click();

  // getByRole('status') targets the ARIA live region. Playwright auto-retries
  // toHaveText until the text appears or the assertion timeout is reached,
  // meaning no explicit waitFor is needed even though the live region is updated
  // asynchronously after the server responds.
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText(
    'Your message has been sent successfully.'
  );

  // Verify that the form is reset after a successful submission so the next
  // user can start fresh without stale input values.
  await expect(page.getByLabel('Your name')).toHaveValue('');
});
```
Tradeoff: asserting on `role="status"` anchors the test to the accessibility contract (the live region that screen readers announce) rather than to a CSS class or data attribute that has no user-facing meaning, making the test both more resilient to markup refactors and more meaningful as a regression guard; the tradeoff is that if the application announces the success message via a `role="alert"` element instead of `role="status"`, the locator will find nothing and time out — audit the rendered ARIA roles in the browser's accessibility tree before writing the assertion to ensure the correct role is targeted.

---

**Pattern 651** — `test.describe.configure({ retries: 2 })` Scoped to a Single Describe Block for Selective Retry Without Global Noise
```typescript
// Applying global retries to an entire test suite masks genuinely flaky tests
// by making them pass eventually. Scoping retries to a specific describe block
// — typically one that covers an inherently non-deterministic subsystem like
// third-party payment widgets or geo-IP routing — limits retry overhead to the
// tests that need it while keeping the rest of the suite zero-tolerance.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Tests for the deterministic parts of the checkout flow — no retries.
test('cart total calculates correctly', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/cart');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-total')).toHaveText('$49.99');
});

// Tests that interact with the third-party Stripe widget inherit the retry config
// declared on this describe block only.
test.describe('Stripe payment widget', () => {
  test.describe.configure({ retries: 2 });

  test('card number field accepts valid input', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    const stripeFrame = page.frameLocator('[name^="__privateStripeFrame"]');
    await stripeFrame.getByRole('textbox', { name: /card number/i }).fill('4242424242424242');
    await expect(
      stripeFrame.getByRole('textbox', { name: /card number/i })
    ).toHaveValue('4242 4242 4242 4242');
  });

  test('expired card shows error message', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    const stripeFrame = page.frameLocator('[name^="__privateStripeFrame"]');
    await stripeFrame.getByRole('textbox', { name: /expiry/i }).fill('01/20');
    await expect(stripeFrame.getByText("Your card's expiration year is in the past")).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: scoping retries to a single `describe` block limits the blast radius of retry-masking to the subsystem that is inherently non-deterministic, preserving zero-tolerance semantics for all other tests; the tradeoff is that when a Stripe-widget test starts failing consistently (e.g., after an SDK update), the two retry attempts delay CI feedback by up to 3x the per-test timeout before the run reports a failure — monitor flaky-test dashboards for tests in retry-enabled blocks that begin reporting "passed on retry" to detect newly broken behaviour early.

**Pattern 652** — Vitest `onTestFinished` Hook for Per-Test Temp-File Cleanup Without a Shared `afterEach`
```typescript
// Tests that write to the filesystem (generating reports, exporting CSVs,
// writing config snapshots) often leave temp files behind when they fail before
// reaching a cleanup block. Registering cleanup via onTestFinished — called from
// inside the test — ties the teardown directly to the test that created the
// resource, running even on assertion failure or uncaught error.
import { it, expect, onTestFinished } from 'vitest';
import { unlinkSync, existsSync } from 'fs';
import { tmpdir } from 'os';
import * as path from 'path';
import { exportConfig } from '../src/config-exporter';

it('exportConfig writes a valid JSON file to the given path', () => {
  const outputPath = path.join(tmpdir(), `config-export-${Date.now()}.json`);

  // Register cleanup before any assertions so it runs even if the test fails
  // partway through. onTestFinished fires after the test completes regardless
  // of whether it passed, failed, or was skipped.
  onTestFinished(() => {
    if (existsSync(outputPath)) {
      unlinkSync(outputPath);
    }
  });

  exportConfig({ output: outputPath, format: 'json' });

  expect(existsSync(outputPath)).toBe(true);
  const contents = JSON.parse(require('fs').readFileSync(outputPath, 'utf-8'));
  expect(contents).toHaveProperty('version');
  expect(contents.version).toMatch(/^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/);
});
```
Tradeoff: `onTestFinished` registration inside the test body ties resource cleanup to the test that allocated the resource, eliminating the "orphaned temp file from a failed test contaminates the next test's glob patterns" class of flakiness without requiring a shared `afterEach` that runs for every test in the file whether or not they used the filesystem; the tradeoff is that `onTestFinished` is not available in Vitest versions below 1.4 — pin the minimum Vitest version in `package.json` and add a `peerDependencies` check in CI to prevent silent regression when the toolchain is downgraded.

---

**Pattern 653** — `page.frameLocator` by `title` Attribute for Stable Assertions Inside Sandboxed iframes
```typescript
// Components embedded in sandboxed iframes (rich text editors, payment widgets,
// embedded dashboards) require crossing the frame boundary for assertions.
// Mixing frameLocator with a title-attribute selector eliminates the brittle
// "find the iframe by index" anti-pattern that breaks when the parent page
// inserts a new iframe above the target.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('rich text editor renders initial content and accepts input', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/editor');

  // Target the editor iframe by its title attribute — more stable than a
  // numeric index that shifts when other iframes are added to the page.
  const editorFrame = page.frameLocator('iframe[title="Rich text editor"]');

  // Verify the editor initialised with the expected placeholder text.
  await expect(editorFrame.getByRole('textbox')).toHaveText('Start typing here…');

  // Clear the placeholder and type new content.
  await editorFrame.getByRole('textbox').click();
  await page.keyboard.press('Control+A');
  await page.keyboard.type('Updated content from test');

  // Confirm the change is reflected in the editor's content area.
  await expect(editorFrame.getByRole('textbox')).toHaveText('Updated content from test');

  // Verify the parent page's character count indicator updates after the edit
  // (cross-frame communication via postMessage).
  await expect(page.getByTestId('char-count')).toHaveText('24 characters');
});
```
Tradeoff: using `frameLocator('iframe[title="..."]')` selects the frame by a stable semantic attribute rather than by DOM index, making the test resilient to frame insertion order changes; the tradeoff is that `frameLocator` re-evaluates the iframe selector on each action call, meaning if the iframe is briefly removed and re-inserted by the framework (e.g., during a hot-module reload in development), `frameLocator` will correctly re-acquire it, but in production builds this re-evaluation adds a small per-action overhead — profile with `--trace on` if iframe-heavy tests are unexpectedly slow and switch to `locator.contentFrame()` on a pre-resolved iframe locator for tight inner loops.

---

**Pattern 654** — `vi.spyOn` With `mockImplementationOnce` Sequence to Test Transient Failure and Recovery Logic
```typescript
// Functions that implement retry-with-backoff, circuit-breaker patterns, or
// graceful degradation are tested by making the dependency fail a known number
// of times then succeed. Using mockImplementationOnce in sequence on a single
// spy is more readable and deterministic than toggling a shared flag variable.
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { fetchWithRetry } from '../src/fetch-with-retry';
import * as httpModule from '../src/http';

describe('fetchWithRetry', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.restoreAllMocks();
  });

  it('retries twice on transient errors and returns the successful response', async () => {
    const spy = vi.spyOn(httpModule, 'get');

    // First attempt: network error.
    spy.mockImplementationOnce(() => Promise.reject(new Error('ECONNRESET')));
    // Second attempt: server error.
    spy.mockImplementationOnce(() =>
      Promise.resolve({ status: 503, body: 'Service Unavailable' })
    );
    // Third attempt: success.
    spy.mockImplementationOnce(() =>
      Promise.resolve({ status: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ id: 42 }) })
    );

    const result = await fetchWithRetry('/api/resource', { maxRetries: 3 });

    expect(spy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
    expect(result).toEqual({ id: 42 });
  });

  it('throws after exhausting all retries', async () => {
    const spy = vi.spyOn(httpModule, 'get');
    spy.mockRejectedValue(new Error('ETIMEDOUT'));

    await expect(fetchWithRetry('/api/resource', { maxRetries: 2 })).rejects.toThrow(
      'Max retries (2) exceeded'
    );
    expect(spy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3); // initial + 2 retries
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: chaining `mockImplementationOnce` calls on a single spy produces a precise, readable failure sequence without shared mutable state, making it easy to verify that the retry count and call count match; the tradeoff is that if `fetchWithRetry` is refactored to call `httpModule.get` more times per attempt (e.g., to emit a pre-flight HEAD request), the call-count assertions break and require updating — document the expected call count in a comment explaining the retry contract so future maintainers understand why the number is non-obvious.

---

**Pattern 655** — `expect(page).toHaveURL` With a Regex After Multi-Step Redirects to Avoid Intermediate-URL Flakiness
```typescript
// Multi-step authentication flows (OAuth, SAML, magic-link) redirect the browser
// through several intermediate URLs before landing on the destination. Asserting
// on a specific intermediate URL is fragile because the redirect chain can change
// its middle steps without altering the final destination. Asserting on the final
// URL with a regex that captures the expected path — not the full origin — is
// resilient to domain changes between environments.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('magic-link login lands on the personalised dashboard', async ({ page, request }) => {
  // Request a magic link via the API rather than going through the email UI.
  const { token } = await request
    .post('/api/auth/magic-link', { data: { email: 'qa+test@example.com' } })
    .then((r) => r.json());

  // Navigate to the magic-link URL. The flow redirects through:
  //   /auth/verify?token=... -> /auth/callback -> /onboarding?step=1 -> /dashboard/jane
  // We only care about the final destination.
  await page.goto(`/auth/verify?token=${token}`);

  // Wait for the redirect chain to settle before asserting. toHaveURL uses
  // Playwright's auto-retry mechanism and will wait until the URL matches or
  // the assertion timeout is reached.
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/dashboard\/[a-z0-9-]+$/);

  // Verify the personalised greeting to confirm the correct user is logged in.
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toContainText('Welcome back');
});
```
Tradeoff: using a regex in `toHaveURL` asserts that the browser reached the destination path family without coupling the test to the full origin (which differs between local, staging, and production) or to intermediate redirect URLs that may change without breaking the user experience; the tradeoff is that the regex `/\/dashboard\/[a-z0-9-]+$/` will also match an error page whose URL happens to include a dashboard-like path segment — always pair the URL assertion with a content assertion (the personalised heading) to confirm the page rendered successfully, not just that the browser was redirected to the right URL shape.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G240** — `page.route` Handlers Registered After `page.goto` Miss Requests Fired During Initial Page Load
Why this matters: `page.route` registers an intercept handler that applies to all future matching requests on the page. If `page.goto` is called before `page.route` is registered, any network request that fires as part of the initial HTML parse and render cycle — including preloaded API calls, web fonts, and inline `<script>` fetches — completes before the handler is ever registered. Tests that rely on intercepting these initial requests (to stub an auth token header, mock a configuration endpoint, or abort a third-party tracker) will see the real responses on the first load and only the mocked responses on subsequent navigations, causing intermittent assertion failures on first run that disappear on retry.
Fix: always call `page.route(...)` before `page.goto(...)`, or register the route at the `browserContext` level so it is active from the moment the context is created and covers all pages including the initial navigation. For routes that must be registered conditionally per-test, use Playwright's `test.beforeEach` hook to ensure the handler is in place before any page is opened.

**G241** — Vitest `vi.mock` Hoisting Silently Wins Over a `beforeEach` `vi.spyOn` When Both Target the Same Module Export
Why this matters: Vitest hoists `vi.mock(...)` calls to the top of the test file during transformation, so a `vi.mock('../../src/logger')` declared anywhere in the file — including after a `describe` block — replaces the entire module before any `beforeEach` or `it` block runs. A subsequent `vi.spyOn(logger, 'warn')` in `beforeEach` operates on the already-replaced mock object, not on the real implementation. This produces unexpected behaviour: `spyOn` believes it is wrapping the mock's no-op function, `mockRestore()` restores the no-op (not the original), and any call-count assertion using `toHaveBeenCalledWith` may pass vacuously because the spy and the mock's internal call recorder are tracking different invocations.
Fix: choose one strategy per module per test file — either use `vi.mock` for full module replacement (and configure return values with `mockReturnValue` / `mockImplementation` inside the `vi.mock` factory), or use `vi.spyOn` without `vi.mock` for selective wrapping. If both are needed, use `vi.mock` with `vi.importActual` inside the factory to keep the real implementation and add the spy on top: `vi.mock('../../src/logger', async (importOriginal) => ({ ...await importOriginal(), warn: vi.fn() }))`.

**G242** — `page.evaluate` Closures Capture Serialised Copies of Variables, Not Live References
Why this matters: `page.evaluate((value) => window._testValue = value, myObject)` serialises `myObject` to JSON, sends it across the browser-Node.js boundary, and deserialises it in the browser context. If `myObject` contains non-serialisable properties (functions, `undefined` values, `Symbol` keys, circular references, `Map`/`Set` instances), the serialisation silently drops or corrupts those properties. Tests that pass a rich domain object into `page.evaluate` and then assert on the result often see mysterious failures only when the object grows a function property, or when the test runs in a worker that uses a stricter JSON serialiser (e.g., `structuredClone` with `transfer` restrictions in Chromium's worker boundary).
Fix: only pass primitive values, plain objects, and arrays to `page.evaluate`. For complex domain objects, extract the scalar values needed in the browser and pass only those, or expose a browser-side API (a global function registered with `page.exposeFunction`) that accepts primitives and reconstructs the domain object internally. Add a `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(myObject))` round-trip assertion in the test setup to detect serialisation loss before it reaches `page.evaluate`.

**G243** — `toMatchSnapshot()` Files Committed on macOS Fail on Linux CI Due to Font-Rendering Pixel Differences in Screenshots
Why this matters: Playwright's `page.screenshot` and `locator.screenshot` render text using the platform's default font stack. On macOS, fonts are rendered with sub-pixel antialiasing; on Linux CI (Ubuntu, Debian), fonts are rendered with greyscale antialiasing at a different pixel grid. A snapshot committed from a developer's macOS workstation produces a PNG that differs by hundreds of pixels from the Linux-rendered screenshot, causing `toMatchSnapshot()` to fail on every CI run with "X pixels differ" even though the UI is visually identical to a human. The failure is consistent (not intermittent in the traditional sense) but is often mis-diagnosed as a test infrastructure problem.
Fix: generate and commit all visual snapshots from within the same environment that runs CI — use the `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright` Docker image locally and in CI so the rendering pipeline is identical. Alternatively, use `toMatchSnapshot({ maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.02 })` with a 2% pixel tolerance as a short-term workaround, but document the tolerance explicitly and set a CI alert when it climbs above 5%, which indicates genuine visual regressions are being masked.

**G244** — `expect(fn).toThrow()` Does Not Catch Errors Thrown Inside `async` Functions Unless the Call Returns a Rejected Promise
Why this matters: `expect(() => asyncFn()).toThrow()` passes the return value of `asyncFn()` — a `Promise` — to Vitest's `toThrow` matcher. Because the promise is returned synchronously without throwing, `toThrow` sees no synchronous exception and the assertion passes vacuously even when `asyncFn` rejects. The test file shows a green tick, but the actual error-handling branch of the code is never exercised. This is the most common source of "tests that pass but don't test anything" in async-heavy codebases discovered during mutation testing.
Fix: always use `await expect(asyncFn()).rejects.toThrow('expected message')` for async functions that are expected to reject. For functions that may throw synchronously in some code paths and asynchronously in others, write two separate test cases — one using `toThrow` on a sync wrapper and one using `rejects.toThrow` on the async path — to ensure both branches are covered. Add `eslint-plugin-vitest`'s `valid-expect` rule to your ESLint config to catch bare `expect(asyncFn()).toThrow` patterns at lint time.

**Pattern 641** — `test.describe.configure({ retries: 2 })` for Scoped Retry Budgets on Known-Unstable Suites
```typescript
// Applying retries globally inflates suite runtime; scoping retries to known-
// unstable describe blocks lets stable suites fail fast while giving fragile
// integration tests the extra attempts they need to surface real failures.

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// This suite calls a live staging API with occasional transient HTTP 503s.
// Grant it two retries so a single spike does not block the merge queue.
test.describe('Checkout integration — staging API', () => {
  test.describe.configure({ retries: 2 });

  test('completes a one-item order successfully', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242424242424242');
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/30');
    await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();

    // Auto-retrying assertion waits up to 5 s by default.
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' }))
      .toBeVisible({ timeout: 10_000 });
  });

  test('shows an error for a declined card', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4000000000000002');
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/30');
    await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();

    await expect(page.getByText('Your card was declined')).toBeVisible();
  });
});

// Stable unit suite — fail fast, no retries needed.
test.describe('CartStore unit', () => {
  test('addItem increments quantity', () => {
    const store = new CartStore();
    store.addItem({ id: 'SKU-1', qty: 2 });
    expect(store.items).toHaveLength(1);
    expect(store.items[0].qty).toBe(2);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.describe.configure({ retries: N })` narrows retry cost to the describe block that actually needs it, preventing global retry inflation from tripling suite wall-clock time; the risk is that a test categorised as "flaky" by the retry report may be masking a real regression in a background service — review the `testInfo.retry` counter in `afterEach` dashboards regularly and drop the retry budget to zero once the root cause is fixed so genuine failures surface immediately.

**Pattern 642** — `testInfo.workerIndex` as a Database-Partition Key to Eliminate Cross-Worker Row Collisions
```typescript
// Parallel workers that share a single test database collide when they insert
// rows with the same unique key. Embedding workerIndex in every seed row
// guarantees each worker operates in an isolated partition without requiring
// a separate database instance per worker.

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { seedUser, deleteUser } from '../helpers/db';

let userId: string;

test.beforeAll(async ({ }, testInfo) => {
  // Each worker gets its own user partition: user_0@test, user_1@test, ...
  const email = `user_${testInfo.workerIndex}@test.example`;
  userId = await seedUser({ email, password: 'Test1234!' });
});

test.afterAll(async () => {
  await deleteUser(userId);
});

test('profile page shows the correct email', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto(`/users/${userId}`);
  await expect(page.getByTestId('profile-email')).toHaveText(
    `user_${test.info().workerIndex}@test.example`
  );
});

test('user can update display name', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto(`/users/${userId}/settings`);
  await page.getByLabel('Display name').fill(`Worker ${test.info().workerIndex}`);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('display-name')).toHaveText(
    `Worker ${test.info().workerIndex}`
  );
});
```
Tradeoff: partitioning by `workerIndex` eliminates unique-key collisions at near-zero overhead cost, but it ties test correctness to the maximum worker count — if `workers` is reduced from 4 to 2 in CI, worker 0 inherits the rows originally created by workers 0 and 2, which can leave stale data; always run `afterAll` cleanup unconditionally and assert the row count before the test to verify isolation rather than relying on partition ownership as a guarantee.

**Pattern 643** — `page.clock.pauseAt` + `page.clock.runFor` to Test Time-Gated UI Without Real Delays
```typescript
// UI that enables a "Resend" button only after 60 seconds cannot be tested
// with real timers — the test would wait a full minute. page.clock.pauseAt
// freezes the browser clock at a known instant; page.clock.runFor advances
// it by an arbitrary amount without any real wall-clock wait.

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('Resend button becomes enabled after the 60-second cooldown', async ({ page }) => {
  // Freeze the browser clock at an arbitrary but deterministic timestamp.
  // install must be called before navigation so the page JS sees the fake
  // clock from its first execution frame.
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-01-15T12:00:00Z') });
  await page.clock.pauseAt(new Date('2026-01-15T12:00:00Z'));

  await page.goto('/login/otp');
  await page.getByLabel('Phone number').fill('+15551234567');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send code' }).click();

  // Immediately after sending, Resend is disabled.
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Resend code' }))
    .toBeDisabled();

  // Advance the fake clock by 59 seconds — still within the cooldown window.
  await page.clock.runFor(59_000);
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Resend code' }))
    .toBeDisabled();

  // Advance one more second — the cooldown has expired.
  await page.clock.runFor(1_000);
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Resend code' }))
    .toBeEnabled();
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.clock.pauseAt` + `page.clock.runFor` collapses minutes of real time into milliseconds of test execution, completely eliminating timer-related flakiness for cooldown, expiry, and retry-after UI; the limitation is that `runFor` fires *all* timers scheduled within the window sequentially in one synchronous burst, so if production code uses `requestAnimationFrame` for smooth countdown animations, the visual frames are skipped — assert on the functional state change rather than the animation progress to keep tests meaningful.

**Pattern 644** — Worker-Scoped `auth` Fixture to Reuse Browser Sessions Across Tests in the Same Worker
```typescript
// Signing in before every test is the single largest source of e2e suite
// slowdown. A worker-scoped fixture signs in once per worker process and
// reuses the storage state across all tests assigned to that worker without
// sharing context between tests (each test still gets its own page).

import { test as base, expect, BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

type WorkerFixtures = {
  workerStorageState: string;
};

const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerFixtures>({
  workerStorageState: [
    async ({ browser }, use, workerInfo) => {
      // One storage-state file per worker so parallel workers never collide.
      const stateFile = path.join(
        __dirname, '..', '.auth',
        `worker-${workerInfo.workerIndex}.json`
      );
      const ctx: BrowserContext = await browser.newContext();
      const page = await ctx.newPage();

      await page.goto('/login');
      await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(`user_${workerInfo.workerIndex}@example.com`);
      await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('TestPass123!');
      await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
      await expect(page).toHaveURL('/dashboard');

      await ctx.storageState({ path: stateFile });
      await ctx.close();
      await use(stateFile);
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],

  // Override the default context to inject the pre-authenticated state.
  context: async ({ browser, workerStorageState }, use) => {
    const ctx = await browser.newContext({ storageState: workerStorageState });
    await use(ctx);
    await ctx.close();
  },
});

export { test, expect };
```
Tradeoff: the worker-scoped auth fixture reduces sign-in overhead from O(tests) to O(workers), which is typically a 10–30× speedup for large suites; the risk is that a mid-suite action that mutates the user account (e.g., changing the password or revoking the session) invalidates the shared storage state for every subsequent test in the same worker — guard account-mutating tests with `test.use({ storageState: undefined })` to force a fresh login for those specific tests.

**Pattern 645** — `route.fulfill` with a JSON Fixture File to Eliminate External API Flakiness
```typescript
// Tests that call real external APIs fail intermittently due to rate limits,
// network latency, and third-party outages. Intercepting every API call with
// a route handler and fulfilling from a versioned fixture file makes tests
// completely deterministic regardless of network conditions.

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import productsFixture from '../fixtures/products-api-response.json';

test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  // Intercept all requests matching the products API glob.
  await page.route('**/api/v2/products**', async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify(productsFixture),
    });
  });
});

test('product grid renders all items from the fixture', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  // The fixture contains exactly 3 products.
  const cards = page.getByTestId('product-card');
  await expect(cards).toHaveCount(productsFixture.items.length);

  // Verify the first card title matches the fixture data.
  await expect(cards.first().getByRole('heading'))
    .toHaveText(productsFixture.items[0].title);
});

test('search filters the product grid client-side', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');
  await page.getByRole('searchbox', { name: 'Search products' })
    .fill(productsFixture.items[1].title);

  // Only the matching card should remain visible.
  await expect(page.getByTestId('product-card')).toHaveCount(1);
  await expect(page.getByTestId('product-card').getByRole('heading'))
    .toHaveText(productsFixture.items[1].title);
});
```
Tradeoff: `route.fulfill` with a fixture file provides zero-latency, zero-flakiness API responses and makes the test contract explicit via a versioned JSON file; the tradeoff is that the fixture can drift from the real API schema over time — run a weekly contract-verification job that calls the real API and diffs the response shape against `*.json` fixtures using `ajv` or `zod` so schema drift is caught before it silently invalidates test coverage.

**Pattern 646** — `page.waitForResponse` with a URL Predicate to Gate Assertions on Specific Network Completions
```typescript
// Asserting UI state immediately after clicking a "Save" button can race
// with the in-flight PATCH request. page.waitForResponse ensures the
// assertion only fires after the specific network response has been received
// and processed by the page, regardless of animation or re-render timing.

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('saving a profile update persists the new display name', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/settings/profile');

  // Register the response waiter BEFORE the action that triggers the request.
  // Registering after the click creates a race: the response may arrive and
  // resolve before waitForResponse is set up.
  const saveResponsePromise = page.waitForResponse(
    (response) =>
      response.url().includes('/api/profile') &&
      response.request().method() === 'PATCH' &&
      response.status() === 200
  );

  await page.getByLabel('Display name').fill('Jane Smith');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save changes' }).click();

  // Wait for the PATCH /api/profile to complete before asserting.
  const saveResponse = await saveResponsePromise;
  const body = await saveResponse.json();

  // Validate round-trip: the server echoed the new name.
  expect(body.displayName).toBe('Jane Smith');

  // Now assert the UI reflects the persisted value.
  await expect(page.getByTestId('profile-display-name')).toHaveText('Jane Smith');
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.waitForResponse` eliminates the race between a user action and its network side-effect, making save/submit flow tests deterministic; the downside is that it couples the test to the exact URL pattern and HTTP method, so renaming or versioning the endpoint breaks the waiter — combine with `route` interception to validate both the request payload and the response in one assertion block rather than relying on the live endpoint URL alone.

**Pattern 647** — `expect.poll` with a Custom Predicate to Tolerate Eventual-Consistency Database Reads
```typescript
// Tests against eventually consistent data stores (DynamoDB, Cassandra,
// Elasticsearch) fail intermittently because a write does not become
// immediately visible on subsequent reads. expect.poll retries the assertion
// on a configurable cadence until the timeout is exceeded.

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { createDocument, getDocument, deleteDocument } from '../helpers/db-client';

test('newly created document is visible in the search index within 5 seconds', async () => {
  const docId = await createDocument({
    title: 'Distributed Consensus Notes',
    tags: ['raft', 'consensus'],
  });

  // The search index is updated asynchronously; the document may not appear
  // immediately. Poll every 500 ms for up to 5 seconds before failing.
  await expect.poll(
    async () => {
      const result = await getDocument(docId);
      return result?.indexed ?? false;
    },
    {
      message: `Document ${docId} was not indexed within 5 seconds`,
      timeout: 5_000,
      intervals: [500, 500, 500, 500, 500, 500, 500, 500, 500, 500],
    }
  ).toBe(true);
});

test('deleted document is removed from the index within 5 seconds', async () => {
  const docId = await createDocument({ title: 'To be deleted', tags: [] });
  // Wait for initial indexing before testing deletion.
  await expect.poll(async () => (await getDocument(docId))?.indexed ?? false, {
    timeout: 5_000,
  }).toBe(true);

  await deleteDocument(docId);

  await expect.poll(
    async () => (await getDocument(docId)) === null,
    { timeout: 5_000, message: `Document ${docId} still present after deletion` }
  ).toBe(true);
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.poll` provides a readable, configurable polling loop that surfaces helpful failure messages when the eventual-consistency window is exceeded, making it far preferable to manual `while` loops with `sleep`; the limitation is that every failed interval attempt is a real async call that consumes test worker CPU and network budget — keep the `intervals` array tight and the `timeout` proportional to the known p99 propagation latency of the specific data store rather than using a blanket 30-second timeout.

**Pattern 648** — `vi.mock` with an Inline Factory and `mockReset` in `beforeEach` to Prevent Cross-Test Module State Leakage
```typescript
// When vi.mock uses a factory function, Vitest hoists the factory to the top
// of the file. If the factory closes over mutable test-scope state (a counter,
// a flag, a spy), that state persists across tests unless explicitly reset.
// An inline factory that creates a fresh vi.fn() paired with mockReset in
// beforeEach avoids this leakage.

import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';

// The factory runs at hoist time; the returned spy is a fresh vi.fn() that
// can be reset between tests without affecting the module registry.
vi.mock('../services/email-service', () => ({
  sendEmail: vi.fn(),
}));

// Import AFTER vi.mock so the test receives the hoisted mock.
import { sendEmail } from '../services/email-service';
import { registerUser } from '../user-registration';

describe('registerUser', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    // Reset call history and any custom implementations set in previous tests.
    vi.mocked(sendEmail).mockReset();
  });

  it('sends a welcome email after successful registration', async () => {
    vi.mocked(sendEmail).mockResolvedValueOnce({ messageId: 'msg-001' });

    await registerUser({ email: 'alice@example.com', password: 'Secure123!' });

    expect(sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ to: 'alice@example.com', subject: 'Welcome!' })
    );
  });

  it('does not send an email when registration fails due to duplicate email', async () => {
    vi.spyOn(console, 'error').mockImplementation(() => {});
    await expect(
      registerUser({ email: 'alice@example.com', password: 'Secure123!' })
    ).rejects.toThrow('Email already registered');

    // The mock reset in beforeEach guarantees this call count is 0, not 1 from
    // the previous test.
    expect(sendEmail).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.mocked(fn).mockReset()` in `beforeEach` guarantees a clean slate for each test at essentially zero cost, eliminating the class of flakiness where test N passes only when run after test N-1 because test N-1 left a `mockReturnValue` on the spy; the subtle risk is that `mockReset` also removes any default implementation set in the factory, so if a test relies on a default return value it must set it up via `mockImplementation` in the test body rather than assuming the factory default persists.

**Pattern 649** — `getByRole` Locators with `name` Option to Resist DOM Refactoring
```typescript
// Tests anchored to CSS class names or XPath positions break silently when
// designers rename classes or developers restructure the DOM. getByRole with
// a name option targets the element by its ARIA role and accessible name,
// which remain stable across visual and structural refactors as long as the
// feature semantics are unchanged.

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('user can submit the contact form and sees a confirmation', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/contact');

  // Role + name locators: resistant to div→section rewraps, CSS class renames,
  // and attribute-list reordering. They break only when the feature changes.
  await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Full name' }).fill('Alice Smith');
  await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Email address' }).fill('alice@example.com');
  await page.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Department' }).selectOption('Support');
  await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Message' }).fill(
    'I need help with my order.'
  );

  // Using getByRole('button') instead of page.locator('.submit-btn') means this
  // locator survives a Tailwind class rename or a button-wrapper div insertion.
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send message' }).click();

  // Assert the success banner by its ARIA role and heading text.
  await expect(
    page.getByRole('status').getByText('Your message has been sent')
  ).toBeVisible();
});

test('form validation rejects a missing email', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/contact');
  await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Full name' }).fill('Bob Jones');
  // Deliberately skip the email field.
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send message' }).click();

  await expect(
    page.getByRole('alert').filter({ hasText: 'Email address is required' })
  ).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `getByRole` with `name` is the most refactor-resilient locator strategy Playwright offers because it mirrors how assistive technology reads the page, meaning tests break only when the feature's accessibility contract changes rather than when the visual implementation changes; the limitation is that elements without explicit ARIA roles or labels produce ambiguous role matches, and adding `aria-label` purely to satisfy a test locator can silently suppress the label text that screen-reader users need — prefer associating a `<label>` element correctly over adding synthetic `aria-label` attributes.

**Pattern 650** — `context.serviceWorkers: 'block'` to Guarantee `page.route` Intercepts in PWA Tests
```typescript
// When a Service Worker is registered on the page, fetch requests flow through
// the SW's fetch handler BEFORE reaching Playwright's network layer. This means
// page.route() mocks are bypassed silently, producing tests where the live API
// is called even though a route interceptor appears to be in place.

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import cartFixture from '../fixtures/cart.json';

// Block all Service Workers for this context so that route mocks are
// guaranteed to intercept every request.
test.use({
  serviceWorkers: 'block',
});

test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('**/api/cart**', async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify(cartFixture),
    });
  });
});

test('cart badge shows the item count from the API response', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/shop');

  // Without serviceWorkers: 'block', the SW might serve a cached empty cart
  // from a previous test run, making the badge show 0 instead of the fixture's
  // expected value.
  await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-badge')).toHaveText(
    String(cartFixture.items.length)
  );
});

test('checkout button is disabled when the cart has a pending lock', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('**/api/cart**', async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify({ ...cartFixture, locked: true }),
    });
  });
  await page.goto('/shop');
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' })).toBeDisabled();
});
```
Tradeoff: `serviceWorkers: 'block'` guarantees Playwright's route layer intercepts every request, making API mocks deterministic even in PWA applications; the cost is that any UI feature that depends on the Service Worker for offline support, background sync, or push notifications will be absent during the test — use a dedicated browser context with Service Workers enabled for offline-mode and push-notification tests and reserve the blocked context for API-mock-dependent tests.

**Pattern 651** — `test.step` with Descriptive Names for Actionable Failure Messages in Long Flows
```typescript
// Multi-action tests that fail deep in a sequence produce cryptic assertion
// errors like "expected 'Loading...' to equal 'Order #1234'" with no indication
// of which step failed. Wrapping logical groups of actions in test.step
// prefixes the error with the step title, reducing debug time from minutes to
// seconds.

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('full order placement flow from product page to confirmation', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('Navigate to product and add to cart', async () => {
    await page.goto('/products/wireless-keyboard');
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Wireless Keyboard' }))
      .toBeVisible();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-badge')).toHaveText('1');
  });

  await test.step('Proceed through checkout and enter shipping details', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Cart' }).click();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Proceed to checkout' }).click();
    await page.getByLabel('Full name').fill('Alice Brown');
    await page.getByLabel('Address line 1').fill('123 Main St');
    await page.getByLabel('City').fill('Portland');
    await page.getByLabel('Postcode').fill('97201');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue to payment' }).click();
  });

  await test.step('Enter payment details and submit', async () => {
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242424242424242');
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/30');
    await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();
  });

  await test.step('Verify confirmation page', async () => {
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/orders\/\d+\/confirmation/);
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /Order #\d+ confirmed/ }))
      .toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.step` wrapping turns a cryptic deep-assertion failure into a structured "Step: Enter payment details and submit > Error: expected element to be visible" trace that pinpoints the exact phase of failure without requiring a trace viewer; the overhead of wrapping every step is that deeply nested `test.step` calls produce verbose HTML reports that are slower to scan — limit steps to logical user-visible phases (navigate, fill, submit, verify) rather than wrapping individual locator actions.

**Pattern 652** — `vi.spyOn(globalThis, 'fetch')` with Scoped `mockRestore` to Prevent Fetch-Mock Leakage Between Tests
```typescript
// Tests that mock globalThis.fetch without restoring the original after each
// run contaminate subsequent tests in the same file, causing them to call the
// mock rather than the real fetch. Using vi.spyOn with mockRestore in afterEach
// guarantees the original is always reinstated.

import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { fetchWeather } from '../services/weather-service';

describe('fetchWeather', () => {
  let fetchSpy: ReturnType<typeof vi.spyOn>;

  beforeEach(() => {
    // Create a fresh spy before each test. vi.spyOn automatically wraps the
    // original so mockRestore() can reinstate it.
    fetchSpy = vi.spyOn(globalThis, 'fetch');
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    // Restores the original globalThis.fetch — not just clears the call log.
    // This prevents the mock from leaking into the next test.
    fetchSpy.mockRestore();
  });

  it('returns the parsed temperature on a 200 response', async () => {
    fetchSpy.mockResolvedValueOnce(
      new Response(JSON.stringify({ temperature: 22, unit: 'C' }), {
        status: 200,
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      })
    );

    const result = await fetchWeather('Portland');

    expect(result.temperature).toBe(22);
    expect(fetchSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.stringContaining('Portland'),
      expect.objectContaining({ method: 'GET' })
    );
  });

  it('throws a NetworkError when fetch rejects', async () => {
    fetchSpy.mockRejectedValueOnce(new TypeError('Failed to fetch'));

    await expect(fetchWeather('Portland')).rejects.toThrow('NetworkError');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.spyOn` + `mockRestore()` is the safest pattern for mocking globals because it returns the real implementation after each test, preventing the accidental live-API calls that a stale mock from a previous test would otherwise trigger; the subtlety is that `mockRestore()` only works for spies created with `vi.spyOn` — calling `mockRestore()` on a `vi.fn()` that was assigned directly to `globalThis.fetch` is a no-op, leaving the global permanently mocked until the test process exits.

**Pattern 653** — `test.use({ locale, timezoneId })` to Pin Locale and Timezone for Date-Formatting Tests
```typescript
// Tests that assert formatted dates (e.g., "May 14, 2026") break in CI when
// the server runs in UTC+0 and the developer's machine is in UTC-8: the same
// timestamp renders as a different date string on each side of midnight.
// test.use pins both locale and timezone for the entire describe block.

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// All tests in this block run in a US English locale with Pacific Time.
test.use({
  locale: 'en-US',
  timezoneId: 'America/Los_Angeles',
});

test('invoice date is displayed in mm/dd/yyyy format', async ({ page }) => {
  // Seed: the invoice was created at 2026-05-14T06:00:00Z.
  // In UTC this is May 14; in PST (UTC-7) this is still May 13 at 11 PM.
  // Without pinning timezoneId, the displayed date depends on CI server TZ.
  await page.goto('/invoices/INV-2026-001');

  // With timezoneId: 'America/Los_Angeles', this is deterministically "05/13/2026".
  await expect(page.getByTestId('invoice-date')).toHaveText('05/13/2026');
});

test('dashboard "today" filter includes invoices created today in LA time', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/invoices?filter=today');

  // In LA time, May 13 invoices are "today" — a UTC-only run would miss them.
  const rows = page.getByTestId('invoice-row');
  await expect(rows).not.toHaveCount(0);
  await expect(rows.first().getByTestId('invoice-date')).toHaveText('05/13/2026');
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.use({ locale, timezoneId })` pins the browser's `Intl.DateTimeFormat` locale and the V8 time zone simultaneously, making every `Date.toLocaleDateString()` call deterministic regardless of where CI runs; the risk is that pinning a single timezone means the test passes on a US developer's machine and in US-hosted CI but fails if the same suite is reused for a European user-facing test that expects `dd/mm/yyyy` format — create a separate describe block with `locale: 'en-GB', timezoneId: 'Europe/London'` for regional format variants rather than patching the existing suite.

**Pattern 654** — `page.on('console', ...)` Collector to Fail Tests on Unexpected `console.error` Calls
```typescript
// Production code that encounters an error often calls console.error but
// continues running, producing a visually passing test that silently swallows
// a React unhandled error boundary trigger, a failed API call, or a 404 asset.
// Collecting console errors during the test and asserting on them converts
// silent failures into explicit test failures.

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('product page loads without console errors', async ({ page }) => {
  const consoleErrors: string[] = [];

  // Attach the listener before navigation so errors from the initial page
  // load are captured.
  page.on('console', (msg) => {
    if (msg.type() === 'error') {
      consoleErrors.push(msg.text());
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/products/widget-pro');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Widget Pro' })).toBeVisible();

  // Interact with the page to trigger lazy-loaded components.
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'View specifications' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('specifications-panel')).toBeVisible();

  // Fail the test if any console.error was emitted, providing the full list
  // as the failure message for immediate diagnosis.
  expect(
    consoleErrors,
    `Unexpected console.error calls:\n${consoleErrors.join('\n')}`
  ).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: a `console.error` collector is a zero-cost smoke test that surfaces a whole class of silent runtime errors (missing images, React prop-type violations, unhandled rejections caught by an error boundary) that functional assertions never catch; the tradeoff is that third-party libraries and browser extensions emit their own `console.error` messages outside your control — maintain an allowlist of known-benign patterns (e.g., `/ResizeObserver loop/, /Non-passive event listener/`) and filter them from `consoleErrors` before the final assertion rather than disabling the collector entirely.

**Pattern 655** — `maxFailures` in `playwright.config.ts` to Fail Fast and Preserve CI Resources on Systemic Failures
```typescript
// A suite with 500 tests where test 10 deletes shared database rows can
// cause all remaining 490 tests to fail with "row not found" errors, consuming
// 30 minutes of CI time to report what is effectively a single root-cause
// failure. maxFailures short-circuits the run as soon as a threshold is crossed.

// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Stop the entire test run after 5 failures. In a healthy pipeline this
  // threshold is never reached; when it is, it signals a systemic failure
  // rather than isolated flakiness.
  maxFailures: process.env.CI ? 5 : 0, // 0 = no limit in local development

  retries: process.env.CI ? 1 : 0,

  use: {
    // Capture trace on first retry so the first failure is always debuggable
    // even though the second failure may trigger maxFailures.
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
    video: 'on-first-retry',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
  },

  reporter: [
    ['html'],
    // Blob reporter merges shard results in matrix CI builds.
    ...(process.env.CI ? [['blob'] as ['blob']] : []),
  ],

  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { browserName: 'chromium' },
    },
  ],
});
```
Tradeoff: `maxFailures: 5` on CI saves significant compute cost when a systemic failure cascades through hundreds of tests, providing a quick signal that "something fundamental is broken" rather than a 30-minute list of 490 individual failures; the risk is that setting the threshold too low (e.g., 1) causes a single legitimate flake on a heavily-used branch to abort the entire run and block the merge queue — calibrate `maxFailures` to roughly 1–2% of the suite size so it distinguishes true systemic failures from acceptable noise while still terminating early enough to matter.

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G240 — `page.clock.install()` Must Be Called Before `page.goto()` or Initial-Load Timers Are Scheduled Against the Real Clock**
Why this matters: `page.clock.install()` replaces the browser's `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `requestAnimationFrame` implementations with Playwright-controlled fakes. If it is called after `page.goto()`, any timers that the page registered during its initial load phase — for example, a session-expiry `setTimeout` set in an inline `<script>` tag or a React `useEffect` — were already scheduled against the real clock and are invisible to the fake clock. The test then observes a hybrid state: some timers are fake and controllable, others are real and fire unpredictably. The result is tests that pass when the page happens to load within a narrow real-time window and fail when CI latency pushes the real timers past their trigger point before the fake clock can be advanced.
Fix: always call `await page.clock.install({ time: <fixed-date> })` before `await page.goto()`. If the test needs to navigate to a specific URL first, use `page.clock.install()` in a `test.beforeEach` hook before any navigation — never after the first `goto` call. Pair `install` with `pauseAt` set to the same timestamp to freeze the clock immediately so subsequent `runFor` calls advance from a deterministic baseline.

**Gotcha G241 — `test.describe.serial()` Causes the Entire Group to Re-Run on Retry, Multiplying Seed-Data Side Effects**
Why this matters: `test.describe.serial()` is intended for tests that share state and must run in order. When retries are enabled globally, a single failure in a serial group causes the entire group to re-run from the beginning in a fresh worker. If the first test in the group seeds data and the failing test is the fifth, the re-run re-executes all five tests — the seed runs twice, potentially creating duplicate rows or conflicting state. If the second run also fails due to the duplicate seed rather than the original defect, Playwright reports the entire group as failed, masking the root cause. Teams often interpret this as intermittent infrastructure failure rather than a serial-group retry side effect.
Fix: avoid `test.describe.serial()` in suites with retries enabled. Instead, make each test individually idempotent using `workerIndex`-based data partitioning (Pattern 642) and `beforeAll` + `afterAll` cleanup that is safe to run multiple times. If serial ordering is truly unavoidable, add `test.describe.configure({ retries: 0 })` inside the serial block to override the global retry count and prevent group re-execution.

**Gotcha G242 — `page.route` Handlers Registered in `beforeEach` Accumulate Across Tests When the Same Page Object Is Reused**
Why this matters: `page.route()` registers a route handler on the page object. When a page is created in `beforeAll` and shared across tests, calling `page.route()` in `beforeEach` adds a new handler each time without removing the previous one. Playwright processes route handlers in LIFO (last-in, first-out) order, so the newest handler always intercepts first — but the old handlers remain active and fire for requests that the new handler passes through via `route.continue()`. After ten tests, ten handlers are stacked. A `route.continue()` call in the tenth handler triggers the ninth handler, which triggers the eighth, and so on, introducing cumulative latency and potential double-fulfillment errors when multiple handlers attempt to `route.fulfill()` the same request.
Fix: call `await page.unroute('**')` in `afterEach` to remove all accumulated route handlers, or use `page.route()` with the `times: 1` option to auto-unregister a handler after a single intercept. Better still, create a fresh page per test (Playwright's default) so route handlers are discarded automatically when the page is closed.

**Gotcha G243 — `vi.setSystemTime` Does Not Update `performance.now()`, Causing Duration-Diff Logic to Return Near-Zero Elapsed Values**
Why this matters: `vi.setSystemTime(date)` updates `Date.now()` and `new Date()` to the specified time, but it does not update `performance.now()`. Code that measures elapsed time using `performance.now()` — common in animation loops, debounce timers, and performance-tracking utilities — continues to read from the real monotonic clock. A test that calls `vi.setSystemTime(Date.now() + 5000)` to simulate 5 seconds of progress and then checks a `performance.now()`-based duration will observe a near-zero elapsed duration, causing the test to fail with a value like `3` instead of the expected `5000`. This is especially confusing because the fix for `Date.now()` (calling `vi.setSystemTime`) appears to work for date-display logic but silently fails for duration logic in the same module.
Fix: use `vi.useFakeTimers()` instead of `vi.setSystemTime` when the code under test uses `performance.now()`. `vi.useFakeTimers()` replaces both `Date` and `performance.now()` with fake implementations that are advanced together via `vi.advanceTimersByTime()`. If only `Date.now()` needs to be faked (e.g., for a pure date-formatting function), `vi.setSystemTime` is safe — verify which time source the production code uses before choosing the faking strategy.

**Gotcha G244 — `locator.filter({ hasText })` Substring Matching Causes Ambiguous Locator Errors When List Items Share a Prefix**
Why this matters: `locator.filter({ hasText: 'Invoice' })` matches any element whose text content *contains* the string "Invoice", including "Invoice #1", "Invoice #10", "Invoice #100", and "Invoice history". When the list has multiple items that share the search term, `filter` returns all of them, and a subsequent `.click()` or `.toHaveCount(1)` assertion fails with "strict mode violation: locator resolved to N elements". This is a common source of test flakiness in tables and lists where item titles follow a predictable pattern: a test passes when the list has few items and fails once the data set grows past the point where duplicated prefixes appear.
Fix: use `locator.filter({ hasText: /^Invoice #42$/ })` with a full-anchor regex (`^...$`) to require an exact full-text match rather than a substring match. Alternatively, combine `filter` with `has` to scope the match by a unique child element: `locator.filter({ has: page.getByTestId('invoice-id-42') })`. For tables, prefer `page.getByRole('row', { name: 'Invoice #42' })` which uses the accessible row name and is exact by default.

## Cycle 67 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 656** — `testInfo.retry` Guard to Reset Server-Side State Before Each Retry Attempt
```typescript
// When a test modifies server state (e.g., creates a record) and then fails,
// a naive retry re-runs against polluted state and fails for an unrelated
// reason. Reading testInfo.retry lets the test clean up before the retry
// begins without incurring a superfluous DELETE on the first attempt.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('create and verify order', async ({ page, request }, testInfo) => {
  if (testInfo.retry > 0) {
    // Clean up any order left by a prior attempt before retrying.
    await request.delete('/api/orders/test-order-cycle67', {
      failOnStatusCode: false, // 404 is fine if the prior attempt failed before creation
    });
  }

  await page.goto('/orders/new');
  await page.getByLabel('Order ID').fill('test-order-cycle67');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Order created');
});
```
Tradeoff: guarding cleanup behind `testInfo.retry > 0` avoids a superfluous `DELETE` on the first attempt and ensures the server is in a known-clean state on every retry; the cost is that cleanup must be idempotent (hence `failOnStatusCode: false`) and requires a stable, predictable resource identifier — tests that generate UUIDs inside the page must persist the ID in a fixture or file so the retry path can reference it.

---

**Pattern 657** — `page.routeFromHAR` in Replay Mode for Recording-Based Network Isolation
```typescript
// HAR replay is the highest-fidelity mocking strategy: responses are recorded
// from a real session and replayed verbatim, preserving headers, timing
// metadata, and binary bodies that are error-prone to hand-craft. Unlike
// route.fulfill, no fixture maintenance is required when response bodies are
// large or binary.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.use({
  // Switch to { update: true } once to re-record against a live environment,
  // then commit the HAR and switch back to { update: false } for CI.
  serviceWorkers: 'block', // prevents MSW from intercepting before Playwright
});

test('dashboard chart loads with recorded data', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.routeFromHAR('./fixtures/dashboard.har', {
    url: '*/**/api/v1/metrics/**',
    update: false,           // replay mode — never hits the real network
    updateContent: 'embed',  // inline binary blobs so the HAR is self-contained
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="revenue-chart"]')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="revenue-chart"]')).not.toBeEmpty();
});
```
Tradeoff: HAR replay eliminates live-network flakiness for entire flows without hand-crafting mocks, and `updateContent: 'embed'` keeps binary responses (images, fonts, wasm) self-contained in a single file; the cost is that HAR files can grow large (>10 MB) and become difficult to review in pull requests — scope the `url` pattern tightly to only the API paths under test and use `.gitattributes` to mark HAR files as binary to prevent diff noise.

---

**Pattern 658** — Worker-Scoped Playwright Fixture for a Single Shared Browser Context Across Read-Only Tests
```typescript
// Creating a new browser context per test adds ~150 ms overhead per test on
// most CI machines. For read-only smoke tests that do not mutate state, a
// worker-scoped context amortises the startup cost across the whole worker.
import { test as base, expect, BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

type WorkerFixtures = { sharedContext: BrowserContext };

const test = base.extend<Record<string, never>, WorkerFixtures>({
  sharedContext: [
    async ({ browser }, use) => {
      // Created once per worker process, not once per test.
      const ctx = await browser.newContext({
        storageState: './auth/read-only-user.json',
      });
      await use(ctx);
      await ctx.close(); // Runs after the last test in the worker completes.
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

test('homepage title is correct', async ({ sharedContext }) => {
  const page = await sharedContext.newPage();
  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page).toHaveTitle(/MyApp/);
  await page.close();
});

test('help link is visible', async ({ sharedContext }) => {
  const page = await sharedContext.newPage();
  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Help' })).toBeVisible();
  await page.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: a worker-scoped context reduces per-test browser startup overhead to near zero for read-only suites; the hazard is that cookies or localStorage mutated by one test (e.g., banner dismissal stored in a cookie) persist into the next test in the same worker — only use worker scope for truly read-only tests and open a fresh `page` per test (not a fresh `context`) to limit shared state surface area.

---

**Pattern 659** — `expect.toPass` With Back-Off `intervals` for Multi-Assertion Eventually-Consistent UI Blocks
```typescript
// `expect.poll` polls a callback that returns a scalar value. `expect.toPass`
// polls an entire assertion block, which is more ergonomic when you need to
// assert on multiple properties of a single locator that stabilises only after
// an async backend operation settles.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('processing badge transitions from "pending" to "done"', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/jobs/42');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Run job' }).click();

  // Poll the entire assertion block with an exponential back-off schedule.
  // Any single assertion failure inside the block triggers a retry.
  await expect(async () => {
    const badge = page.getByTestId('job-status-badge');
    await expect(badge).toBeVisible();
    await expect(badge).toHaveText('done');
    await expect(badge).toHaveAttribute('data-status', 'success');
    // Confirm the orange/pending colour is gone.
    await expect(badge).not.toHaveCSS('background-color', 'rgb(255, 165, 0)');
  }).toPass({ intervals: [500, 1_000, 2_000, 5_000], timeout: 30_000 });
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.toPass` lets you poll a multi-assertion block with a single back-off schedule, removing the need to nest multiple `expect.poll` calls; the downside is that on final failure Playwright reports only the last inner assertion that failed, so it is not immediately obvious which of the four assertions triggered the retry — add a named Playwright step (`test.step`) around the block to improve failure attribution in the trace viewer.

---

**Pattern 660** — `vi.useFakeTimers` With `vi.setSystemTime` to Freeze the Clock During Snapshot Tests
```typescript
// Snapshot tests that render components containing `Date.now()` or
// `new Date()` produce different snapshots on every run unless the clock is
// frozen. `vi.useFakeTimers()` replaces the runtime clock so the rendered
// output is deterministic.
import { describe, it, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { render } from '@testing-library/react';
import { InvoiceTimestamp } from '../components/InvoiceTimestamp';

describe('InvoiceTimestamp', () => {
  afterEach(() => {
    vi.useRealTimers(); // always restore after each test to prevent clock leaks
  });

  it('renders a pinned date in the invoice header', () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    // Pin to a specific UTC instant so the snapshot is identical across all
    // timezones when process.env.TZ is set to 'UTC' in vitest.config.ts.
    vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-01-15T09:00:00.000Z'));

    const { container } = render(<InvoiceTimestamp />);

    // Snapshot is stable: always "Jan 15, 2026, 09:00 AM UTC" on every machine.
    expect(container).toMatchSnapshot();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: freezing the clock with `vi.setSystemTime` makes snapshot output deterministic across all CI environments; the caveat is that `Intl.DateTimeFormat` in Node.js 18+ uses an ICU timezone cache that is not patched by `vi.setSystemTime` — set `process.env.TZ = 'UTC'` in `vitest.config.ts` and assert on UTC-formatted strings to avoid snapshot drift on CI hosts with different system timezone offsets.

**Pattern 661** — `page.on('websocket')` to Inject Deterministic WebSocket Frames Without a Live Server
```typescript
// Tests that assert on WebSocket-driven UI updates are flaky when they depend
// on a live WebSocket server. Playwright's page.on('websocket') lets you
// intercept the connection and inject synthetic frames before the UI sees them.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('live price ticker updates on incoming WebSocket message', async ({ page }) => {
  // Register the WebSocket interceptor before navigating so the connection
  // is captured from the moment the page script opens it.
  page.on('websocket', (ws) => {
    ws.on('framesent', () => {
      // After the client sends its subscription frame, inject a price update.
      ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'price', symbol: 'AAPL', value: 182.55 }));
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/ticker');

  // The UI must reflect the injected WebSocket message.
  const priceCell = page.getByTestId('ticker-AAPL-price');
  await expect(priceCell).toHaveText('$182.55');
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.on('websocket')` + `ws.send` injects deterministic server frames without running a real WebSocket server, eliminating the most common source of timing-driven WebSocket test flakiness; the limitation is that `ws.send` handles only text frames — binary (ArrayBuffer) messages require `ws.sendBinary`, and because the `framesent` handler fires asynchronously with respect to the UI render cycle, always follow the `ws.send` call with an auto-retrying `expect` rather than a synchronous assertion.

**Pattern 662** — `vi.mock` With `vi.importActual` to Stub Only the Network Layer of a Service Module
```typescript
// Mocking an entire module replaces all exports with vi.fn(), breaking imports
// that the module-under-test relies on for non-network logic. Spreading the
// actual module and overriding only the fetch wrapper keeps pure business logic
// untouched while isolating network calls.
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';

vi.mock('../services/productService', async (importOriginal) => {
  const actual = await importOriginal<typeof import('../services/productService')>();
  return {
    ...actual, // preserve all non-network helpers: formatPrice, sortByName, etc.
    fetchProducts: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue([
      { id: 'p1', name: 'Widget A', price: 9.99 },
      { id: 'p2', name: 'Widget B', price: 14.99 },
    ]),
  };
});

import { getFilteredProducts } from '../services/productService';

describe('getFilteredProducts', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.clearAllMocks();
  });

  it('returns only products above the price threshold', async () => {
    const result = await getFilteredProducts({ minPrice: 12 });
    expect(result).toHaveLength(1);
    expect(result[0].name).toBe('Widget B');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: spreading `importOriginal` preserves business-logic helpers so tests exercise the real filtering/sorting code while isolating the network layer; the footgun is that if `fetchProducts` is invoked inside a closure at module-load time rather than at call time, the `vi.fn()` stub arrives too late — verify the mocked export is not called in a top-level IIFE or module-level side effect before relying on this pattern.

**Pattern 663** — `testInfo.workerIndex` for Per-Worker Database User Isolation in Parallel Test Suites
```typescript
// Parallel workers that write to a shared database table race each other
// and produce intermittent "duplicate key" or "wrong row count" failures.
// Using testInfo.workerIndex as a namespace suffix gives each worker an
// isolated slice of data without requiring a separate database per worker.
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

type WorkerFixtures = { dbUser: string };

const test = base.extend<Record<string, never>, WorkerFixtures>({
  dbUser: [
    async ({}, use, workerInfo) => {
      const user = `test_worker_${workerInfo.workerIndex}`;
      // Upsert so the fixture is safe to call even if a prior run left debris.
      await globalThis.dbClient.query(
        'INSERT INTO test_users (username) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING',
        [user],
      );
      await use(user);
      await globalThis.dbClient.query(
        'DELETE FROM test_users WHERE username = $1',
        [user],
      );
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

test('user can update their profile', async ({ page, dbUser }) => {
  await page.goto(`/users/${dbUser}/profile`);
  await page.getByLabel('Display name').fill('New Name');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Saved');
});
```
Tradeoff: `workerIndex`-namespaced database users eliminate cross-worker data collisions with zero per-test overhead because the fixture is worker-scoped; the tradeoff is that `workerIndex` values are reused across retries in the same worker, so if a retry begins before teardown of the previous attempt completes the `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` clause silently masks a genuine collision — add an explicit `DELETE` at the top of the setup block to guarantee a clean slate on each fixture initialisation.
