**Pattern 664** — `page.clock.install` + `page.clock.runFor` to Advance Countdown Timers Without Real Waiting
```typescript
// Tests that assert on countdown timers, session-expiry warnings, or
// debounced auto-save dialogs must either wait for real time (slow,
// unreliable) or manipulate the browser clock. page.clock.install gives full
// control over setTimeout, setInterval, Date, and performance.now inside
// the browser context.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('session expiry warning appears after 25 minutes of inactivity', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install the fake clock BEFORE goto so all timers registered during
  // page initialisation are controlled by the fake clock from the start.
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-03-01T10:00:00Z') });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Advance the browser clock by 25 minutes in one step — the test runner
  // thread is not blocked; no real sleep occurs.
  await page.clock.runFor(25 * 60 * 1_000);

  const warning = page.getByRole('alertdialog', { name: /session expiring/i });
  await expect(warning).toBeVisible();

  await warning.getByRole('button', { name: 'Stay signed in' }).click();
  await expect(warning).not.toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.clock.runFor` advances all browser-side timers synchronously, making a 25-minute inactivity scenario complete in under one second; the caveat is that `page.clock` patches only the in-browser clock — server-side session expiry that checks `Date.now()` at the API layer is unaffected, so this pattern tests UI timer logic in isolation and must be paired with a separate API-level test that exercises real server-side expiry or uses a server-clock mock.

**Pattern 665** — `serviceWorkers: 'block'` to Prevent MSW From Intercepting Before Playwright Route Handlers
```typescript
// Mock Service Worker registers a service worker that intercepts fetch calls
// at the browser level before Playwright's page.route handlers can process
// them. When both are active, MSW returns a mock response and Playwright's
// handler never fires, causing request-interception assertions to fail
// non-deterministically based on service-worker registration timing.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Applied globally in playwright.config.ts or per-file via test.use().
test.use({
  contextOptions: {
    serviceWorkers: 'block', // prevents service worker registration entirely
  },
});

test('GET /api/orders is intercepted by Playwright route handler', async ({ page }) => {
  let intercepted = false;

  await page.route('*/**/api/orders', async (route) => {
    intercepted = true;
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify([{ id: 'ord-1', total: 99.99 }]),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/orders');
  await expect(page.getByRole('row')).toHaveCount(2); // header + 1 data row
  expect(intercepted).toBe(true);
});
```
Tradeoff: `serviceWorkers: 'block'` guarantees Playwright route handlers are the sole network interceptors, making request-interception assertions reliable; the cost is that any feature genuinely requiring a service worker (offline caching, background sync, push notifications) will not function in tests using this context option — maintain a separate context without the block flag for PWA-specific tests.

**Pattern 666** — Soft Assertions With `expect.configure({ soft: true })` for Full-Page Audit Tests
```typescript
// Accessibility audits, SEO meta-tag checks, and visual spot-checks must
// report every failure on the page, not just the first one. A hard assertion
// terminates at the first failure; a soft assertion accumulates all failures
// and reports them together at the end of the test.
import { test, expect as baseExpect } from '@playwright/test';

// Pre-configure a soft-by-default expect instance for audit-style tests.
const expect = baseExpect.configure({ soft: true });

test('homepage passes all SEO and accessibility spot-checks', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  // All assertions run regardless of whether earlier ones have failed.
  await expect(page).toHaveTitle(/MyApp — Home/);
  await expect(page.locator('meta[name="description"]')).toHaveAttribute(
    'content',
    /.{50,160}/, // description should be 50–160 characters
  );
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('navigation')).toHaveAttribute('aria-label', /.+/);
  await expect(page.locator('h1')).toHaveCount(1); // exactly one H1 per page
  await expect(page.locator('img:not([alt])')).toHaveCount(0); // no missing alt text

  // Hard assertion for a blocking issue — still uses baseExpect.
  await baseExpect(page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Home' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.configure({ soft: true })` surfaces every SEO or accessibility violation in one CI run rather than requiring iterative fix-and-rerun cycles; the downside is that a soft assertion that fails does not halt the test, so a later assertion that depends on a previous one (e.g., clicking a button confirmed by a prior soft assertion to exist) will throw a confusing locator error — use soft assertions only for independent, read-only checks and switch back to hard assertions for action-gated steps.

**Pattern 667** — `vi.spyOn(globalThis, 'fetch')` With `mockResolvedValueOnce` for Per-Call Fetch Error Injection
```typescript
// Components that call fetch directly (without an abstraction layer) are
// hard to test with vi.mock because fetch is a global. Spying on
// globalThis.fetch lets you inject resolved or rejected values per-call
// without mocking an entire module, and restoring in afterEach prevents
// the stub from leaking into other tests.
import { describe, it, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { renderHook, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react';
import { useProductDetails } from '../hooks/useProductDetails';

describe('useProductDetails error branch', () => {
  afterEach(() => {
    vi.restoreAllMocks(); // restore fetch so other tests use the real implementation
  });

  it('returns an error state when the API responds with 500', async () => {
    vi.spyOn(globalThis, 'fetch').mockResolvedValueOnce(
      new Response(JSON.stringify({ message: 'Internal Server Error' }), {
        status: 500,
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      }),
    );

    const { result } = renderHook(() => useProductDetails('prod-99'));

    await waitFor(() => {
      expect(result.current.isError).toBe(true);
    });

    expect(result.current.errorMessage).toMatch(/Internal Server Error/i);
    expect(result.current.data).toBeNull();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.spyOn(globalThis, 'fetch')` targets only the specific test's call sequence via `mockResolvedValueOnce` without permanently replacing the global; the caveat is that `mockResolvedValueOnce` is consumed on the first call — if the hook internally calls `fetch` more than once (e.g., a retry loop), later calls fall through to the real implementation unless you chain additional `mockResolvedValueOnce` calls or switch to the non-`Once` variant for persistent stubbing.

**Pattern 668** — `page.addLocatorHandler` to Dismiss Non-Deterministic Cookie Consent Banners Transparently
```typescript
// Cookie banners, session-expiry modals, and subscription pop-ups appear at
// unpredictable times during multi-step flows. Without a handler they block
// clicks and cause "strict mode violation" or "element not visible" errors
// that are indistinguishable from real application failures.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  // Register once — fires whenever the overlay becomes visible, regardless of
  // which navigation or action triggered its appearance.
  await page.addLocatorHandler(
    page.getByRole('dialog', { name: /cookie/i }),
    async (dialog) => {
      const acceptBtn = dialog.getByRole('button', { name: /accept all/i });
      if (await acceptBtn.isVisible()) {
        await acceptBtn.click();
      }
    },
    { noWaitAfter: false, times: 5 }, // allow up to 5 dismissals per test
  );
});

test('checkout flow completes without cookie banner interference', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/shop');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).first().click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'View cart' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Your cart' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `addLocatorHandler` intercepts the overlay at Playwright's between-action checkpoint, making it transparent to every subsequent `click`/`fill`/`navigate` call without per-test boilerplate; the risk is over-dismissal — if the cookie dialog is the subject of a specific test the handler will dismiss it before the assertion fires, so call `page.removeLocatorHandler(locator)` at the top of any test that intentionally asserts on the overlay.

**Pattern 669** — `page.route` + `route.fulfill` With a JSON Fixture File for Deterministic API Responses
```typescript
// Tests that call a real API are brittle: rate limits, schema changes, and
// network latency all produce failures invisible in unit tests. Intercepting
// with route.fulfill and a committed fixture file makes responses
// reproducible and eliminates the network dependency entirely.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import productsFixture from './fixtures/products.json';

test('product grid renders all items from API', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('*/**/api/v2/products', async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify(productsFixture),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/products');

  // Count is driven entirely by the fixture — zero network variance.
  const cards = page.getByRole('article', { name: /product/i });
  await expect(cards).toHaveCount(productsFixture.items.length);
});
```
Tradeoff: fulfilling with a committed JSON fixture gives full control over response shape and eliminates external network calls; the tradeoff is fixture drift — when the real API changes its schema the fixture silently diverges, so pair every fixture file with a nightly contract-test job that fetches the live endpoint, diffs against the fixture, and fails the build when the schema has changed.

**Pattern 670** — `test.step` Wrappers Around Multi-Action Sequences to Surface Exact Failure Points in Traces
```typescript
// Long end-to-end tests with 10+ actions are hard to debug when a single
// assertion fails: the trace viewer shows all actions but does not group
// them semantically. Wrapping logical phases in test.step gives each phase
// a label that appears in the trace viewer, HTML report, and CI log output.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('complete multi-step registration flow', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('Navigate to registration', async () => {
    await page.goto('/register');
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Create account' })).toBeVisible();
  });

  await test.step('Fill in account details', async () => {
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('new-user@example.com');
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('Secur3P@ssword');
    await page.getByLabel('Confirm password').fill('Secur3P@ssword');
  });

  await test.step('Submit and verify confirmation', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create account' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Check your email' })).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByText('new-user@example.com')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.step` labels appear in the HTML report and trace viewer, reducing mean-time-to-diagnose when a step fails in CI because the step name pinpoints the phase without requiring the developer to count action indices in the full trace; the tradeoff is that each `test.step` call introduces a slight overhead (~1 ms) and creates an additional nesting level in the report — avoid steps finer-grained than a logical user action sequence (e.g., do not wrap individual `fill` calls) or the report becomes harder to read than the flat action list it was meant to improve.

### Community Gotchas

**G245** — `page.clock.install` Must Be Called Before `page.goto` or In-Page Timers Registered During Load Will Use the Real Clock
Why this matters: `page.clock.install` patches `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `Date`, and `performance.now` inside the browser context, but only for timers registered after the patch is applied. If `page.goto` is called first, any `setInterval` or `setTimeout` registered during module initialisation — e.g., an auto-refresh polling loop in a React context provider — will use the real clock and are invisible to the fake clock. Calls to `page.clock.runFor` advance the fake clock without affecting those already-scheduled real timers, producing a hybrid state where the UI updates at unpredictable times. Tests pass locally (where system and fake time happen to coincide) and fail on slow CI machines where the real timers fire before the fake clock can be advanced.
Fix: always call `await page.clock.install(...)` before `await page.goto(...)`. If the application registers timers in a lazy-loaded service (only triggered by a user action), install the clock before the action that triggers lazy loading. For cases where the page must load before the target time is known, call `page.evaluate(() => Date.now())` after `goto` to read the current real time, install with that value, then advance from there to minimise drift.

**G246** — Playwright `workers: 'auto'` on Virtualised CI Cores Can Saturate CPU and Cause Timeouts That Look Like Flakiness
Why this matters: `workers: 'auto'` spawns one worker per logical CPU core. Cloud CI machines (GitHub Actions, CircleCI, Bitbucket Pipelines) typically report 2–4 logical cores but those cores are virtualised and shared with co-tenanted containers. When all workers launch browser instances simultaneously, CPU contention causes navigation timeouts (`page.goto` exceeds its `timeout` because the browser process is starved for CPU) and rendering stalls. These failures are indistinguishable from real application bugs in the Playwright report, causing developers to investigate non-existent race conditions.
Fix: set `workers: process.env.CI ? 2 : undefined` in `playwright.config.ts` to cap parallel workers on CI while preserving auto-scaling on developer machines. Alternatively, use `--shard` to distribute the suite across multiple CI jobs rather than packing all workers into one job. Identify CPU-saturation flakiness by checking whether all workers consistently timeout at the same instant in the timeline report — that pattern signals resource contention rather than application flakiness.

**G247** — `vi.clearAllMocks` Resets Call History But Does NOT Restore Original Implementations — Use `vi.restoreAllMocks` After `vi.spyOn`
Why this matters: `vi.clearAllMocks()` resets `mock.calls`, `mock.instances`, and `mock.results` but leaves the mock implementation installed. A spy created with `vi.spyOn(obj, 'method').mockImplementation(...)` will still return the stub in the next test even after `clearAllMocks`. The next test therefore receives the stubbed return value rather than the real implementation, producing incorrect results that look like a component bug rather than a leaked spy. The problem is especially common when test files mix `vi.spyOn` and `vi.fn()`, and developers apply a global `clearAllMocks` assuming it handles both cases identically.
Fix: use `vi.restoreAllMocks()` in `afterEach` (or set `restoreMocks: true` in `vitest.config.ts`) whenever any test in the file uses `vi.spyOn`. `restoreAllMocks` both clears call history and restores the original implementation. Reserve `vi.clearAllMocks` for files that use only standalone `vi.fn()` mocks with no original implementation to restore. Add a lint rule targeting `vi.clearAllMocks` in files that also call `vi.spyOn` to catch the mismatch at review time.

**G248** — Using `await locator.count()` Directly Inside `expect(...)` Bypasses Auto-Retry and Races Async Removals
Why this matters: `expect(locator).toHaveCount(0)` is auto-retrying and polls until the count is zero. The pattern `expect(await locator.count()).toBe(0)` evaluates the count synchronously at the exact moment of the call. After a `click` or `fill` action that triggers an async deletion (toast close, list-item removal via API), the element may still be in the DOM when the non-retrying assertion runs, causing an intermittent failure. The failure passes locally (where the deletion is fast) and fails on CI (where the event loop is more congested or the API is slower).
Fix: always use the auto-retrying form `await expect(locator).toHaveCount(0)` or `await expect(locator).not.toBeAttached()` after actions that trigger async DOM removals. Pass an explicit `{ timeout: 10_000 }` when removals are known to be slow, rather than raising the global timeout. Grep the test suite for `await locator.count()` used inside `expect(...)` and replace each occurrence with the auto-retrying locator assertion form.

**G249** — `page.waitForLoadState('networkidle')` Hangs Indefinitely for SPAs With Persistent WebSocket or SSE Connections
Why this matters: `waitForLoadState('networkidle')` resolves only when there are no open network connections for 500 ms. SPAs that maintain a persistent WebSocket or EventSource (SSE) for live updates never enter this state — the open connection is counted as active network activity. Tests that call `waitForLoadState('networkidle')` as a post-navigation readiness gate will wait until the configured timeout (default 30 s) before failing. The failure appears as a generic timeout in CI logs, masking the real cause (the persistent socket), and is often misdiagnosed as a slow application or resource exhaustion.
Fix: replace `waitForLoadState('networkidle')` with a content-based readiness gate: `await expect(page.getByTestId('app-shell')).toBeVisible()` or `await page.waitForSelector('[data-ready="true"]', { state: 'attached' })`. For pages with loading spinners, use `await expect(page.getByRole('progressbar')).not.toBeAttached()`. If a true networkidle check is genuinely required during `globalSetup`, block persistent connections first with `page.route('*/**/ws', route => route.abort())` before navigating.

## Cycle 68 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 671** — `page.clock.pauseAt` + `page.clock.resume` for Asserting Time-Gated UI Segments Without Timer Drift
```typescript
// Some components render different UI based on a time window (e.g., a banner
// that only shows between 09:00 and 17:00 local business hours). Testing both
// states requires the clock to be deterministically positioned at a known time,
// then advanced past the boundary, and assertions must not race the fake timers.
// pauseAt freezes the clock at a precise instant; resume restarts timer callbacks.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('business-hours banner appears inside window and hides after close', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install the fake clock BEFORE navigation so any timers created during page
  // load are already under synthetic control.
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-06-10T08:59:00.000Z') });
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Just before the 09:00 window opens — banner must not be visible.
  await expect(page.getByTestId('business-hours-banner')).toBeHidden();

  // Jump to exactly 09:00 and pause; fires setInterval/setTimeout callbacks
  // registered by the component without letting time continue to drift.
  await page.clock.pauseAt(new Date('2026-06-10T09:00:00.000Z'));
  await expect(page.getByTestId('business-hours-banner')).toBeVisible();

  // Jump to 17:01 — past the close boundary — and assert the banner collapses.
  await page.clock.pauseAt(new Date('2026-06-10T17:01:00.000Z'));
  await expect(page.getByTestId('business-hours-banner')).toBeHidden();

  // Resume the clock so any cleanup timers registered by the component can
  // fire during teardown without leaving dangling interval handles.
  await page.clock.resume();
});
```
Tradeoff: `pauseAt` gives pixel-perfect control over time-window boundary assertions with no wall-clock wait, making the test deterministic even when deployed to CI workers in different timezones; the cost is that any component code that uses `setTimeout` with a very short delay (< 1 ms) to defer a microtask may not fire between successive `pauseAt` calls unless you interleave `page.clock.runFor(1)`, requiring careful choreography when the component has multiple timer layers.

---

**Pattern 672** — `expect.toPass` Retry Block for Asserting External State That Converges Asynchronously
```typescript
// Some UI actions trigger background jobs (email dispatch, webhook delivery,
// cache invalidation) whose effects are visible only after the server finishes
// processing. Hard-coding a sleep races against server load; expect.toPass
// retries the entire assertion block until it succeeds or times out.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('invoice email is delivered after checkout', async ({ page, request }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' })).toBeVisible();

  // Poll the test-only email capture endpoint until the invoice email appears.
  // expect.toPass retries the entire async callback with the configured intervals.
  await expect(async () => {
    const response = await request.get('/api/test/emails?subject=invoice&limit=1');
    expect(response.ok()).toBeTruthy();
    const body = await response.json();
    expect(body.emails).toHaveLength(1);
    expect(body.emails[0].to).toMatch(/^customer@/);
  }).toPass({
    intervals: [500, 1000, 2000, 4000],
    timeout: 15_000,
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.toPass` eliminates arbitrary `page.waitForTimeout` sleeps and gives the assertion a clean retry loop with configurable back-off intervals, making the test resilient to server processing jitter without masking genuine failures; the cost is that a poorly scoped retry block can hide performance regressions (a job that previously finished in 200 ms now takes 12 seconds) because the test still passes as long as it converges within the timeout — always log or assert on a timing metric separately when processing latency is a quality concern.

---

**Pattern 673** — `test.use({ timezoneId, locale })` Per-Describe-Block to Eliminate Locale-Driven Date Rendering Flakiness
```typescript
// Components that call Intl.DateTimeFormat or Date.toLocaleDateString produce
// different rendered strings depending on the browser's timezone and locale.
// Tests that assert on formatted date text fail on CI runners in UTC+0 when
// the developer machine is UTC-5, or when the OS locale differs.
// test.use scopes the override to a single describe block without polluting
// the rest of the suite.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('invoice date display — Eastern US locale', () => {
  test.use({ timezoneId: 'America/New_York', locale: 'en-US' });

  test('invoice date renders in M/D/YYYY format', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/invoices/42');
    // With timezoneId and locale pinned, this assertion is stable regardless
    // of the CI runner's host timezone or OS locale configuration.
    await expect(page.getByTestId('invoice-date')).toHaveText('6/15/2026');
  });
});

test.describe('invoice date display — German locale', () => {
  test.use({ timezoneId: 'Europe/Berlin', locale: 'de-DE' });

  test('invoice date renders in DD.MM.YYYY format', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/invoices/42');
    await expect(page.getByTestId('invoice-date')).toHaveText('15.06.2026');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: scoping `test.use({ timezoneId, locale })` to a describe block makes locale-sensitive assertions fully deterministic without requiring any application code change or environment variable; the cost is that the browser context is re-created for each scope boundary, adding roughly 100–200 ms of context startup overhead per describe group — which is acceptable for correctness but can inflate suite runtime when dozens of locale variants are tested in separate scopes rather than being collapsed into a single parameterised test.

**Pattern 674** — `vi.waitFor` With `timeout` and `interval` for Asserting Eventual Reactive State Updates in Vitest
```typescript
// Vue, MobX, and Zustand stores sometimes apply state changes in batched
// microtask flushes that complete asynchronously relative to the triggering
// action. Asserting synchronously on store.state after an action can read stale
// state because the reactive scheduler has not yet committed. vi.waitFor retries
// the callback until it passes or the timeout expires.
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { createPinia, setActivePinia } from 'pinia';
import { useCartStore } from '@/stores/cart';

describe('CartStore reactive update', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    setActivePinia(createPinia());
  });

  it('total recalculates after async coupon validation resolves', async () => {
    const cart = useCartStore();
    cart.addItem({ id: 'prod-1', price: 100, quantity: 2 });

    // applyCoupon dispatches an async validation that resolves in the next
    // microtask tick and then updates the discount via a reactive setter.
    cart.applyCoupon('SAVE10');

    // vi.waitFor retries the assertion every 50 ms until total converges.
    await vi.waitFor(
      () => {
        expect(cart.total).toBe(180); // 200 - 10%
      },
      { timeout: 2000, interval: 50 }
    );
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.waitFor` with explicit `timeout` and `interval` replaces both `nextTick` chains and `flushPromises` patterns and survives even when the reactive scheduler introduces additional intermediate ticks, making tests resilient to internal scheduler implementation changes; the cost is that a failing assertion burns the full timeout before reporting failure — keep timeout values as small as possible (≤ 500 ms for unit tests) and complement `vi.waitFor` with `vi.useFakeTimers` when the delay is itself timer-driven so the timeout can be advanced synthetically rather than wall-clock waiting.

**Pattern 675** — Per-Worker `storageState` Files to Isolate Authenticated Sessions in Parallel Playwright Tests
```typescript
// When multiple parallel workers all share the same storageState file and a
// test modifies the authenticated user's profile (e.g., changes the email
// address or resets a password), subsequent tests in other workers read stale
// or corrupt session data. Per-worker auth files fence each worker's session.
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  globalSetup: './global-setup.ts',
  use: {
    // Each worker receives its own session file keyed by worker index.
    storageState: ({ workerIndex }) => `playwright/.auth/worker-${workerIndex}.json`,
  },
});

// global-setup.ts — logs in once per worker with a dedicated test account.
import { chromium, FullConfig } from '@playwright/test';

async function globalSetup(config: FullConfig) {
  const { workers } = config;
  const browser = await chromium.launch();

  for (let i = 0; i < (workers ?? 1); i++) {
    const context = await browser.newContext();
    const page = await context.newPage();
    await page.goto(`${config.projects[0].use.baseURL}/login`);
    // Use pre-seeded per-worker test accounts to avoid session collisions.
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(`worker${i}@test.example`);
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('TestPass123!');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
    await page.waitForURL('**/dashboard');
    await context.storageState({ path: `playwright/.auth/worker-${i}.json` });
    await context.close();
  }

  await browser.close();
}

export default globalSetup;
```
Tradeoff: per-worker storageState files eliminate session collision flakiness in suites that mutate authenticated user state by giving each worker a fully isolated identity backed by a dedicated test account; the cost is that the global setup duration scales linearly with the number of workers (each worker requires a full login round-trip), so for large parallelism counts (> 8 workers) consider using an API endpoint that issues short-lived test tokens directly rather than driving a browser login for every worker.

**Pattern 676** — `page.routeFromHAR` With `updateMode: 'minimal'` to Record Live API Responses as Deterministic Test Fixtures
```typescript
// Integration tests that call a real backend are flaky because the backend can
// return different data on each run (different IDs, timestamps, pagination
// cursors). routeFromHAR replays a recorded HAR file for matching requests,
// making the test deterministic without requiring a full mock layer.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const HAR_FILE = path.resolve(__dirname, 'fixtures/products-api.har');

test.describe('product listing with HAR replay', () => {
  test.use({ serviceWorkers: 'block' }); // prevent SW from intercepting routes

  test('renders 12 products from HAR fixture', async ({ page }) => {
    // In CI: replay the HAR — requests never hit the real server.
    // To update the fixture: run with UPDATE_HAR=1 env var set.
    const shouldUpdate = !!process.env.UPDATE_HAR;
    await page.routeFromHAR(HAR_FILE, {
      url: '**/api/products**',
      update: shouldUpdate,
      updateMode: shouldUpdate ? 'minimal' : undefined,
    });

    await page.goto('/products');
    const cards = page.getByTestId('product-card');
    await expect(cards).toHaveCount(12);

    // Spot-check deterministic data from the recorded HAR.
    await expect(cards.first()).toContainText('Widget Pro');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `routeFromHAR` with `updateMode: 'minimal'` records only the subset of response fields that change between runs, keeping the HAR file small and diff-friendly in version control while making all assertions against stable fixture data; the cost is that the fixture must be refreshed when the API contract changes (new fields, renamed endpoints), so teams must establish a clear "refresh the HAR" workflow and commit updated fixtures in the same PR as the application change — otherwise tests pass against the old contract while the live API diverges.

**Pattern 677** — `test.describe.configure({ retries })` for Shard-Local Retry Budgets That Do Not Inflate Global Pipeline Duration
```typescript
// When a CI pipeline shards across 8 machines, global retries configured in
// playwright.config.ts apply per-test but do not respect shard boundaries —
// a flaky test retried on shard 3 can delay the entire pipeline if it consumes
// its full retry budget. Scoping retries to the describe block that owns the
// flaky tests lets other shards complete independently.

// playwright.config.ts — global retries kept low; per-suite retries override locally.
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  retries: 1, // one global retry for all tests; locally-scoped overrides go higher
  reporter: [['blob'], ['html', { open: 'never' }]],
});

// tests/checkout/payment.spec.ts — elevated retries scoped to the unstable sandbox.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('payment provider sandbox', () => {
  // Grant up to 3 retries only within this describe scope.
  test.describe.configure({ retries: 3 });

  test('card tokenisation succeeds on sandbox', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout/payment');
    await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4111111111111111');
    await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
    await page.getByLabel('CVV').fill('123');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('payment-success')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 20_000 });
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.describe.configure({ retries })` scopes elevated retry budgets to the specific flaky subsystem without inflating retry counts globally, preventing one unstable sandbox integration from tripling the worst-case duration of the entire shard; the cost is that retry configuration is now distributed across many spec files rather than centralised in `playwright.config.ts`, making it harder to audit the total retry budget and potentially masking permanently broken tests if retries are set too generously in individual files.

**Pattern 678** — `test.step` With Descriptive Labels to Produce Trace-Viewer–Readable Flaky-Test Diagnostics
```typescript
// When a long Playwright test flakes in CI, the trace viewer shows a flat list
// of Playwright actions without logical groupings — it is hard to identify
// which business step failed. Wrapping logical phases in test.step produces
// named segments in the trace timeline that immediately reveal which phase
// failed without needing to correlate action indices to test logic manually.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('complete order lifecycle — place, confirm, track', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('navigate to product and add to cart', async () => {
    await page.goto('/products/widget-pro');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-count')).toHaveText('1');
  });

  await test.step('proceed through checkout', async () => {
    await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'View cart' }).click();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('buyer@example.com');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' }).click();
  });

  await test.step('confirm order and capture order ID', async () => {
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
    const orderId = await page.getByTestId('order-id').textContent();
    expect(orderId).toMatch(/^ORD-\d{6}$/);
  });

  await test.step('verify order appears in tracking page', async () => {
    await page.goto('/orders');
    await expect(page.getByText('Widget Pro')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.step` labels produce named segments in the Playwright trace viewer and HTML report, cutting mean time-to-diagnose on flaky CI failures from minutes to seconds by showing exactly which logical phase failed; the cost is that wrapping every action in a `test.step` adds two async function boundary overhead per step (roughly 0.5–1 ms each), which is negligible for most tests but adds measurable overhead in extremely tight loops — reserve `test.step` for coarse logical phases (3–8 per test) rather than wrapping individual locator actions.

**Pattern 679** — `vi.fn().mockResolvedValueOnce` Chaining for Deterministic Retry-Sequence Unit Tests
```typescript
// Services that implement client-side retry logic (e.g., exponential back-off
// after a 503) are flaky when tested with a mock that always resolves or always
// rejects — the test cannot verify that the retry fired, or that the third
// attempt used a different payload. mockResolvedValueOnce lets you script a
// precise call-by-call sequence without timer gymnastics.
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { fetchWithRetry } from '@/lib/fetchWithRetry';

const mockFetch = vi.fn();
vi.stubGlobal('fetch', mockFetch);

describe('fetchWithRetry — exponential back-off sequence', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    mockFetch.mockReset();
    vi.useFakeTimers();
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });

  it('retries twice on 503 and resolves on the third call', async () => {
    // Script: call 1 → 503, call 2 → 503, call 3 → 200.
    mockFetch
      .mockResolvedValueOnce(new Response(null, { status: 503 }))
      .mockResolvedValueOnce(new Response(null, { status: 503 }))
      .mockResolvedValueOnce(new Response(JSON.stringify({ ok: true }), { status: 200 }));

    const promise = fetchWithRetry('/api/data', { retries: 3, baseDelay: 100 });

    // Advance through the two back-off delays synthetically.
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(100); // first retry delay
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(200); // second retry delay (doubled)

    const result = await promise;
    expect(await result.json()).toEqual({ ok: true });
    expect(mockFetch).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: chaining `mockResolvedValueOnce` scripts the exact call sequence without coupling the test to timing assumptions about the real network, making the retry unit test fully deterministic and fast under fake timers; the cost is that the chain is positionally dependent — inserting an extra internal `fetch` call inside `fetchWithRetry` (e.g., for telemetry) shifts the sequence and causes the third mock value to be consumed by a non-retry call, breaking the test in a confusing way — always assert `expect(mockFetch).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(n)` to catch unexpected extra invocations immediately.

**Pattern 680** — `page.waitForResponse` With URL Predicate and Status Check to Gate Assertions on Specific API Round-Trips
```typescript
// Clicking "Save" on a form triggers an XHR PATCH request. Asserting on the
// success toast immediately after click races against the network round-trip:
// on a fast developer machine the response arrives before the assertion, but on
// a CI runner with a throttled loopback interface the toast has not yet rendered.
// Register the waiter BEFORE the triggering action to eliminate the race.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('profile update persists and shows confirmation', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/settings/profile');

  // Register the response waiter BEFORE triggering the network request to
  // avoid a race where the response arrives before the waiter is installed.
  const saveResponsePromise = page.waitForResponse(
    (response) =>
      response.url().includes('/api/users/me') &&
      response.request().method() === 'PATCH' &&
      response.status() === 200,
    { timeout: 10_000 }
  );

  await page.getByLabel('Display name').fill('Jane Doe');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save changes' }).click();

  // Await the response before asserting on UI state that depends on it.
  const response = await saveResponsePromise;
  const body = await response.json();
  expect(body.displayName).toBe('Jane Doe');

  // Now safe to assert on the toast — the response has arrived.
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: 'Profile updated' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: registering `page.waitForResponse` before the triggering action eliminates the response-arrival race entirely, making assertions on downstream UI state deterministic even under network latency; the cost is that the predicate must be specific enough (URL + method + status) to not match unrelated background requests — an overly broad predicate (matching only on URL substring) can be satisfied by a prefetch request that fires before the save action, causing the test to proceed with the wrong response and produce confusing assertion failures.

**Pattern 681** — Vitest `worker`-Scoped Fixtures for Expensive DB Connections That Must Not Be Re-Created Per Test
```typescript
// Opening a real database connection takes 200–800 ms. Creating one per test
// in beforeEach multiplies suite runtime and, when tests run in parallel across
// multiple workers, can exhaust the database connection pool, causing random
// "too many connections" failures in tests that happen to overlap.
// Worker-scoped fixtures create the connection once per worker process.
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { Pool } from 'pg';

// Extend Vitest's base test with a worker-scoped DB pool fixture.
export const test = base.extend<
  Record<string, never>,       // test-scoped fixtures (empty here)
  { dbPool: Pool }             // worker-scoped fixtures
>({
  dbPool: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      const pool = new Pool({
        connectionString: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL,
        max: 3, // hard cap per worker to prevent pool exhaustion
      });
      // Verify the pool is healthy before any test in this worker runs.
      await pool.query('SELECT 1');
      await use(pool);
      // Teardown: drain all idle connections when the worker exits.
      await pool.end();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },       // runs once per worker, not once per test
  ],
});

// In any spec file, import the extended test and use the pool directly:
// test('inserts a user', async ({ dbPool }) => {
//   await dbPool.query('INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ($1)', ['a@b.com']);
// });
```
Tradeoff: a worker-scoped DB pool fixture amortises connection overhead across the full set of tests in a worker, reducing test suite runtime by up to 60% on database-heavy suites and preventing connection-pool exhaustion under high parallelism; the cost is that all tests in a worker share the same pool, so any test that leaves an open transaction or holds a lock (e.g., due to an uncaught exception in a `beforeEach`) will block subsequent tests in the same worker until the connection is recycled — always wrap test DB operations in explicit transactions with rollback in `afterEach` when using a shared pool.

---

**Pattern 682** — `page.mouse` Low-Level Coordinate Drag to Bypass `pointer-events: none` Overlay Layers in Drag-and-Drop Tests
```typescript
// Playwright's locator.dragTo targets the topmost element at the drop
// coordinates. When a drag-and-drop zone is covered by a transparent overlay
// with pointer-events: none, dragTo may silently fail to trigger the drop
// handler. Using page.mouse with explicit coordinates bypasses CSS
// pointer-events checks at the Playwright action level.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dragging a task card between Kanban columns re-assigns it', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/kanban');

  const sourceCard = page.getByTestId('task-card-101');
  const targetColumn = page.getByTestId('column-in-progress');

  // Get bounding boxes to compute precise centre coordinates.
  const sourceBBox = await sourceCard.boundingBox();
  const targetBBox = await targetColumn.boundingBox();

  if (!sourceBBox || !targetBBox) throw new Error('Element not visible');

  const sourceX = sourceBBox.x + sourceBBox.width / 2;
  const sourceY = sourceBBox.y + sourceBBox.height / 2;
  const targetX = targetBBox.x + targetBBox.width / 2;
  const targetY = targetBBox.y + targetBBox.height / 2;

  // Low-level mouse sequence fires all drag events in the correct order.
  await page.mouse.move(sourceX, sourceY);
  await page.mouse.down();
  // Move in small increments to trigger dragover on intermediate elements.
  await page.mouse.move(sourceX + 10, sourceY, { steps: 5 });
  await page.mouse.move(targetX, targetY, { steps: 20 });
  await page.mouse.up();

  // Assert the card is now inside the target column.
  await expect(targetColumn.getByTestId('task-card-101')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.mouse` low-level drag bypasses CSS `pointer-events` restrictions and generates the full `mousedown` → `mousemove` → `mouseup` sequence that real drag-and-drop libraries (react-beautiful-dnd, dnd-kit) require, making the test robust against DOM layering; the cost is that coordinate arithmetic is brittle when the page layout changes — a responsive layout shift or a new sidebar that alters column widths will change the bounding box values and silently cause the drag to land in the wrong position, so always assert the card's new column membership rather than just that no error was thrown.

---

**Pattern 683** — `expect.soft` Aggregation for Multi-Field Form Validation Tests That Must Report All Failures at Once
```typescript
// A checkout form has 8 required fields. A test that validates error-message
// display for all fields stops on the first failing assertion when using hard
// expect calls, so a developer sees only the first regression even if multiple
// fields are broken. expect.soft accumulates all failures and reports them
// together at the end of the test.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('all required-field errors display on empty checkout submission', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  // Submit the form without filling any fields.
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();

  // Hard assertion: verify the error container exists before soft-checking text.
  await expect(page.getByTestId('validation-summary')).toBeVisible();

  // Soft assertions collect all failures; the test continues past each one.
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('error-first-name')).toHaveText('First name is required');
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('error-last-name')).toHaveText('Last name is required');
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('error-email')).toHaveText('Email is required');
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('error-phone')).toHaveText('Phone is required');
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('error-address')).toHaveText('Address is required');
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('error-city')).toHaveText('City is required');
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('error-postcode')).toHaveText('Postcode is required');
  await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('error-country')).toHaveText('Country is required');

  // Final hard assertion ensures the form did not navigate away on empty submit.
  await expect(page).toHaveURL('/checkout');
  // Playwright re-raises all soft failures collected above at this point.
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.soft` surfaces all failing field assertions in a single test run rather than stopping at the first regression, dramatically reducing the number of run/fix/re-run cycles needed to fully restore a multi-field validation feature; the cost is that a soft-assertion test cannot use the result of a failing assertion to guard subsequent assertions — if the error element does not exist at all (as opposed to having the wrong text), the soft assertion swallows the locator failure and the test reports a confusing "expected text X but element was missing" message rather than "element not found", so always combine soft assertions with a prior hard assertion that the form's error-summary container is visible.

---

**Pattern 684** — `vi.setTimerTickMode('interval')` to Drain Mixed `setInterval` + `setTimeout` Queues Without Masking Ordering Bugs
```typescript
// Components that mix setInterval polling with setTimeout debounce produce
// interleaved timer queues. vi.runAllTimers drains the entire queue at once,
// which fires all timers simultaneously and can mask ordering bugs. Setting
// tick mode to 'interval' advances time in configurable steps, allowing
// assertions between timer firings to validate intermediate states.
import { describe, it, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { createAutoSave } from '@/lib/autoSave';

describe('AutoSave — mixed timer queue ordering', () => {
  afterEach(() => {
    vi.useRealTimers();
  });

  it('debounces rapid keystrokes and then persists on interval', async () => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    // interval tick mode preserves intermediate timer callbacks' correct ordering.
    vi.setTimerTickMode('interval');

    const persistFn = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ saved: true });
    const autoSave = createAutoSave(persistFn, {
      debounceMs: 300,   // debounce fires 300 ms after last keystroke
      intervalMs: 5000,  // interval triggers a force-save every 5 s
    });

    autoSave.onChange('Hello');
    autoSave.onChange('Hello W');
    autoSave.onChange('Hello World');

    // Advance 299 ms — debounce must NOT have fired yet.
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(299);
    expect(persistFn).not.toHaveBeenCalled();

    // Advance 1 more ms — debounce fires now.
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1);
    expect(persistFn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
    expect(persistFn).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Hello World');

    // Advance to the interval boundary — force-save fires.
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(5000 - 300);
    expect(persistFn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.setTimerTickMode('interval')` preserves the relative ordering of debounce and interval callbacks when time is advanced in precise increments, making intermediate-state assertions possible and catching bugs where the interval fires before the debounce has resolved; the cost is that setting a global tick mode in one test can bleed into adjacent tests if `vi.useRealTimers()` is not called in `afterEach` — always restore real timers unconditionally in teardown and avoid calling `vi.setTimerTickMode` outside a fake-timer context.

---

**Pattern 685** — `page.route` REST Handler Factory for Reusable Per-Test API Stub Composition
```typescript
// Repeating full page.route(..., route.fulfill({...})) blocks across many test
// files couples every test to the response shape and causes cascade failures
// when the API contract changes. A factory function composes route handlers
// from per-test overrides merged onto sensible defaults, giving each test the
// minimal stub it needs without duplicating boilerplate.
import { Page, Route } from '@playwright/test';

type ProductsStubOptions = {
  items?: Array<{ id: string; name: string; price: number }>;
  status?: number;
  delay?: number;
};

/** Default product list — update here when the API response shape changes. */
const defaultProducts = [
  { id: 'p1', name: 'Widget Pro', price: 99 },
  { id: 'p2', name: 'Widget Lite', price: 49 },
];

export async function stubProductsApi(
  page: Page,
  overrides: ProductsStubOptions = {}
): Promise<void> {
  const { items = defaultProducts, status = 200, delay = 0 } = overrides;

  await page.route('**/api/products**', async (route: Route) => {
    if (delay > 0) await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, delay));
    await route.fulfill({
      status,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify({ data: items, total: items.length }),
    });
  });
}

// Usage — each test calls the factory with only the overrides it needs:
// test('renders empty state', async ({ page }) => {
//   await stubProductsApi(page, { items: [] });
//   await page.goto('/products');
//   await expect(page.getByText('No products found')).toBeVisible();
// });
//
// test('renders 503 error state', async ({ page }) => {
//   await stubProductsApi(page, { status: 503 });
//   await page.goto('/products');
//   await expect(page.getByTestId('error-banner')).toBeVisible();
// });
```
Tradeoff: a route-handler factory with merge semantics centralises the API stub contract in one place so that a field rename in the response only requires a single update to the factory's default, eliminating the cascade of failures caused by individually authored `route.fulfill` blocks scattered across spec files; the cost is that the factory abstraction can mask the intent of a specific test — a reviewer reading `stubProductsApi(page, { items: [] })` must navigate to the factory to understand what the full response body looks like, so always keep factory signatures small and document the default shape in a JSDoc comment directly above the function.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G250** — `waitForLoadState('networkidle')` Produces False Positives on Pages With Long-Poll or WebSocket Connections
Why this matters: `waitForLoadState('networkidle')` resolves when there are no in-flight network connections for 500 ms. Pages that open a WebSocket connection or a long-polling XHR during initialization never reach the idle threshold — the navigation wait times out and the test fails with a generic timeout. More subtly, pages that batch analytics beacons 400 ms after `DOMContentLoaded` satisfy the 500 ms idle window momentarily and then open more connections, causing `networkidle` to resolve between beacon batches even though the page is still loading content.
Fix: replace `waitForLoadState('networkidle')` with a content-based readiness gate: `await expect(page.getByTestId('product-grid')).toBeVisible()`. This waits for exactly the readiness signal your test cares about rather than a heuristic network-silence window. For pages with persistent background connections, use `waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded')` paired with an explicit content assertion rather than relying on network silence.

**G251** — Fixture Teardown Errors in Playwright Swallow the Original Test Failure
Why this matters: when a test fails and its `afterEach` hook (or fixture teardown function) also throws, Playwright records only the teardown error in the test report and discards the original test failure. The original failure — which is the actual bug — disappears from the output, replaced by a misleading "page closed" or "context already destroyed" error from the teardown code that tried to interact with a page that had already failed. Developers spend time investigating the teardown error rather than the root cause.
Fix: wrap teardown code so that `await use(fixture)` is called inside a `try` block with teardown in the `finally` block so that fixture cleanup runs even if the test throws, but teardown errors do not replace the original failure. For `afterEach` hooks that close pages or reset DB state, add explicit null guards (`if (page && !page.isClosed())`) before performing teardown actions to prevent teardown from throwing when the test has already torn down the context.

**G252** — `vi.mock` Hoisting Does Not Apply to Dynamic `await import()` Calls Inside Async Factory Functions
Why this matters: Vitest hoists `vi.mock('module-name', factory)` calls to the top of the file at transform time, ensuring the mock is registered before any `import` statement at module scope resolves. However, when application code uses `await import('@/lib/feature-flags')` inside an async function body (a dynamic import), the mock registry is checked at the time of the `await import()` call — and if the module was already loaded into the real module registry before the mock was registered (e.g., because a different test file imported it first in the same worker), the dynamic import returns the real module rather than the mock, causing the test to run against live code without any warning.
Fix: use `vi.doMock` instead of `vi.mock` for modules that are loaded via `await import()` inside async functions, and call `vi.doMock` immediately before the `await import()` call in the test body rather than at module scope. Alternatively, ensure `vi.resetModules()` is called in `beforeEach` when testing code paths that use dynamic imports, then require the module under test fresh within `vi.isolateModulesAsync` to guarantee the mock registry is consulted against a clean module graph.

**G253** — Reusing a `storageState` File Across Test Runs Without Expiry Validation Causes Silent Authentication Failures Hours Later
Why this matters: `playwright/.auth/user.json` is typically written once during `globalSetup` and reused for the entire CI pipeline run. If the test account's session token expires during a long-running pipeline (e.g., a 4-hour nightly suite against a server with 2-hour session TTLs), every test that relies on `storageState` silently lands on the login redirect rather than the authenticated page — there is no error; locator assertions simply time out on elements that are present on the dashboard but absent from the login screen, and the failure message says "element not found" rather than "session expired".
Fix: add a session-validity probe at the end of `globalSetup` by navigating to a protected endpoint and asserting the authenticated page title or a sentinel element; if the probe fails, re-run the login flow before saving `storageState`. For long pipelines, configure server session TTLs to exceed the expected pipeline duration, or add a `beforeAll` hook in your fixtures that performs a lightweight `request.get('/api/me')` and reloads `storageState` if the response is 401.

**G254** — `page.clock.install()` Called After `page.goto()` Does Not Control Timers Created During Page Initialisation
Why this matters: `page.clock.install()` patches the browser context's timer and Date APIs from the point of installation forward. Any `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, or `new Date()` call that executed before `install()` was called used the real clock and is not retroactively brought under synthetic control. When `install()` is called after `goto()` — even if the navigation `await` has resolved — timers created by module-level code or by script tags that ran during the HTML parse phase are already scheduled on the real clock. Tests that try to advance fake time with `page.clock.runFor(5000)` after `goto()` will not fire those early-registered timers, causing assertions on their side effects to fail or time out.
Fix: always call `await page.clock.install({ time: new Date(...) })` before `await page.goto(...)`. If the test must navigate to a page first, use `page.clock.setFixedTime()` immediately after `install()` to position the clock before navigation, ensuring both Date and timer APIs are synthetic for every script that executes during page load.

**Pattern 686** — `locator.ariaSnapshot({ mode: 'ai' })` for LLM-Assisted Flaky Selector Diagnosis
```typescript
// When a test fails intermittently because a locator matches the wrong element or
// matches nothing at all, the default error message shows only the selector string.
// locator.ariaSnapshot({ mode: 'ai' }) produces a snapshot containing element refs
// (e.g., [ref=e42]) and bounding boxes so an AI agent — or a developer using an LLM
// tool — can pinpoint the correct selector from the current DOM structure in one pass.
//
// Mode 'ai' differs from the default mode in three ways:
//   1. It includes element references like [ref=e42] for programmatic targeting.
//   2. It embeds bounding-box coordinates [box=x,y,w,h] when boxes:true is set.
//   3. It does NOT wait for elements matching the locator to exist — it throws
//      immediately when the locator finds nothing (use default mode for assertions).
//
// Safe usage: call only in afterEach/onTestFailed diagnostic handlers, never in
// the main test body where an empty locator would throw and mask the real failure.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.afterEach(async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  if (testInfo.status !== 'passed') {
    // Capture an AI-mode snapshot of the entire page body for LLM triage.
    // The snapshot includes [ref=eN] anchors that a repair agent can target directly.
    try {
      const snapshot = await page.locator('body').ariaSnapshot({
        mode: 'ai',
        depth: 5,       // enough to surface the problem element without flooding context
        boxes: true,    // include bounding boxes for layout-sensitive flakiness diagnosis
        timeout: 3_000, // fail fast — do not block teardown for a diagnostic
      });
      await testInfo.attach('aria-snapshot-ai', {
        body: snapshot,
        contentType: 'text/plain',
      });
    } catch {
      // Swallow — page may already be closed if the test threw before navigation.
    }
  }
});

test('product search returns results', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/search');
  await page.getByRole('searchbox').fill('widget');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Search' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('result-count')).toContainText(/\d+ results/);
});
```
Tradeoff: `ariaSnapshot({ mode: 'ai' })` captures structured element refs and bounding-box coordinates that an AI repair agent (or developer using an LLM tool) can use to identify the correct resilient locator without re-running the failing test — significantly cutting the investigation cycle for intermittent selector failures where the DOM differs between environments; the cost is that `mode: 'ai'` throws immediately when the locator matches nothing rather than waiting, so it must never be placed in the main test path where an empty page could interrupt the test before the actual assertion runs — always gate it behind `testInfo.status !== 'passed'` or a `try/catch` in diagnostic teardown code only.

**Pattern 687** — `locator.highlight({ style })` for Headed-Only Visual Debugging During Flakiness Investigation  [official]
```typescript
// When investigating a locator that intermittently fails, running the test in headed
// mode with locator.highlight() makes the matched element visually obvious, confirming
// that the locator is finding the right element before the action is attempted.
// Unlike locator.focus() or keyboard focus, highlight() adds a configurable CSS
// overlay without altering the element's state — click targets, disabled states,
// and focus rings are unaffected.
//
// IMPORTANT: highlight() returns a Disposable. The overlay persists until the
// disposable is disposed or the page navigates. Do NOT use in CI (headed: false)
// — it has no effect in headless mode and adds 10–50 ms of IPC overhead per call.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Guard: only run with headed flag to prevent CI overhead.
test.skip(!process.env.HEADED, 'highlight debugging — run with HEADED=1 only');

test('confirm locator uniqueness before fixing flaky click', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Highlight the suspected flaky locator with a distinctive outline.
  // Returns a Disposable — use `await using` (TS 5.2+) for scoped cleanup.
  await using _highlight = await page
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Export' })
    .highlight({
      style: 'outline: 3px solid red; background: rgba(255,0,0,0.15)',
    });

  // Pause execution — developer inspects the highlighted element visually.
  // Remove this line once the locator is confirmed correct.
  await page.pause();

  // Now assert: if this is the only red-outlined element, the locator is unique.
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Export' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('export-modal')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `locator.highlight()` with a custom `style` provides immediate visual confirmation that a locator resolves to exactly the intended element during headed debugging sessions, removing the guesswork about whether an intermittent "element not found" error is a timing issue or an ambiguous selector issue; the cost is that the method has zero effect in headless environments (`headed: false`) and introduces 10–50 ms of DevTools Protocol round-trips per call — guard every call site with a `HEADED` environment check or a `test.skip` so the highlight code is never present in CI runs, where it wastes time without providing any diagnostic value.

**Pattern 688** — Playwright v1.56 Test Agents (Planner / Generator / Healer) for Automated Locator Self-Healing  [official]
```typescript
// Playwright v1.56 introduced Test Agents — three AI-backed worker processes that
// run alongside the test executor and operate on test files and the live browser:
//
//   planner  — breaks a natural-language test description into steps
//   generator — writes or edits .spec.ts files to implement the steps
//   healer    — repairs locator failures in failing tests without manual intervention
//
// The healer agent is the most directly relevant to flakiness: when a test fails
// because a locator no longer matches (e.g., a class name hash changed, a label
// text was renamed), the healer inspects the current DOM via ariaSnapshot(mode:'ai'),
// infers the best replacement locator, updates the .spec.ts file, and re-runs
// the test — all without developer involvement.
//
// Configuration: add the 'agents' block to playwright.config.ts.
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Agents section configures all three agent workers.
  // Each agent is opt-in — omit any block to disable that agent.
  agents: {
    // Healer agent: automatically repairs broken locators.
    healer: {
      enabled: true,
      // Confidence threshold: 0.0–1.0. Below this, the healer writes a
      // FIXME comment instead of auto-committing the locator change.
      confidence: 0.8,
      // Maximum retries after heal before the test is still marked failed.
      maxHealAttempts: 2,
    },
    // Generator agent: off here — only use for spec scaffolding, not healing.
    generator: { enabled: false },
  },
  retries: 1, // keep at least 1 retry so the healer has a second attempt after repair
  reporter: [['html', { open: 'never' }], ['json', { outputFile: 'results.json' }]],
});
```
```typescript
// The healer agent watches for TestInfoError objects whose message matches
// 'locator.click: Error: strict mode violation' or 'locator resolved to N elements'.
// It uses ariaSnapshot(mode:'ai') on the failing step's parent locator to build
// a candidate list, then applies a semantic similarity score to pick the best match.
//
// Anti-pattern that confuses the healer: wrapping locators in custom helpers that
// catch errors and return null — the healer never sees the original locator error.
// Pattern: keep locator calls direct in test bodies so the healer can intercept them.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('user profile page — locator-resilient test for healer agent demo', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/profile');

  // Direct locator calls — healer can intercept and repair these.
  await page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'My Profile' }).waitFor();
  await page.getByLabel('Display name').fill('Jane Doe');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save changes' }).click();

  // Role-based assertions are healer-friendly: they express intent, not implementation.
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Saved');
});
```
Tradeoff: the healer agent eliminates the most common source of "locator drift" flakiness — tests that fail only after a UI change because a class name, label text, or DOM structure changed — by automatically committing the corrected locator to the spec file before the next CI run; the cost is that the healer can accept false positives at confidence levels below 0.9 (it repairs the locator to the wrong element but the test still passes because the wrong element happens to produce the expected text), so always review healer-authored commits in PR diff and set `confidence: 0.85` or higher in production pipelines; also note that healer repairs are only deterministic when tests use semantic locators (`getByRole`, `getByLabel`, `getByText`) — tests written with CSS selectors or XPath produce ambiguous repair candidates.

**Pattern 689** — Vitest 4.1 Test Tags With Per-Environment Retry Budget for CI-Only Retries  [official]
```typescript
// A common flakiness management mistake: setting a high global retryTimes in
// vitest.config.ts to handle CI flakiness, which also masks failures locally
// (developers re-run once and assume the test passed) and inflates local
// test suite runtime by 2–3x when running the full suite.
//
// Vitest 4.1 test tags with per-tag options solve this cleanly: tests known to be
// flaky in CI (e.g., integration tests hitting a real DB, tests spawning child
// processes) receive 3 CI retries via a 'flaky-ci' tag, while the global retry
// stays at 0 so local runs report the failure on first attempt.
//
// The tag is also a quarantine signal: the presence of { tags: ['flaky-ci'] }
// on a test is a searchable marker for quarterly flakiness review — grep for it,
// file tracking issues, and remove it once the root cause is fixed.
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Global retry is 0 — no retry by default (fast local feedback).
    retry: 0,
    // Tag-level overrides: 'flaky-ci' gets 3 retries only when running in CI.
    tags: [
      {
        name: 'flaky-ci',
        // CI-only retry budget. On developer machines, still fails on first attempt.
        retry: process.env.CI ? 3 : 0,
        // Longer timeout for integration tests on constrained CI runners.
        timeout: process.env.CI ? 60_000 : 10_000,
      },
      {
        name: 'db-integration',
        // DB tests need more time on CI without needing extra retries.
        timeout: process.env.CI ? 30_000 : 5_000,
        retry: 0,
      },
    ],
  },
});
```
```typescript
// Usage: tag only the tests known to be flaky in CI — not entire describe blocks.
// A tracking comment documents WHY the tag is present and when it should be removed.
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { sendEmailVerification } from '@/services/email';

describe('email verification service', () => {
  // [FLAKY-CI] 2026-05-14: AWS SES sandbox has 2–3 s cold-start on first call.
  // Tracking: https://github.com/org/repo/issues/1234
  // Remove tag once: SES connection pooling lands in email.service.ts
  it('sends verification email within SLA', { tags: ['flaky-ci'] }, async () => {
    const result = await sendEmailVerification('user@test.example');
    expect(result.status).toBe('queued');
    expect(result.messageId).toMatch(/^[0-9a-f-]{36}$/);
  });

  // Non-flaky test in same suite — no tag, uses global retry: 0.
  it('rejects invalid email format immediately', async () => {
    await expect(sendEmailVerification('not-an-email')).rejects.toThrow(
      'Invalid email format',
    );
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: per-tag retry budgets in Vitest 4.1 let teams surgically apply CI retries to the exact test cases that need them without inflating local runtime or masking failures for developers — the `{ tags: ['flaky-ci'] }` annotation is also a self-documenting quarantine marker that survives refactoring and is greppable for quarterly review; the cost is that the tag can become permanent if no one owns the quarterly cleanup — add a `// Remove tag once: <condition>` comment on every tagged test and enforce via a linting rule (`no-permanent-flaky-tag`) that fails if the tag appears without a removal condition comment.

### Community Gotchas (continued)

**G255** — `locator.ariaSnapshot({ mode: 'ai' })` Throws Immediately When the Locator Matches No Elements — Use Default Mode for Structural Assertions  [community]
Why this matters: `ariaSnapshot({ mode: 'ai' })` differs from the default mode in one critical way: it does not wait for the locator to resolve — it throws synchronously if zero elements match. Developers who discover `mode: 'ai'` and add it to snapshot assertion calls expecting the usual retry-with-timeout behaviour end up with tests that fail immediately on the first render frame, producing a misleading "locator not found" error on pages that require a brief loading period before elements appear. The actual assertion that was intended (structure matches expected snapshot) is never reached.
Fix: use `mode: 'ai'` exclusively in diagnostic teardown code (`afterEach`, `onTestFailed`, custom reporters) where you want an immediate snapshot of whatever is currently in the DOM — not in test bodies. For structural assertions, use `expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot(template)` (default mode) which retries with the configured timeout before failing.

**G256** — Vitest `tags` Config-Level Options Apply to ALL Tests Tagged — Accidentally Tagging Stable Tests With a High-Retry Tag Inflates Runtime Without Warning  [community]
Why this matters: when a developer adds `{ tags: ['flaky-ci'] }` to a test that shares a describe block with other tests they want to group, and later another developer adds the same tag to a fast, stable unit test to avoid filtering it from a CI report, that stable test now inherits 3 retries on every CI run — tripling its contribution to pipeline duration without any visible warning. Vitest emits no warning when a tag override matches a test that never fails; the retry budget is silently consumed on the first successful attempt.
Fix: document a strict convention: `'flaky-ci'` is a quarantine marker, not a grouping tool. Use a separate tag like `'integration'` or `'slow'` for timeout adjustments on stable-but-slow tests. Add a lint rule or `beforeAll` assertion that queries `expect(test.meta.tags ?? []).not.toContain('flaky-ci')` in suites where no flakiness is expected, catching misuse before it reaches CI.

**Pattern 690** — Playwright v1.52 `failOnFlakyTests` + Per-Project `workers` as a Two-Layer CI Gate  [official]

Playwright v1.52 introduced both `failOnFlakyTests` (config-level) and a per-project `workers` override. Together they form a two-layer CI gate: `failOnFlakyTests` ensures any test that passes on retry (i.e., was flaky rather than genuinely failing) blocks the merge, while per-project workers lets you run the known-flaky projects with `workers: 1` (serial execution) to isolate order-dependency from concurrency-induced flakiness — without slowing down the stable projects.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — two-layer CI gate for flakiness
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // LAYER 1: any test that passes on retry is reported as flaky and the overall
  // run exits with a non-zero code — blocking merges on new flakiness.
  // Only enable in CI; locally this would block development on known-flaky tests
  // that are already tracked with test.fixme().
  failOnFlakyTests: !!process.env.CI,

  // Default: up to 2 retries in CI so flaky detection works.
  // If retries were 0, failOnFlakyTests would never trigger (no retry → no flaky signal).
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,

  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium-stable',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
      // Fast, stable unit and component tests — run in parallel.
      workers: undefined, // inherits global default (typically 50% of CPUs)
    },
    {
      name: 'e2e-db-heavy',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
      // LAYER 2: integration/E2E tests that hit a real DB or shared service.
      // workers: 1 ensures order-dependency and port collisions are eliminated
      // from the flakiness signal — if a test still flakes serially, it is a
      // genuine timing or external-dependency issue, not a parallelism artifact.
      workers: 1,
      // Longer timeout for slower serial runs.
      timeout: 60_000,
    },
  ],
});
```

```typescript
// Marking pre-existing known-flaky tests with test.fixme() prevents
// failOnFlakyTests from blocking unrelated PRs while the root cause is tracked.
// test.fixme() marks the test as "expected to fail" — if it passes, it is
// reported as "unexpectedly passed" (not flaky), so it does not trigger failOnFlakyTests.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// [QUARANTINE] 2026-05-14: DB connection pool exhaustion under load.
// Tracking: https://github.com/org/repo/issues/5678
// Remove fixme once: connection pool size is configurable per test environment.
test.fixme('checkout flow completes under load', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
});
```

Tradeoff: the `failOnFlakyTests` + `workers: 1` combination makes new flakiness visible and actionable at merge time — a developer cannot land code that introduces a new flaky test, because the retry will flip the test from "failed" to "flaky" and the run will fail; the cost is that pre-existing flaky tests not yet marked with `test.fixme()` will block all PRs until they are tagged, so the right rollout sequence is: (1) audit existing suite for flaky tests using `--repeat-each 5` nightly, (2) mark confirmed-flaky tests with `test.fixme()`, (3) enable `failOnFlakyTests: true` in CI; rolling it out without step 2 will produce immediate CI noise on unrelated PRs.

**Pattern 691** — Playwright v1.53 `locator.describe()` for Human-Readable Locator Labels in Trace Viewer  [official]

Playwright v1.53 added `locator.describe(label)`, which attaches a human-readable string to a locator that appears in trace viewer step names, HTML reporter output, and error messages. In flakiness postmortems, the most common confusion is "which of the 3 `.submit-btn` elements failed?" — `locator.describe()` eliminates this by surfacing a meaningful name in the trace without changing the locator's selector logic.

```typescript
// Before v1.53: trace viewer shows "locator('.submit-btn').nth(1).click"
// — ambiguous which button in a multi-form page.
// After: "Submit payment form > .submit-btn:nth(1) > click"
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('payment flow submits successfully', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/payment');

  // Wrap the locator with a descriptive label.
  // The label appears in trace viewer and error messages but does NOT change the
  // element matched — it is purely diagnostic metadata.
  const submitBtn = page
    .locator('.submit-btn')
    .nth(1)
    .describe('Submit payment form primary CTA');

  // Now trace shows: "Submit payment form primary CTA > click" instead of
  // a raw CSS selector string, making flakiness postmortems faster.
  await submitBtn.click();

  await expect(
    page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Payment confirmed' }).describe('Payment success heading'),
  ).toBeVisible();
});
```

```typescript
// Composing described locators in page objects — the describe label is
// preserved through chaining, so fixture-based page objects get readable
// trace output automatically.
import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export class CheckoutPage {
  readonly submitButton;
  readonly errorBanner;

  constructor(private readonly page: Page) {
    this.submitButton = page
      .getByRole('button', { name: /pay/i })
      .describe('Checkout > Pay button');
    this.errorBanner = page
      .getByRole('alert')
      .describe('Checkout > Inline error banner');
  }

  async submitPayment() {
    await this.submitButton.click();
  }

  async waitForError(expectedText: string) {
    // Trace: "Checkout > Inline error banner > toContainText"
    await expect(this.errorBanner).toContainText(expectedText);
  }
}
```

Tradeoff: `locator.describe()` dramatically reduces the time spent correlating trace viewer steps to source code during flakiness investigation — a labelled trace step pinpoints both the locator and its semantic role in the user journey, whereas an unlabelled CSS/XPath step requires cross-referencing the test source and the page DOM; the cost is that labels must be kept in sync with UI changes (a label reading "Submit payment form primary CTA" becomes misleading if the button is later replaced with a link), so adopt a convention of using the same text as the accessible name where possible (e.g., `.describe('Pay button')` mirrors `getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' })`), and avoid labels that embed selector details (`'nth(1) .submit-btn'`) since that defeats the readability purpose.
